title: Spectral origin of the topological gap exponent d + η: mechanism, kernel, decomposition, and scope
summary: The topological gap $Δ$ -- the excess $H_1$ total persistence of a critical point cloud over a density-matched null -- scales as $Δ\sim L^{d+η}$. We derive this analytically: the spectral integral $I(α) = \sum_{k\neq 0} S_{\mathrm{conn}}(k)\,|k|^α$ scales as $L^{2-α-η}$ when IR-dominated, giving $I(-2η) \sim L^{d+η}$. The decomposition $I(-2η) = I_0 \cdot I_{\mathrm{shape}}$ separates volume ($I_0 \propto N(1-m^2) \sim L^d$) from anomalous dimension ($I_{\mathrm{shape}} \sim L^η$); the volume factor accounts for the magnetization-driven per-configuration variance of $Δ$. We prove the mechanism requires $d < 2 + η$ (IR dominance), confining it to $d = 2$ for physical systems; in $d = 3$ the spectral integral is UV-dominated, explaining why density normalization is needed. An $α$-sweep for Potts $q = 4$ at $L = 32$--$256$ finds $α_{\mathrm{opt}}$ in $[-0.75, -0.5]$, consistent with $-2η_{\mathrm{Ising}}$ and inconsistent with $-2η_{q=4} = -1$; we flag this as tentative pending $L \geq 1024$ confirmation. The $\langle m^2 \cdot I(-2η)\rangle$ hyperscaling product is dominated by the correlation $r(m^2, I) \approx -0.98$ via the shared $I_0$ amplitude, so we report it as a covariance-correction analysis. Under a heuristic argument extending Divol--Polonik to inhomogeneous Poisson intensities, the bare PH kernel is flat; the effective kernel acquires $k$-dependence only at criticality. The per-configuration agreement between $Δ$ and $I(-0.5)$ is primarily a magnetization correlation: $R^2 = 0.91$ at $L = 256$ collapses to $R^2 \approx 0$ once $|M|$ is partialed out. Per-configuration evidence corroborates the $I_0$ Parseval identity but not the $|k|^{-2η}$ shape factor; the latter is established by ensemble $L$-scaling.

AI.tldr: Topological gap Δ scales as Δ ∼ L^{d+η} in IR-dominated regimes (d<2+η); decomposition I(−2η)=I0·Ishape separates volume and anomalous-dimension effects, with magnetization driving per-configuration variance. In 2D this mechanism holds; in 3D UV-dominance requires density normalization. Empirical checks with Potts q=4 show α_opt roughly −0.75 to −0.5, consistent with −2ηIsing but not with −2ηq=4. Evidence links Δ and I(−2η) primarily through magnetization, though |k|^{−2η} shape factor is not solidly supported by ensemble scaling; per-configuration data support I0 (Parseval) but not the shape factor. Overall, the results establish a scaling framework tying persistent topology to spectral content and critical exponents, with caveats on finite-size and dimensionality.
AI.motivation: To understand finite-size scaling of the topological gap Δ in critical point clouds via spectral methods, and to connect Δ with the anomalous dimension η and magnetization fluctuations, clarifying when IR versus UV physics dominates and how density normalization enters in higher dimensions.
AI.method: Analytic derivation of the spectral integral I(α)=∑_{k≠0} S_conn(k)|k|^α; show IR-dominance leads to I(α) ∼ L^{2−α−η}; set α=−2η to obtain Δ ∼ L^{d+η}. Decompose I(−2η)=I0·I_shape with I0 ∝ N(1−m^2) ∼ L^d and I_shape ∼ L^η. Extend Divol–Polonik to inhomogeneous Poisson intensities to argue bare PH kernel is flat; the effective kernel acquires k-dependence at criticality. Empirical analysis includes α-sweep for Potts q=4 at L=32–256 to locate α_opt, and per-configuration covariance and correlation analyses (e.g., R^2 for m^2 vs I, partialing out M).
AI.result: Δ scales as L^{d+η} under IR dominance (d<2+η); I(−2η) factorizes into volume and shape components, with I0 driving per-configuration variance through magnetization. In 2D, the mechanism is valid; in 3D UV-dominated, density normalization is required. For Potts q=4, α_opt ≈ [−0.75,−0.5], consistent with −2η_Ising and not with −2η_q=4 (−1), though requires L≥1024 for confirmation. The hyperscaling product ⟨m^2 I(−2η)⟩ is dominated by r(m^2,I) ≈ −0.98 via shared I0; per-configuration data support I0 Parseval identity but not a robust |k|^{−2η} shape factor, which is only supported by ensemble L-scaling. The magnetization drives most of the observed covariance; Δ–I correlation largely reflects this.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a coherent scaling picture linking topological gap Δ to spectral content and critical exponents, with IR-dominated scaling in low dimensions and a need for density normalization in 3D. Empirical checks in 2D are encouraging but limited by system size; larger L needed to firmly establish η via α_opt. The per-configuration analysis highlights magnetization as the dominant source of variance, and the Parseval-based I0 contribution is validated, while the proposed |k|^{−2η} shape factor remains unconfirmed at finite ensembles.

title: Physics-informed neural networks by Gradient-Guided Gaussian Adaptive Sampling (3GAS-PINNs)
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for solving partial differential equations, yet their performance in nonlinear problems is often limited by slow convergence, gradient imbalance, and insufficient resolution to capture localized intermittent structures such as shock waves[1]. These issues arise primarily from the use of fixed weights of loss and uniform collocation point distributions, which cannot adapt to the evolving complexity of the solution field during training. To address these challenges, Gradient-Guided Gaussian Adaptive Sampling Physics-Informed Neural Networks (3GAS-PINNs) is proposed in this paper, which combines uniform probability distribution and Gaussian-smoothed probability distribution derived from the spatial gradients of solution, to maintain global constraint satisfaction as well as concentrating collocation points in regions of high gradient. Thus, intermittency structures like shock wave and solitons can be accurately captured. The method is evaluated on three benchmark nonlinear problems, including one-dimensional forced Burgers equation, Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation and nonlinear Schrodinger equation, all of which exhibit steep gradients or strong nonlinearity. In comparison with baseline PINNs, 3GAS-PINNs can effectively promote the physical consistency in intermittent regions. The accuracy of the numerical simulation can be improved by a factor of up to 14.

AI.tldr: Gradient-guided Gaussian adaptive sampling for PINNs (3GAS-PINNs) adaptively concentrates collocation points in high-gradient regions by blending uniform and Gaussian-smoothed gradient-based sampling, improving nonlinear PDE solving and capturing shocks/solitons with up to 14x accuracy gains over baseline PINNs on Burgers, KdV, and nonlinear Schrödinger equations.
AI.motivation: PINNs often underperform on nonlinear problems due to slow convergence, gradient imbalance, and inability to resolve localized intermittent structures (e.g., shocks) caused by fixed loss weights and uniform collocation points.
AI.method: Introduce a sampling strategy that combines uniform sampling with a Gaussian-smoothed probability distribution derived from spatial solution gradients to guide collocation point placement, concentrating points where gradients are large while maintaining global constraint satisfaction.
AI.result: Evaluated on 1D forced Burgers, KdV, and nonlinear Schrödinger equations. 3GAS-PINNs show improved physical consistency in intermittent regions and up to 14x improvement in accuracy compared to baseline PINNs.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-guided adaptive sampling enhances PINN performance for nonlinear PDEs by dynamically focusing resolution on high-gradient/intermittent regions, enabling better capture of shocks/solitons and improved overall accuracy.

title: World-Time Compute with Verified Code World Models
comment: 36 pages, 16 figures, 12 tables. Code and data available at https://github.com/quome-cloud/openworld
summary: LLMs generalize across a domain only after seeing many real, labeled examples, which most domains lack. We study a way to manufacture it cheaply. When a domain's dynamics can be written as code, one template instantiates into many world models: executable, verifiable programs over symbolic state, each an inexhaustible source of exactly-labeled trajectories. Fine-tuning an LLM on trajectories through many such worlds, which we call world-time compute, a training-time analogue of test-time compute, lifts generalization to held-out worlds it never trained on (synthesized world families). Gains are largest where capability is scarcest: +29 points at 0.5B; the largest model's lift is within noise, consistent with saturation. Labels can be trusted because the worlds are verified code: synthesized-then-checked dynamics are exact over 20-step rollouts and answer 10x out-of-distribution probes exactly (100%), whereas per-step LLM and MLP predictors compound error and collapse. Unlike domain randomization, each world is independently authored and verified; a corrupted-label control shows label exactness, not task variety, drives the gains. On real benchmarks (ARC-AGI grids, List Functions, CLRS) the same lever holds as per-world test-time training. On List Functions the harder cross-world form holds: one adapter trained on 128 disjoint worlds reaches 40% on held-out worlds versus 6% for a corrupted-label control (+34 points, CI [29, 39]). The gain is a saturating regularity, not a law: largest for few-step reasoning and small/weak models, fading for long chains, perception-induced tasks, and saturated tasks; cross-task transfer is weak without shared skill. Worlds are authored and served by OpenWorld, a zero-dependency framework (companion paper). Scope: symbolic state; pixel-native domains remain territory of learned models. All code, recipes, and this manuscript regenerate from one repository.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs on trajectories from many independently authored, verified synthetic world models enables cross-world generalization to held-out, synthesized world families, with large gains for small models and few-step reasoning; gains saturate for longer chains and perception tasks.
AI.motivation: Generalization of LLMs typically requires many real, labeled examples per domain, which are scarce. The work proposes a cheap, scalable data-generation paradigm by exploiting programmable world dynamics to generate exactly labeled trajectories for training.
AI.method: Represent dynamics as executable code templates that instantiate many world models. Generate labeled trajectories in these worlds (world-time compute). Fine-tune LLMs on these trajectories. Worlds are authored/verified as exact over short rollouts (20 steps) and assessed with OOD probes. Compare against per-step predictors and corrupted-label controls. Use OpenWorld framework to host worlds.
AI.result: Training on synthesized worlds yields up to +29 points improvement at 0.5B models; gains are largest for small models and few-step reasoning; cross-world transfer is weaker for long chains and perception tasks and saturates with model size. On List Functions, adapter trained on 128 disjoint worlds achieves 40% on held-out worlds vs 6% with corrupted-label control. Across ARC-AGI grids, List Functions, CLRS, the world-time compute lever remains beneficial. 20-step rollouts and exact 100% accuracy on 10x-ODD probes for synthesized dynamics; per-step predictors accumulate error.
AI.conclusion: World-time compute offers a scalable path to generalization across unseen world families within symbolic-state domains. Worlds are authored/verified and served by OpenWorld; results are reproducible in a single repo. Domain: symbolic state; not yet pixel-native tasks.

title: Scaling Post-Training Ternarisation to Qwen3-8B Capability Retention, Reproduction, Lossless Packing, and Packed Execution
summary:
Ultra-low-bit language models promise reductions in storage and memory traffic, but a nominal "1.58-bit" label does not specify the deployed representation or its execution cost. We study a scale-up of an aggressive post-training conversion pipeline from Qwen3-4B to Qwen3-8B.
  The conversion uses KOTMS rotation, E2M-ATQ adaptive ternarisation, and GPTQ-style error compensation in a weight-only A16 configuration. We do not claim these algorithms as new. Our contribution is the end-to-end scale-up characterisation: an external reproduction gate, matched 4B/8B capability analysis, cross-corpus perplexity, effective-bit accounting, lossless lattice-aware packing, and direct packed execution.
  The 8B model reaches a three-corpus perplexity ratio of 1.361x, with WikiText-2, C4, and PTB ratios of 1.318x, 1.393x, and 1.371x. On eight zero-shot tasks at n = 500, mean accuracy is 64.6% versus 72.4% for FP16, corresponding to 78.5% chance-corrected retention and a 7.8-point absolute cost. The matched 4B run retains 69.6%, yielding an 8.9-point 8B advantage.
  The packed checkpoint is 8.24 GiB and preserves the recorded perplexity to measurement precision. Direct packed execution reaches 15.52 tokens/s in 7.35 GiB, while a preliminary packed GEMV remains slower than FP16 cuBLAS. The result is a validated scale-up baseline: model size improves robustness to aggressive post-training discretisation, actual serialisation is solved for the measured artefact, and direct execution is feasible, while broader seeds, calibration distributions, and kernel optimisation remain open.

AI.tldr: End-to-end scale-up characterization of ultra-low-bit Qwen3 models (4B→8B) using a post-training quantization pipeline (KOTMS rotation, E2M-ATQ ternarisation, GPTQ-like error compensation) in a weight-only A16 setting, with lossless lattice-aware packing and direct packed execution. The 8B model shows perplexity improvements (ratios ~1.32–1.39 across WikiText-2, C4, PTB) and a mean zero-shot accuracy drop from FP16 of ~7.8 points on eight tasks; a matched 4B run retains ~69.6% accuracy. The packed checkpoint is 8.24 GiB; direct execution achieves ~15.5 tokens/s in 7.35 GiB, while a preliminary packed GEMV lags behind FP16 cuBLAS. The work provides a validated scale-up baseline and confirms robustness to aggressive discretisation, while seeds, calibration distributions, and kernel optimization remain open.
AI.motivation: To quantify what an ultra-low-bit label means in deployed reality, by providing an end-to-end, reproducible scale-up study from 4B to 8B, including model size, perplexity, zero-shot performance, and deployment metrics, rather than focusing on algorithmic novelty.
AI.method: Post-training quantization scale-up using KOTMS rotation, E2M-ATQ adaptive ternarisation, and GPTQ-style error compensation applied in a weight-only A16 configuration. The evaluation includes an external reproduction gate, cross-corpus perplexity (WikiText-2, C4, PTB), lossless lattice-aware packing, and direct packed execution. Eight zero-shot tasks at n=500 assess accuracy; comparisons are made against FP16 baselines. The packed checkpoint is 8.24 GiB; runtime metrics include 15.52 tokens/s on 7.35 GiB and a preliminary packed GEMV.
AI.result: 8B perplexity ratios: WikiText-2 1.318x, C4 1.393x, PTB 1.371x; overall 1.361x across three corpora. Eight zero-shot tasks: mean accuracy 64.6% vs FP16 72.4% (78.5% chance-corrected retention; 7.8-point absolute cost). Matched 4B: 69.6% accuracy (8B advantage = 8.9 points). Packed checkpoint: 8.24 GiB and preserves perplexity. Direct packed execution: 15.52 tokens/s in 7.35 GiB; packed GEMV slower than FP16 cuBLAS.
AI.conclusion: Validated scale-up baseline: larger models exhibit improved robustness to aggressive post-training discretisation, serialization is resolved for measured artefacts, and direct packed execution is feasible; however broader seeds, calibration distributions, and kernel optimization remain open areas.

title: Identifying Habit, Physics, and Nuisance in Robot World Models
summary: Teleoperated demonstrations are often multimodal even when the underlying dynamics are nearly deterministic given the executed action. We argue that this multimodality typically mixes three factors--operator habit in action selection, shared physics, and observation nuisance--and that entangled next-observation predictors absorb all three. We formalize the split with a structural causal model a=g(h,z,u), z'=f(z,a), o=r(z,c), and test it with complementary interventions: replacing or shuffling actions at fixed state sharply increases next-state error, whereas appearance and camera changes should not; habit-aware reverse scoring improves ranking of feasible pasts without rewriting the dynamics. The associated adaptation rule is to freeze a shared physics readout and update only a thin interface. On StackCube, DROID, and RH20T this rule improves low-shot transfer relative to training from scratch, retains cleaner dynamics under corrupted adaptation data, and extends from proprioception to pixel observations with multi-view and multi-step checks. We do not equate latent actions with operator habit, and we do not target large-scale video generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Entangled multimodal signals in teleoperation can be better understood and addressed via a structural causal model; interventions show action misalignment affects next-state predictions, while habit-aware fitting plus a freeze of shared physics improves transfer and robustness across modalities.
AI.motivation: Teleoperated demonstrations exhibit multimodality even when dynamics are near-deterministic, due to operator habits, shared physics, and observation nuisance. Disentangling these factors is essential for robust learning, transfer, and prediction of next observations.
AI.method: Propose a structural causal model a=g(h,z,u), z'=f(z,a), o=r(z,c). Use targeted interventions: replace/shuffle actions at fixed state to test effect on next-state error; test effect of appearance/camera changes; employ habit-aware reverse scoring to re-rank feasible pasts. Derive an adaptation rule: freeze shared physics readout and update only a thin interface. Validate on StackCube, DROID, RH20T with low-shot transfer and robustness to corrupted adaptation data; extend from proprioception to pixel observations with multi-view/multi-step checks.
AI.result: Intervening on actions sharply increases next-state error, while appearance/camera changes do not. Habit-aware reverse scoring improves ranking of feasible pasts without altering dynamics. The adaptation rule—freeze shared physics readout and adjust a thin interface—improves low-shot transfer, preserves cleaner dynamics under corrupted data, and extends to pixel observations across modalities and views.
AI.conclusion: Latent actions are not simply operator habit; the proposed causal decomposition and thin-interface adaptation provide robust transfer and prediction across modalities without relying on large-scale video generation benchmarks.

title: Evidence-Order Calibration for Selective Visual Reasoning under Progressive Loss of Question-Critical Evidence
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Code and supplementary materials: https://github.com/aacaas5/evidence-order-calibration-vlm
summary: Vision-language model (VLM) confidence may change in aggregate when visual evidence is degraded while remaining structurally inconsistent within individual examples. We study answer-level reliability along five-step, question-conditioned evidence-loss trajectories. Using a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct model, we construct 176 accepted GQA-derived trajectories (880 masking conditions) by progressively masking scene-graph-localized question-critical regions. Native sequence confidence has an evidence monotonicity violation rate (EMVR) of 0.436, and 92.0% of trajectories contain at least one adjacent violation. A matched non-critical-region control shows that full critical masking reduces accuracy by 28.2 percentage points, compared with 0.6 points for equally sized non-critical masks; the paired difference is 27.6 points (95% CI [20.0, 34.7]). We train a lightweight post-hoc reliability head on frozen hidden states, sequence confidence, and entropy. Adding evidence-order supervision to binary cross-entropy (BCE) reduces masking EMVR from 0.330 to 0.303 (paired difference -0.027, 95% CI [-0.044, -0.010]). The same mask-trained objective reduces EMVR from 0.449 to 0.402 on held-out question IDs under unseen local Gaussian blur (difference -0.0468, 95% CI [-0.0739, -0.0199]). AUROC, Brier, and AURC differences between the two learned heads are statistically inconclusive, and native confidence remains stronger for selective-risk ranking. The results separate evidence-order consistency from conventional correctness discrimination rather than establishing generic confidence superiority.

AI.tldr: Masking evidence in a vision-language model reveals high evidence-order violations and large accuracy drops; a post-hoc reliability head modestly reduces EMVR but does not establish universal confidence superiority.
AI.motivation: Quantify answer-level reliability under stepwise, question-conditioned evidence loss and disentangle evidence-order consistency from conventional correctness discrimination.
AI.method: Use a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct model to create 176 GQA-derived evidence-loss trajectories (880 masking conditions) by masking scene-graph-localized, question-critical regions. Measure native sequence confidence EMVR, accuracy drop under full vs non-critical masks, and train a lightweight post-hoc reliability head on frozen hidden states, sequence confidence, and entropy. Compare evidence-order supervision in BCE; test on held-out IDs under unseen Gaussian blur; evaluate AUROC, Brier, AURC.
AI.result: Native sequence confidence exhibits an evidence monotonicity violation rate (EMVR) of 0.436; 92.0% of trajectories contain at least one adjacent violation. Full critical masking reduces accuracy by 28.2 percentage points vs 0.6 points for non-critical masks; paired difference 27.6 points (CI [20.0, 34.7]). Post-hoc reliability head reduces EMVR from 0.330 to 0.303 (paired diff -0.027, CI [-0.044, -0.010]). On held-out questions under unseen local Gaussian blur, EMVR falls from 0.449 to 0.402 (CI [-0.0739, -0.0199]). AUROC, Brier, AURC differences between two heads are inconclusive; native confidence remains stronger for selective-risk ranking.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-order consistency differs from conventional correctness discrimination; the approach does not establish universal confidence superiority and highlights the need for more nuanced reliability mechanisms that separate order-consistency from plain accuracy.

title: OpenDiscoveryTrace: Process Traces for Evaluating AI Scientist Workflows
comment: Best Dataset Award, ICML 2026 Workshop on AI for Science (AI Scientists: Tools, Co-authors, or Founders?). Code: https://github.com/aayambansal/OpenDiscoveryTrace Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/aayambansall/OpenDiscoveryTrace
summary: Existing benchmarks for autonomous AI scientists evaluate only final outputs---generated code, hypotheses, or papers---yet discard the reasoning process by which those outputs were obtained. This makes it impossible to audit scientific methodology, diagnose failure modes, or distinguish systematic reasoning from fortunate guessing. We present \textbf{OpenDiscoveryTrace}, a public dataset of 558 complete AI scientific agent trajectories that captures how models reason, not just what they produce. Each trajectory records a structured 9-field-per-step trace---including thoughts, tool calls, observations, errors, revision triggers, and self-reported confidence---as models execute 124 scientific tasks spanning drug discovery, materials science, genomics, and scientific literature analysis. The dataset covers seven models: three frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 Pro; 124 trajectories each, fully balanced across domains and difficulty levels) and four open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Phi-3.5-mini, and Qwen2.5-1.5B; 30 each), plus 60 live-retrieval variant trajectories. Pilot analysis on 363 LLM-judged trajectories reveals that process traces expose behavioral differences invisible to output-only evaluation: all three frontier models achieve comparable success rates (84--89%), yet Claude Opus 4.6 produces 30$\times$ more errors than GPT-5.4 (2.5 vs. 0.08 per trajectory, $p < 0.0001$, Cliff's $δ= 0.613$), with qualitatively different error profiles---66.7% tool misuse for Claude versus 83.6% reasoning errors for GPT-5.4. We define five benchmark tasks with baselines from logistic regression, random forests, LSTMs, and Transformer models. The dataset, trace schema, agent harness, and benchmark definitions are publicly available under CC BY 4.0 to support research on process-level evaluation, scientific agent auditing, and AI governance.

AI.tldr: OpenDiscoveryTrace provides 558 complete AI scientific agent trajectories with per-step reasoning traces across 124 tasks, enabling process-level evaluation and governance beyond output-only benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To enable auditability and diagnosis of AI scientific reasoning, addressing the gap in current benchmarks that only consider outputs and not the reasoning process.
AI.method: Collect 558 trajectories from 7 models (3 frontier: GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro with 124 trajectories each; 4 open-weight: Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Phi-3.5-mini, Qwen2.5-1.5B with 30 each) plus 60 live-retrieval variants, across 124 tasks and 7 domains (drug discovery, materials science, genomics, literature analysis). Each trajectory records a 9-field-per-step trace (thoughts, tool calls, observations, errors, revision triggers, self-reported confidence, etc.). A public dataset with a benchmark foundation (logistic regression, random forests, LSTMs, Transformers).
AI.result: Pilot analysis shows process traces reveal behavioral differences invisible to outputs: frontier models have similar success rates (84–89%), but Claude Opus 4.6 makes ~30x more errors than GPT-5.4 (2.5 vs 0.08 per trajectory; p<0.0001; Cliff’s δ=0.613). Error profiles differ: Claude shows 66.7% tool misuse; GPT-5.4 shows 83.6% reasoning errors. The dataset exposes failure modes and supports process-level evaluation; results are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: OpenDiscoveryTrace enables auditability and governance of AI scientific agents, offering dataset, trace schema, and benchmarks for research on process-level evaluation; encourages better transparency and methodological scrutiny in AI-driven science.

title: The Hyperbolic Surface Distance, Diameter, and Dirichlet Problems
summary: Despite the prominence of hyperbolic surfaces in mathematics, basic algorithmic questions about them, even computing the distance between two points, have remained open, leaving many features of these surfaces inaccessible. The classical machinery assumes a polyhedral structure absent on a smooth surface. We remove these obstacles. We begin with an efficient $O(g^2)$ algorithm for the distance between two points, where $g$ is the genus of the surface. Building on it, we obtain an $O(g^2 \log g)$ method for answering distance queries from a fixed source and, as a consequence, for recentering a Dirichlet domain around an arbitrary point. This understanding of distances on the surface then lets us approximate the diameter to within any $\eps$ in time $O(g^3 \log g / \eps^2)$. We further show that the diameter, a single real number encoding a great deal about the surface, is exactly computable. Its hyperbolic cosine is an algebraic number over the field encoding the coefficients of the hyperbolic isometries defining the surface.

AI.tldr: Efficient intrinsic algorithms on hyperbolic surfaces: compute distances in O(g^2), answer distance queries in O(g^2 log g), approximate diameter in O(g^3 log g / ε^2), and exactly compute the diameter; the diameter’s hyperbolic cosine is algebraic over the coefficient field of the defining isometries.
AI.motivation: Address computation on smooth hyperbolic surfaces, removing polyhedral assumptions; enable practical distance queries, diameter computations, and understanding the surface’s geometry.
AI.method: Develop an intrinsic, polyhedral-free framework for hyperbolic geometry on genus-g surfaces. Create an O(g^2) distance algorithm, extend to O(g^2 log g) distance-query machinery from a fixed source and to recenter Dirichlet domains. Use these primitives to approximate the diameter within ε in O(g^3 log g / ε^2) and show the diameter is exactly computable with its hyperbolic cosine algebraic over the field generated by the isometry coefficients.
AI.result: An explicit, polyhedral-free algorithmic toolkit for hyperbolic surfaces: exact two-point distance in O(g^2); distance queries and Dirichlet domain recentering in O(g^2 log g); approximate diameter in O(g^3 log g / ε^2); diameter computable exactly; cosine of diameter is algebraic over the coefficient field of the defining isometries.
AI.conclusion: Distances on hyperbolic surfaces can be computed efficiently without triangulations; the diameter is not only computable but algebraically constrained, linking geometry to the algebra of Fuchsian group coefficients.

title: Distribution-Consistent Inference for Dynamic Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have emerged as a powerful paradigm for scaling model capacity while preserving efficient inference in large foundation models. However, most MoE models use a fixed top-$k$ expert selection policy, assigning the same expert budget to every token even when fewer experts may be sufficient. Inference-time dynamic top-$k$ routing can reduce computation without retraining, but existing methods often overlook the distributional shift caused by deviating from the training-time routing configuration. We show that reducing the number of activated experts consistently increases the RMS scale and variance of SMoE outputs, inducing a representation mismatch that contributes to downstream performance degradation in addition to the loss of expert capacity. To address this correctable component, we propose Layer-wise Distribution Alignment (LDA), a lightweight inference-time correction that uses layer-wise calibration statistics to align reduced-routing representations with the default configuration. Across multiple SMoE LLMs, benchmarks, and routing strategies, LDA recovers much of the performance lost induced by the distributional shift under reduced routing while preserving sparse-inference efficiency with negligible overhead.

AI.tldr: Inference-time dynamic top-k routing for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reduces computation but induces distributional shift; Layer-wise Distribution Alignment (LDA) corrects this shift at inference, recovering performance with negligible overhead.
AI.motivation: Mitigate inefficiency of fixed top-k routing and the performance drop caused by reduced routing without retraining by aligning representations between reduced routing and training-time routing.
AI.method: Introduce LDA: a lightweight layer-wise calibration that uses per-layer statistics to calibrate reduced-routing representations to match the default MOE routing, enabling better alignment at inference.
AI.result: Across multiple SMoE LLMs, benchmarks, and routing strategies, LDA recovers a large portion of the performance lost due to distributional shift, while maintaining sparse inference and minimal overhead.
AI.conclusion: LDA is an effective, easy-to-implement correction for distributional shift in inference-time reduced routing for MoE models, enabling efficient yet high-performing sparse inference.

title: Geometry Conditioning in an Embodied SLM: Training Controls and Robustness Diagnostics in a 0.8B Hybrid Model
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures. Includes ancillary data and analysis code
summary: We study how physical-state inputs affect a 0.8B hybrid language model adapted for manipulation with 6.2M trainable parameters. Six conditions are trained on three LIBERO-Spatial tasks and evaluated over three seeds and 540 held-out rollouts. Conditioning recurrent decay gates on geometric increments yields 28.9% success, compared with 36.7% when those increments are shuffled during training and 24.4% without explicit object/goal geometry. Both geometry policies receive correct inputs at evaluation. A token adapter using the same increments scores 27.8%; differences vary across seeds and remain inconclusive. Token-clock conditioning scores 11.1%, including one seed that fails to converge. In separate robustness tests, a state-only relative-coordinate policy retains 7/10 success under frame relabeling, whereas all four tested visual policies fall to at most 3/20 after a 5 cm object displacement. These results show no reliable advantage from training-time geometric alignment under this recipe and illustrate the gap between coordinate invariance and physical-layout generalization. Episode records, seed-level analyses, and figure-generation code accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: Training-time geometric conditioning yields no clear advantage for a 0.8B hybrid LM used in manipulation when evaluated on LIBERO-Spatial tasks; results are inconsistent across seeds and input modalities, with several robustness tests showing limited generalization. The study highlights a gap between coordinate invariance and physical-layout generalization.
AI.motivation: Assess whether incorporating physical-state inputs and geometric alignment during training improves manipulation performance and cross-scenario generalization, and whether different geometric conditioning mechanisms yield consistent benefits.
AI.method: Six training conditions are evaluated on three LIBERO-Spatial tasks, across three seeds and 540 held-out rollouts. The study compares conditioning recurrent decay gates on geometric increments versus shuffling those increments during training and versus not providing explicit object/goal geometry. It also compares a token adapter using the same increments, token-clock conditioning, and several robustness tests including frame relabeling (relative-coordinate policy) and four visual policies. Episode records, seed-level analyses, and figure-generation code accompany the work.
AI.result: Geometry-conditioned decay-gate inputs achieved 28.9% success, while increments shuffled during training yielded 36.7% and lack of explicit geometry yielded 24.4%. Token adapter scored 27.8%; token-clock conditioning 11.1% (one seed did not converge). Robustness tests showed state-only relative-coordinate policy maintained 7/10 under frame relabeling, but all four visual policies dropped to at most 3/20 after a 5 cm object displacement. Overall, there is no reliable advantage from training-time geometric alignment under this approach; results illustrate the gap between coordinate invariance and physical-layout generalization.
AI.conclusion: Training-time geometric alignment, as implemented, does not produce consistent performance gains across seeds/tasks. The study underscores the need to disentangle coordinate invariance from physical-layout generalization and suggests that geometry-aware conditioning alone may be insufficient for robust manipulation generalization.

title: Integrating Unimodal and Vision-Language Representations in Latent Space for Multi-Label Chest X-Ray Classification
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables (main text); 12 pages, 1 figure, 13 tables (supplementary material)
summary:
Multi-label chest X-ray classification has attracted considerable attention in recent years, with the effective use of visual representations and clinical semantic knowledge playing an important role. This study proposes a framework that combines unimodal representations from RAD-DINO with vision--language representations from BioViL-T for the classification of 14 labels in the MIMIC-CXR-JPG dataset. The RAD-DINO and BioViL-T embeddings and their combined representation are refined separately in latent space before being normalized and fused across the three branches. In addition to improving classification performance, the study aims to clarify the role of each embedding source and the degree to which they complement one another.
  Experiments show that RAD-DINO outperforms BioViL-T when used independently, whereas early fusion further improves the results, indicating that the two embedding sources contain complementary information. The best-performing model achieves a mean AUROC of 0.840 and an mAP of 0.467. Ablation analysis shows that hybrid fusion provides consistent and statistically significant improvements over early fusion when each embedding source is refined in latent space, suggesting that fusion effectiveness depends on the quality of the representation supplied by each branch. However, the study has only been evaluated internally on MIMIC-CXR-JPG; its generalizability to data from other healthcare institutions therefore remains to be validated. The source code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/mimic-report-C210/.

AI.tldr: A three-branch fusion framework combines RAD-DINO unimodal visual representations with BioViL-T vision-language embeddings for 14-label chest X-ray classification on MIMIC-CXR-JPG. Latent-space refinement and normalization are applied per-branch before fusion; hybrid fusion outperforms early fusion. Best results: mean AUROC 0.840 and mAP 0.467. Evaluation is internal only; code is released.
AI.motivation: To exploit complementary information from visual-only and vision-language representations, aided by clinical semantic knowledge, to improve multi-label chest X-ray classification and to quantify each source's contribution.
AI.method: Three-branch architecture: RAD-DINO (unimodal visual), BioViL-T (vision-language), and their fused representation. Each embedding is refined in latent space, normalized, and then fused across the three branches. The study compares early fusion versus hybrid fusion, with ablations to assess the impact of latent-space refinement and fusion strategy. Evaluated on 14-label classification on the MIMIC-CXR-JPG dataset; internal validation only.
AI.result: RAD-DINO alone outperforms BioViL-T alone. Early fusion further improves performance, suggesting complementary information. Hybrid fusion provides consistent and statistically significant gains over early fusion when each embedding source is refined in latent space. Best overall metrics: mean AUROC 0.840 and mAP 0.467. Generalizability to other institutions remains untested; source code is available at the provided link.
AI.conclusion: Combining unimodal visual and vision-language representations with latent-space refinement and a thoughtful fusion strategy yields performance gains in multi-label chest X-ray classification, and clarifies the complementary roles of each embedding source. External validation is needed to establish generalizability.

title: Adaptive Entangled Game Modules in Artificial General Intelligence
summary: We introduce a probability-wave framework for modeling the collective behavior of interacting adaptive agents, deriving testable eigenmodes through a generalized behavioral intelligence (GBI) nonlocal probability-wave equation. This framework captures a broad range of human intelligence behaviors with analytical mechanisms and offers an indirect method to examine the Liu-Chen-Ao (LCA) hypothesis of nonlocal entangled nerve fibers in the brain through collective trader behaviors. Our empirical analysis of Chinese intraday stock market data demonstrates that adaptive entangled game modes explain 82-94% (89% overall) of observed decision patterns, a sharp contrast to the predictions of neoclassical finance based on independent rational agents. Moreover, 2-12% of behaviors show adaption to intraday news, events, and environments, characterized by dual equilibrium states and abrupt reference point shifts, while purely independent modes occur in less than 5% of cases. These findings empirically support the LCA hypothesis, as observable trading behaviors reflect underlying brain mechanisms and internal intelligence decision-making in behavioral psychology. Our results highlight the necessity of incorporating adaptive entangled game modules into artificial general intelligence (AGI) architectures, addressing the limitations of conventional artificial neural network (ANN)-based AI, which relies on trillions of opaque parameters. By integrating ANN-based AI with probability-wave-based entangled-brain simulations, machine learning can enrich AGI foundation models (FMs) and facilitate the development of human-like processing units (HPUs) that leverage brain-inspired mechanisms. Such HPUs may ultimately create more compact, efficient, and robust AGI systems, particularly for embodied intelligence and robotics.

AI.tldr: A probability-wave, nonlocal GBI framework for collective adaptive agents; empirical evidence from Chinese intraday stocks shows adaptive entangled game modes explain ~89% of decisions; supports LCA brain-initiated nonlocal entanglement; advocates integrating entangled-brain modules into AGI and HPUs for brain-inspired, compact AI.
AI.motivation: Bridge behavioral neuroscience (Liu-Chen-Ao nonlocal entangled nerves) with market data to validate a nonlocal probability-wave model and motivate brain-inspired AGI architectures.
AI.method: Derive a generalized behavioral intelligence (GBI) nonlocal probability-wave equation; perform empirical analysis on Chinese intraday stock market data; quantify share of behavior explained by adaptive entangled game modes versus independent modes; identify dual equilibria and reference-point shifts.
AI.result: Adaptive entangled game modes explain 82-94% (89% overall) of decision patterns; 2-12% adapt to intraday news/events; independent modes <5%; findings support LCA hypothesis; evidences that brain-like mechanisms underlie trading behavior; AGI implications.
AI.conclusion: Incorporate adaptive entangled game modules into AGI architectures; combine ANN-based AI with probability-wave entangled-brain simulations to create brain-inspired HPUs for more compact, robust AGI, beneficial for embodied intelligence and robotics.

title: A 2.37332-Competitive Algorithm for Online Square Packing with Gravity
summary: We consider online packing of axis-parallel squares into a unit-width strip under the Tetris and gravity constraints: An incoming square must be lowered from above along a monotonic downwards path until it reaches support from below. Fekete, Kamphans, and Schweer [Algorithmica, 2014] gave an algorithm with asymptotic competitive ratio $34/13\approx2.6154$ in this model. We present $\mathrm{AsymmetricSlots}$, a recursive algorithm based on splitting each slot into a wide and narrow subslot. The proof uses a local charging argument: squares that are large relative to its associated slot pay for the height they create with their own area, while smaller squares are balanced between the two subslots and may use a bounded temporary credit. For a suitable split parameter $p^\star$, we prove $\mathrm{AsymmetricSlots}{p^\star}(σ)\le 2.37332 \operatorname{OPT} (σ)+O(1)$ for every input sequence $σ$. Additionally, we show that the same framework gives an algorithm with asymptotic competitive ratio $O(κ)$ for rectangles of aspect ratio at most $κ$, and a matching $ Ω(κ)$ lower bound shows that the dependence on $κ$ is asymptotically optimal. For the square algorithm, we give a lower bound of $2$ on its asymptotic competitive ratio.

AI.tldr: AsymmetricSlots is a recursive online packing algorithm for axis-aligned squares in a unit-width strip under gravity, achieving a competitive ratio of at most about 2.37332 times OPT (plus constants) via splitting slots into wide/narrow subslots and a local charging analysis; it also extends to rectangles with aspect ratio κ with matching κ-dependent bounds, while establishing a 2 lower bound for the square case.
AI.motivation: Improve upon the previous best asymptotic competitive ratio for online square packing under gravity (34/13 ≈ 2.6154) and develop a framework that handles rectangles of bounded aspect ratio, with rigorous analysis via a local charging scheme.
AI.method: Introduce AsymmetricSlots, recursively partitioning each slot into a wide and narrow subslot using a split parameter p*. Use a local charging argument: large squares contribute height via their own area (paying for created height), while smaller squares are balanced between subslots and receive bounded temporary credit; analyze to obtain a bound of 2.37332 OPT + O(1) for an optimal p*, and show the framework yields O(κ) asymptotic competitive ratio for rectangles of aspect ratio at most κ.
AI.result: Main: AsymmetricSlots(p*) achieves ≤ 2.37332·OPT(σ) + O(1) for every input sequence σ for squares; also yields O(κ) asymptotic bound for rectangles with aspect ratio ≤ κ and a matching Ω(κ) lower bound; for the square-only algorithm, a lower bound of 2 on the asymptotic competitive ratio.
AI.conclusion: The slot-splitting framework with local charging improves the online-square packing bound under gravity and extends to bounded-aspect-ratio rectangles, indicating the approach is near-optimal in κ-dependence and establishing a concrete square-case lower bound of 2.

title: DiffLUT-Net: Differentiable Training of FPGA LUT Networks with Learnable Connectivity
summary: Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) enable efficient neural-network inference, but most deployment flows either accelerate multiply-accumulate operations or convert pretrained quantized models into lookup tables (LUTs). We present DiffLUT-Net, an FPGA-native network connected by six-input LUTs that are trained from scratch. We jointly learn the 64 truth-table entries of a LUT and the source to each of its six input ports using a differentiable LUT function relaxation and hardware source selection. After training, the truth tables and connections are discretized, unused logic can be pruned, and the network is exported directly as synthesizable Verilog. Across five benchmarks, DiffLUT-Net achieves favorable accuracy-resource trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly learning LUT functions and sparse connectivity for compact FPGA-native inference. The code is available at https://github.com/TUDa-HWAI/DiffLUT-Network.

AI.tldr: An FPGA-native neural network built from trainable six-input LUTs; jointly learning LUT truth tables and input connections to enable compact, synthesizable Verilog export; shows favorable trade-offs across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To enable end-to-end differentiable training of neural networks mapped directly to FPGA LUTs, avoiding full precision DSP/lookup-table conversion and enabling compact, hardware-efficient inference.
AI.method: Train-from-scratch network of six-input LUT blocks (LUT-6). Jointly optimize each LUT’s 64-entry truth table and the source of each input port via a differentiable LUT relaxation and hardware source selection. After training, discretize the truth tables and connections, prune unused logic, and export a synthesizable Verilog netlist.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks, DiffLUT-Net achieves favorable accuracy-resource trade-offs, demonstrating that jointly learning LUT functions and sparse connectivity can yield compact FPGA-native inference. Code is available.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning LUT logic and sparse connectivity enables compact, FPGA-native neural inference with a straightforward Verilog export path, suggesting a promising direction for end-to-end FPGA deployment of neural networks.

title: Design and Attitude Control of an Underwater Quadruped Robot
summary: Legged robots are versatile on land, but their use in underwater environments remains limited. Extending quadruped locomotion to water enables amphibious mobility with applications in inspection, environmental monitoring and disaster response. This paper presents the design, modeling, and experimental validation of a reproducible underwater quadruped robot. The robot is built around custom waterproof motor housings machined from polyoxymethylene plastic, which use off-the-shelf O-rings and dynamic shaft seals. A simplified model is derived to describe the dynamics of this underwater legged system, capturing how drag forces on spherical end effectors transmit torque to the floating base. Building on this model, a closed-loop attitude controller is developed using an error formulation defined on the special orthogonal group SO(3). The controller is evaluated both in simulation and experimentally in a water tank, where the robot tracks desired orientation setpoints in roll, pitch and yaw.

AI.tldr: An underwater quadruped with a reproducible waterproof design, a simplified drag-based dynamics model, and an SO(3) attitude controller validated in simulation and a water tank.
AI.motivation: Extend quadrupedal locomotion to underwater environments to enable amphibious inspection, environmental monitoring, and disaster response; address design and control challenges of underwater legged robots.
AI.method: Design of waterproof motor housings from POM with off-the-shelf O-rings and shaft seals; derive a simplified dynamics model capturing drag forces on spherical end effectors and their torque transmission to the floating base; develop a closed-loop attitude controller on SO(3) using an error formulation; evaluate via simulation and water-tank experiments tracking orientation setpoints in roll, pitch, and yaw.
AI.result: The model captures the key dynamics of drag-driven torque transfer on the floating base, and the attitude controller achieves orientation tracking in both simulation and water-tank experiments.
AI.conclusion: Provides a reproducible underwater quadruped design, a tractable dynamic model for drag-induced coupling, and a practical SO(3) attitude control framework with experimental validation, advancing amphibious robotic capabilities.

title: M2LG-DG: A Multi-modal Local-Global Domain Generalization Framework for Cross-site Major Depressive Disorder Classification
summary: Classification models based on resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) often show lower performance at imaging sites not included during model development, which can limit their use in clinical settings. Domain generalization (DG) addresses this issue by learning representations from source sites that remain effective for unseen target sites. However, existing DG approaches for psychiatric disorder classification commonly rely on a single imaging modality and may not fully account for site-specific acquisition effects on the learned representation space. Subjects scanned at the same site share scanner hardware, acquisition settings, and preprocessing characteristics, which can cause representations to reflect acquisition conditions rather than diagnostic information. In this work, we present M2LG-DG, a source-only multimodal local-global framework for cross-site major depressive disorder (MDD) classification. The framework employs a dual-stream rs-fMRI encoder, where the global pathway models inter-regional dependencies through self-attention and the local pathway performs graph-constrained aggregation over functional connectivity-derived brain graphs. Imaging and non-imaging representations are decomposed into shared and private components and integrated through bidirectional cross-attention with a learned modality gate. A cross-site supervised contrastive objective forms positive pairs from same-class subjects acquired at different source sites, encouraging the fused representation to preserve diagnostic information across acquisition domains. On four held-out REST-meta-MDD sites, M2LG-DG achieves an AUC of 69.48% and exceeds the closest comparison method by 2.18 percentage points. Experiments on the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) dataset further support its applicability to other psychiatric neuroimaging classification tasks.

AI.tldr: Introduces M2LG-DG, a source-only multimodal cross-site domain generalization framework for MDD classification from rs-fMRI, combining a global self-attention encoder and a local graph-based encoder; decomposes imaging/non-imaging features into shared/private components, fuses them via bidirectional cross-attention with a modality gate, and uses a cross-site supervised contrastive loss to align same-class samples from different sites. Achieves 69.48% AUC on four held-out REST-meta-MDD sites, outperforms the closest method by 2.18 points, with ABIDE results suggesting applicability to other psychiatric tasks.
AI.motivation: Domain shifts across imaging sites (scanner/hardware/settings) degrade cross-site performance in rs-fMRI psychiatric classification. Existing DG methods are often single-modality and may not adequately account for site acquisition effects on representations.
AI.method: A dual-stream rs-fMRI encoder: a global pathway using self-attention to model inter-regional dependencies; a local pathway performing graph-constrained aggregation over FC-derived brain graphs. Imaging and non-imaging representations are decomposed into shared and private components and fused via bidirectional cross-attention with a learned modality gate. A cross-site supervised contrastive objective creates positive pairs from same-class subjects across different source sites to encourage domain-invariant, diagnostic-rich representations.
AI.result: On four held-out REST-meta-MDD sites, the model achieves an AUC of 69.48%, surpassing the closest comparison method by 2.18 percentage points. Additional experiments on ABIDE demonstrate applicability to other psychiatric neuroimaging classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a source-only multimodal DG framework with cross-attention fusion and cross-site contrastive learning can improve cross-site generalization for psychiatric MRI classification and may generalize to other disorders/datasets.

title: Subagents vs Agent Skills: Executing Reusable Knowledge for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
summary: How can language model agents effectively leverage libraries of reusable knowledge to solve long-horizon tasks? Recent work has increasingly focused on agent skills: reusable capabilities represented as skill packages, i.e., multi-file bundles containing instructions, scripts, and other resources that help agents perform specific tasks. Agent skills are typically executed by loading their skill instructions into an agent's context and relying on the agent to follow them. As task horizons grow, however, this approach becomes increasingly brittle, because reasoning quality degrades as more information accumulates in the context window. We investigate an alternative approach in which skill packages are instead invoked as subagents. Rather than loading skill instructions into the main context, subagent execution spawns fresh context windows dedicated to solving individual subtasks. We show that subagent execution outperforms agent-skill execution when skill packages expose clear input-output contracts and their instructions encode the procedural knowledge needed to fulfill those contracts. The tradeoff is additional communication overhead, as extra tokens are required to coordinate between the main agent and its subagents. Our results show that the benefit of reusable knowledge depends not only on its content, but also on how it is organized and invoked.

AI.tldr: Subagent-based invocation of skill packages outperforms direct loading of skill instructions for long-horizon tasks when the packages expose clear input–output contracts; however, this approach introduces extra communication overhead. Effectiveness depends on how knowledge is organized and invoked.
AI.motivation: Address brittleness and context-window limitations in long-horizon agent reasoning by exploring an alternative design for reusable knowledge—invoking skill packages as subagents rather than loading them into the main context.
AI.method: Systematically compare two architectures: (1) agent-skill where skill instructions are loaded into the main agent context; (2) subagent invocation where skill packages are executed as separate, fresh-context subagents solving subtasks. Use skill packages that provide clear input–output contracts and encode procedural knowledge; vary organization/invocation strategies and measure task performance and communication overhead.
AI.result: Subagent execution outperforms agent-skill when skill packages expose clear IO contracts and contain procedural knowledge; the gain comes with increased communication overhead due to coordination between the main agent and subagents. The magnitude of improvement depends on how knowledge is organized and invoked.
AI.conclusion: Invoking reusable knowledge as subagents is a viable and often superior approach for long-horizon tasks, contingent on clear input–output contracts and deliberate organization/invocation design; the benefits must be weighed against the coordination overhead.

title: iLogMap: Geodesic Polar Coordinates Parameterization with the Magnetic Laplacian
summary: Geodesic polar coordinates (GPCs) provide an intrinsic parameterization over curved surfaces, but their accurate estimation remains challenging, particularly in the presence of anisotropic metrics, high curvature and complex topology. We introduce iLogMap, a method for computing GPCs in curved domains that recasts the angular component of the logarithmic map to a ground-state magnetic eigenproblem over the circumferential direction field of geodesic distance. Our method effortlessly extends to anisotropic metric tensors and solid volumes, enabling cylindrical and spherical parameterizations in tetrahedral meshes. Experiments on diverse shapes with varying genus confirm competitive angular accuracy and reduced metric distortion relative to heat-based methods, with improved performance on surfaces with boundary and domains with anisotropy. We demonstrate the utility of iLogMap in computational cardiology applications, where we use it to initialize spiral phases on atrial surfaces and estimate local activation patterns in ventricular models.

AI.tldr: iLogMap introduces a magnetic-eigenproblem formulation for geodesic polar coordinates (GPCs) on curved domains, enabling anisotropic and volumetric parameterizations (including cylindrical and spherical maps in tetrahedral meshes). It shows competitive angular accuracy and reduced metric distortion compared with heat-based methods, particularly for surfaces with boundary or anisotropy, and supports cardiology-oriented applications (atrial spiral phase initialization and ventricular activation estimation).
AI.motivation: Geodesic polar coordinates aim to parameterize curved surfaces intrinsically, but estimation is hard under anisotropic metrics, high curvature, and complex topology. Existing approaches (e.g., heat-based methods) can yield larger angular errors and metric distortions, and extending GPCs to anisotropic tensors and solid volumes is challenging.
AI.method: iLogMap recasts the angular component of the logarithmic map as a ground-state magnetic eigenproblem over the circumferential direction field of geodesic distance. The framework naturally extends to anisotropic metric tensors and solid volumes, enabling cylindrical and spherical parameterizations in tetrahedral meshes.
AI.result: Experiments on shapes with varying genus demonstrate competitive angular accuracy and reduced metric distortion relative to heat-based methods. The approach shows improved performance on surfaces with boundaries and under anisotropy. In computational cardiology, iLogMap is used to initialize spiral phases on atrial surfaces and to estimate local activation patterns in ventricular models.
AI.conclusion: iLogMap provides a robust, versatile method for computing GPCs on curved domains, including anisotropic metrics and volumes, with improved angular accuracy and lower metric distortion compared with heat-based methods. It enables practical cylindrical/spherical parameterizations in meshes and demonstrates utility in biomedical applications.

title: Accountable and uncertainty-aware evaluation of sensor-based AI under distribution shift: devices, subjects, and nearly three years underground
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Manuscript prepared for Measurement Science and Technology
summary: Sensor-based AI systems are rarely operated under the conditions under which they were trained: devices, personnel and recording epochs change, and each change degrades performance in ways a random train-test split cannot reveal. We propose a staged, accountable evaluation protocol that treats the evaluation of a deployed model as a measurement with declared reference levels and a quantified uncertainty. Four cumulative generalisation stages hold out devices, subjects and time. Each stage is judged on quantiles of repeated trainings against chance references with the correct class count, an out-of-present-scope rate exposes silent misdirection towards classes that are no longer present in deployment relative to training, and an explicit decision rule ties roll-out decisions not to means but to 5% quantiles. We demonstrate the protocol on infrastructure-free geomagnetic localisation with smartphone-based recurrent classifiers in two real underground mines, including a replication of the scheme's training stages at the second site. Unchanged models are re-evaluated on data recorded 34 months after the training campaign, on a device generation unknown at training time and with a held-out surveyor. The 5% quantile of their present-conditioned precision there is 0.39 over 299 repeated trainings, 16.5 times the chance level; across the composition of the 42 reachable location classes the figure varies by +/-0.08, several times the spread between repeated runs. Repeated trainings of a single configuration show why means mislead: a bimodal configuration passes a mean-based test decisively while its 5% quantile lies more than an order of magnitude below chance.

title: Learning to Fly: Stable Vision-Guided UAV Servoing with Compact Target-Centric Cues and Reinforcement Learning
summary: Vision-guided reinforcement learning for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) remains challenging due to unstable policy optimisation, aggressive exploration, and the cost of high-dimensional visual perception. In this work, we investigate long-horizon UAV visual servoing using compact target-centric cues combined with low-dimensional sensor measurements. Rather than learning directly from RGB images, lightweight target segmentation provides image-space offsets and relative depth, which are combined with quadrotor velocity and projected-gravity measurements into a compact 12D policy observation. We compare Direct PPO with three matched-budget curriculum strategies: a Visual curriculum that progressively expands target placement difficulty, a Dynamics curriculum that gradually relaxes action constraints and smoothing, and a Joint curriculum that combines both progressions. All strategies reach comparable nominal performance, with complementary advantages across tracking metrics. Observation ablations show that proprioceptive measurements are critical for stable flight and image-space cues for target alignment, while explicit depth is not necessary for strong performance in the evaluated setting. Against tuned classical visual-servo controllers, learned policies show greater robustness to strong control and visual perturbations, while the Visual curriculum exhibits the smallest degradation under unseen target motion. Overall, the results demonstrate that compact target-centric representations can support robust long-horizon aerial visual servoing and that visual curriculum training can improve robustness to dynamic distribution shifts despite limited gains in nominal performance.

AI.tldr: Compact target-centric visual servoing for UAVs using a 12D observation space with lightweight cues, showing competitive nominal performance but improved robustness via curriculum training; proprioceptive and image-space cues are key, depth not essential.
AI.motivation: To enable robust, long-horizon UAV visual servoing under high-dimensional perception and unstable policy optimization by leveraging compact target-centric cues and curriculum learning.
AI.method: Train Direct PPO using a 12D observation that fuses target-space offsets, relative depth from segmentation, quadrotor velocity, and projected-gravity measurements. Compare three matched-budget curricula (Visual, Dynamics, Joint) against a baseline. Conduct ablations on sensor modalities and compare to tuned classical visual-servo controllers.
AI.result: All strategies achieve similar nominal performance with complementary strengths. Proprioceptive measurements are essential for stability; image-space cues aid target alignment; explicit depth is not critical. Learned policies show greater robustness to strong control and visual perturbations; the Visual curriculum offers the smallest degradation under unseen target motion. Curriculum training improves robustness to distribution shifts with limited gains in nominal performance.
AI.conclusion: Compact, target-centric representations enable robust long-horizon UAV visual servoing, and curriculum training can enhance robustness to dynamic distribution shifts even if nominal gains are modest.

title: AgenticGen: Reward-Guided Agentic Video Generation for Advertising
summary: Advertising video generation is not only a video synthesis task, but also a product-conditioned reasoning problem whose success is measured by online business metrics. Recent video foundation models can generate realistic clips from multimodal conditions, yet they do not optimize how a product should be transformed into an effective advertisement or how future generation should be improved from online business feedback. To close this loop, we propose AgenticGen, a reward-guided agentic framework that decomposes advertising video generation into two trainable reasoning stages, strategy selection and draft generation, thereby exposing optimization targets that online business feedback can supervise. AgenticGen learns a performance-based reward from accumulated online feedback and a complementary rubric-based reward aligned with human quality standards, then uses them to supervise policy optimization. DPO first moves the agentic policies toward online preferences, and GRPO further refines both stages with process and outcome rewards. Offline experiments validate the reward models and successive policy optimization. Online A/B experiments in the TikTok advertising system show that AgenticGen after DPO and GRPO improves CTR by 2.72%, CVR by 2.63%, and Advv by 9.61% over the SFT baseline.

AI.tldr: Introduces AgenticGen, a reward-guided agentic framework for advertising video generation with two trainable reasoning stages, optimized via online feedback and rubric rewards; achieves CTR, CVR, and Advv gains in TikTok ads.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap between video synthesis and advertising effectiveness by treating ad generation as a product-conditioned reasoning problem that should be supervised by online business feedback and human-quality rubrics.
AI.method: AgenticGen decomposes generation into two trainable stages: strategy selection and draft generation. It learns a performance-based reward from accumulated online feedback and a rubric-based reward aligned with human quality standards, then uses them to supervise policy optimization. It applies DPO to align policies with online preferences, followed by GRPO to refine both stages with process/outcome rewards. Evaluation includes offline validation of reward models and successive policy optimization, plus online A/B testing in TikTok showing improvements over an SFT baseline.
AI.result: Reward models are validated and policy optimization improves under offline tests. Online A/B experiments show substantial gains: CTR +2.72%, CVR +2.63%, Ad-viewability/Advv +9.61% over the SFT baseline.
AI.conclusion: A reward-guided, two-stage agentic framework can align ad-video generation with business metrics; iterative policy optimization using online feedback can meaningfully boost key performance indicators in an industrial advertising system.

title: Gradland: On Phenomenal Experience, Differentiated Across Many Dimensions
summary: This paper investigates the hypothesis that the first-order structure of physical interactions, i.e. gradients or Jacobians, characterizes the structure of phenomenal experience. It does so in an idealized world inhabited by neural networks, Gradland, where the physics are known and the functions are (mostly) differentiable. The paper introduces two measures of Jacobian structure: effective rank and cohesion, based on Kirchhoff complexity. Applying the measures to a series of worked examples shows the hypothesis accounts for: (1) the duration of experience, that it can prolong over hundreds of milliseconds; (2) the difference between what is experienced vividly and obscurely; (3) the experience of texture; (4) the blooming buzzing confusion presumably experienced by newborns; (5) the difference between ideas that are held distinctly in mind and ideas that are confused; (6) what learning is like; and finally (7) the paper explains the function of rich, dense experience.

AI.tldr: Two Jacobian-based measures (effective rank and cohesion) relate first-order interaction structure to phenomenological experience in an idealized differentiable world, explaining seven qualitative aspects of conscious experience.
AI.motivation: Bridge between the mathematics of first-order dynamics (gradients/Jacobians) and the structure of conscious experience, using Kirchhoff-complexity-based metrics in Gradland.
AI.method: Define effective rank and cohesion from Jacobian structure; compute within worked examples; apply to several experiential phenomena (duration, vividness, texture, newborn experience, mental clarity, learning, richness of experience).
AI.result: Accounts for all seven phenomena via Jacobian structure; demonstrates explanatory power of the measures.
AI.conclusion: Supports hypothesis that experiential structure is encoded in first-order Jacobian structure; proposes Jacobian-based metrics as a unifying framework for conscious experience.

title: Literati: Towards Anytime Optimal Shape Generalized Trees via AO*
summary: Decision trees are prized for their interpretability and strong performance on tabular data, but popular greedy top-down induction algorithms can yield suboptimal and unnecessarily complex structures. Optimal decision tree methods address this through global optimization, yet remain restricted to axis-aligned threshold splits, which limit the expressivity of each node and often force deep, complex trees to capture non-linear feature effects. Shape Generalized Trees (SGTs) generalize threshold splits to learnable univariate shape functions, improving expressivity and enabling more compact trees. However, existing SGT induction algorithms are greedy and offer no optimality guarantees. In this work, we introduce Literati, the first algorithm for optimal SGT induction. We propose a novel AND/OR graph formulation of the problem that jointly optimizes tree structure and shape function complexity. To solve this AND/OR graph, we develop an AO*-based algorithm with two enhancements that improve anytime performance while preserving optimality: a secondary heuristic for OR-node selection and a round-robin policy for AND-node exploration. Across 24 real-world datasets, Literati achieves higher training and test accuracy than state-of-the-art tree approaches.

AI.tldr: Introduces Literati, the first optimal induction algorithm for Shape Generalized Trees (SGTs). It uses an AND/OR graph and an AO*-based search to jointly optimize tree structure and shape-function complexity, with enhancements for better anytime performance. Empirically, it achieves higher training and test accuracy than state-of-the-art tree methods on 24 real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Overcome suboptimality of greedy, axis-aligned decision trees and expand expressivity through learnable univariate shape functions; provide optimality guarantees for SGT induction.
AI.method: Formulates optimal SGT induction as an AND/OR graph problem and solves it with an AO*-based algorithm augmented by (i) a secondary heuristic for OR-node selection and (ii) a round-robin exploration policy for AND-nodes, enabling anytime performance while preserving optimality; jointly optimizes tree structure and shape-function complexity.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 24 real-world datasets shows Literati yields higher training and test accuracy compared to state-of-the-art tree approaches, indicating improved performance and effective use of expressive SGTs.
AI.conclusion: Literati establishes the first optimal induction procedure for Shape Generalized Trees, delivering more expressive yet optimally learned trees and demonstrating practical gains over existing tree methods on tabular data.

title: No Free Checker: A Survey of Verifiers for Robot Policies
comment: Survey. 31 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables, 187 references. Covers reward models, success and failure detection, temporal-logic and formal verification, world-model evaluation, and reward hacking. Project page: https://github.com/ZJUSCL/Awesome-Robot-Verifier
summary: A verifier for robot policies reads a candidate behavior and returns a score for how well it did, used both to evaluate vision-language-action policies and to train them. Verifiers range from success detectors and reward models to runtime monitors, safety filters, and temporal-logic specifications. We survey roughly 150 verifiers and compare them along two properties. Availability is how much a verdict costs, how early in a rollout the verdict arrives, and how often a verdict can be asked for. Availability rises as verdicts get cheaper, earlier, and denser. Credibility is how much a high score tells us about the task. Credibility falls as the judgment becomes gameable and self-serving. We group the verifiers by who supplies the judgment: human verifiers, rule-based and formal verifiers, learned and pretrained verifiers, and model-intrinsic verifiers. Across the four families, we find that credibility falls as availability rises. Regardless of who supplies the judgment, there is no free checker. We then examine what validates a verifier itself, and how much a high score tells us. Three measures appear in the literature: agreement with human labels, the performance of the policy it trains, and behavior under reward hacking. We close with nine metrics that make a verifier claim checkable, and coordinates for the verifiers still to be built.

AI.tldr: Survey of ~150 verifiers for robot-policy evaluation/training; trade-off: higher availability implies lower credibility; four verifier families; three validation measures; proposes nine metrics and future directions.
AI.motivation: To map the verifier landscape for robot policies, quantify tradeoffs between availability and credibility, and identify validation practices and gaps.
AI.method: Literature survey across diverse verifiers (human, rule-based/formal, learned/pretrained, model-intrinsic); categorize by supply source and analyze availability/credibility; assess validation measures and propose practice-oriented metrics.
AI.result: Credibility declines as availability rises across all verifier families; no verifier is free of bias or gaming risk; cross-family patterns and common validation measures identified; nine metrics proposed to check verifier claims; coordinates for future verifiers outlined.
AI.conclusion: A comprehensive but heterogeneous verifier ecosystem exists; effective verification requires balancing availability and credibility, plus standardized evaluation metrics. The paper offers a framework and roadmap for building and validating verifiers.

title: Lensless Gaze Is Not Private by Default: Auditing Identity Leakage Across Disclosure Surfaces
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the PFATCV Workshop, ECCV 2026. Code available at https://github.com/xoxo121/Lensless-Gaze-Is-Not-Private-by-Default
summary: Lensless near-eye sensing is often described as privacy-friendly because its coded measurements are visually unintelligible. Yet visual unintelligibility reflects human interpretation, not what a learned adversary can recover. We therefore treat identity privacy as a systems property of disclosure surfaces: representations crossing sensing, storage, computation, and output boundaries. We audit a simulated lensless gaze pipeline under a 36-subject known-gallery closed-set identification protocol with a fixed, known PSF; privacy from an unknown or varying optical key is outside our scope. Reported accuracies are empirical attack success rates under matched linear and MLP probes and do not upper-bound stronger adversaries. Simulated lensless measurements yield 96.7% top-1 identification versus 97.7% for matched original eye crops, while an MAE embedding retains 94.3%. Compression alone offers little protection: 8-D PCA and a matched 8-D bottleneck retain 93.2% and 91.8%, whereas separately trained 8-D GSPL bottlenecks yield 77.5% mean recovery across three seeds. A released 128-way gaze token lowers single-frame recovery to 38.1%, while its residual and continuous gaze output expose 62.1% and 72.6%, respectively. Under a source-frame-disjoint tiled protocol, token summaries reach 39.9% at T=25, showing that repeated-output risk depends on representation and aggregation. These rates reflect all subject-correlated information in the evaluated dataset, including acquisition and behavioral cues, rather than isolating intrinsic ocular biometrics. Ordinary least squares residualization against a six-dimensional crop geometry and intensity summary still leaves lensless recovery at 95.1%. Our results show that privacy claims for lensless sensing must be tested at disclosure boundaries rather than inferred from appearance.

AI.tldr: Lensless gaze sensing reveals substantial identity leakage; privacy claims based on visual indistinguishability are insufficient, as disclosure-boundary attacks can still recover subjects with high accuracy, even after compression or tokenization.
AI.motivation: Challenge the assumption that lensless sensing is privacy-friendly due to visual obscurity; treat privacy as a systemic property across sensing, storage, computation, and output; quantify actual disclosure risk under realistic identification settings.
AI.method: Simulated lensless gaze pipeline evaluated on a 36-subject known-gallery closed-set with fixed PSF. Assessed privacy against matched linear and MLP probes; compared original eye crops, compressed bottlenecks (8-D PCA, 8-D GSPL), and a 128-way gaze token. Also tested under source-frame-disjoint tiled protocol and used residualization against crop geometry/intensity. Reported attack rates reflect actor with standard priors rather than optimal adversaries.
AI.result: High re-identification rates from lensless data: 96.7% top-1 identification vs 97.7% for original crops; MAE embedding 94.3%. Compression reduced but did not eliminate risk: 8-D PCA 93.2%, 8-D bottleneck 91.8%, GSPL bottlenecks 77.5%. Gaze token reduces single-frame recovery to 38.1%, but residual and continuous outputs reveal 62.1% and 72.6%. In a source-frame-disjoint protocol, token summaries reach 39.9% at T=25. Repeated-output risk depends on representation; ordinary least squares residualization leaves recovery at 95.1%.
