AI.conclusion: Privacy claims for lensless sensing must be tested at the disclosure boundary, not inferred from appearance; substantial subject-correlated information persists across representations and aggregations, undermining assumed privacy advantages.

title: An Autonomous GeoAI Agent for Arctic Eco-Navigation
summary: Arctic maritime navigation is becoming increasingly important as changing sea-ice conditions expand seasonal accessibility while simultaneously introducing substantial operational, environmental, and community risks. Arctic route planning is inherently a multi-criteria problem: routes that improve vessel safety or efficiency may increase exposure to sea ice, sensitive ecosystems, or nearby communities. Existing routing methods prioritize travel time, fuel use, and navigational risk, often overlooking ecological and community impacts. We introduce a human-in-the-loop, multi-agent GeoAI system for Arctic eco-navigation that integrates operational, physical, ecological, and community-related criteria within a unified routing framework. Multiple specialized agents coordinate geospatial data acquisition and preparation, multi-objective route generation, and skyline-based decision support. The ecological criteria explicitly account for exposure to sensitive areas, including Essential Fish Habitat and seal critical habitat. By considering these ecosystem impacts and potential community burdens while keeping consequential value judgments under human control, the framework supports safer, more transparent, and socially responsible Arctic navigation. Project page and code are publicly available. https://samiraat.github.io/Arctic-Eco-Navigation-Agent/, https://github.com/samiraat/Arctic-Eco-Navigation-Agent

AI.tldr: A human-in-the-loop multi-agent GeoAI system for Arctic eco-navigation that unifies operational, ecological, and community criteria into a skyline-based multi-objective routing framework; enables safer, more transparent, and socially responsible Arctic navigation; code and project resources available.
AI.motivation: Arctic sea-ice changes create new route opportunities but also heightened risks; traditional routing focuses on time, fuel, and navigational risk, neglecting ecological and community impacts, necessitating a holistic, transparent decision-support system.
AI.method: Develop a multi-agent GeoAI architecture with data acquisition/preparation, multi-objective route generation, and skyline-based decision support; integrate operational, physical, ecological (e.g., Essential Fish Habitat, seal habitat), and community criteria; incorporate human-in-the-loop for value judgments; provide open-source implementation.
AI.result: Conceptual framework with an implemented prototype and public resources; no empirical results reported in abstract, but claims integration and openness; system supports eco-friendly route planning.
AI.conclusion: The framework advances safer, more transparent, and socially responsible Arctic navigation by explicitly accounting for ecosystem and community burdens while keeping human oversight; public code fosters reproducibility and broader adoption.

title: Explaining f-Divergence-Based Regularization via Local Curvature and Sharpness-Aware Minimization
comment: Published at 5th Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs), 2026
summary: Divergence-based regularization and Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) are two prominent approaches for improving generalization in deep learning, both motivated by robustness to perturbations. However, their relationship has remained largely unexplored. Building on classical second-order expansions of $f$-divergences, we show that the two methods are locally consistent under parameter-space perturbations: both induce curvature-sensitive penalties, with divergence regularization yielding a Fisher-weighted quadratic form and SAM penalizing sharpness through the dominant Hessian eigenvalue. For negative log-likelihood objectives with exponential-family output distributions, this correspondence becomes especially transparent, since the Fisher and Gauss-Newton matrices coincide. We further show that the same local geometric perspective extends to input-space perturbations, where divergence-based regularization is defined through transformations of the input. In this setting, the regularizer induces a pullback quadratic form on the input space, providing a more general perturbation framework than standard SAM while preserving the same local sensitivity interpretation. To validate the analysis empirically, we use the asymmetric $α$-skew Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) family as a controlled testbed. Its local curvature coefficient scales as $α(1-α)$ and is maximized at the symmetric point $α=\tfrac12$, which recovers the standard JSD. Loss-landscape visualizations in the input-perturbation regime show that stronger induced curvature penalization is associated with flatter local minima. Experiments on four benchmark datasets further demonstrate that both accuracy and negative log-likelihood are consistently best near this regime of maximal curvature penalization.

AI.tldr: Divergence-based regularization and Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) are locally consistent under perturbations, both imposing curvature penalties: divergence regularization yields a Fisher-weighted quadratic form in parameter space, while SAM penalizes sharpness via the largest Hessian eigenvalue; in input space, divergence regularization induces a pullback quadratic form. With exponential-family NLL objectives, Fisher and Gauss-Newton coincide. Using asymmetric α-skew Jensen-Shannon divergence as a controlled testbed shows maximum curvature at α=1/2, corresponding to standard JSD; empirical loss-landscape visualizations reveal that stronger curvature penalization yields flatter minima. Four datasets show both accuracy and negative log-likelihood are best near this maximal-curvature regime.
AI.motivation: Clarify the relationship between two major robustness-oriented regularization strategies (divergence-based regularization and Sharpness-Aware Minimization) and provide a unified local geometric perspective for both parameter- and input-space perturbations.
AI.method: Employ classical second-order expansions of f-divergences to derive curvature-based penalties; relate these penalties to SAM; analyze negative log-likelihood objectives under exponential-family output distributions where Fisher and Gauss-Newton coincide; extend the framework to input-space perturbations via input transformations and pullback quadratic forms; use asymmetric α-skew Jensen-Shannon divergence as a controllable testbed with curvature scaling α(1-α); visualize loss landscapes and perform empirical evaluations on four benchmark datasets.
AI.result: Divergence regularization yields a Fisher-weighted quadratic form in parameter space, whereas SAM imposes a penalty tied to the dominant Hessian eigenvalue (curvature in the most sensitive direction). In the exponential-family NLL case, the Fisher and Gauss-Newton matrices coincide, aligning the two views. In input space, the regularizer induces a pullback quadratic form via input transformations, offering a broader perturbation framework than standard SAM with the same local sensitivity interpretation. The α-skew JSD testbed shows curvature scales as α(1-α) and is maximized at α=1/2; loss-landscape analyses demonstrate that stronger curvature penalization corresponds to flatter minima, and four datasets reveal that both accuracy and NLL are best near this maximal-curvature regime.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified local geometric interpretation linking divergence-based regularization and SAM, extends the perspective to input perturbations, and proposes a general perturbation framework beyond conventional SAM. Empirical results support that maximizing curvature penalization (near α=1/2 in the skew JSD) yields flatter minima and better generalization in terms of accuracy and NLL.

title: AccelMPC: High-Rate, Low-Power FPGA-Accelerated Model Predictive Control for Tiny Drones
summary: Unlocking the potential of tiny aerial robots requires order of magnitude improvements in the performance of embedded edge control. In particular, although recent cached model predictive control (MPC) solvers can handle the fast system dynamics and complex constraints required for agile drone flight, their computational demands remain prohibitive for resource-constrained robots, forcing prior implementations to operate at reduced control rates. AccelMPC overcomes this challenge through an end-to-end co-design approach that jointly optimizes the solver algorithm, numerical representation, hardware mapping, and physical integration. AccelMPC pairs a co-designed FPGA-accelerated alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-based MPC solver with a custom 6g PCB, providing high-bandwidth communication for deployment on a 35g Crazyflie. Hardware experiments demonstrate 1 kHz onboard constrained MPC with dynamic obstacles, up to 15.6x faster solve times and 195.4x improvement in energy-delay product over state-of-the-art embedded microcontroller-based solvers, all while scaling to optimization problems with over 20,000 optimization variables and a comparable number of constraints. We release our PCB design files, firmware, and FPGA solver code open source.

AI.tldr: FPGA-accelerated ADMM-based MPC (AccelMPC) enables 1 kHz onboard constrained MPC on a 35g quadcopter, with large-scale optimization (20k+ vars) and major speed/energy-delay improvements; open-source hardware and solver.
AI.motivation: Enable real-time, constraint-aware control for tiny aerial robots where traditional embedded MPC is too slow and energy-inefficient, hindering agile flight and obstacle avoidance.
AI.method: End-to-end co-design of solver, numerical representation, hardware mapping, and physical integration. Deploys a co-designed FPGA-accelerated ADMM-based MPC solver on a custom 6g PCB with high-bandwidth communication for a 35g Crazyflie.
AI.result: Achieves 1 kHz onboard constrained MPC with dynamic obstacles; up to 15.6× faster solve times and 195.4× energy-delay improvement over state-of-the-art MCU-based solvers; scales to optimization problems with >20,000 variables and a similar number of constraints.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability of FPGA-accelerated MPC for tiny aerial robots and releases PCB design, firmware, and FPGA solver code as open source, enabling broader adoption and further research.

title: MLLMs Hallucinate when Information Distribution Drifts in Synergy Heads
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often struggle with hallucinations, thus hindering their reliable practical applications. Existing attention-based mitigation methods mainly rely on indirect signals (e.g., attention weights) that fail to accurately reflect the actual information shift underlying hallucination generation. In this paper, we propose HEAL, Head-lEvel information disentAnglement and caLibration for identifying and mitigating hallucinations. HEAL first employs causal noise intervention on multi-head outputs to filter out causally redundant heads. Subsequently, it disentangles information distribution within the remaining heads via the counterfactual Difference-in-Differences, categorizing heads into four types. Through analysis, we observe: hallucinations happen when information distribution drifts away from a healthy equilibrium in synergy heads, not strongly correlated with the quantity or strength of modality-specific heads. Motivated by this insight, HEAL injects dynamic information calibration factors into the value vectors of synergy heads, and actively regulates visual-language dependencies, steering the output distribution towards factual evidence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HEAL effectively reduces hallucinations across multiple MLLMs, offering a simple and interpretable pathway to enhance model trustworthiness.

AI.tldr: HEAL provides a causal, head-level mitigation for hallucinations in multimodal LLMs: filter redundant heads via causal noise intervention, disentangle information distribution with counterfactual Difference-in-Differences to categorize heads, and inject dynamic calibration into synergy heads to regulate visual-language dependencies, yielding improved factuality across models.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer from hallucinations; existing attention-based mitigations rely on indirect signals that poorly reflect actual information shifts; need a causal, interpretable approach to identify and control information flow across heads.
AI.method: 1) apply causal noise intervention on multi-head outputs to prune causally redundant heads; 2) use counterfactual Difference-in-Differences to disentangle information distribution within remaining heads and categorize into four types; 3) inject dynamic information calibration factors into value vectors of synergy heads to steer dependencies toward factual evidence.
AI.result: Empirical results show HEAL reduces hallucinations across multiple MLLMs, offering a simple, interpretable pathway to improve model trustworthiness.
AI.conclusion: HEAL demonstrates that controlling head-level information distribution and calibrated synergy heads can effectively mitigate hallucinations in MLLMs, with broad applicability and interpretability.

title: The Menu Is an Execution Prior: State-Path Tool Menus for Online Agents
summary: Language models act through tools, yet practical agents face libraries containing thousands of interfaces. We introduce the tool menu as the short, ordered subset of available tools shown to an agent before execution. The agent can call only tools in this menu. Multi-step tasks require the final action and the prerequisite tools that create its inputs in a usable order. Current constructors rank tools by request relevance, which can surface the final action while omitting or delaying less obvious producers. We introduce the state path, a pre-execution route from the observable request state to the desired outcome, and propose State-Path Tool Menu to learn it. Our framework treats the menu as an execution prior over these routes. Its encoder represents which tools can run from the current state, how their outputs satisfy later inputs, and which orders recur in training paths. A retriever covers an executable entry, the missing-input producers, and the final action. A reranker then places producers before consumers. On ToolBench, our menu raises online success from 0.737 to 0.898 and outperforms retrieval, reranking, generation, and routing baselines without changing the agent. The State-Path menu also covers more complete chains with 32 tools than the official list covers with 128, and its success gain persists across executor families with different model capacities. Our code is at https://github.com/Met2348/State-Path.

AI.tldr: State-Path Tool Menu frames tool invocation as pre-execution state-path routes, using an encoder-retriever-reranker pipeline to assemble executable tool chains. It improves multi-step task success by prioritizing necessary input producers and sequencing them before final actions, outperforming baselines on ToolBench and generalizing across model capacities.
AI.motivation: Practical agents face thousands of interfaces and must choose a compact tool menu. Current ranking tends to surface final actions while neglecting prerequisite producers, hindering multi-step task execution.
AI.method: Define a State-Path as a pre-execution route from the observable request state to the desired outcome. Treat the tool menu as an execution prior over routes. Use an encoder to represent available tools and input-output dependencies, a retriever to assemble executable entries, missing-input producers, and final action, and a reranker to order producers before consumers.
AI.result: Empirically, the State-Path Menu on ToolBench raises online success from 0.737 to 0.898 and outperforms baselines (retrieval, reranking, generation, routing) without changing the agent. It covers more complete chains (32 tools) than the official list (128 tools) and maintains gains across executor families with varying model capacities.
AI.conclusion: The State-Path Menu improves tool-chain generation and execution quality, offering a scalable approach that captures longer, prerequisite-aware tool chains and generalizes across model variants. Code is available at the referenced GitHub repository.

title: Constraint-Aware Discrete Black-Box Optimization Using Tensor Decomposition
comment: 32 pages, including supplementary material. ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Discrete black-box optimization is often addressed using approaches such as Sequential Model-Based Optimization (SMBO), which aims to improve sample efficiency by fitting surrogate models that approximate a costly objective function over a discrete search space. In many real-world problems, the set of feasible inputs is often given by logical constraints known in advance. However, existing surrogate modeling techniques generally fail to capture the symbolic rules governing feasibility in discrete input spaces. In this paper, we propose a surrogate modeling approach based on tensor decomposition that captures the structure of discrete search spaces while directly integrating feasibility information. To implement this approach, we formulate surrogate model training as a constrained polynomial optimization problem and solve a relaxed formulation using a differentiable penalty term derived from T-norms. Our experiments on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including a pressure vessel design task, demonstrate that the proposed method improves sample efficiency by effectively guiding the search away from infeasible regions.

AI.tldr: A tensor-decomposition surrogate model for discrete black-box optimization with explicit feasibility constraints, optimized via a constrained polynomial objective and a differentiable T-norm penalty, improves sample efficiency by avoiding infeasible regions in SMBO; validated on synthetic benchmarks and a pressure-vessel design task.
AI.motivation: Discrete optimization with logical feasibility constraints often lacks surrogates that capture the symbolic structure governing feasibility, limiting sample efficiency in SMBO.
AI.method: Introduce a tensor-decomposition-based surrogate that models the discrete search space structure and integrates feasibility. Train via a constrained polynomial optimization problem solved in a relaxed form using a differentiable penalty derived from T-norms to enforce feasibility during optimization.
AI.result: Empirical results on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including a pressure vessel design task, show that the proposed approach improves sample efficiency by guiding searches away from infeasible regions.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating feasibility information through a tensor-decomposition surrogate and a differentiable T-norm penalty yields more sample-efficient discrete SMBO by effectively exploiting symbolic feasibility structure.

title: A Decade of Bayesian Optimization for Controller Tuning and Robot Learning: Tutorial, Review, and Future Prospects
summary: In the past decade, Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a powerful and adaptable framework for automatic controller tuning and robot learning. This article offers a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in BO, designed to support both researchers and practitioners in understanding recent advancements, practical applications, and future research directions. We begin by adopting a practitioner's perspective, illustrating how to effectively set up BO through a representative controller tuning example. We position BO within the broader context of learning paradigms, ranging from deep reinforcement learning to data-driven control, and highlight scenarios where BO is most advantageous. Next, we discuss the diverse range of BO methods that have been developed to tackle complex problems and specific applications. This article provides a unified perspective on the current landscape of BO, emphasizing its relevance to control systems and robotics, and it highlights future prospects by identifying key research challenges and promising avenues for advancing BO in the field. This includes addressing a significant gap in the BO landscape: the lack of standardized benchmark problems specifically for control-related applications. To foster future research and ensure rigorous evaluation, we start an effort towards a lightweight benchmark suite for control engineering and robotics. We also present metrics and best practices to facilitate direct comparisons between new BO algorithms and established state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: Comprehensive survey of Bayesian optimization (BO) in controller tuning and robot learning, addressing practical setup, benchmarking, and future directions; highlights the lack of standardized control benchmarks and proposes a lightweight benchmark suite with evaluation guidelines.
AI.motivation: Provide a practitioner-friendly, unified overview of BO in control and robotics, bridging theory and application while highlighting gaps in benchmarking and evaluation.
AI.method: Literature survey and synthesis; illustrative controller-tuning example; situating BO among learning paradigms; proposal of a lightweight control/robotics benchmark suite; discussion of metrics and best practices for fair comparisons.
AI.result: A unified landscape of BO for control/robotics; identification of gaps (notably standardized benchmarks); initiation of benchmark development and evaluation guidance; practical recommendations for comparing BO methods.
AI.conclusion: BO remains a powerful framework for control and robotics; future work should emphasize benchmarks, robust/multi-fidelity methods, and rigorous evaluation protocols to advance the field.

title: Video-MOPD: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Video Understanding
summary: Video understanding demands a convergence of complementary capabilities across perception, temporal understanding, and complex reasoning, which are difficult to jointly optimize within a single model. We introduce Video-MOPD-8B, an open-weight model dedicated to video understanding tasks. To fundamentally enhance its capabilities, we conduct targeted reinforcement learning (RL) optimization across three core domains: video temporal grounding (VTG), general video comprehension, and video STEM reasoning. We then unify their complementary capabilities via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), which consolidates expert knowledge by supervising student-generated trajectories with routed teacher feedback. We further introduce Reliability-Aware Informative Sampling (RAIS), which selects examples with consistently reliable teacher supervision and large teacher-student performance gaps. Together, these components enable Video-MOPD-8B to achieve coordinated and comprehensive performance gains across diverse video understanding tasks. Extensive experiments on comprehensive benchmarks covering general video understanding, temporal grounding, video reasoning, and video STEM tasks demonstrate that Video-MOPD-8B achieves state-of-the-art performance among existing models at a comparable scale. The trained model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/LandH/Video-MOPD-8B.

AI.tldr: Video-MOPD-8B is an open-weight model for video understanding optimized via three RL domains (VTG, general video comprehension, and video STEM reasoning) and unified with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) guided by Reliability-Aware Informative Sampling (RAIS). It achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse video benchmarks at a comparable scale, with released weights on HuggingFace.
AI.motivation: Video understanding requires a blend of perception, temporal grounding, and advanced reasoning, which are challenging to optimize jointly in a single model. The paper proposes a framework to systematically enhance capabilities in distinct yet related domains and unify them through distillation.
AI.method: 1) Targeted RL optimization across three domains: video temporal grounding (VTG), general video comprehension, and video STEM reasoning. 2) Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to consolidate expert knowledge by supervising student trajectories with routed teacher feedback. 3) Reliability-Aware Informative Sampling (RAIS) to select examples with consistently reliable teacher supervision and large teacher-student performance gaps.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmarks spanning general video understanding, temporal grounding, video reasoning, and video STEM tasks show Video-MOPD-8B achieving state-of-the-art performance among models of comparable scale. Model weights are publicly available at HuggingFace.
AI.conclusion: The combination of targeted RL optimization, MOPD, and RAIS yields coordinated, comprehensive gains across diverse video understanding tasks, enabling an effective open-weight model for broad video understanding.

title: Decision-Focused Active Learning for Scale-Aware Critical-Materials Recovery
summary:
Choosing a recovery process for scale-up requires connecting laboratory results with product requirements, process costs, and scale effects. We analyze records from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's Computer Intelligence for Critical Element Recovery and Optimization (CICERO) workflow for autonomous selective precipitation. Active learning uses prior results to choose experiments. In a conditional retrospective benchmark with fitted models and recycled neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnet records, active learning finds the best recorded result with fewer experiments than nonadaptive space filling. Enrichment is the selected rare-earth-to-iron ratio relative to that in the feed. Adaptive policies reach the recorded enrichment maximum by 16 to 24 wells (individual experiments), versus 48. Our two-stage reconstruction ties two adaptive alternatives at 16 wells. Conditional analyses of recycled samarium-cobalt (SmCo) magnets show a Round 2 tradeoff between purity and nominal yield, the recovery fraction calculated from an assumed starting amount - NdFeB Round 1 routes differ in enrichment. Rankings for produced water from oil and gas extraction depend on phase and dilution assumptions requiring confirmation.
  We propose choosing batches by their expected reduction in downstream Bayes risk: the minimum expected loss among available process decisions under current beliefs. In exploratory simulations, a hybrid that filters candidates has lower estimated loss than the implemented joint search across routes and conditions. Differences involving the synthetic two-stage policy are small relative to estimation uncertainty. We outline a pre-registered prospective test under a shared loss and logging standard, requiring clarified measurements and records, a defined process decision and relevant outputs, credible economic inputs, and validation at the intended scale.

AI.tldr: Active-learning guided recovery-process selection for autonomous selective precipitation reduces experiments and approaches optimal enrichment in recycled NdFeB/SmCo magnets; introduces a Bayes-risk-based batch selection framework and outlines prospective validation.
AI.motivation: Bridge laboratory results and scale-up constraints in rare-earth recovery; reduce experimental burden; handle multiple material routes and uncertainties in production water rankings.
AI.method: Apply CICERO autonomous selective precipitation with active learning to select experiments; perform conditional retrospective benchmarks on recycled NdFeB magnet data with fitted models; two-stage reconstruction; analyze SmCo magnets; rank produced water by phase/dilution assumptions; propose Bayes-risk minimization for batch decisions; conduct exploratory simulations comparing candidate-filtering hybrid vs joint search; outline pre-registered prospective test with logging standard.
AI.result: Active learning identifies best recorded results with fewer experiments than nonadaptive space-filling; enrichment reaches the maximum with 16–24 wells vs 48; two-stage reconstruction aligns two adaptive methods at 16 wells; SmCo analyses show a Round 2 purity–yield tradeoff; produced-water rankings depend on assumptions; a candidate-filtering hybrid lowers estimated Bayes risk versus full joint search; policy differences are small relative to estimation uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Advocate batch selection by minimum expected Bayes risk under current beliefs; demonstrate potential reductions in experimentation; propose a pre-registered prospective test with standardized logging and measurements and plan validation at intended scale.

title: XAI-Refine: An Automated Explanation-Knowledge Loop for Brain-Age Prediction
summary: Brain-age prediction models are commonly evaluated by predictive accuracy, yet accurate predictions alone do not establish that a model relies on reproducible or neurobiologically supported mechanisms. Post-hoc explanation methods can expose these mechanisms, but existing workflows typically stop at diagnosis or require correction targets to be specified before model analysis. We propose XAI-Refine, an automated explanation-knowledge loop for brain-age prediction from resting-state functional connectivity. At each iteration, XAI-Refine consolidates complementary post-hoc analyses across repeated training runs into reliable, structured model explanations. It converts each reliable explanation into a neutral neurobiological question, retrieves and verifies relevant literature, and compiles the verified evidence into an admissible set in the same typed explanation space. The target for refinement is defined as the minimal projection of the current model explanation onto the admissible set induced by applicable verified knowledge. This revised explanation is then translated into a differentiable constraint while preserving the originating model variable, measurement operator, and applicable scope. Candidate updates are promoted only when multi-seed validation confirms target-directed explanatory movement, predictive performance remains within a prespecified guardrail, and non-target explanatory drift remains bounded. Experiments on functional-connectivity-based brain-age prediction evaluate predictive performance, explanation reliability, literature alignment, and target-specific model revision, illustrating a structured route from post-hoc analysis to evidence-guided model refinement.

AI.tldr: Introduces XAI-Refine: an automated explanation-knowledge loop for brain-age prediction using RSFC, converting reliable post-hoc explanations into neurobiological constraints guiding model refinement, with evaluation on reliability, literature alignment, and performance.
AI.motivation: Beyond predictive accuracy, models should reflect reproducible, neurobiologically grounded mechanisms. Existing workflows either stop at diagnosis or require predefined targets. The paper proposes an iterative framework that integrates post-hoc explanations with verified literature to yield admissible explanations and constraint-based updates.
AI.method: Iterative loop: aggregate explanations across training runs to identify reliable patterns; translate each into a neutral neurobiological question; retrieve and verify relevant literature; form an admissible knowledge set in the same explanation space; define the target as the minimal projection of the current explanation onto this set; translate this revised explanation into a differentiable constraint, preserving model variables, measurement operator, and scope; promote candidate updates only if multi-seed validation shows movement toward the target, performance remains within guardrails, and non-target explanatory drift is bounded.
AI.result: Evaluated on resting-state functional connectivity–based brain-age prediction, focusing on predictive performance, explanation reliability, literature alignment, and target-directed model revision; demonstrates a structured route from post-hoc analysis to evidence-guided refinement.
AI.conclusion: XAI-Refine provides a principled framework to move from explanations to evidence-guided model refinement, improving neurobiological plausibility and reproducibility while maintaining predictive performance.

title: Actuator Dynamics Curricula for Narrow-Viability Tasks in Legged Robot Learning
comment: Accepted at 2026 Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL)
summary: Reinforcement learning has produced capable controllers across a broad range of legged-robot tasks, but a subset of these tasks fail to converge under standard training: those for which most exploration trajectories terminate before producing useful gradient signal. To address such tasks we introduce the \emph{Actuator Dynamics Curriculum}, a procedure that initializes joint stiffness at a high value and anneals it toward the system-identified value as completed episode lengths grow. Using a cart-pole system as a representative example, we show that higher closed-loop joint natural frequency under critical damping enlarges the viability kernel of the underlying Markov Decision Process, increasing the fraction of initial states from which the task is feasible. We validate the kernel monotonicity on the cart-pole and apply the curriculum to a quadrupedal-to-handstand transition on the Boston Dynamics Spot, a narrow-viability task where training under fixed identified stiffness plateaus at a policy that never completes the transition. The trained policy executes the transition in simulation across 10 seeds and transfers to hardware. More broadly, our results suggest that simulated actuator dynamics is a useful axis along which to design curricula for tasks in which exploration is bottlenecked by termination conditions rather than by reward signal.

AI.tldr: Introduces Actuator Dynamics Curriculum: start with high joint stiffness and anneal to the identified value as episodes lengthen to expand the viability kernel and improve RL success for torque-sensitive tasks; demonstrated on cart-pole and Spot to enable training and sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Exploration bottlenecks in RL for legged robots where most trajectories terminate early, leading to poor gradient signal and convergence; need a curriculum to shape actuator dynamics to widen the set of feasible initial states.
AI.method: Propose Actuator Dynamics Curriculum: initialize joint stiffness high, then anneal toward the system-identified stiffness as episode lengths grow. Analyze how higher closed-loop natural frequency under critical damping enlarges the viability kernel (set of states from which the task is feasible). Validate kernel monotonicity on cart-pole; apply curriculum to a quadrupedal-to-handstand transition on Spot (narrow-viability task); train across seeds in simulation and transfer to hardware.
AI.result: The curriculum enlarges the viability kernel, increasing feasible initial states. Kernel monotonicity holds on cart-pole. Trained policy achieves the handstand transition in simulation across 10 seeds and transfers to hardware. The approach suggests actuator dynamics as a useful axis for curricula in exploration-bottlenecked RL tasks.
AI.conclusion: Simulated actuator dynamics can be exploited to design curricula that mitigate termination-driven exploration bottlenecks, aiding convergence and sim-to-real transfer for legged-robot control tasks.

title: DensePol: Dense-Angle Polarization Dataset for Learning-Based Polarimetric Vision
summary: Polarimetric vision is gaining increasing attention because it provides physical cues about scene shape, material, and reflection that are difficult to recover from RGB alone. Recent work has therefore explored predicting polarization directly from conventional RGB images; however, the fidelity of these methods strongly depends on the polarization supervision used for training. Most existing datasets rely on Division-of-Focal-Plane (DoFP) cameras with four spatially interleaved analyzer orientations, which provide limited angular redundancy and introduce interpolation and instantaneous-field-of-view errors. We introduce DensePol, a high-redundancy RGB--polarization dataset based on Division-of-Time (DoT) acquisition, capturing 180 full-resolution analyzer orientations at $1^\circ$ intervals. DensePol contains 2,018 paired RGB--polarization images with the angular measurements and fitting residuals retained. Dense angular sampling substantially improves polarization stability, reducing AoLP deviation from $13.36^\circ$ to $2.21^\circ$. We further introduce a deterministic diffusion-based RGB-to-polarization framework with cyclic AoLP representation and a local DoLP refiner. Experiments demonstrate improved polarization prediction and downstream surface-normal estimation. The dataset and code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: DensePol provides a high-redundancy RGB–polarization dataset using Division-of-Time (DoT) acquisition (180 orientations at 1°), plus a diffusion-based RGB-to-polarization method with cyclic AoLP and a local DoLP refiner, improving polarization fidelity and downstream surface-normal estimation; dataset/code to be released.
AI.motivation: Current DoFP-based polarization datasets offer limited angular coverage, leading to interpolation errors and poorer supervision for learning-based polarization prediction. A dense, high-angular-redundancy dataset can substantially improve polarization fidelity and downstream tasks.
AI.method: DoT acquisition capturing 180 full-resolution analyzer orientations at 1° intervals; retention of angular measurements and fitting residuals. A deterministic diffusion-based RGB-to-polarization framework with cyclic AoLP representation and a local DoLP refiner.
AI.result: AoLP deviation reduced from 13.36° to 2.21°; improved polarization prediction and downstream surface-normal estimation. Dataset comprises 2,018 paired RGB–polarization images with angular measurements and residuals.
AI.conclusion: DensePol enables high-fidelity polarization supervision for learning-based methods and enhances downstream tasks; the dataset and code will be publicly available.

title: Valerant: An Automatic Navigable Game Map Generator via Action-Conditioned World Model Exploration
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) couple predictive world modeling with action generation, allowing anticipated future states to guide agent behavior. Although WAMs are rapidly advancing embodied AI, general-purpose counterparts remain largely unexplored in games. Existing game-oriented approaches often combine action-conditioned world models with external policies and reward functions to realize WAM-like decision-making, yet they operate mainly in 2D visual observation space and do not instantiate persistent 3D geometry. Extending this paradigm to 3D games introduces a distinct challenge. In autonomous driving and robotics, the physical environment exists independently of the model, providing a persistent 3D world in which selected actions can be executed. Games have no such external substrate; the virtual world itself must be instantiated. Most playable games require a persistent and navigable space, while 3D games additionally require explicit geometry that supports movement and interaction. Action-conditioned video rollouts provide visual observations but not this spatial representation. We present \textsc{Valerant}, a training-free framework that transforms a pretrained action-conditioned world model into a WAM for exploring and constructing 3D game maps. By coupling predictive visual rollouts with SLAM-based spatial reconstruction and exploration-driven action selection, \textsc{Valerant} progressively transforms a single image into a persistent 3D game map. This framework extends WAM-based interaction beyond 2D visual simulation and offers a new approach to reducing manual effort in 3D game-map creation.

AI.tldr: Training-free Valerant converts a pretrained action-conditioned world model into a 3D world model for exploring and constructing persistent 3D game maps by fusing predictive visual rollouts with SLAM-based reconstruction and exploration-driven action selection.
AI.motivation: Extend WAMs from 2D visual domains to fully persistent 3D game worlds, which require explicit geometry and a substrate to execute actions; reduce manual 3D map creation in games.
AI.method: Integrate a pretrained action-conditioned world model with SLAM-based spatial reconstruction and exploration-driven action selection; progressively transform a single image into a persistent 3D map; training-free.
AI.result: Feasibility demonstrated: can produce and refine persistent 3D maps from visual inputs, enabling 3D WAM interactions and reducing manual map creation effort.
AI.conclusion: Valerant extends WAM-based interaction to 3D games and provides a practical route to automated 3D map construction without extra training, bridging 2D WAMs and persistent 3D game worlds.

title: Applying foundation model embeddings towards urban livability evaluation
summary: While accurate measurement of socioeconomic indicators remains challenging in data-scarce regions, which limits policy interventions and resource allocation, high-resolution geospatial data is widely available and can contain information on various livability statistics. We investigate which physical features are encoded within foundation model embeddings, such as AlphaEarth, AnySat, and TerraMind, and provide a systematic framework for identifying the most predictive geospatial indicators. By analyzing how different types of geospatial data influence urban livability predictions, our approach enables researchers to prioritize the most informative features for their specific applications. Additionally, we demonstrate how to leverage foundation model embeddings to enhance prediction performance for these outcomes. This work contributes a principled methodology for extracting actionable information from satellite imagery while accounting for complex spatial dependencies, with applications in predicting urban livability in regions with limited observation data.

AI.tldr: identifies which physical cues in foundation-model embeddings from satellite imagery best predict urban livability in data-scarce regions, providing a framework to rank geospatial indicators and enhance predictions.
AI.motivation: Data scarcity impedes accurate socioeconomic measurement; abundant high-resolution geospatial data may encode livability signals. Leveraging foundation-model embeddings could reveal the most informative indicators and improve policy-relevant predictions in data-poor contexts.
AI.method: Systematically analyze how different geospatial data types influence urban livability predictions using foundation-model embeddings (AlphaEarth, AnySat, TerraMind) and develop a principled framework to extract and rank predictive indicators, accounting for spatial dependencies and enabling enhanced prediction performance.
AI.result: A principled methodology to extract actionable information from satellite imagery is proposed, with a framework to identify the most informative geospatial features and a demonstration that embeddings can enhance prediction performance for urban livability in data-limited regions.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes a systematic approach to leveraging foundation-model embeddings for geospatial prediction, enabling researchers to prioritize features and improve livability predictions while accommodating complex spatial dependencies.

title: Agentic AI-enabled Semantic Commissioning of a Cognitive Digital Twin for Reconfigurable Manufacturing
summary: Rapid bespoke commissioning of the Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) is a major challenge in reconfigurable manufacturing. Traditional digital twin (DT) construction methods primarily focus on geometric reconstruction, often neglecting the deep semantic integration and functional interoperability necessary for autonomous reasoning. This paper proposes an agent-based, AI-driven workflow to automate end-to-end CDT debugging. The system utilises LangGraph as a multi-agent orchestration engine to achieve dual-path synthesis: the semantic path extracts technical specifications from unstructured documents using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), while the functional path autonomously discovers and binds to real-time industrial telemetry data using Model Context Protocol (MCP). Experimental validation in a robotic machining cell demonstrates that the system achieves a mean average accuracy (mAP) of 97.2% in perception and reduces the deployment cycle from several weeks to an average of 2 hours, marking a paradigm shift from manual scripting to autonomous orchestration.

AI.tldr: Agent-based, AI-driven workflow using LangGraph for rapid CDT debugging with dual-path synthesis (semantic via RAG; functional via MCP), achieving 97.2% mAP and ~2 h deployment cycle.
AI.motivation: Overcome slow, geometry-centric DT construction by enabling rapid, semantically integrated, autonomously orchestrated CDT deployment in reconfigurable manufacturing.
AI.method: Dual-path synthesis orchestrated by LangGraph: semantic path uses Retrieval Augmented Generation to extract technical specs from unstructured documents; functional path autonomously binds to real-time industrial telemetry using Model Context Protocol.
AI.result: Experiments in a robotic machining cell show mean average precision (mAP) of 97.2% in perception and deployment cycle reduced from weeks to about 2 hours, demonstrating autonomous orchestration supplanting manual scripting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AI-driven, agent-based workflow enables rapid, semantically rich CDT commissioning and end-to-end debugging, marking a paradigm shift from geometry-focused DT construction to autonomous, interoperable CDT deployment.

title: The Living Library: Transforming Archival Collections into Conversational Knowledge Systems -- Lessons from the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
summary:
We present the Living Library, an end-to-end framework for transforming fragmented digital archives into governed, conversational, in-person exhibit experiences. Developed and deployed at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library, the framework comprises four layers: digitization and corpus creation, AI-powered processing, retrieval and reasoning, and an optional embodied conversational interface. The first three layers aggregate a 300,000-record collection, apply OCR and structured metadata enrichment for expert curatorial review, and publish records to a hybrid dense/semantic index. Expert review is conducted through the Archivist App, a curator-facing interface that supports correction of AI-generated transcriptions and metadata.
  The governed corpus powers both a researcher-facing interface and Talk to TR, a continuously operating exhibit that embodies Theodore Roosevelt as a full-scale digital human within a museum environment. To support live, face-to-face interactions, Cross-Era Analogical Grounding reframes contemporary questions through documented historical parallels, allowing Roosevelt to address present-day topics without inventing facts. Dual-path retrieval and end-to-end streaming keep responses grounded and responsive. Layered watchdogs, visitor-session isolation, automated conversation management, and independently restartable services enable reliable unattended operation for hundreds of visitors. Avatar realism, spatial audio, lighting, staging, and conversational design are developed and evaluated as an integrated experience. Rather than report a controlled benchmark, we describe lessons from operating Talk to TR as a public exhibit and offer a transferable model for transforming archival collections into believable, in-person conversational experiences.

AI.tldr: End-to-end Living Library framework turning fragmented archives into grounded, embodied conversational exhibits, with a four-layer pipeline, archival governance, and a public digital human (Talk to TR).
AI.motivation: Enable engaging, accurate, and responsible in-person experiences from archival collections by integrating digitization, AI processing, retrieval, and governance; address fidelity, scalability, and live operation for hundreds of visitors.
AI.method: Four-layer architecture: digitization and corpus creation; AI-powered processing; retrieval and reasoning; optional embodied interface; Archivist App for expert review; Cross-Era Analogical Grounding for grounding; dual-path retrieval; end-to-end streaming; watchdogs and session isolation; expressive avatar design.
AI.result: Describes lived deployment and lessons, not fixed benchmarks; provides a transferable model for transforming archives into believable conversational exhibits; demonstrates feasibility and operational reliability in a public setting.
AI.conclusion: Offers a transferable, governance-driven blueprint for converting archival collections into believable, in-person conversational experiences, with attention to grounding, reliability, and curator involvement.

title: XAI-Arena: Can LLMs Assess the Quality of XAI Explanations?
summary: Evaluating the quality of explanations produced by explainable AI (XAI) methods remains challenging because existing approaches often rely on subjective human judgment, limiting reproducibility, scalability, and comparability between studies. We examine whether LLMs can serve as a reproducible and scalable mechanism to make comparative assessments of the quality of XAI explanations. We introduce XAI-Arena, an LLM-as-a-judge framework for scalable, reproducible, multidimensional, and stakeholder-sensitive evaluation of XAI explanation quality. XAI-Arena then allows us to compare XAI explanations along various dimensions, namely, perceived simplicity, clarity, task adequacy, trust calibration, actionability, transparency, faithfulness, and overall interpretability. We then benchmark XAI explanation methods across various datasets, machine learning models, and stakeholder personas. Human validation shows a strong positive association between LLM-generated and human ratings (Spearman's rho=.693, p<.001). Together, LLM-based evaluations can capture systematic differences in XAI explanation quality and provide a scalable and reproducible framework for comparative assessment of XAI explanations.

AI.tldr: LLM-based XAI-Arena enables scalable, reproducible, multidimensional evaluation of XAI explanations, with moderate-to-strong alignment to human judgments and cross-domain applicability.
AI.motivation: Subjective, human-centered evaluation of XAI explanations impedes reproducibility, scalability, and comparability across studies; a reproducible, scalable evaluation framework is needed.
AI.method: XAI-Arena uses LLMs as judges to assess XAI explanations along dimensions such as simplicity, clarity, task adequacy, trust calibration, actionability, transparency, faithfulness, and overall interpretability; benchmarks explanations across diverse datasets, models, and stakeholder personas; human validation shows significant association with human ratings (Spearman 0.693, p<0.001).
AI.result: LLM-based evaluations reveal systematic differences in XAI explanation quality and provide a scalable, reproducible method for comparative assessment across methods, datasets, models, and stakeholders.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven evaluation is a viable, scalable approach for comparative XAI assessment with strong alignment to human judgments; further work should address prompts, biases, and generalization across domains.

title: SCCM : Stream Cruise Control Method for Automated Drift Detection and Adaptation
summary: Real-world datasets often exhibit evolving distributions, known as concept drift. Ignoring drift degrades predictive performance, while reliance on fixed hyperparameters further limits model adaptability under changing conditions. Adaptive learning addresses this challenge by continuously updating models online, allowing them to incrementally adjust and remain effective as data distributions evolve. This paper presents the Stream Cruise Control Method (SCCM), a comprehensive framework for drift detection and adaptation in online regression. SCCM enables automated adaptation through early-response, pre-update drift detection, drift magnitude quantification, KPI-window-based thresholding for local false-alarm mitigation, dynamic hyperparameter tuning, and model recalibration. SCCM also adopts an in-memory design for real-time adaptability, unlike purely reactive methods that typically activate adaptation only after performance degradation is observed. By using dynamic thresholding and remaining agnostic to data distributions, SCCM supports KPI-based monitoring across varying data streams, including high-dimensional and large-scale settings. SCCM is integrated with four online regression models and evaluated on 18 synthetic datasets covering abrupt, incremental, and alternating gradual drift, together with eight real-world datasets. The evaluation uses both R2 and MSE and compares against eight detector--adaptation baselines. Results show improved predictive performance and effective drift handling across the evaluated online regression settings.

AI.tldr: SCCM is an in-memory, KPI-driven drift detection and adaptation framework for online regression, enabling early response, dynamic hyperparameter tuning, and recalibration to handle concept drift across diverse data streams.
AI.motivation: Real-world data often exhibits concept drift; fixed hyperparameters hinder adaptation; there is need for online, automated drift detection and model recalibration.
AI.method: SCCM framework: early-response pre-update drift detection, drift magnitude quantification, KPI-window-based local false-alarm mitigation, dynamic hyperparameter tuning, model recalibration, in-memory real-time design; integrates with four online regression models; evaluated on 18 synthetic and 8 real-world datasets with R2 and MSE; compared to eight detector-adaptation baselines.
AI.result: SCCM achieves improved predictive performance and effective drift handling across abruptly, incrementally, and gradually drifting data settings; performs well in high-dimensional/large-scale streams.
AI.conclusion: SCCM provides automated, robust online regression adaptation with distributed KPI-based monitoring and real-time recalibration, suitable for diverse drift scenarios.

title: Compact Visuotactile World Models for Lifting: Prediction, Reward Alignment, and Force Constraints
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Code and tabulated results included as ancillary material
summary: Accurate contact prediction is useful for robotic manipulation only if it supports effective decisions. We investigate this connection using a compact, randomly initialized visuotactile world model, trajectory-level uncertainty calibration, and behavior-initialized actor-critic learning in imagination. On 160 MuJoCo Lift episodes, adding touch reduces endpoint-force prediction error from 1.058 to 0.228 N and interval-peak error from 2.724 to 0.523 N across three training seeds. However, tactile persistence achieves lower errors of 0.095 and 0.498 N, respectively. Two exploratory control rounds comprise 680 executions on 40 independent test initial conditions. A matched reward revision on fresh test environments increases in-distribution 10 cm lifting success from 20.0% to 93.3%, while success within an 8 N per-finger budget reaches only 33.3%, compared with 70.0% for force feedback. Calibration margins reduce force violations at the cost of task completion. In a separate study of public GelSight recordings, a force regressor achieves 0.04234 N error, but frame-level calibration covers only 15.80% of complete trajectories; trajectory-level calibration raises this to 87.36% at nominal 90% coverage. Together, these findings distinguish improvements in sensing and task reward from improvements in force-constrained control. The evidence is limited to public sensing records and simulator execution, without a demonstrated transfer between them.

AI.tldr: Touch improves contact prediction and lifting performance in a visuotactile world model, but gains depend on calibration level; improvements in sensing and task rewards are not yet transferred to force-constrained control, and evidence is limited to simulator data and public sensing records.
AI.motivation: To understand when contact prediction benefits decision-making in robotic manipulation and to disentangle improvements from sensing versus task reward/control.
AI.method: Evaluate a compact, randomly initialized visuotactile world model with trajectory-level uncertainty calibration and behavior-initialized actor-critic learning in imagination. Experiments include 160 MuJoCo Lift episodes comparing touch vs no-touch, tactile persistence, two exploratory control rounds (680 executions on 40 test initial conditions), and a reward revision on fresh environments. A public GelSight dataset analyzes force regression with frame- and trajectory-level calibration.
AI.result: With touch, endpoint-force error drops from 1.058 to 0.228 N and interval-peak error from 2.724 to 0.523 N; tactile persistence yields 0.095 and 0.498 N. Lifting success rises from 20.0% to 93.3% after reward revision; within an 8 N per-finger budget, success is 33.3% vs 70.0% with force feedback. Calibration margins reduce force violations but can slow task completion. GelSight analysis shows force regressor error of 0.04234 N, but frame-level calibration covers only 15.80% of trajectories while trajectory-level calibration covers 87.36% at 90% nominal coverage.
AI.conclusion: Sensing improvements (contact prediction/calibration) and task reward improvements can enhance performance, but improvements in force-constrained control remain distinct. The evidence is confined to simulation and public sensing data, with no demonstrated transfer between the two domains.

title: OmniPoint: Universal Monocular Metric Pointcloud from Any Camera
summary: Recovering metric 3D geometry from monocular images is a fundamental computer vision task, yet current methods remain heavily fragmented by fixed camera model assumptions and inflexible input schemes. We present OmniPoint, a unified framework designed to generalize metric reconstruction across diverse imaging sensors, including pinhole, fisheye, and equirectangular projections, while accommodating varying geometric priors. To overcome projection rigidity, OmniPoint abandons conventional planar depth regression. It instead adopts a decoupled ray and distance representation alongside a decoupled training objective, explicitly separating the camera projection model from the scene structure. To address the severe scarcity of training data for alternative cameras, we introduce a bidirectional augmentation strategy that explicitly bridges labeled perspective data and unlabeled omnidirectional domains in 3D space. Furthermore, to seamlessly integrate optional inputs like camera intrinsics or sparse depth without destabilizing the network through feature distribution shifts, we propose a robust information injection mechanism. This mechanism utilizes learnable input state embeddings to resolve architectural ambiguity and applies vectorized Gaussian smoothing to densify irregular measurements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniPoint achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across multiple benchmarks, establishing a robust new standard for unified monocular 3D reconstruction.

AI.tldr: OmniPoint introduces a unified, projection-agnostic framework for monocular 3D reconstruction that generalizes across pinhole, fisheye, and equirectangular cameras without fixed depth regression, using a decoupled ray-distance representation, decoupled training objective, bidirectional data augmentation bridging perspective and omnidirectional domains, and a robust information injection strategy with learnable input embeddings and Gaussian smoothing, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot results.
AI.motivation: Current monocular metric reconstruction methods are constrained by fixed camera models and rigid input pipelines, limiting generalization to diverse sensors. A unified approach is needed to perform reliable 3D reconstruction across varied projections and priors.
AI.method: 1) Replace planar depth regression with a decoupled ray-and-distance representation, separating camera projection from scene geometry. 2) Use a decoupled training objective to prevent projection-model bias. 3) Implement bidirectional augmentation to connect labeled perspective data with unlabeled omnidirectional domains in 3D space. 4) Introduce a robust information injection mechanism with learnable input state embeddings to handle optional inputs and apply vectorized Gaussian smoothing to dense irregular measurements.
AI.result: OmniPoint achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen camera models and inputs.
AI.conclusion: A unified, projection-agnostic framework with decoupled representations and data augmentation establishes a new standard for monocular 3D reconstruction across diverse imaging sensors.

title: Do Agents Know When They Succeed? Calibrating Agent Confidence from Internal Representations
summary: As agentic systems getting adopted rapidly in safety critical applications, it is vital to measure the confidence associated with the agentic actions. In comparison to the traditional machine learning systems, agentic workflows have complex failure modes with planning, tool invocation and dynamic environment interactions. In this paper, we investigate whether model's internal representations provide stronger signals of eventual task success in multi-turn agentic setups. We introduce two complementary methods: Latent Trajectory Dynamics (LTD), which summarizes changes in residual-stream representations across an an interaction trajectory, and the Action Representation Probe (ARP), which predicts success from representations formed at action decisions. Across three interactive benchmarks (Bash, SQL, Python) and three model families (Qwen14B, Qwen7B, DeepSeek6.7B), our methods consistently outperform surface level generation and sequence-based calibration baselines providing a zero-overhead reliability monitor that requires neither prompt alterations nor multi-sample rollouts.

AI.tldr: LTD and ARP offer zero-overhead, internal-signal reliability monitoring for multi-turn agentic systems, outperforming baselines across Bash/SQL/Python and multiple models.
AI.motivation: Agentic workflows in safety-critical settings require reliable confidence signals. Traditional generation calibration may miss failure modes arising from planning, tool use, and dynamic interaction. Internal model representations may encode predictive cues of success.
AI.method: Latent Trajectory Dynamics (LTD) tracks residual-stream dynamics along an interaction trajectory; Action Representation Probe (ARP) predicts task success from representations formed at action decisions. Evaluated on three benchmarks (Bash, SQL, Python) and three model families (Qwen14B, Qwen7B, DeepSeek6.7B).
AI.result: LTD and ARP consistently outperform surface-level generation and sequence-based calibration baselines, providing a zero-overhead reliability monitor that requires neither prompt alterations nor multi-sample rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Internal, representation-based probes (LTD and ARP) provide robust, model-agnostic reliability signals for agentic tasks in multi-turn settings and can be deployed without changes to prompts or sampling strategies.

title: Efficient Leakage-Free Neural Architecture Search under Leave-One-Subject-Out Evaluation
summary: Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) evaluation estimates generalisation performance for subject-based classification but makes Neural Architecture Search (NAS) computationally expensive because a fully nested implementation requires N independent architecture searches and, assuming approximately linear training cost, scales as O(N^2). We propose a leakage-free, block-based approach that shares NAS runs across subjects. On the BioVid Heat Pain dataset, our approach increased the mean accuracy from 82.79% to 83.39% while reducing the number of parameters by up to 99.2%.

AI.tldr: Leakage-free, block-based NAS that shares NAS runs across subjects for LOSO evaluation; achieves small accuracy gain with large parameter reduction (BioVid Heat Pain).
AI.motivation: LOSO is accurate for generalization but computationally expensive; previous setups require N independent NAS runs, scaling as O(N^2).
AI.method: Block-based, leakage-free NAS approach that reuses NAS runs across subjects, ensuring leakage-free design while sharing computation across subject folds.
AI.result: Mean accuracy on BioVid Heat Pain improved from 82.79% to 83.39%; parameter count reduced by up to 99.2%.
AI.conclusion: Block-based NAS sharing across subjects reduces computational cost in LOSO settings while maintaining or slightly improving performance.

title: MuJoCable: Reduced-Order Surface-Routed Cable Transmission for Tendon-Driven Robots
summary: Tendon transmissions reduce distal inertia and add compliance, yet routing, slack, and friction govern motion and force transfer. Mainstream rigid-body robotics simulators such as MuJoCo do not jointly resolve moving noncircular contact, unilateral tension, and segment friction. We present MuJoCable, which adds a reduced-order, configuration-dependent cable transmission to MuJoCo. Its routing algorithm jointly optimizes an ordered path across moving analytic and mesh surfaces. A unilateral axial law, directional Capstan propagation, and nodal virtual work map this path to segment tensions and body forces. The warm-started engine plugin applies these forces during simulation and exposes route and load states for design. Pulley benchmarks recover analytical transmission relations with a Capstan-ratio error below 0.5%. On the underactuated 18-joint SpiRobs, MuJoCable reveals friction-driven load growth and proximal redistribution of joint rotation that the native tendon does not represent. Hardware tests on SpiRobs and a tendon-route-coupled finger reproduce observed motion sequences. By making physical threading executable, MuJoCable brings transmission sources of the simulation-to-reality gap into route, cable, and actuator design before fabrication.

AI.tldr: A reduced-order cable transmission (MuJoCable) added to MuJoCo enables routing of tendon-like cables across moving surfaces with unilateral tension, Capstan effects, and friction; validated via benchmarks and hardware, revealing previously unmodeled friction-driven load dynamics and closer simulation-to-reality fidelity.
AI.motivation: Mainstream rigid-body simulators struggle to jointly resolve moving noncircular contact, unilateral tension, and segment friction in tendon-driven systems; a joint transmission model is needed to close the simulation-to-reality gap.
AI.method: Develop a configuration-dependent cable routing algorithm that optimizes an ordered path across moving analytic and mesh surfaces, implement a unilateral axial law and Capstan-based propagation, and map to segment tensions via nodal virtual work. Integrate as a warm-started MuJoCo engine plugin exposing route/load states for design; validate with pulley benchmarks and hardware experiments on SpiRobs and a tendon-route-coupled finger.
AI.result: Pulley benchmarks reproduce analytical transmission relations with Capstan-ratio error < 0.5%. On an 18-joint SpiRob, MuJoCable shows friction-driven load growth and proximal redistribution of joint rotation not captured by native tendon models. Hardware tests corroborate observed motion sequences; the approach enables executable physical threading and improves design fidelity before fabrication.
AI.conclusion: MuJoCable extends MuJoCo to include tendon transmission physics, reducing the simulation-to-reality gap by enabling route-, cable-, and actuator-level design prior to fabrication and providing observable effects of friction and routing on actuation in hardware.

title: VANTAGE-Bench: Evaluating the Infrastructure AI Gap in Vision-Language Models
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://vantage-bench.org/; dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/PhysicalAI-VANTAGE-Bench;
summary:
As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance toward physical deployment, the focus has remained on action-oriented Embodied AI evaluated on subject-centric consumer video. This overlooks a pervasive class of Physical AI: Infrastructure AI, which relies on fixed cameras for open-loop insights like safety monitoring and operational logging. We introduce VANTAGE-Bench, a benchmark measuring this "Infrastructure AI Gap." It spans three operational domains (Logistics, Transportation, and Smart Spaces), unifies image and video evaluation across semantic, spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal capabilities, and moves beyond multiple-choice to eight task formulations including dense captioning and spatio-temporal grounding. It adds a single-pass trajectory protocol for Single Object Tracking and, to our knowledge, the first such evaluation on fixed-camera infrastructure video, scored against specialist trackers. Annotation spans three regimes over 3,346 media assets: 3,342 video-task annotations, 4,281 image-grounding annotations, and 27,404 detection boxes.
  Evaluating 17 models zero-shot, we find the shortfall relative to consumer-centric benchmarks is concentrated, not general. Event verification, referring expressions, and temporal localization fall roughly 9 to 24 points at every model scale, while video question answering stays within 5.3 points of VideoMME and 2D spatial pointing shows no shortfall against BLINK. The temporal pillar is weakest in absolute terms: no system exceeds 55.7 mIoU on temporal localization or 37.3 SODA_c on dense video captioning. On tracking, frontier models come within roughly 5 points of specialist trackers over short horizons but separate as the horizon extends. Open-weight models lead 2D object localization outright, so neither scale nor proprietary access explains the pattern. Data, evaluation harness, and leaderboard: https://vantage-bench.org/

AI.tldr: VANTAGE-Bench introduces Infrastructure AI benchmark for fixed-camera open-loop tasks across Logistics, Transportation, and Smart Spaces; extends to eight tasks including dense captioning and spatio-temporal grounding with a single-pass SOT protocol; evaluates 17 models in zero-shot; identifies a persistent infrastructure AI gap especially in temporal localization and complex reasoning, with frontier models approaching but not surpassing specialist trackers for short horizons; data and leaderboard at vantage-bench.org.
AI.motivation: To address the underexplored Infrastructure AI gap—perception and reasoning from fixed cameras for safety, monitoring, and operational logging—by creating a unified, multi-domain benchmark that covers image/video understanding across semantic, spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal dimensions and moves beyond multiple-choice tasks.
AI.method: Proposes VANTAGE-Bench with three operational domains (Logistics, Transportation, Smart Spaces), unifying image and video evaluation across semantic/spatial/temporal capabilities and eight task formulations (including dense captioning and spatio-temporal grounding). Introduces a single-pass trajectory protocol for Single Object Tracking on fixed-camera infrastructure video. Annotations span 3 regimes over 3,346 media assets (3,342 video-task annotations, 4,281 image-grounding annotations, 27,404 detection boxes). Zero-shot evaluation of 17 models.
AI.result: Gap relative to consumer-centric benchmarks is concentrated rather than general. Event verification, referring expressions, and temporal localization drop roughly 9–24 points across models; video QA remains within 5.3 points of VideoMME; 2D spatial pointing shows parity with BLINK. Temporal localization is the weakest: no system exceeds 55.7 mIoU; dense video captioning lags at 37.3 SODA_c. Frontier models are within ~5 points of specialist trackers for short horizons, but diverge over longer horizons. Open-weight models lead in 2D object localization, not explained by data scale or access.
AI.conclusion: Infrastructure AI demands dedicated benchmarks and evaluation protocols; current models struggle in temporal and complex reasoning tasks, highlighting the need for more infrastructure-specific training and evaluation. Open-weight models show promise for 2D localization; data, evaluation harness, and leaderboard are available at vantage-bench.org.

title: ContractEval: Query-Conditioned Execution Matching for Procedural Instruction Conformance
summary: As LLM agents move from answering questions to carrying out procedures, failures can be unwarranted rather than visibly wrong: the final response looks acceptable even though the system skipped the check, branch, dependency, or invariant that made the answer justified. Output-only evaluation sees the answer, and trace-aware judging sees activity, but neither identifies which obligations were active for the query. We introduce CONTRACTEVAL, a diagnostic framework for making those active obligations explicit. It represents procedural instructions as query-active obligations and matches them against response or trace evidence, turning omissions, wrong branches, ordering errors, extra actions, invariant breaches, and output-contract violations into distinct conformance failures. On a controlled suite of audited procedural contracts, output-only and trace-aware LLM judges miss many injected structural failures; under gold expected and observed graphs, ContractEval detects and localizes all of them. LLM-backed extraction preserves much of this signal but remains calibration-sensitive. ContractEval is therefore not a compliance guarantee; it makes procedural conformance auditable rather than implicit in final-answer quality.

AI.tldr: A diagnostic framework that makes active procedural obligations explicit and uses them to audit LLM-based procedures for conformance, revealing omissions and missteps beyond traditional evaluation.
AI.motivation: Final outputs can appear correct even when required checks were skipped; existing output-only and trace-aware evaluations fail to flag active obligations; need auditable, obligation-based evaluation.
AI.method: Represent procedural instructions as query-active obligations; match against response and trace evidence; classify failures into omissions, wrong branches, ordering errors, extra actions, invariant breaches, and output-contract violations; evaluate on a controlled suite of audited procedural contracts; compare gold expected vs observed graphs; use LLM-backed extraction to get signals.
AI.result: In controlled suite, standard judges miss many injected structural failures; ContractEval detects and localizes all of them under gold graphs; extraction preserves much signal but is calibration-sensitive.
AI.conclusion: Not a guarantee; enables auditable conformance; useful for diagnosing, auditing, and improving procedural safety; complements final-answer quality.

title: Tensor-Train Weak SINDy: Identifying High-Dimensional Nonlinear Dynamics
summary: In recent years, weak-form methods have made significant advances in data-driven discovery of dynamical systems. However, in high-dimensional settings, current techniques can prove expensive in both computation and memory. In this work, we introduce TT-WSINDy, which combines techniques of the Multidimensional Approximation of Nonlinear Dynamics (MANDy) and Weak Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (WSINDy) methods, implementing requisite computations in the tensor-train (TT) format. We demonstrate that this method is able to search an exponentially-growing space of candidate functions -- performing weak-form transformation, regression, and sparsification -- without suffering from the curse of dimensionality.

AI.tldr: TT-WSINDy enables high-dimensional weak-form sparse identification by using tensor-train representations to search an exponentially large candidate function space while avoiding the curse of dimensionality.
AI.motivation: Address computational and memory barriers in data-driven discovery of dynamical systems with weak-form methods at high dimensionality.
AI.method: Integrate MANDy and WSINDy into a tensor-train framework; perform weak-form transformation, regression, and sparsification within TT format to efficiently explore candidate functions.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the approach can search an exponentially growing space of candidate functions without suffering from the curse of dimensionality.
AI.conclusion: TT-WSINDy offers scalable, high-dimensional data-driven discovery of nonlinear dynamics by exploiting TT decompositions to mitigate computational/memory constraints.

title: JEPA Policy: Diffusion-Free Imitation Learning via Paired Action and Future Representation Prediction
comment: 17 pages. Code: https://github.com/jiejie567/JEPA-Policy . Project page: https://jiejie567.github.io/JEPA-Policy/
summary: Standard behavior cloning supervises actions without explicitly constraining the future representation paired with each demonstrated action chunk. We introduce JEPA Policy, a diffusion-free framework that uses the action chunk and its observed future representation as paired training targets. Action and future-representation tokens interact in a shared Transformer and are refined through two forward passes. Future prediction can therefore shape the representation used to generate actions. Dual-branch and gradient-routing controls attribute the gain to this shared topology rather than to an auxiliary prediction head alone. Across nine simulated tasks, JEPA Policy improves mean success over the action-only MIP baseline and outperforms Diffusion Policy under the evaluated configurations, while adding 0.29 ms to MIP's model latency. A five-task, 630-episode physical-robot study produces the same pooled ranking. Further audits find no complete representation collapse under action supervision and identify a task-conditioned failure-ranking signal in future-prediction error. These results support paired future-representation supervision as a practical approach to low-latency visuomotor imitation without iterative generative sampling.

AI.tldr: JEPA Policy: a diffusion-free visuomotor imitation framework that pairs action chunks with their future representations in a shared Transformer, improving success with minimal latency vs action-only baselines and diffusion policies.
AI.motivation: Standard behavior cloning lacks constraints on the future representation accompanying each action chunk; leveraging paired future representations could guide action generation and reduce iterative sampling.
AI.method: Train with paired targets: action chunk and observed future representation, both fed into a shared Transformer with two forward passes; dual-branch and gradient-routing to attribute gains to shared topology rather than a separate head; evaluate across nine simulated tasks and a physical-robot study; compare to MIP and Diffusion Policy.
