AI.result: Across nine simulations, JEPA Policy increases mean success over the action-only MIP baseline and outperforms Diffusion Policy under evaluated configs, adding 0.29 ms to MIP's latency; a five-task, 630-episode robot study shows the same ranking; audits indicate no complete representation collapse under action supervision and reveal a task-conditioned failure-ranking signal in future-prediction error.
AI.conclusion: Paired future-representation supervision enables low-latency visuomotor imitation without iterative sampling, with gains attributable to the shared Transformer topology rather than an auxiliary predictor.

title: Vision-language models know more about agriculture than they show and rubric-grounded verifications close the gap
comment: Submitted to the AI for Science Workshop (NeurIPS Workshops 2026)
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for agricultural classification, but zero-shot performance on disease, pest, damage, quality, and species identification remains poor, and it is unclear whether this reflects weak visual features or a failure to connect them to domain knowledge. We build a benchmark of 116 datasets, 834 classes, and 8,324 images spanning these tasks to isolate where the gap arises. Linear probing shows VLM vision encoders already encode agricultural features nearly as separable as a self-supervised DINOv3 baseline, ruling out weak visual representations as the primary bottleneck. Conditioning each model on an oracle reference description (an upper bound on its parametric knowledge) closes most of the gap left by an unaided lower bound, showing VLMs already know more about agriculture than they show. To close this gap without an oracle description at inference time, we structure test-time reasoning around a fixed, per-task diagnostic rubric: the model generates $K$ candidate responses and a Probabilistic Pivot Tournament (PPT) verifier, scored pairwise against the rubric, selects the best one. This nearly doubles judged F1 over the lower bound and matches or exceeds the upper bound on several tasks, notably pushing Gemma 4 E4B-it's disease F1 to 0.71, above its own upper bound of 0.60. However, the verifier's letter-scale confidence score has the opposite of its intended effect: filtering to its most confident predictions does not improve accuracy and correlates negatively with correctness across every model and pool size tested, so the score cannot serve as a measure of predictive uncertainty, and most of the observed gain likely comes from rubric-grounded generation rather than pairwise verification.

AI.tldr: A large agricultural benchmark reveals VLMs have strong visual features; using an oracle description reduces the gap; a rubric-based test-time reasoning (PPT) improves F1 substantially, while a verifier's confidence is unreliable, suggesting gains mainly come from rubric-grounded generation.
AI.motivation: Determine whether zero-shot failures in agricultural tasks stem from weak visuals or missing domain knowledge by isolating performance across disease, pest, damage, quality, and species classification.
AI.method: Create a benchmark with 116 datasets, 834 classes, and 8,324 images. Compare linear probing of VLM vision encoders against a self-supervised DINOv3 baseline. Condition models on an oracle reference description to bound knowledge. Propose test-time reasoning with a fixed per-task rubric: generate K candidate responses and a Probabilistic Pivot Tournament (PPT) verifier scored against the rubric, selecting the best. Evaluate against lower/upper bounds and analyze calibration of the verifier's confidence.
AI.result: Vision encoders are nearly as separable as the DINOv3 baseline in linear probing, indicating visuals are not the primary bottleneck. Oracle conditioning closes much of the gap. The rubric-plus-PPT approach nearly doubles judged F1 over the lower bound and matches or exceeds the upper bound on several tasks (e.g., disease F1 for Gemma 4 E4B-it reaches 0.71, above its 0.60 upper bound). However, the verifier’s letter-scale confidence score negatively correlates with correctness, indicating it is not a reliable uncertainty measure; most gains appear to come from rubric-guided generation rather than the verification step.
AI.conclusion: Agricultural knowledge is largely embedded in VLMs; test-time rubric-guided generation can unlock that knowledge without oracle descriptions, but the current uncertainty signal is unreliable and future work should focus on robust uncertainty estimation and further rubric design.

title: Multi-Agent Agentic Graph Learning via Structural Signatures
summary: Agentic graph learning (AGL) has recently achieved promising results on graph reasoning tasks, where an agent powered by a large language model (LLM) sequentially samples the graph as evidence to support its final prediction. Existing methods either employ a single agent or orchestrate multiple role-based agents to reason and learn over the entire graph, but both essentially rely on a shared reasoning policy across different graph regions, which can be suboptimal for graphs with heterogeneous structural and semantic patterns. Inspired by the progress of multi-agent collaboration on complex reasoning tasks, a natural remedy is to let multiple agents own different memory and collaborate; however, applying this paradigm to graphs directly faces two challenges. First, existing AGL methods typically verbalize graph structures into natural-language descriptions for LLM agents, making the reasoning process sensitive to the ordering of structural information and thereby breaking the permutation-invariant nature of graphs. Second, incorporating increasingly large sampled neighborhoods leads to rapidly growing contexts. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a multi-agent agentic graph learning (i.e., MAAGL) framework. MAAGL partitions the graph into communities and assigns an independent agent to each community for region-specific specialization. MAAGL represents structural and semantic evidence separately. Structural evidence is summarized by a dynamically updated structural signature that is permutation-invariant and fixed in size, while semantic evidence is filtered to the top-k nodes ranked by relevance. Based on historical trajectories with similar signatures, agents estimate their confidence and trigger debate-style collaboration when needed. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets show that MAAGL outperforms SOTA AGL methods.

AI.tldr: MAAGL is a multi-agent, region-aware graph-learning framework that partitions graphs into communities, uses permutation-invariant structural signatures and top-k semantic evidence, and enables debate-style collaboration, achieving state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Graphs exhibit heterogeneous structural/semantic patterns. Shared reasoning policies hamper performance; verbalizing graph structures breaks permutation invariance; growing neighborhoods lead to large contexts. MAAGL targets region-specific reasoning with scalable memory.
AI.method: Partition the graph into communities; assign an independent agent per community. Represent evidence in two streams: (1) structural evidence via a dynamically updated, fixed-size, permutation-invariant structural signature; (2) semantic evidence via top-k nodes by relevance. Agents estimate confidence from historical trajectories with similar signatures and trigger debate-style collaboration when needed.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four benchmark datasets shows MAAGL achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing AGL methods.
AI.conclusion: MAAGL effectively handles regional heterogeneity and scalability in agentic graph learning by separating structural/semantic evidence and enabling selective collaboration, suggesting promise for more scalable, permutation-safe multi-agent graph reasoning.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Sea-Ice Type Mapping with Multiple Ice Charts
summary: Sea-ice stage of development (SoD) describes the age and associated thickness of sea ice and provides important information for navigation, and operational ice monitoring. SoD labels are obtained from operational ice charts, where trained analysts interpret satellite observations and assign standardized stage codes to regions with similar ice conditions. These codes often represent ranges of compatible ice thicknesses rather than exact physical values. Deep-learning methods can automate SoD mapping and commonly adopt operational ice charts as reference labels for training. These annotations are not exact, however; this is because chart interpretation relies on analyst judgement and on the observations available at the time, so different ice services may assign different SoD labels to the same conditions. We term this variation across independently produced expert annotations multi-annotator label uncertainty; collapsing the annotations into a single deterministic target discards this variation. A second source of uncertainty originates in the learned model itself. In this paper, we quantify both sources: annotation uncertainty from disagreement among independent ice-service charts and model uncertainty from the learned predictive models. We then evaluate their relationship by testing whether model uncertainty is higher where ice services disagree. We observe that supervision incorporating information from multiple annotators can improve this correspondence, with soft supervision achieving the highest overall correlation of 0.256. The relationship becomes substantially stronger near the ice edge, where model predictive uncertainty closely tracks multi-annotator disagreement, reaching a correlation of 0.704 within 0--10 km. Among the uncertainty-estimation approaches, Monte Carlo dropout provides the best-calibrated confidence estimates, with an expected calibration error of 0.050.

AI.tldr: Quantifies and compares two sources of uncertainty in sea-ice stage-of-development mapping: annotator disagreement and model uncertainty; shows soft supervision and MC dropout improve alignment, especially near the ice edge.
AI.motivation: Improve reliability and interpretability of automated SoD mapping by explicitly accounting for both annotation uncertainty across expert charts and model uncertainty.
AI.method: Quantify annotation uncertainty from disagreement among independent ice-service charts; quantify model uncertainty from learned predictive models; test whether model uncertainty correlates with multi-annotator disagreement; evaluate soft supervision that integrates information from multiple annotators; compare uncertainty-estimation approaches, with Monte Carlo dropout reported as best-calibrated.
AI.result: Overall correlation between model uncertainty and multi-annotator disagreement: 0.256; near ice edge (0--10 km): 0.704; soft supervision yields highest correlation; Monte Carlo dropout provides best calibration with expected calibration error 0.050.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating multi-annotator information improves the correspondence between predicted uncertainty and annotator disagreement, particularly near the ice edge; MC dropout offers strong calibration for uncertainty estimates; results highlight the value of modeling multiple uncertainty sources in operational SoD mapping.

title: A Risk-Sensitive and Uncertainty-Aware Decision-Making and Control Framework for Safe and Robust Autonomous Driving
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated considerable potential for autonomous driving decision-making. However, its deployment in urban autonomous driving, particularly at highly interactive unsignalized intersections, remains challenging, as learned policies may struggle to maintain both safety and robust decision-making in complex traffic situations. Conventional safety-filtering approaches typically employ fixed conservative constraints, which may improve safety at the cost of excessive intervention and degraded traffic efficiency. To address these limitations, we propose a Risk-sensitive and Uncertainty-aware Decision-making and Control (RUDC) framework for safe and robust autonomous driving. RUDC couples risk-sensitive distributional RL with ensemble-based policy uncertainty quantification, jointly accounting for tail risks in return distributions and uncertainty in learned policies. An uncertainty-aware high-order control barrier function (HOCBF)-based safety correction mechanism adaptively adjusts constraint strictness according to policy uncertainty, while a learnable residual predictor compensates for CBF model mismatches and discretization errors. Extensive simulations at unsignalized intersections demonstrate that RUDC achieves a favorable balance among safety, efficiency, and robustness, outperforming representative safe RL baselines under both nominal and challenging OOD and long-tail scenarios while satisfying real-time requirements.

AI.tldr: Introduces RUDC, a risk-sensitive distributional RL framework with ensemble uncertainty for safe, robust autonomous driving at unsignalized intersections, augmented by an uncertainty-aware HOCBF safety correction and a learnable residual to mitigate model errors; demonstrates improved safety, efficiency, and robustness in simulations, including OOD/long-tail scenarios.
AI.motivation: Conventional safety filters use fixed conservatism that can hamper traffic efficiency and may not capture tail risks or policy uncertainty in highly interactive urban intersections; a framework that jointly addresses tail risk and policy uncertainty is needed for reliable, real-time decision-making.
AI.method: RUDC fuses (i) distributional RL with ensemble-based uncertainty estimation to model tail risk in returns, (ii) an uncertainty-aware high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) safety correction that adaptively tightens/loosens constraints based on policy uncertainty, and (iii) a learnable residual predictor to compensate for CBF model mismatches and discretization errors; designed for real-time operation at unsignalized intersections.
AI.result: In simulations of unsignalized intersections, RUDC achieves a favorable balance among safety, efficiency, and robustness, and outperforms representative safe RL baselines under nominal, OOD, and long-tail challenging scenarios while meeting real-time requirements.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a principled integration of risk-sensitive RL and uncertainty-aware safety control for safe and robust autonomous driving in complex urban traffic, with strong performance in diverse scenarios. Future work may include real-world validation, scalability analyses, and exploring computational trade-offs.

title: Longitudinal tracking of multiple sclerosis lesions in the spinal cord: A validation study
summary: Longitudinal characterization of multiple sclerosis (MS) lesions remains constrained by the lack of frameworks capable of establishing consistent instance-level correspondences across time. Conventional segmentation approaches produce semantic lesion masks at each visit and therefore fail to capture the complex instance temporal patterns associated with lesion appearance, disappearance, splitting, or merging. This study presents a comparative evaluation of five strategies for automated tracking of spinal cord MS lesions in longitudinal MRI data from a multi-site cohort. The investigated strategies rely either on deformable registration or on a spinal anatomical reference system, and encompass overlap-based matching, coordinate-based Hungarian algorithm, gradient-boosted classification, and Siamese model classification. Tracking accuracy is quantified using instance-level true positives, false positives, and false negatives, allowing to assess the presence of one-to-many and many-to-one associations. Results show best performance for the registration-based overlap method. This study provides the first systematic analysis of lesion-instance correspondence in the spinal cord and outlines the strengths and limitations of registration-based and registration-free paradigms for longitudinal MS assessment. The code is available at http://github.com/ivadomed/longitudinal-sc-ms-lesion-tracking .

AI.tldr: Comparative evaluation of five spinal cord MS lesion-tracking methods in longitudinal MRI; best results from a registration-based overlap approach; first systematic analysis of lesion-instance correspondence in the spinal cord; code released.
AI.motivation: Overcome the lack of instance-level temporal correspondences for MS lesions—moving beyond semantic segmentation to track appearance, disappearance, splitting, and merging across time in the spinal cord.
AI.method: Evaluate five strategies derived from deformable-registration or spinal anatomical reference frameworks, including overlap-based matching, coordinate-based Hungarian algorithm, gradient-boosted classification, and Siamese model classification. Use instance-level TP/FP/FN metrics to assess one-to-many and many-to-one associations on a multi-site longitudinal dataset.
AI.result: Registration-based overlap method yields the best tracking accuracy. The study provides a first systematic analysis of lesion-instance correspondence in the spinal cord and discusses strengths/limitations of registration-based vs. registration-free approaches. Code available at the stated GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a baseline for lesion-instance tracking in the spinal cord, clarifies trade-offs between registration-based and registration-free paradigms, and supports reproducibility through public code.

title: CityPlanner: A Sandbox Agent for Executable Urban Planning
summary: Urban planning is a real-world spatial optimization problem that requires selecting feasible actions from large candidate spaces under practical objectives such as cost and service quality. Existing optimization and reinforcement learning methods are effective for fixed formulations, but often depend on task-specific representations and constraint handling. We propose \emph{CityPlanner}, a sandbox-agent framework for executable urban planning. CityPlanner introduces \emph{UrbanSandbox}, a unified file-based environment where agents inspect task files, generate plans, run evaluators, and revise decisions based on executable feedback. To make learning tractable, we further propose atomic-task reinforcement learning, which decomposes long sandbox trajectories into \emph{BuildPlan} for initial construction and \emph{ImprovePlan} for feedback-based refinement. Experiments on a real-world benchmark show that CityPlanner consistently outperforms heuristic, task-specific RL, and general LLM-agent baselines. Ablations verify the contributions of UrbanSandbox, atomic-task RL, and iterative deployment. We release the code and dataset at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/co-agent-C1C8

AI.tldr: CityPlanner is a sandbox-agent framework for executable urban planning, introducing UrbanSandbox (file-based environment) and atomic-task RL to decompose planning into BuildPlan and ImprovePlan. It claims superior performance over heuristics, task-specific RL, and general LLM-agent baselines on a real-world benchmark, with ablations validating the components.
AI.motivation: Urban planning involves large candidate spaces and practical objectives (cost, service quality), and existing methods struggle with task-specific representations and constraint handling. A generalizable, executable framework is needed to enable learning from executable feedback.
AI.method: UrbanSandbox provides a unified, file-based interface where agents read task files, generate plans, execute evaluators, and update decisions. Atomic-task RL splits long trajectories into BuildPlan (initial construction) and ImprovePlan (iterative refinement) to make learning tractable.
AI.result: Empirical results show CityPlanner consistently surpasses heuristic approaches, task-specific RL, and general LLM-based agents on a real-world benchmark. Ablations demonstrate the importance of UrbanSandbox, the atomic-task RL decomposition, and iterative deployment.
AI.conclusion: CityPlanner offers a generalizable, executable framework for urban planning that integrates planning, evaluation, and learning from executable feedback, with reported performance gains and ablation-supported contributions. Code and dataset are released.

title: Exact-Form Regret for Gradient Descent, Mirror Descent and Follow-the-Regularized-Leader
summary: Online gradient descent is usually studied through external regret, where the learner competes with fixed alternatives. Recent work shows that first-order methods control richer action-dependent deviations. We ask for a geometric characterization of the deviations with respect to which online gradient descent, mirror descent, and follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) achieve no regret. We identify exactness as the common principle. Exactness means that the relevant displacement field is generated by a scalar potential, or equivalently that the associated one-form is exact in the geometry used by the algorithm. This geometry depends on the algorithm. For gradient descent it is Euclidean geometry, for mirror descent it is the geometry induced by the regularizer, and for FTRL it is the cumulative dual state. Under mild regularity conditions, exactness yields sublinear regret, while nonzero circulation provides the complementary obstruction and leads to linear regret. This gives a unified geometric framework for understanding the deviation classes controlled by these algorithms and reveals that different first-order methods can control genuinely different classes of deviations. These deviation classes have direct consequences for learning, particularly in games. We study the equilibrium notions induced by exact-form deviations and introduce conservative correlated equilibrium, reflecting both the conservative geometry of the underlying displacement fields and the restricted family of deviations available to the players. We characterize its relation to correlated equilibrium, determine when the resulting equilibrium notions coincide and when they separate, and show how these relationships depend on the geometry and the learning algorithm. Overall, this work gives a unified geometric account of what first-order online learning algorithms are no-regret with respect to, beyond fixed comparators.

AI.tldr: Unifies OGD, mirror descent, and FTRL via exactness: sublinear regret arises when displacement fields are exact (generated by a scalar potential) in the algorithm's geometry; nonzero circulation causes linear regret. Introduces conservative correlated equilibrium and links to correlated equilibrium, depending on the algorithm's geometry.
AI.motivation: To geometrically characterize the action-dependent deviation classes that yield no-regret for first-order online learning algorithms, extending beyond fixed comparators, and to understand the induced equilibrium notions in games.
AI.method: Develop a geometric/differential-geometry framework: treat displacement fields in the respective geometries (Euclidean for gradient descent, Bregman geometry for mirror descent, cumulative dual state for FTRL); characterize exactness vs. non-exactness (circulation) of the associated one-forms; derive regret implications; define conservative correlated equilibrium and analyze its relation to standard correlated equilibrium across geometries.
AI.result: Exactness ensures sublinear regret for OGD, MD, and FTRL; nonzero circulation yields linear regret. The work provides a unified geometric account of deviation classes controlled by these algorithms, showing that different first-order methods control genuinely different deviations. It also introduces conservative correlated equilibrium and characterizes when it coincides with or differs from correlated equilibrium, depending on geometry and learning algorithm.
AI.conclusion: Offers a unified geometric explanation of no-regret phenomena beyond fixed comparators and reveals that gradient-descent, mirror-descent, and FTRL govern different deviation classes, with concrete implications for learning in games.

title: CT-SAFR: Safe and Interpretable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Autonomous Robots: A Multi-Layered Verification Framework for Trustworthy AI-Driven Robotic Decision Making
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Accepted version. Published in 2026 IEEE Conference on Artificial Intelligence (CAI), pp. 598-603
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enables LLMs to perform explicit, step-by-step reasoning, creating opportunities for sophisticated autonomous robots. However, recent research reveals that reasoning models verbalize their actual decision processes only 25-39% of the time, with faithfulness degrading 44% on complex tasks. This paper presents CT-SAFR (Chain-of-Thought Safety and Faithfulness for Robotics), a multi-layered verification framework achieving 94.2% hallucination detection (n = 500, 95% CI: 91.8-95.9%) with sub-500ms latency. Through a warehouse robot case study, this work demonstrates 87% reduction in unsafe reasoning outputs (p < 0.001) and provides recommendations for responsible deployment of reasoning-capable autonomous robots.

AI.tldr: CT-SAFR: a multi-layered verification framework to improve safety and faithfulness of chain-of-thought in robotics, achieving high hallucination-detection accuracy with low latency and a substantial reduction in unsafe reasoning in a warehouse-robot case study.
AI.motivation: Address faithfulness and safety issues in Chain-of-Thought for reasoning-capable robots, where models often reveal non-faithful or unsafe decision processes; ensure reliable, verifiable reasoning for real-world deployment.
AI.method: A multi-layered verification framework (CT-SAFR) that detects and mitigates hallucinations in CoT. Evaluation includes a large-scale detection metric (n=500) with sub-500 ms latency, and a warehouse-robot case study measuring unsafe reasoning outputs (87% reduction, p<0.001).
AI.result: Achieves 94.2% hallucination detection (95% CI: 91.8–95.9%) with sub-500 ms latency; 87% reduction in unsafe reasoning outputs in the case study.
AI.conclusion: Results support the feasibility of safe, faithful reasoning in robotics via CT-SAFR, with strong detection performance and practical deployment benefits; suggests guidelines for responsible deployment of reasoning-capable autonomous robots.

title: Low-Rank Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models with Fixed-Token Bases
summary: Prompt learning adapts CLIP to downstream recognition by replacing hand-written templates with learned continuous context vectors, which in Context Optimization (CoOp) form a dense prompt matrix $\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ trained from only a few examples per class. We study whether this matrix is over-parameterized by factorizing it as $\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}$, which cuts the trainable prompt parameters from $md$ to $r(m+d)$, and to $rd$ once the token-side factor $\mathbf{B}$ is fixed. Across seven few-shot benchmarks and two CLIP backbones, low-rank prompts match or improve dense CoOp at far fewer parameters, with the clearest gains on low-shot base-to-new generalization. We then find that the token-side factor need not be learned at all: fixing $\mathbf{B}$ to a Gaussian, orthogonal, SVD-derived, or even random basis and training only the embedding-side factor $\mathbf{A}$ stays on par with the fully trainable factorization, and a source-trained $\mathbf{B}$ offers no advantage over a random one. A prompt-factor asymmetry and a local update-space dimension gap show why fixing $\mathbf{B}$ is far less restrictive than fixing $\mathbf{A}$, and a smoothness-only guarantee certifies that optimizing $\mathbf{A}$ over a fixed $\mathbf{B}$ converges. In the CLIP prompt setting, the embedding-side coefficients carry the adaptation while the token basis can simply be fixed.

AI.tldr: Low-rank factorization of CoOp prompts into P = B A yields parameter-efficient prompts that match or surpass dense CoOp across seven few-shot benchmarks and two CLIP backbones. The token-side basis B can be fixed (random or otherwise) without hurting performance, while the embedding-side factor A carries the adaptation. This explains a prompt-factor asymmetry, a dimension-gap in update space, and a smoothness guarantee for convergence. In CLIP prompts, adaptation resides in embedding-side coefficients; fixing B simplifies design without loss.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether the dense prompt matrix in CLIP prompt learning (CoOp) is over-parameterized and whether a low-rank decomposition suffices. Determine which factor (B or A) carries the adaptation, and whether fixing B hurts performance, with implications for generalization, especially in few-shot scenarios.
AI.method: Factorize P as P = B A to reduce trainable parameters from m d to r(m+d) (and to r d when B is fixed). Evaluate low-rank prompts against dense CoOp across seven few-shot benchmarks and two CLIP backbones. Experiment with fixing B using Gaussian, orthogonal, SVD-derived, or random bases, and train only A. Compare with source-trained B. Provide theoretical intuition: prompt-factor asymmetry, update-space dimension gap, and a smoothness-based convergence guarantee. In CLIP prompting, assess whether embedding-side coefficients suffice for adaptation while token-side basis can be fixed.
AI.result: Low-rank prompts match or improve dense CoOp with substantially fewer parameters. Gains are most pronounced in low-shot base-to-new generalization. Fixing B (to Gaussian, orthogonal, SVD-derived, or random) while training only A performs on par with fully trainable P; a source-trained B offers no advantage over a random one. The results reveal a clear asymmetry: A carries adaptation, B can be fixed. Theoretical considerations explain convergence and the dimension gap in update space. In CLIP prompts, embedding-side coefficients are the main adaptation channel, not the token basis.
AI.conclusion: Embedding-side coefficients are the primary locus of adaptation in CLIP prompts; the token-side basis can be fixed without performance loss, enabling highly parameter-efficient prompt learning. This provides practical design guidance (fix B, learn A) and theoretical understanding (asymmetry and convergence) for Prompt learning with CLIP.

title: A Function-Space Approach to the Statistical Mechanics of Learning Dynamics
summary:
Deep neural networks exhibit regular macroscopic behavior despite highly nonlinear dynamics in vast parameter spaces. We develop a statistical-mechanical description of learning directly in function space, treating parameter configurations as microscopic realizations and functions with their dynamical operators as macroscopic variables. For mean-squared loss, the exact error dynamics are governed by the learning operator \(M=JJ^\ast\). Combining the dynamical Boltzmann weight of the conditional stochastic dynamics with the parameter-space density of states, whose local curvature defines a statistical operator \(B\), and integrating over local fluctuations yields
  $$ Φ_{\mathrm{fluc}}(M;B)=\frac{σ_ξ^2}{2}\log\det(M^{-1}+B)+\mathrm{const}. $$
  At fixed spectrum, this term is rotationally stationary when \([M,B]=0\), is minimized by pairing large eigenvalues of \(M\) with small eigenvalues of \(B\), and generates a local restoring contribution against rotational mismatch. For ReLU-type function spaces under mild stable statistical conditions, \(B=σ_ξ^2L^\ast\mathcal K L\), where \(L\) measures coarse-grained second-order structure. Thus the low-\(B\) sector corresponds, up to bounded anisotropy of \(\mathcal K\), to low structural curvature, implying a preference for faster relaxation along smooth, data-adaptive directions. These results identify function space as a natural macroscopic level for studying stable collective organization in learning.

AI.tldr: A statistical-mechanical, function-space description of learning yields a fluctuation term Φ_fluc ∝ log det(M^{-1}+B); under [M,B]=0, rotationally stationary and favors pairing large eigenvalues of the learning operator M with small eigenvalues of B; for ReLU spaces B = σ_ξ^2 L^* K L, implying faster relaxation along smooth, data-adaptive directions. Function space emerges as a natural macroscopic level to study stable learning organization.
AI.motivation: Bridge microscopic parameter dynamics and macroscopic learning behavior by treating functions as macroscopic variables and characterizing fluctuations in the learning process to explain stable, regular macroscopic activity in deep nets.
AI.method: Derive exact mean-squared loss error dynamics with learning operator M = JJ^*; model fluctuations via dynamical Boltzmann weight and the parameter-space density of states with curvature-defining operator B; integrate over local fluctuations to obtain Φ_fluc(M;B) = (σ_ξ^2/2) log det(M^{-1}+B) + const; analyze spectral properties, implying rotational invariance under [M,B]=0 and optimal eigen-direction pairing.
AI.result: Fluctuation term is rotationally stationary when M and B commute; the term is minimized by aligning large eigenvalues of M with small eigenvalues of B, yielding a local restoring force against rotational misalignment; in ReLU-like spaces with B = σ_ξ^2 L^* K L, small B corresponds to low curvature, hence faster relaxation along smooth, data-adaptive directions.
AI.conclusion: Function space serves as a natural macroscopic framework to study stable collective organization in learning, linking eigenstructure and curvature to dynamic relaxation properties and suggesting directions for efficient learning dynamics in neural networks.

title: Building the Harness Automatically: Self-Play in Code Distills a Text Harness for Black-Box Optimization
summary: Can an agent learn a numerical search strategy through executable practice and then transfer that strategy as text? We study low-budget black-box optimization, where unaided language models remain well below strong classical optimizers. During development, an agent repeatedly writes and evaluates optimizer programs. It then distills the resulting program and practice record once into a 197-word primary Harness A, which is frozen before evaluation. Harness A reduces Gemini Flash regret by 48\% in an independent $N=30$ study ($p<.001$), enters the GP-BO performance range on the practice family, and lowers mean regret on all three held-out BBOB landscapes. The same text improves every tested Gemini executor and transfers to Claude Sonnet, reducing regret by 43\% and 49\% ($p\leq.005$). An independent end-to-end replication produces Harness B, a different program and text at the same performance tier. The same framework also attains the lowest regret on a sealed YouTube reward-tuning production benchmark. Executable practice is thus a viable way to discover a search policy, and language a portable medium for deploying it.

AI.tldr: Executable practice learns a numerical search strategy and distills it into a 197-word Harness A, enabling cross-model transfer and performance gains across multiple black-box optimization benchmarks; independent replication yields Harness B; language serves as a portable deployment medium.
AI.motivation: Low-budget black-box optimization where unaided language models underperform strong classical optimizers; a data-efficient, transferable method to discover and deploy search policies is needed.
AI.method: An agent repeatedly writes and evaluates optimizer programs (executable practice), distills the resulting program and practice record into a 197-word Harness A (frozen before evaluation), and evaluates on Gemini Flash regret, GP-BO performance on the practice family, and BBOB landscapes; the same Harness text transfers to other models (Claude Sonnet) and improves their regret; independent end-to-end replication yields Harness B with similar performance; the framework also achieves strong results on a sealed YouTube reward-tuning benchmark.
AI.result: Harness A reduces Gemini Flash regret by 48% (N=30, p<.001); enters GP-BO performance range on the practice family; lowers mean regret on all three BBOB landscapes. The Harness text improves every tested Gemini executor and transfers to Claude Sonnet, reducing regret by 43% and 49% (p≤.005). An independent replication produces Harness B at the same performance tier. The framework attains the lowest regret on a sealed YouTube reward-tuning production benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Executable practice is a viable approach to discovering a search policy, and a short textual artifact (Harness) can serve as a portable medium for deploying it across models and benchmarks; this demonstrates cross-model transfer and reproducibility in low-budget optimization settings.

title: PccDiffuser: Multi-solution Motion Planning for Continuum Robots
summary: We present the PccDiffuser, a conditional diffusion framework for continuum robots that learns a multimodal distribution over complete configuration-space paths and samples multiple candidate solutions in parallel, which are subsequently converted into an executable trajectory by time allocation considering actuator constraints. Under the piecewise constant-curvature model, we use exponential co-ordinates to describe the robot kinematics, and use graph neural network to encode a variable number of environment obstacles. Analytical differential kinematics is incorporated in the denoising process to improve terminal accuracy and whole-body clearance. On a mixed test set comprising workspace with zero to four obstacles, PccDiffuser achieved a success rate of 91\%. Compared with existing sampling- and optimisation-based benchmarks, it delivered both a higher success rate and greater computational efficiency, with the latter advantage becoming more substantial when sampling more candidate solutions. Experiments on a three-section tendon-driven continuum robot further demonstrate consecutive planning, multi-solution planning, and whole-body obstacle avoidance.

AI.tldr: A conditional diffusion framework (PccDiffuser) for continuum robots that learns multimodal path distributions in configuration space, enabling parallel sampling of multiple candidate trajectories and efficient conversion to executable trajectories, with favorable results (91% success) and obstacle-aware planning.
AI.motivation: Robust, multimodal, and computationally efficient planning for continuum robots in cluttered environments; existing methods struggle with multimodality and planning speed.
AI.method: Conditional diffusion model that learns a distribution over complete configuration-space paths conditioned on the environment; samples multiple candidate solutions in parallel; converts to executable trajectories via time allocation respecting actuator limits; uses piecewise constant-curvature kinematics with exponential coordinates; encodes variable obstacles using a graph neural network; incorporates analytical differential kinematics in the denoising step to improve terminal accuracy and whole-body clearance.
AI.result: Achieves 91% success on a mixed test set with up to four obstacles; outperforms existing sampling- and optimization-based benchmarks in both success rate and computational efficiency, with efficiency gains increasing as more candidates are sampled; validated on a three-section tendon-driven continuum robot for consecutive and multi-solution planning with obstacle avoidance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective multimodal, efficient planning for continuum robots and shows potential for real-time or near-real-time planning in obstacle-rich environments, with applicability to tendon-driven designs and scalable sampling of multiple candidate trajectories.

title: LeCor: Learning to Be Corrected by Meta-Learned Test-Time Training for Interactive 3D Lung-Tumour Segmentation
summary: Delineating lung tumours on computed tomography (CT) takes a considerable share of the time spent on radiotherapy planning, and a contour proposed by a model can be refined interactively by the clinician. Promptable foundation models such as SAM 3 support this workflow by writing each correction into a session memory that conditions the remaining slices, while the model weights stay fixed. On 690 test cases from five public CT cohorts, fine-tuning SAM 3 on lung tumours raises the Dice obtained from a single point prompt from 0.298 to 0.757, and seven rounds of corrections raise it further to 0.765, but under memory conditioning alone the accuracy on slices the annotator has not touched stops improving after six rounds. We therefore treat each correction as a training signal and propose LeCor, which performs test-time training on a small set of case adapters that are reset for every case and meta-learned such that a single gradient step driven by a click improves the slices that were not clicked. On the 133 test cases that span at least eight slices, LeCor raises the Dice reached after seven correction rounds from 0.787 with the fine-tuned model to 0.827, reduces the number of cases that never reach a Dice of 0.80 from 47 to 27, and reaches in three correction rounds the accuracy that the fine-tuned model attains in seven.

AI.tldr: Two-stage approach to interactive lung-tumor segmentation: memory-conditioned fine-tuning of SAM 3 with CT prompts yields large Dice gains but saturates; LeCor adds test-time adapters with meta-learning, enabling faster corrections and higher Dice, reducing hard failures.
AI.motivation: Reduce radiotherapy contouring time by making foundation models accurately adapt to active clinician corrections with minimal retraining.
AI.method: 1) Fine-tune SAM 3 on lung tumours and evaluate with a session-memory correction workflow on 690 CT cases from five public cohorts; memory conditioning improves Dice from 0.298 (single point) to ~0.757–0.765, saturating after ~6 rounds. 2) Propose LeCor, test-time training on a small per-case adapter set reset per case and meta-learned so a single gradient update from a click improves neighboring slices; evaluate on 133 cases with >=8 slices.
AI.result: Fine-tuning with memory yields Dice 0.757 after a single point; 0.765 after seven rounds. LeCor raises Dice after seven corrections from 0.787 (fine-tuned baseline) to 0.827, reduces cases never reaching 0.80 from 47 to 27, and with three corrections matches the seven-round accuracy of the fine-tuned model.
AI.conclusion: LeCor enhances robustness and data-efficiency of promptable segmentation in CT lung-tumour segmentation, enabling faster convergence to high accuracy than standard memory-conditioned fine-tuning.

title: From State Synchronization to Cognitive Self-Evolution: An Operational Architecture for Cognitive Digital Twins
summary: As Digital Twin (DT) systems evolve beyond state synchronization toward task-oriented and knowledge-driven operation, Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) have emerged as an extension that incorporates cognitive capabilities into twin operation. Existing CDT studies often focus on specific enabling techniques, such as learning modules, knowledge graphs, and large language models, while providing limited insight into how cognition can be systematically integrated into DT architectures. To address this issue, this paper proposes a four-layer CDT architecture consisting of the physical layer, digital-twin layer, cognitive layer, and task layer. The proposed architecture establishes a self-evolving closed operational loop spanning these four layers, in which physical states are synchronized into digital representations, cognition constructs task-specific cognitive models through knowledge, memory, and attention, and task-level decisions are generated under practical constraints. Operational feedback further refines cognitive experience and updates relationships and annotations in the digital representation, enabling subsequent task interpretation, initiation, and reasoning to evolve with system operation. Based on this framework, two representative operation modes are characterized: user-request-driven cognition and self-driven cognition. We further discuss key enabling mechanisms and deployment challenges associated with semantic communication, knowledge querying, task orchestration, and closed-loop synchronization. A lightweight simulation study illustrates reliable closed-loop task feasibility under limited semantic information and improved operational efficiency through accumulated task experience. The proposed framework provides a structured foundation for the design and development of future CDT systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes a four-layer Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) architecture with a self-evolving, closed operational loop for task-oriented cognition, identifies two operation modes, and discusses enabling mechanisms and deployment challenges; supported by a lightweight simulation validating task feasibility and efficiency gains.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of a systematic approach for integrating cognition into Digital Twins, moving beyond isolated learning, knowledge-graph, or LLM components toward a coherent, action-oriented CDT framework.
AI.method: Define a four-layer CDT architecture (physical, digital-twin, cognitive, task), establish a self-evolving closed loop across layers, model cognition via task-specific cognitive models built from knowledge, memory, and attention, delineate two operation modes (user-request-driven and self-driven), analyze enabling mechanisms (semantic communication, knowledge querying, task orchestration, closed-loop synchronization), and present a lightweight simulation to demonstrate feasibility and efficiency.
AI.result: Demonstrates reliable closed-loop task execution under limited semantic information and shows improved operational efficiency through accumulated task experience; asserts the framework as a solid foundation for future CDT design and deployment.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a structured, extensible foundation for CDT development, highlights critical enabling mechanisms and deployment challenges, and paves the way for systematic cognition integration into DT architectures.

title: From Fixed Keys to Readable Schemas: Small Language Models for Vehicle Agent Function Calls
summary: In-vehicle assistants must translate natural-language requests into accurate vehicle function calls under strict memory and latency constraints, making small language models (SLMs) attractive for on-device deployment. For such models, a key design choice is how the available function surface is presented. Two approaches are to represent each function with a dedicated Functional Token (FT) or provide function schemas directly in the prompt. FTs enable compact inference but are restricted to functions learned during training, whereas Schema-in-Prompt (SIP) can generalize to unseen functions at the cost of longer prompts and higher inference overhead. We introduce a benchmark of 9,822 single-turn examples spanning 79 vehicle functions derived from Android Automotive, including held-out functions and requests requiring refusal. We compare both approaches under matched fine-tuning across four SLMs from 270M to 1.7B parameters. On functions seen during training, scaling provides limited benefit: the 270M model can match the 1.7B model, while the strongest overall performance occurs at 0.6B. On held-out functions, FT achieves zero accuracy by construction, whereas SIP generalizes and improves substantially with scale. On out-of-scope requests, FT can invoke an unavailable function it was trained to emit, while SIP more reliably refuses based on the functions offered. This flexibility comes with higher memory use and latency. Our theoretical analysis explains how SIP enables generalization and why longer schema contexts increase inference cost. Overall, function-surface representation, rather than model scale alone, determines the capabilities and failure modes of SLM-based vehicle function calling.

AI.tldr: Schema-in-Prompt (SIP) enables generalization to unseen or refused vehicle functions on-device LMs, outperforming Functional Tokens (FT) in held-out cases; scaling yields limited gains for seen functions; FT may hallucinate or refuse poorly; SIP trades higher memory/latency for better generalization; function-surface representation drives capabilities more than model size.
AI.motivation: Enable accurate and safe on-device function calling in in-vehicle assistants under memory/latency constraints; compare two surface representations (FT vs SIP) across diverse functions.
AI.method: Construct benchmark of 9,822 single-turn requests across 79 Android Automotive-derived functions, including held-out and refusal cases; train/fine-tune four SLMs (270M–1.7B parameters); evaluate FT vs SIP on seen and held-out/unavailable function scenarios; analyze inference cost and memory implications.
AI.result: For seen functions, scaling benefits are limited; the 270M model matches 1.7B, peak at ~0.6B. For held-out functions, FT yields zero accuracy by construction; SIP generalizes with scale and improves. For out-of-scope requests, FT may emit unavailable functions; SIP more reliably refuses. SIP incurs higher memory usage and latency. Theoretical analysis explains SIP's generalization and cost of longer schemas.
AI.conclusion: Function-surface representation determines SLM-based vehicle function calling capabilities and failure modes; SIP generalizes to unseen/refusal cases, FT restricted to trained functions; model size alone insufficient; trade-offs between generalization and efficiency.

title: HiRAD: A Flexible Large-Scale AGV Routing System
summary: Automatic Guided Vehicles (AGVs) substantially boost warehouse throughput, but routing large-scale AGV fleets remains challenging. Classical Multi-Agent Pathfinding solvers suffer from exploding combinatorial complexity and super-quadratic runtime, while relying on idealized grid or piecewise-linear motion models that mismatch real-world kinematics. Recent Reinforcement Learning (RL) solutions improve flexibility via decentralized agent policies but depend on discretized spatiotemporal representations, require millions of episodes to converge, and incur full-map observation at every step, which leads to large models, slow convergence, and high inference latency that violates real-time industrial control constraints. To address these bottlenecks, we propose HiRAD, a hierarchical RL framework for continuous-space AGV routing with real-time guarantees: (1) a step-level spatiotemporal representation that translates continuous motion into a differentiable RL problem, (2) a hierarchical strategy that splits heading choice from velocity control to reduce the action space, and (3) an asynchronous event-driven decision pipeline that lowers inference complexity from O(n^2) to O(n) and cuts per-step latency by as much as 71 percent. Across random graphs and two warehouse maps, HiRAD reduces makespan by 45 percent to 63 percent and shortens end-to-end runtime.

AI.tldr: HiRAD is a hierarchical RL framework for continuous-space AGV routing that achieves real-time guarantees, reducing latency and improves throughput compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Large-scale AGV routing is limited by combinatorial MAPF complexity and the mismatch between idealized models and real-world kinematics; current RL methods have high sample costs, large models, and latency due to full-map observations.
AI.method: HiRAD introduces (1) a step-level spatiotemporal representation converting motion into a differentiable RL problem, (2) a hierarchical policy that separates heading control from velocity, reducing action space, and (3) an asynchronous event-driven pipeline that lowers per-step complexity from O(n^2) to O(n) and reduces latency; evaluated on random graphs and two warehouse maps.
AI.result: HiRAD reduces makespan by 45–63% and shortens end-to-end runtime; inference latency is substantially reduced due to the O(n) pipeline, outperforming baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: A scalable, real-time capable hierarchical RL framework for continuous-space AGV routing is feasible; the combination of a step-level representation, hierarchical actions, and event-driven computation yields significant performance gains that support deployment in warehouse environments.

title: Infra-Bench CLS: A Global, Open-Source Benchmark for Critical Infrastructure Classification with Earth Observation Foundation Models
comment: 9 figures. Supporting information with 10 figures and 13 tables. Submitted to Big Earth Data
summary: Critical infrastructure location data is often incomplete and unevenly distributed globally, especially in developing regions. Earth observation foundation models are proposed as a new step in enabling us to more efficiently understand the natural and built environment, raising questions as to their effectiveness in performing challenging downstream tasks. Yet, foundation models remain largely untested for detecting and classifying the facility-scale critical infrastructure that underpins a range of important societal and economic functions. Subsequently, Infra-Bench CLS is introduced as a benchmark to test foundation models on 18,756 Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral facility-scale critical infrastructure asset images covering seven continents and 13 infrastructure classes, with results reported for the 10 retained classes. Using linear probing and fine-tuning for two training dataset levels (1.0x and 0.3x), seven foundation models are evaluated (SatlasPretrain S2, SatlasPretrain S1, CROMA, Prithvi-EO-2.0, AlphaEarth Foundations, OlmoEarth v1.1-Base, and DINOv3 ViT-L/16). When comparing macro F1 scores to a ResNet-18 supervised baseline of 39.2 percent, the best foundation model achieved 57.9 percent, a 48 percent improvement. Top performing classes were airports (F1 85.3 percent), train stations (F1 82.1 percent), and data centers (F1 77.6 percent). By contrast, many of the power sector classes perform poorly (F1 27.5-46.2 percent). These findings suggest foundation models can enable superior critical infrastructure classification, but future work should evaluate performance on higher-resolution imagery, particularly for poorly performing sectors, such as power.

AI.tldr: Foundation models trained on Sentinel imagery outperform a supervised ResNet-18 baseline for facility-scale critical infrastructure classification, with strong results on airports, train stations, and data centers, but weaker performance on power-related classes; suggests potential with higher-resolution data.
AI.motivation: Assess whether earth observation foundation models can effectively detect and classify facility-scale critical infrastructure globally, addressing data gaps in developing regions.
AI.method: Infra-Bench CLS benchmark: 18,756 Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral facility-scale infrastructure images across seven continents and 13 classes (reported for 10 retained classes). Evaluates seven foundation models (SatlasPretrain S2, SatlasPretrain S1, CROMA, Prithvi-EO-2.0, AlphaEarth Foundations, OlmoEarth v1.1-Base, DINOv3 ViT-L/16) using linear probing and fine-tuning at two training data levels (1.0x and 0.3x); compares against ResNet-18 supervised baseline (39.2% macro F1).
AI.result: Best foundation model achieved 57.9% macro F1 (vs 39.2% baseline, ~48% relative improvement). Top classes: airports 85.3% F1, train stations 82.1%, data centers 77.6%. Poor performance for power sector classes (27.5–46.2%). Overall, foundation models can enable superior infrastructure classification, but higher-resolution imagery may be needed, especially for underperforming sectors like power.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models show potential for superior facility-scale infrastructure classification across global regions, but their effectiveness is limited by class-specific performance (notably power) and would benefit from higher-resolution imagery and targeted improvements for challenging sectors.

title: Seven Sources of Physical AI Capability Formation
summary: Capabilities relevant to Physical AI can arise from materially different formation histories, yet existing taxonomies organized by morphology, architecture, learning algorithm, task, or domain do not directly answer what gives rise to a capability. We define a capability-formation source as a factor materially contributing to capability formation, distinct from components or construction steps. We identify seven non-exclusive sources: Recorded-Experience (RE), Predictive-Modeling (PM), Evaluative-Interaction (EI), Surrogate-Environment (SE), Mechanism-Grounded (MG), Embodied-Coupling (EC), and Evolution-Driven (ED) Formation. Using reconstructive induction with theoretical saturation, we traced a research matrix to primary studies, deduplicated the literature, set coding rules, and conducted three rounds of maximum-difference and negative-case sampling. Challenges included curriculum and self-supervised learning, active inference, open-ended and developmental learning, planning and search, neuro-symbolic architectures, digital twins, generative physical world models, and morphology-control co-design. Within the scope and criteria fixed as of September 4, 2026, all 49 evidence records were explainable by the seven sources individually or in combination. No R1-R3 challenge produced an irreducible eighth source, and R3 required no new core definition or substantive boundary rule. We therefore claim theoretical saturation within the stated scope, not logical completeness or exhaustive future coverage. The framework distinguishes similarity in observed capability from similarity in how it was formed, supporting analysis of explanation, transfer, replication, dependencies, governance evidence, and geoeconomic foundations.

AI.tldr: Seven non-exclusive sources (RE, PM, EI, SE, MG, EC, ED) explain capability formation in Physical AI. Through reconstructive induction and theoretical saturation, 49 records map to these sources (individually or in combination); no irreducible eighth source identified within the scope (as of 2026-09-04). The framework separates similarity of observed capabilities from formation, enabling analyses of explanation, transfer, replication, dependencies, governance, and geoeconomic foundations.
AI.motivation: Address fragmentation in taxonomies by grounding capability emergence in formation sources, not only morphology/architecture or tasks; provide a theory-grounded, testable framework to analyze how capabilities arise and how to compare, replicate, or govern them.
AI.method: Reconstructive induction with theoretical saturation. Build a research matrix, deduplicate literature, set coding rules, and perform three rounds of maximum-difference and negative-case sampling. Map to primary studies and adjudicate sources. Rigorously test for additional sources; assess challenges across curriculum/self-supervised learning, active inference, open-ended/developmental learning, planning/search, neuro-symbolic architectures, digital twins, generative world models, morphology-control co-design.
AI.result: All 49 evidence records are explainable by the seven sources, individually or in combination. No irreducible eighth source emerged. R3 required no new core definition or substantive boundary rule. The authors claim theoretical saturation within the stated scope, not logical completeness. The framework distinguishes similarity of observed capability from similarity of formation and supports analysis of explanations, transfer, replication, dependencies, governance evidence, and geoeconomic foundations.
AI.conclusion: The seven-source capability-formation framework offers a robust, scalable lens to understand how Physical AI capabilities arise, beyond conventional taxonomies. It supports cross-domain explanation, transfer, replication, and governance considerations, with explicit caveats about scope and future expansion.

title: Unthrottling the Tanh Jacobian in SAC: A Negative Result on Bang-Bang Control and MetaDrive
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Technical report. Negative result. Code: https://github.com/fshamass/Tanh-Bypass
summary:
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) represents a continuous policy as an unbounded Gaussian that is squashed by tanh. The Jacobian of that map is $\partial a/\partial u = 1-a^2$, which vanishes as $|a|\to 1$. A natural concern is that this throttle starves the actor of critic signal exactly where extreme actions (full brake, full throttle) are optimal. We test a minimal intervention that restores the missing signal: one extra term in the actor loss whose gradient on the pre-tanh mean is the detached action-gradient of $Q$, with no gain parameter.
  On a minimum-time double integrator whose optimum is bang-bang at the action bounds, vanilla SAC already reaches near-optimal return ($-31.6$ vs. a calibrated optimum of $-30.3$) across ten paired seeds. An ungated bypass does saturate the policy (99% of eval steps with $|a|\ge 0.9$) and collapses return to $-195.5$. A gated bypass that fires only on the flat shoulder $|a|\in[0.9,0.999]$ also fails, and does so without leaving a saturated policy. Warm-started MetaDrive fine-tuning shows the same pattern: the bypass does not improve return, and where collision rate falls it is typically traded for out-of-road departures. Auto-tuned entropy coefficient rises against the bypass, which is a push toward the tails.
  The Jacobian effect is real. Treating it as a bug to be undone is not free, and on the tasks studied here it is not helpful. Saturating a bound is not the same as solving a problem whose optimum lives on that bound.

AI.tldr: Jacobian-induced throttle in SAC near action bounds is real; a minimal bypass to inject the Q-gradient into the actor loss does not improve performance on studied tasks and often harms it. Vanilla SAC already achieves near-optimal results; saturating actions at bounds is not a universal fix; attempting to 'undo' the Jacobian introduces trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Assess whether the tanh-squashed Gaussian policy in SAC loses critical critic signal near action bounds and whether a simple additive gradient term to the actor loss can mitigate any adverse effects.
AI.method: Add an extra term to the actor loss whose gradient with respect to the pre-tanh mean equals the detached action-gradient of Q, with no gain parameter. Compare vanilla SAC, an ungated bypass that can drive saturation, and a gated bypass restricting the trigger to the shoulder region. Evaluate on a minimum-time double integrator with bang-bang optimal control, across seeds; analyze saturation behavior and returns. Extend evaluation with warm-started MetaDrive fine-tuning to observe transfer effects on collisions and road departures. Monitor entropy coefficient dynamics.
AI.result: Vanilla SAC attains near-optimal returns on the tested task (-31.6 vs -30.3). The ungated bypass causes extreme saturation (about 99% of eval steps have |a| ≥ 0.9) and collapses performance to -195.5. The gated bypass fails as well and does not evoke saturation. In warm-started MetaDrive fine-tuning, the bypass does not improve return and often trades improved collision rates for more off-road exits. Auto-tuned entropy rises in the presence of the bypass, indicating a push toward heavier tails. The Jacobian effect is real; treating it as a bug to be undone is not cost-free and does not universally improve performance.
AI.conclusion: The Jacobian-induced throttle in tanh-squashed SAC is a real effect that, on the studied tasks, is not ameliorated by the proposed bypass. Saturating the policy at bounds is not a general remedy; in fact, it can degrade performance or shift metrics unfavorably. Careful evaluation shows that vanilla SAC remains competitive or superior here, and the optimum may lie on the action bounds rather than in their interior.

title: GTA-2: A Multi-VLM Framework for Synthesizing Robot Manipulation Skills via Grounded Task Axes
summary: Robotic manipulation tasks are often decomposed into behaviors or skills. However, one often needs to predefine these behaviors for specific tasks or try to cover a wide range of tasks using generic skills. As a result, these behaviors can remain too coarse to expose the geometric, control, and scene-dependent decisions required for execution. We introduce Grounded Task Axes v2 (GTA-2), a modular multi-VLM framework that constructs executable, task-bespoke manipulation skills from reusable object-centric task-axis components. Rather than predicting actions end-to-end or composing fixed task-level primitives, GTA-2 represents each skill as semantic subtasks comprising task-relevant keypoints and axes, controller compositions, and scene-dependent parameters. Four specialized VLM agents separately decompose the task, construct an abstract task-axis skill, assign controller parameters, and ground the required visual features from RGB-D observations. This abstraction-to-grounding factorization enables zero-shot skill generation without task-specific robot demonstrations, policy training, or fine-tuning. It also keeps intermediate decisions explicit, allowing targeted human feedback to refine an incorrect stage while preserving correct components. We evaluate GTA-2 on 14 real-robot manipulation tasks against a VLA policy pi_{0.5} and two Code-as-Policies baselines using task-axis controllers or conventional robot primitives. GTA-2 achieves an average zero-shot success rate of 73.9%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 31.4 percentage points, while targeted refinement raises GTA-2's average success rate to 90.7%. Project page: https://gta2-project.github.io/

AI.tldr: GTA-2 introduces a modular, grounding-based approach to robotic manipulation by constructing task-axis, object-centric skills from semantic subtasks, enabling zero-shot execution and interpretable refinement; achieves 73.9% zero-shot accuracy across 14 tasks, 90.7% with human-in-the-loop refinement.
AI.motivation: Address the rigidity of fixed-task primitives and end-to-end policies; require reusable, interpretable skill representations that expose geometric, control, and scene-dependent decisions; enable zero-shot skill generation without task-specific data.
AI.method: Four specialized VLM agents decompose task, build abstract task-axis skills, assign controller parameters, and ground RGB-D features; represent skills as subtasks with keypoints and axes, controller compositions, and scene-dependent parameters; zero-shot generation without demonstrations or fine-tuning; supports targeted human feedback at intermediate stages.
AI.result: 14 real-robot tasks; GTA-2 avg zero-shot success 73.9%, 31.4-point improvement over strongest baseline; targeted refinement raises to 90.7% average success; compared to VLA pi_0.5 and two Code-as-Policies baselines; uses task-axis controllers or conventional primitives; project page.
AI.conclusion: Shows that abstraction-to-grounding factorization yields executable, task-bespoke skills without task-specific data; increases interpretability and editability; strong zero-shot performance with room for refinement via human feedback; suggests modular multi-VLM strategy as a path to generalizable robot manipulation.

title: Learning Global Camera Poses from Noisy View-Graphs for Structure from Motion
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://vgpa-sfm.github.io/
summary: Camera pose estimation is a key step in 3D reconstruction and view-synthesis pipelines. We present a deep, global Structure-from-Motion framework based on learned view-graph aggregation. Our method employs a permutation-equivariant, edge-conditioned graph neural network that takes noisy pairwise relative poses as input and outputs globally consistent camera extrinsics. The network is trained without ground-truth supervision, relying solely on a relative-pose consistency objective. This is followed by 3D point triangulation and robust bundle adjustment. Our approach is efficient, scalable to more than a thousand images, and robust to graph density. We evaluate our method on MegaDepth, 1DSfM, Strecha, and BlendedMVS. These experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior rotation and translation accuracy compared to deep track-centric methods while registering more images across many scenes, and competitive results compared to state-of-the-art classical pipelines, while being much faster.

AI.tldr: A global, learned view-graph aggregation method for camera pose estimation using a permutation-equivariant, edge-conditioned GNN that fuses noisy pairwise relative poses into globally consistent extrinsics, trained with a relative-pose consistency objective, followed by triangulation and robust bundle adjustment; scalable to 1000+ images and faster than classical pipelines with competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Global Structure-from-Motion remains challenging due to noisy pairwise relative poses, graph density variation, and the need for scalability. A learned, permutation-equivariant aggregation of the view-graph can exploit relational structure to produce robust, globally consistent poses without ground-truth supervision.
AI.method: A deep, global SfM framework that uses a permutation-equivariant, edge-conditioned graph neural network. It ingests noisy pairwise relative poses as edges and outputs globally consistent camera extrinsics. Training uses a relative-pose consistency objective (no ground-truth poses). After pose estimation, standard 3D triangulation and robust bundle adjustment are applied. The approach emphasizes efficiency and scalability across large graphs.
AI.result: Evaluations on MegaDepth, 1DSfM, Strecha, and BlendedMVS show the method achieves superior rotation and translation accuracy compared with deep track-centric methods, while registering more images across scenes, and is competitive with state-of-the-art classical pipelines while being much faster.
AI.conclusion: Global, learned view-graph aggregation for SfM yields accurate, scalable camera pose estimation that integrates well with standard 3D reconstruction steps, offering speed advantages over classical pipelines and robustness across varying graph densities.

title: RobustSGPO: Search-Space Control for Agent Harness Evolution
summary: Semantic-gradient-based prompt optimization (SGPO) improves agent harnesses using execution feedback, but its local update rule leaves the choice of edit scope and operation unresolved. We introduce RobustSGPO, which specifies the requested edit, constructs and checks the patch, and continues search from either the incumbent or retained snapshots. We evaluate permission scheduling, cumulative controls, and task-family transfer in the AgentX brainstorming workflow using 120 tasks, 95 runs, and 7,350 candidate attempts. Periodic $1\to2\to3$ scheduling exceeds fixed maximum permission by 0.28 test-score points. RobustSGPO increases completion on 30 held-out tasks from 60.0% to 80.0% and improves test quality from 3.77 to 4.14 under a 20-million-token budget. Category retention reduces source-task degradation after a shift, whereas random retention reaches a higher destination endpoint. Search-space control benefits quality through executable edits and alternative starting points, with measurable retention overhead.

AI.tldr: RobustSGPO enhances SGPO by explicitly specifying edits, validating patches, and allowing search to continue from incumbent or retained snapshots. It shows improved task-completion and test quality in AgentX brainstorming with explicit scheduling and retention strategies.
AI.motivation: SGPO's local update rule leaves edit scope and operation unresolved, limiting robust search. RobustSGPO introduces explicit edit specification and patch validation to enable controlled, repeatable edits and better search behavior.
AI.method: Specify the requested edit, construct and check the patch, and continue search from the incumbent or retained snapshots. Evaluate permission scheduling, cumulative controls, and task-family transfer in AgentX with 120 tasks, 95 runs, and 7,350 candidate attempts. Compare periodic 1→2→3 scheduling against a fixed maximum permission. Measure held-out-task completion and test quality under a 20M-token budget. Compare category retention vs random retention. Assess search-space control via executable edits and alternative starting points and report retention overhead.
AI.result: Periodic 1→2→3 scheduling surpasses fixed maximum permission by 0.28 test-score points. RobustSGPO raises held-out task completion from 60% to 80% and improves test quality from 3.77 to 4.14 under a 20M-token budget. Category retention reduces source-task degradation after a shift, while random retention reaches a higher destination endpoint. Search-space control improves quality through executable edits and alternative starting points, with measurable retention overhead.
AI.conclusion: Explicit edit specification and robust search strategies can improve performance in agent-thinking workflows. Scheduling patterns and retention strategies influence transfer and degradation, and search-space control yields higher quality at some overhead.

title: Efficient Fairness Auditing Across Guidance Scales in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models via Causal Abstraction
summary: Fairness auditing of text-to-image diffusion models often requires generating large numbers of images across sampling configurations, making comprehensive evaluation computationally expensive. We propose a causal-abstraction-based audit instrument for efficiently evaluating fairness under interventions on the classifier-free guidance scale. Given a fixed prompt and a target feature function, we represent the diffusion process as a low-level structural causal model and construct a corresponding high-level model over abstract denoising states. We characterize the projected causal structure, establish identifiability of the fairness-relevant interventional query, and provide sufficient conditions under which the high-level model preserves this query. A probabilistic transformer implements the high-level model as an amortized predictor of target-feature distributions across guidance scales. Experiments evaluate distributional fidelity, fairness-query accuracy, and computational efficiency. We present two auditing demonstrations: one using standard Stable Diffusion 1.5 and another using StayFair, a fairness-enhanced Stable Diffusion model, to examine their behavior across guidance scales.

AI.tldr: A causal-abstraction audit framework to efficiently test fairness in diffusion models under classifier-free guidance interventions, using a low-level SCM and a high-level abstract denoising model, with a probabilistic transformer predictor and experiments across Stable Diffusion variants.
AI.motivation: Fairness auditing of text-to-image diffusion models requires exploring many sampling configurations, which is computationally expensive; an efficient auditing instrument is needed to reliably assess fairness under interventions.
AI.method: Construct a structural causal model of the diffusion process at a low level and derive a corresponding high-level model over abstract denoising states; analyze the projected causal structure and identifiability of the fairness-relevant interventional query; provide conditions under which the high-level model preserves the query; implement a probabilistic transformer to amortize prediction of target-feature distributions across guidance scales.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates distributional fidelity, accuracy of the fairness query, and computational efficiency; two auditing demonstrations are conducted on Stable Diffusion 1.5 and StayFair across guidance scales, illustrating the approach's practical utility.
AI.conclusion: A causal-abstraction audit instrument can efficiently and reliably assess fairness in diffusion models across guidance scales, with an amortized predictor enabling scalable querying; results show fidelity and improved efficiency, and the method accommodates different model variants (e.g., StayFair).

title: ViBe: Visual Behavior Adaptation for Perceptive Humanoid Whole-Body Control
summary: Motion tracking provides a scalable recipe for humanoid whole-body control. By design, the resulting trackers lack exteroceptive feedback hence reacting to the environment remains the responsibility of a higher-level planner. Existing perceptive controllers train geometry-only encoders from scratch, trading semantics for sim-to-real ease, and typically rely on teacher-student distillation for a task of interest. We present ViBe, a post-training framework for adapting motion trackers to perceptive control tasks. We leverage pre-trained visual encoders with a multi-query extractor module to learn task-relevant perceptive feedback. This feedback is grafted onto the tracker's input via low-rank adapters, enabling parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Given a task reward and a reference dataset, this modular controller can be adapted directly via policy optimization. Across four tasks, ViBe shows zero-shot sim-to-real transfer spanning perceptive walking on curbs and parkour, Repose Cube, omni-object loco-manipulation, and dodgeball, with visually robust performance across outdoor, low-light, and RGB distractor conditions. Finally, we solve a goal-oriented Repose Cube task with a deliberately simple planner, demonstrating the efficacy of perceptive controllers, adapted by our approach.

AI.tldr: ViBe enables post-training adaptation of motion trackers to perceptive control by grafting task-specific perceptive feedback from pre-trained visual encoders via low-rank adapters, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across diverse tasks.
AI.motivation: To overcome the lack of exteroceptive feedback in humanoid motion trackers and reduce sim-to-real gaps by leveraging perceptive feedback without re-training geometry from scratch.
AI.method: Use pre-trained visual encoders with a multi-query extractor to learn task-relevant perceptive feedback. Inject this feedback into the tracker input via low-rank adapters for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Given a task reward and reference dataset, adapt the modular controller directly through policy optimization.
AI.result: Achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across four tasks: perceptive walking on curbs and parkour, Repose Cube, omni-object loco-manipulation, and dodgeball. Robust performance across outdoor, low-light, and RGB distractor conditions. Also solves a goal-oriented Repose Cube task with a simple planner, showcasing efficacy of perceptive controllers.
AI.conclusion: Perceptive controllers adapted by ViBe can effectively integrate perceptive feedback into motion trackers, enabling scalable, robust humanoid control with efficient, parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

title: RoMa-$Ω$: What Feed-Forward 3D Models Know About Image Matching
summary: Learned image matching has experienced significant progress in recent years, culminating in robust and accurate matchers such as RoMa, whose robustness is often attributed to its use of frozen DINO features. In a parallel development, feed-forward reconstruction models, such as VGGT, have been trained on ever-growing datasets to accurately regress dense 3D point maps and camera poses. The distinction between matchers and feed-forward reconstruction models has become increasingly blurred with the introduction of matching losses in models such as MASt3R and VGGT-$Ω$. This raises a natural question: what do feed-forward 3D models know about image matching? In this work, we answer this question by analyzing three scenarios: (i) zero-shot matching of patch features, (ii) direct matching of 3D point predictions, and (iii) training a full matcher on top of the learned representations.
