We find that, despite performing poorly in zero-shot matching, especially in later layers, feed-forward reconstruction models provide strong representations for linear probing and full matching pipelines. We further show that, even without any training, their raw predictions alone enable competitive matching, albeit only under moderate viewpoint changes and modality gaps. Based on these insights, we retrain RoMa v2 by replacing its DINO backbone with VGGT-$Ω$. Our resulting model, \ours, outperforms state-of-the-art matchers on a wide range of benchmarks, e.g. +8.1 mAA compared to RoMa v2 on WxBS.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes what feed-forward 3D reconstruction models (VGGT-Ω) know about image matching, across zero-shot patch matching, direct 3D-point matching, and learning a full matcher on learned representations. It finds limited zero-shot transfer but strong linear probing and matching capabilities, and even raw predictions aid matching under moderate changes. They retrain RoMa v2 with VGGT-Ω to form OURS, achieving state-of-the-art results (e.g., +8.1 mAA on WxBS).
AI.motivation: To understand whether dense 3D reconstruction models trained with large-scale data encode useful information for image matching, and how they can be integrated with or repurpose existing matchers.
AI.method: 1) Evaluate zero-shot patch feature matching with feed-forward 3D models. 2) Assess direct matching using predicted 3D points. 3) Train a full matcher on top of learned VGGT-Ω representations. 4) Retrain RoMa v2 by replacing its DINO backbone with VGGT-Ω to form a new model (OURS). 5) Benchmark across standard datasets, notably WxBS, to compare with state-of-the-art.
AI.result: Zero-shot matching from later layers is weak, but feed-forward models provide strong representations for linear probing and full matching pipelines. Their raw 3D predictions can yield competitive matching under moderate viewpoint shifts and modality gaps. The proposed OURS model, obtained by swapping RoMa v2's backbone with VGGT-Ω, achieves state-of-the-art performance, e.g., +8.1 mAA on WxBS compared to RoMa v2.
AI.conclusion: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models encode useful information for image matching; with appropriate integration (backbone substitution and/or training a matcher on their representations) they can surpass traditional matchers on diverse benchmarks, highlighting a path for cross-pollination between 3D reconstruction and image-matching research.

title: Black-Box Red Teaming of Agentic AI: A Taxonomy-Driven Framework for Automated Risk Discovery
summary: Agentic systems are rapidly moving to production, where they read untrusted inputs, call tools with real permissions, and act autonomously, expanding the security surface beyond chat-only models. Yet standard evaluations remain single-turn and fail to capture multi-step agent vulnerabilities. We present a systematic black-box framework for risk-aware agent evaluation requiring only basic system descriptions. Our approach introduces: (1) a seven-domain taxonomy mapping observable behaviors to risk categories, (2) fully automated SAGE-RT red teaming producing 120 adversarial scenarios per domain, and (3) human-validated evaluation using LLM judges. Empirical validation across two agent architectures (CrewAI and AutoGen) with four base models reveals alarming patterns: 56.25\% average governance risk, 65\% privacy risk in multi-agent configurations, and agent behavior vulnerabilities reaching 85\%. Our black-box approach effectively identifies critical architectural vulnerabilities without privileged access, providing a scalable path toward safer agent deployments.

AI.tldr: A scalable black-box framework (SAGE-RT) for risk-aware evaluation of agentic systems, combining a seven-domain taxonomy, automated adversarial red-teaming, and human LLM judgment, revealing significant governance and privacy risks across architectures.
AI.motivation: Traditional single-turn evaluations miss multi-step vulnerabilities in production-grade agentic systems; a scalable, risk-aware assessment is needed to identify architectural weaknesses without privileged access.
AI.method: Develop a seven-domain taxonomy mapping agent behaviors to risk categories; automated SAGE-RT red-teaming producing 120 adversarial scenarios per domain; human validation using LLM judges; empirical validation across two agent architectures (CrewAI and AutoGen) with four base models.
AI.result: Identified notable risk levels: governance risk 56.25% average; privacy risk 65% in multi-agent configurations; agent behavior vulnerabilities reaching 85%. Black-box approach identifies architectural vulnerabilities without privileged access and is scalable for safer deployments.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a scalable, architecture-agnostic tool for risk-aware evaluation of agentic systems, uncovering critical vulnerabilities and enabling safer deployments through systematic, multi-domain testing and human-in-the-loop assessment.

title: A Statistical Approach to Estimating Sample Size of Machine Learning Models
summary: Sample size determination for machine learning (ML) prediction models is challenging because conventional power analysis typically requires the predictor-outcome relationship and effect structure to be specified a priori. Nonlinear ML models learn complex prediction surfaces that do not admit straightforward analytical power calculations. We propose a framework that approximates nonlinear ML models with localized linear representations and estimates sample size requirements by evaluating statistical power across these local regions.

AI.tldr: A framework to estimate sample size for nonlinear ML models by approximating with localized linear representations and evaluating power across local regions.
AI.motivation: Conventional power analyses require predefined predictor–outcome relationships, which is difficult for nonlinear ML models with complex prediction surfaces.
AI.method: Approximate nonlinear ML models with localized linear representations and assess statistical power within local regions to determine sample size requirements.
AI.result: A practical approach to ML sample size planning by local linear surrogates and region-specific power evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Localized linear surrogates enable practical sample size estimation for ML prediction models.

title: HaWMPO: Hallucination-Aware World Model-based Policy Optimization for Generalist Robot Policy
summary: Generalist robot policies have demonstrated strong generalization across robotic manipulation tasks, yet their success rates remain limited in com- plex long-horizon scenarios. Recent methods improve Visual-Language-Action (VLA) policies through online reinforcement learning on real robots, but such training relies on costly physical interactions, suffers from low sample efficiency, and may introduce hardware and safety risks. World models offer a promising alternative by enabling policy optimization with imagined rollouts. However, long-horizon rollouts generated by world models often suffer from prediction hal- lucinations, producing biased state transitions that can mislead policy learning. To address this issue, we propose Hallucination-aware World Model-based Pol- icy Optimization (HaWMPO), a closed-loop reinforcement learning pipeline for VLA policy post-training with world models. Specifically, HaWMPO introduces an action-conditioned hallucination-aware model to estimate the reliability of gen- erated image sequences, and incorporates hallucination scores into group relative policy optimization through a Reward-Soft mechanism, suppressing unreliable ac- tion chunks during training. On the LIBERO benchmark, HaWMPO achieves the best average success rate, with gains of 15.0% over the base model and 2.8% over the strongest baseline; real-world experiments on a G1 robot further validate its effectiveness, raising the average success rate on two manipulation tasks from 67.5% to 80.0%.

AI.tldr: HaWMPO mitigates hallucination in world-model rollouts for VLA policy optimization by using an action-conditioned hallucination-aware model and a Reward-Soft mechanism, yielding state-of-the-art LIBERO performance and real-world gains.
AI.motivation: To address long-horizon hallucinations in world-model-based RL, which degrade learning and safety; reduce dependence on costly real-world data.
AI.method: Train an action-conditioned hallucination-aware world model to estimate the reliability of generated image sequences; integrate hallucination scores into group-relative policy optimization via a Reward-Soft mechanism that suppresses unreliable action chunks during training.
AI.result: On LIBERO, HaWMPO achieves best average success rate, +15.0% over base model and +2.8% over strongest baseline. Real-world G1 robot experiments raise average success rate on two tasks from 67.5% to 80.0%.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination-aware world-models with Reward-Soft improve VLA policy optimization, offering safer, more sample-efficient learning and strong generalization in long-horizon robotic manipulation.

title: AnimalLift: Reconstructing Animatable 3D Animals from a Single Image by Learning Canonical Shape, Texture, and Fur Maps
summary: Reconstructing a fully animatable 3D animal from a single image remains challenging because animation-ready assets require not only plausible geometry, but also a unified topology, editable appearance, and fur representations compatible with deformation and simulation. Existing image-to-3D approaches often rely on implicit or loosely structured representations that are difficult to rig or edit, while parametric animal models support animation but cannot capture detailed texture and fur appearance. We present AnimalLift, a framework for reconstructing structured, animation-compatible 3D animal assets with explicit fur from a single image. Our method lifts an input image into a shared canonical space with a consistent topology and UV parameterization across the dataset, enabling joint prediction of canonical geometry, texture, and fur in a unified feed-forward architecture. A key component of our representation is a UV-aligned fur map that encodes strand geometry in a surface-aligned canonical domain, allowing explicit fur reconstruction compatible with mesh deformation and fur simulation. To train the model, we introduce a procedural data generation pipeline that provides large-scale supervision with aligned geometry, texture, and fur across diverse animal species and appearances. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction quality and generalization across animal categories. Beyond reconstruction, our structured representation directly supports downstream applications including animation, pose transfer, fur editing, and simulation-compatible rendering.

AI.tldr: AnimalLift reconstructs a fully animatable 3D animal with explicit fur from a single image by mapping to a canonical UV-aligned space and predicting geometry, texture, and fur in a unified, feed-forward architecture, trained with a procedural data generator; supports animation, pose transfer, fur editing, and simulation.
AI.motivation: To enable animation-ready 3D animal assets from single images, addressing the gap between implicit/loose representations and editable, animation-compatible geometry; requires consistent topology, unified UVs, and explicit fur that can deform and simulate.
AI.method: Lift the input image into a shared canonical space with consistent topology and UV parameterization; jointly predict canonical geometry, texture, and fur in a unified feed-forward model; use a UV-aligned fur map to encode strand geometry in a surface-aligned canonical domain for explicit fur reconstruction compatible with mesh deformation and fur simulation; employ a procedural data generation pipeline to provide large-scale supervision with aligned geometry, texture, and fur across diverse species; evaluate on synthetic and real datasets; demonstrate animation- and editing-friendly assets.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show strong reconstruction quality and generalization across animal categories; the structured representation enables downstream tasks such as animation, pose transfer, fur editing, and simulation-ready rendering.
AI.conclusion: The proposed structured, animation-compatible representation with explicit fur and a procedural training pipeline enables robust single-image reconstruction of animatable 3D animals, with direct applicability to animation, editing, and simulation workflows.

title: RESCUE-BENCH: Towards Relation-Aware Multi-Party Emotional Support Conversation Systems
summary: Existing emotional support conversation systems mainly focus on one-on-one seeker-supporter interactions and individual emotional states, leaving interpersonal relations in multi-party scenarios underexplored. In this work, we introduce relation-aware emotional support conversation, a new task that evaluates whether LLMs can capture and utilize the evolving dynamics of relationships to offer more effective emotional support. We construct RESCUE (Relation-aware Emotional Support Conversation Understanding and Evaluation Benchmark) from real couple and family interview conversations, containing 191 samples, 7,079 annotated turns, and 1,064.8 minutes of video. Based on rich annotations of socio-emotional and support-related dynamics, RESCUE defines six tasks that evaluate two core capabilities required for relation-aware emotional support: Relational Understanding and Relation-Sensitive Support. Experiments with ten LLMs show that current models perform relatively well on tasks relying on local emotional or intervention cues, but struggle with relation-intensive tasks such as relation pattern prediction, viewpoint prediction, and support strategy prediction. These findings reveal the limitations of current LLMs in modeling interpersonal relations and making relation-sensitive support decisions.

AI.tldr: A new RESCUE benchmark for relation-aware emotional support conversations, built from real couple/family interviews, assessing Relational Understanding and Relation-Sensitive Support across six tasks. Ten LLMs show strong performance on local cues but struggle with relation-heavy tasks like predicting relation patterns, viewpoints, and support strategies.
AI.motivation: To address the gap that existing emotional support systems focus on single interlocutors and local emotions, neglecting evolving interpersonal relationships in multi-party settings; propose a benchmark to evaluate and foster relationally aware support in LLMs.
AI.method: Construct RESCUE from real couple/family interview data (191 samples, 7,079 turns, 1,064.8 minutes of video), with rich socio-emotional and support dynamics annotations. Define six tasks targeting Relational Understanding and Relation-Sensitive Support. Evaluate ten LLMs on these tasks.
AI.result: LLMs perform well on tasks driven by local emotional or intervention cues but underperform on relation-intensive tasks such as relation pattern prediction, viewpoint prediction, and support strategy prediction, highlighting limitations in modeling interpersonal relations and making relation-aware decisions.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs struggle to capture evolving interpersonal relations in multi-party emotional support; the RESCUE benchmark reveals gaps and points to the need for improved relational reasoning and evaluation protocols to advance relation-aware support in LLMs.

title: Robust Industrial Cyber Physical Classification Using Neuromorphic Temporal Embeddings and Hybrid SNN XGBoost Under Machine Unlearning Attacks
summary: The digitalisation of electrical distribution networks has increased the exposure of power-grid infrastructure to cyber attacks. Existing intrusion detection systems (IDSs), however, often rely on computationally expensive deep learning models that are difficult to deploy at the edge. Periodic retraining also exposes these systems to machine unlearning attacks, where selective data removal can degrade detection performance. We propose a hybrid Spiking Neural Network (SNN) and XGBoost architecture that combines efficient temporal encoding with a lightweight classifier and provides structural resilience to such attacks. The SNN is trained once on clean data and used as a fixed feature extractor, while only the XGBoost classifier is retrained during model updates. Evaluated on two real-world public power-system datasets, the proposed method achieves 99.9\% accuracy (F1-macro 0.999) on the Synchrophasor dataset and 95.0\% accuracy (F1-macro 0.943) on the MSU/ORNL dataset, outperforming standalone baselines. Under selective label-flipping attacks, the hybrid model loses only 0.9\% F1-macro at 10\% poisoning and delays target-class collapse from 60\% to 70\% poisoning compared with raw models. These results demonstrate that neuromorphic temporal encoding can provide both accurate cyber-attack detection and improved resilience to data poisoning in cyber-physical systems.

AI.tldr: Hybrid Spiking Neural Network (SNN) and XGBoost for edge-friendly IDS in power grids; fixed SNN feature extractor with retrainable XGBoost classifier; strong accuracy and enhanced resilience to data poisoning and unlearning.
AI.motivation: Enable accurate, efficient intrusion detection at the network edge for modern digitalized power grids while mitigating vulnerabilities to model unlearning and data-poisoning attacks.
AI.method: Train the SNN once on clean data as a temporal feature extractor; keep the SNN fixed and retrain only the XGBoost classifier during model updates; evaluate on two real-world public power-system datasets (Synchrophasor and MSU/ORNL) and compare against baselines; assess robustness to selective label-flipping attacks.
AI.result: Accuracies: Synchrophasor 99.9% (F1-macro 0.999); MSU/ORNL 95.0% (F1-macro 0.943). Under 10% poisoning, F1-macro drops by only 0.9%; target-class collapse delayed from 60% to 70% poisoning. Outperforms standalone baselines.
AI.conclusion: Neuromorphic temporal encoding via SNNs provides accurate cyber-attack detection with improved resilience to data poisoning, and is well-suited for edge deployment in cyber-physical systems.

title: RoboDrop: Curating VLA Post-Training Data via Local Gradient Compatibility
summary: Vision--language--action (VLA) models acquire broad generalization through large-scale pretraining, yet adapting them to a new task and robot embodiment still requires post-training on newly collected data. Unlike pretraining, post-training targets task- and embodiment-specific adaptation, making it particularly sensitive to data quality. In practice, collected robot datasets often contain heterogeneous errors, including execution mistakes, sensor drift, and timestamp misalignment, which can impair post-training and policy performance. Manual inspection is costly, while existing data-cleaning methods are typically tailored to particular corruption types. To address these challenges, we introduce \textsc{RoboDrop}, a data-curation framework that audits supervision using local gradient compatibility measured along the training trajectory as a proxy for its effect on post-training performance. During a one-epoch warm-up run, RoboDrop scores each candidate sample online by comparing its gradient with those of task-semantic and visually matched validation samples. The resulting sample scores are aggregated at the episode level, and a simple automatic post-processing rule converts them into filtering decisions. We evaluate RoboDrop on controlled observation--action corruptions, naturally suboptimal demonstrations in simulation, and real-robot datasets containing non-expert collection errors. Across these settings, RoboDrop more accurately distinguishes unreliable demonstrations than prior methods, while post-training on the curated data consistently yields stronger downstream policies, with average real-robot rollout success rising from $35.0\%$ to $67.5\%$. These results establish training-trajectory-aware, context-conditioned supervision auditing as an effective approach to robust VLA post-training.

AI.tldr: RoboDrop is a data-curation framework for VLA post-training that audits supervision via local gradient compatibility during a warm-up, filters data, and improves downstream policy performance (real-robot rollout success rises from 35% to 67.5%).
AI.motivation: Post-training of vision-language-action models is highly sensitive to data quality and embodiment; existing cleaning methods are often limited to specific corruption types. There is a need for task- and embodiment-aware data auditing that can predict the impact of supervision on post-training performance.
AI.method: During a one-epoch warm-up, RoboDrop online scores each candidate sample by computing gradient compatibility with gradients from task-semantic and visually matched validation samples. Scores are aggregated at the episode level, then a simple automatic post-processing rule converts them into filtering decisions. The framework is evaluated on controlled observation-action corruptions, suboptimal demonstrations in simulation, and real-robot datasets with non-expert errors.
AI.result: RoboDrop more accurately identifies unreliable demonstrations than prior methods; post-training on curated data yields stronger downstream policies, with real-robot rollout success increasing from 35.0% to 67.5%.
AI.conclusion: Training-trajectory-aware, context-conditioned supervision auditing is an effective approach for robust VLA post-training.

title: MotionBlind: Probing the Illusion of Motion Understanding in Video-LLMs
summary: Video large language models (Video-LLMs) are increasingly used as the perceptual front end of world models, a role that assumes they can read motion: how fast something moves, which way it travels, how hard it is pushed. We show they cannot. A Video-LLM can watch two clips of the same person in the same room, name every object in both, and still fail to say which clip moves faster. We introduce MotionBlind, a contrastive benchmark of self-recorded video for physically grounded motion(speed, magnitude, and direction), the variables a world model must predict. Each instance is a pair of near-identical clips that differ only in motion. Each clip carries two complementary yes/no questions, giving four items per instance, and a model earns credit only if all four are correct. We report Instance Accuracy(IAcc), which has a 6.25% chance floor. Single-frame, appearance, and language-only shortcuts all collapse to it. MotionBlind complements the recent TimeBlind benchmark. We run a controlled study of six open and two frontier Video-LLMs, varying whether the video is present, whether frames are shown in the correct temporal order, and how frames are sampled (1 to 24 frames, four selection strategies). Open models sit near the 6.25% floor, and scale does not help. Removing the video drops every model to zero IAcc, and shuffling frames collapses IAcc to chance, so the task genuinely needs video in order. Neither more frames nor smarter frame selection closes the gap, because these change which frames are seen, not whether motion is read. Only Gemini3.1 Pro clears the benchmark overall, and even it fails on speed. A frontend that cannot tell two speeds of the same action apart is not yet a trustworthy source of supervision, reward, or evaluation for a world model.

AI.tldr: Video-LLMs struggle with physically grounded motion understanding; a new MotionBlind benchmark reveals they cannot reliably infer speed, magnitude, or direction from pairs of near-identical clips; current models perform near chance, even with more frames, structured sampling, or larger models, while only Gemini3.1 Pro shows marginal gains but still fails on speed.
AI.motivation: Assess whether Video-LLMs can read motion to support physically grounded world models and evaluation; demonstrate gaps between perceptual capabilities and motor-relevant reasoning; provide a benchmark to quantify motion understanding.
AI.method: Create MotionBlind: for each instance, two near-identical video clips that differ only in motion; each clip has two complementary yes/no questions (four items per instance); measure Instance Accuracy (IAcc), with a 6.25% random-floor; evaluate six open and two frontier Video-LLMs under various conditions (video presence, temporal order, frame sampling 1–24 frames, four selection strategies); compare to TimeBlind.
AI.result: Most models hover near the chance floor (6.25% IAcc); removing video drops performance to zero; shuffling frames collapses IAcc to chance; additional frames or smarter sampling do not fix motion-reading; Gemini3.1 Pro is the only model that performs better overall but still fails on speed; motion understanding from video remains unreliable for supervising or evaluating world models.
AI.conclusion: Video-LLMs are not yet reliable sources for perceiving physically grounded motion; MotionBlind effectively tests motion-reading ability and highlights limitations across current models; caution is warranted when using Video-LLMs as supervision/evaluation for world models; further targeted benchmarks and model developments are needed for robust motion understanding.

title: PRAGMA: Evaluating Personalized Guidance with Memory Alignment in Lifelong Conversations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as personalized assistants that interact with users over extended periods of time. As conversations grow longer, relying on full interaction histories becomes increasingly inefficient and unreliable: long contexts introduce substantial computational overhead, making it difficult for models to consistently identify and utilize the most relevant information for the current request. These challenges have motivated memory systems that structure and retrieve user-specific information. In realistic interactions, users often seek practical guidance such as recommendations, planning, and decision support. Unlike factual recall tasks, personalized guidance requires models to integrate information across multiple past conversations and reason about changing user preferences and experiences. However, existing conversational memory evaluations mainly focus on retrieval and factual recall. To study this challenge, we introduce PRAGMA, a benchmark for evaluating personalized guidance in long-term conversations. PRGAMA contains curated longitudinal conversation histories, evidence annotations, and guidance scenarios grounded in evolving user contexts and incorrect user assumptions. Experiments across retrieval systems, memory systems, and long-context models reveal that current systems struggle both to recover the appropriate conversational evidence and to effectively use it for personalized guidance. Our results highlight the need for memory architectures that support robust conversational retrieval and memory-grounded reasoning beyond evidence recall.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (PRAGMA/PRGAMA) for evaluating personalized guidance in long-term conversations, highlighting retrieval and memory-grounded reasoning gaps; calls for memory-augmented architectures beyond simple evidence recall.
AI.motivation: As conversations accumulate, long contexts incur computational overhead and make it harder for LLMs to identify relevant information. Personalized guidance demands integrating information across multiple past interactions and adapting to evolving user preferences, which existing memory evaluations largely emphasize retrieval/recall rather than guided reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce PRAGMA/PRGAMA benchmark with curated longitudinal conversation histories, evidence annotations, and guidance scenarios grounded in evolving contexts and incorrect user assumptions. Conduct experiments across retrieval systems, memory systems, and long-context LLMs to assess performance on personalized guidance tasks.
AI.result: Current systems struggle to recover appropriate evidence and to use it effectively for personalized guidance. Evidence recall is insufficient for robust guidance, indicating gaps in memory-grounded reasoning and integration.
AI.conclusion: There is a need for memory architectures that support robust conversational retrieval and memory-grounded reasoning beyond evidence recall, including better integration of past evidence, dynamic user modeling, and evaluation metrics that capture guidance quality.

title: Positional task conditioning for scalable defect detection across product families in large product catalogs
summary: Product families in large product catalogs suffer from inconsistencies such as duplicates and unit mismatches that degrade customer experience. Detecting these requires reasoning over multiple error types across lengthy product listings, where LLM classification quality degrades due to long-context limitations. We address this by decomposing detection into focused sub-tasks that reduce context and isolate error types, improving F1 from 52\% to 87\%. For scalable deployment, we introduce Positional Task Conditioning (PTC), which distills this capability into a single smaller model by reinforcing task identity at structural prompt boundaries. PTC outperforms rationale-based distillation across five models and two architecture families, achieving within 1.79\% F1 of the frontier at upto 98\% lower cost. Our system is deployed across multiple countries processing 10+ million product families.

AI.tldr: Decomposing multi-type catalog errors into focused sub-tasks improves detection accuracy and scalability: F1 rises from 52% to 87%, aided by Positional Task Conditioning (PTC) that distills to smaller models with near-frontier performance at much lower cost; deployed across countries on 10+ million product families.
AI.motivation: Large product catalogs suffer from duplicates and unit mismatches that harm customer experience. Reasoning over multiple error types requires long context, which degrades LLM classification quality. A modular, scalable approach is needed to handle diverse errors efficiently.
AI.method: Decompose detection into focused sub-tasks to reduce context and isolate error types. Introduce Positional Task Conditioning (PTC) to reinforce task identity at structural prompt boundaries and distill the capability into smaller models. Compare PTC against rationale-based distillation across five models and two architecture families.
AI.result: F1 improved from 52% to 87%. PTC achieves within 1.79% F1 of the frontier while delivering up to 98% cost reductions. System deployed across multiple countries processing 10+ million product families.
AI.conclusion: Structured decomposition with PTC enables scalable, accurate catalog error detection. The approach delivers near-frontier performance at significantly lower cost and is ready for wide deployment in large-scale catalogs.

title: AXON: A ROS 2 RMW with Shared-Memory/QUIC Transport and QKD/ML-KEM Key Establishment
summary: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) standardizes application code against a middleware interface (RMW) whose reference implementations are built on the Data Distribution Service (DDS). We present AXON, an alternative ROS 2 RMW implementation that separates transport policy by deployment scope. A Rust core and C++ adapter use POSIX shared-memory rings for same-host communication, QUIC for remote communication, and a daemon for discovery and graph synchronization. We then describe two fail-closed TLS 1.3 key-establishment configurations for remote traffic. The classic configuration offers only the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 group, preventing negotiation of a classical-only group. The qkd configuration imports a 256-bit key obtained through the ETSI GS QKD 014 API as a pairwise external PSK and offers no Diffie-Hellman group. Its default messages10 strategy additionally protects remote application messages with AES-256-GCM, rotating KME material after ten outgoing messages and using a fresh nonce per envelope; session relies on QUIC protection alone. The external-PSK path requires a narrow extension to rustls, now bundled with AXON. We define the threat model, distinguish peer authentication in the two configurations, and delimit the implementation-level validation from ROS 2 conformance, comparative performance, and physical-QKD validation.

AI.tldr: AXON: a ROS 2 RMW that separates transport policy by deployment scope using a Rust core and C++ adapter; same-host comm via POSIX shared-memory rings, remote comm via QUIC; supports two TLS 1.3 key-establishment configurations (classic X25519-based and QKD-based external-PSK); adds a messages10 strategy with AES-256-GCM and per-envelope nonces, with KME rotation; external-PSK path requires a rustls extension; defines threat model and validation scope for ROS 2 conformance, performance, and physical-QKD validation.
AI.motivation: To move beyond DDS-based RMWs by decoupling transport policy per deployment scope, enabling secure, flexible inter-process and inter-machine communication for ROS 2 with advanced security options including QKD-derived keys.
AI.method: Architectural separation of transport policy; Rust core with C++ adapter; same-host via POSIX shared-memory rings; remote via QUIC; daemon for discovery/graph sync; two TLS 1.3 configurations (classic and QKD-external-PSK); messages10 strategy with AES-256-GCM and KME rotation; external-PSK path requires rustls extension; threat model formulation; implementation-level validation vs ROS 2 conformance and performance evaluation plan.
AI.result: The work defines AXON’s architecture and security configurations, delineates threat models and authentication modes for the two TLS setups, and outlines a validation framework distinguishing implementation-level checks, ROS 2 conformance, comparative performance, and physical-QKD validation.
AI.conclusion: AXON offers a modular, deployment-scope aware RMW for ROS 2 with secure transport options (including QKD-based keys) and a path to ROS 2 conformance verification and physical-QKD validation, while highlighting the need for rustls extensions to support external-PSK.

title: RouteBridge: Reliability-Routed Bidirectional Distillation Between Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) encode a scene with complementary inductive biases, but existing cross-representation distillation typically fixes one representation as teacher for the entire scene. A globally fixed teacher can propagate local reconstruction errors. We present RouteBridge, a bidirectional framework that selects the teaching direction for each ray. Its reliability estimator combines photometric residuals with representation-specific geometric evidence and routes supervision from NeRF to 3DGS, from 3DGS to NeRF, or abstains. A renderer-independent interface transfers color, opacity, and normalized depth without shared features or point correspondence. On mip-NeRF 360, the NeRF and 3DGS exports reach 28.56 and 28.77 dB, respectively. The 3DGS export improves over 3DGS by 1.56 dB and over NeRF-GS by 0.45 dB while reducing LPIPS to 0.207. On static three-view DTU, RouteBridge obtains 21.12 dB. Ablations show that both adaptive routing and geometric ray targets contribute to the improvement.

AI.tldr: RouteBridge enables per-ray bidirectional distillation between NeRFs and 3D Gaussian Splatting, using adaptive routing informed by photometric and geometric cues.
AI.motivation: Cross-representation distillation often fixes a global teacher, causing propagation of local reconstruction errors; a per-ray reliable guidance mechanism leveraging both NeRF and 3DGS is desired.
AI.method: A reliability estimator combines photometric residuals with representation-specific geometric evidence to decide, for each ray, whether to teach NeRF from 3DGS, 3DGS from NeRF, or abstain; uses a renderer-independent interface to transfer color, opacity, and normalized depth without shared features or point correspondences.
AI.result: On mip-NeRF 360, NeRF export 28.56 dB, 3DGS export 28.77 dB; the 3DGS export improves over standard 3DGS by 1.56 dB and over NeRF-GS by 0.45 dB, with LPIPS 0.207. On static three-view DTU, RouteBridge achieves 21.12 dB. Ablations show that both adaptive routing and geometric ray targets contribute to the improvement.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, bidirectional routing with a reliability-guided per-ray strategy yields complementary gains for NeRF and 3DGS; geometry-aware targets and per-ray routing are key to performance improvements.

title: Safe to Stop? Risk-Constrained Stopping for Sequential Clinical Diagnosis Agents
summary: Clinical diagnosis agents must decide not only what test to request next, but also when to diagnose or defer. Existing agent benchmarks largely evaluate accuracy after fixed or unconstrained interaction, leaving autonomous stopping reliability implicit. We present Cros, a risk-constrained stopping layer combining state-wise error ranking, policy design on disjoint development splits, and LTT-style exact tests of selective diagnostic error and minimum autonomous coverage for complete sequential policies. Its finite-sample guarantee requires the candidate family, testing rule, and any randomization to be frozen before calibration labels are accessed. On a 1,834-episode MIMIC-derived abdominal-pain benchmark, the full ranker achieves exploratory state-error AUROC 0.853, compared with 0.715 for maximum class probability and 0.552 for the backbone's native stop score. On the previously viewed 367-episode evaluation split, analytically averaging over the frozen Cros weights yields 16.9% selective error at 78.8% coverage, cost 5.57, and 0.68 tests, versus 30.8% error at 100% coverage, cost 8.14, and 1.53 tests under native stopping. Forced continuation is non-monotone: error is 28.3% with HPI alone and 34.3% after full workup. However, the uniform-weight mixture ablation is cheaper on this viewed split despite missing the locked development margins, and Cros nominally satisfies the joint criterion in only 6 of 20 development resplits. Because evaluation labels were inspected during earlier development, these findings provide exploratory feasibility and audit evidence, not a confirmatory safety certificate.

AI.tldr: Cros is a risk-constrained stopping layer for clinical diagnosis agents that optimizes when to diagnose, using state-wise error ranking and LTT-style exact tests within a finite-sample, frozen-calibration framework. It improves selective error and efficiency over baselines on MIMIC-like abdominal-pain tasks but remains exploratory and not a confirmatory safety certificate.
AI.motivation: Existing clinical decision agents are evaluated mainly on accuracy after fixed or unconstrained interactions, neglecting reliable autonomous stopping; there is a need for principled, auditable stopping guarantees that balance diagnostic error, coverage, and resource use.
AI.method: Cros combines (i) state-wise error ranking, (ii) policy design on disjoint development splits, (iii) LTT-style exact tests of selective diagnostic error and minimum autonomous coverage, with finite-sample guarantees that require the candidate family, testing rule, and randomization to be frozen before access to calibration labels.
AI.result: On a 1,834-episode MIMIC-derived abdominal-pain benchmark, the full ranker achieves exploratory state-error AUROC 0.853 (vs 0.715 for max class probability and 0.552 for the backbone's native stop score). On a previously viewed 367-episode split, averaging over frozen Cros weights yields 16.9% selective error at 78.8% coverage, cost 5.57, and 0.68 tests, versus 30.8% error at 100% coverage, cost 8.14, and 1.53 tests under native stopping. Forced continuation is non-monotone (28.3% error with HPI alone; 34.3% after full workup). A uniform-weight mixture ablation is cheaper on the viewed split but misses locked margins, and Cros satisfies the joint criterion in only 6 of 20 resplits. Evaluation labels were inspected during development, so findings are exploratory feasibility and audit evidence, not a confirmatory safety certificate.
AI.conclusion: Cros demonstrates exploratory feasibility for risk-constrained stopping in clinical decision agents, provides a framework for auditable, finite-sample stopping guarantees, but its safety claims require careful, non-exploitative evaluation design and are not yet a formal safety certificate.

title: Teacher Geometry Shapes Learnability in Teacher-Student Networks
summary: Teacher-student systems, in which a teacher neural network generates training labels so that a student neural network can learn to implement the same function, are widely used as an abstract setting to study learning. However, the structure of the teachers is often overlooked by assuming randomly-generated, normally-distributed parameters. This hides substantial variation in how learnable different teachers are. We formalize learnability as the success rate of converging to the global minimum, as a function of overparameterization, learning algorithm, student initialization distribution, and teacher geometry. We both identify an easy distribution that maximizes node dissimilarity and a hard distribution that minimizes it, and show that these two distributions induce markedly different success rates across a large range of settings and for different activation functions. To explain the gap, we study the loss landscape of small neural networks that contain two distinct kinds of suboptimal local minima, out-of-bounds (OOB) minima at the edge of the data distribution and interior minima within. Assuming infinite data and a fast readout layer, we analytically reduce the loss landscape of small networks to two dimensions, showing that the region of attraction of interior minima changes as a function of teacher structure. In larger networks, maximally dissimilar teachers induce more interior minima, while minimally dissimilar teachers induce more OOB minima. Motivated by these analyses, we show that differentially increasing the learning rate of the readout layer and decreasing the learning rate of the inner biases increases success rates. These findings provide an important step in narrowing the gap between the study of teacher-student networks and more structured functions that arise in practice.

AI.tldr: Formalizes teacher-student learnability as the probability of converging to the global minimum under overparameterization, revealing how teacher geometry and parameter-dissimilarity affect learning dynamics across architectures and activations.
AI.motivation: To understand how the structure of the teacher (beyond random Gaussian parameters) affects the learnability of the student in teacher-student networks, and to connect abstract theory with practical function classes.
AI.method: Analyses of loss landscapes for small networks with two types of suboptimal local minima (OOB and interior), two-dimensional reduction under infinite data and fast readout, and empirical/analytic exploration of larger networks with varying teacher dissimilarity; investigation of learning-rate schedules focusing on the readout layer and inner biases.
AI.result: Demonstrates that easy vs hard teacher-distribution choices lead to markedly different success rates. Shows that interior minima regions expand with higher teacher dissimilarity in larger networks, while OOB minima are more prevalent with low dissimilarity. Proposes learning-rate adjustments—boosting readout LR while reducing inner-bias LR—to increase convergence to the global minimum.
AI.conclusion: Teacher geometry and parameter dissimilarity significantly shape learnability in teacher-student networks. The work bridges abstract learning theory with structured function classes, offering practical training strategies and highlighting the role of loss landscape structure (OOB vs interior) in overparameterized regimes.

title: What Symmetry Buys a Learned Motion Planner
summary:
Learning-based motion planners pay at training what classical planners pay per query. Trained in world coordinates, they relearn the same motion at every position and orientation. Existing work restores the missing rigid-body equivariance in the training data, in the inference operator, or in the weights, and each carries a cost. We ask how much of that equivariance the planning query supplies for free.
  A start s and a goal g determine a frame in closed form, with origin at their midpoint and first axis along g-s. Expressing trajectory and obstacles in that frame removes three translations and two rotations of SE(3), at initialisation, for one cross product per query and with no constraint on the architecture. A single rotation about the start-goal axis remains, and no continuous rule removes it. On a cluttered 3D benchmark, holding architecture, data and budget fixed, the frame raises the held-out collision-free rate from 14.60% to 51.10%, where a straight segment from start to goal scores 15.6% and the world-frame model does not beat it. We build all three mechanisms for the residual rotation and each is worth under a point, though the equivariant backbone reaches any given level two to three times sooner. What the representation supplies therefore dominates what any mechanism enforces, and the standard diagnostic does not see the difference: two models with indistinguishable non-equivariance residuals differ by 28 points. Calibrated against a non-symmetry intervention, the frame is not even the largest effect available, since local geometry is worth +40.0 where the frame is worth +36.5.

AI.tldr: A problem-specific canonical frame anchored by start and goal substantially reduces SE(3) variability in learning-based motion planning, yielding major performance gains and often surpassing learned equivariant mechanisms. The frame representation dominates the benefit over residual rotation mechanisms, though some residual symmetry handling can help speed up training. Local geometry can provide even larger gains than the frame in certain metrics.
AI.motivation: Quantify how much of the needed geometric equivariance in motion planning can be supplied by the planning query itself through a canonical frame, reducing the need for complex equivariant architectures or data transformations.
AI.method: Define a closed-form frame from start s and goal g: origin at the midpoint, first axis along g−s. Transform trajectory and obstacle representations into this frame to remove three translations and two rotations of SE(3) at initialization. Retain a single rotation about the start–goal axis. Evaluate on a cluttered 3D benchmark with fixed architecture, data, and budget; compare against a world-frame baseline and a straight-line planner; implement three residual-rotation mechanisms; calibrate against a non-symmetry intervention; compare against geometry-based baselines.
AI.result: Frame-based representation raised the collision-free rate from 14.60% (world frame / baseline) to 51.10% on the cluttered 3D benchmark, while a straight segment achieved 15.6%. The world-frame model did not beat the straight-line baseline. The three residual-rotation mechanisms contributed less than a point each, but the equivariant backbone accelerated reaching the target by two-to-three times. Two models with indistinguishable non-equivariance residuals differed by 28 points. Calibrated against a non-symmetry intervention, local geometry yielded +40.0 whereas the frame yielded +36.5.
AI.conclusion: The choice of representation (the problem-informed frame) provides the dominant gain over added equivariant mechanisms; the planning query’s structure supplies most of the required equivariance. However, local geometric cues can surpass the frame in some metrics, indicating that representation and geometry together govern performance; careful framing can reduce reliance on specialized equivariant design and improve data efficiency.

title: Marker-free eye-gaze estimation using a single image and depth from defocus
summary: This paper presents a marker-free eye-gaze estimation approach using a single 2D camera, such as an integrated laptop webcam. The gaze-related features are estimated from iris localization and head pose estimated by using depth from defocus. A variational Bayesian multinomial logistic regression framework is used as mapping from the estimated features to the position of regard, based on an 8-dimensional feature vector of head-pose and iris-displacement parameters. No external marker is needed. Experiments were conducted by estimating the gaze of people watching a computer screen at different distances and compared against five existing methods. The obtained scores demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Marker-free gaze estimation from a single 2D camera using iris localization and depth-from-defocus head pose, with an 8D feature vector mapped to gaze position via variational Bayesian multinomial logistic regression; evaluated against five methods across different distances.
AI.motivation: Develop a practical, markerless gaze-tracking solution using a common 2D camera (e.g., laptop webcam) without external markers.
AI.method: Extract head pose via depth from defocus and iris localization to form an 8-dimensional feature vector (head-pose and iris-displacement). Use a variational Bayesian multinomial logistic regression to map these features to the gaze position (position of regard). No external markers are required.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across varying distances shows the proposed method outperforms or is competitive with five existing gaze-estimation methods, with scores indicating effective gaze prediction.
AI.conclusion: A feasible marker-free gaze-estimation pipeline using a single 2D camera is demonstrated, with VB multinomial logistic regression effectively translating 8D eye/head features into gaze position; suitable for consumer devices and real-world usage.

title: Decision Shifts, Lost Label Functionality, and an Inconclusive Grounding Audit in Correctness-Gated Multi-Teacher Distillation
summary: Candidate decision correctness and rationale grounding are different objectives. We examine correctness-gated multi-teacher distillation in a fixed experiment. Eight arms share 4,330 sources, a 63.9M-parameter student, 12,990 optimization rows, 406 updates, evidence inputs, and a decoder; seven teacher-based arms use one fixed three-response pool. Three seeds are evaluated on 267 held-out examples. Relative to unfiltered distillation, the correctness-weighted arm differed in accuracy by +0.1660 (95% observed-matrix interval [0.0670, 0.2455]), five-label macro-F1 by +0.1323 ([0.0916, 0.1731]), and task-defined conditional unsafe-action rate by -0.4979 ([-0.5926, -0.3686]). These shifts do not imply uniformly better behavior. Source-label SFT had the highest mean macro-F1 (0.586). The weighted arm had zero Refuted recall in every seed, and two seeds assigned NotEnoughInfo to all 167 claim examples. In an availability-amended audit at one reference seed, weighted and unfiltered outputs had 0/20 versus 1/20 evidence-supported positives and 20/20 versus 19/20 positives containing unsupported material. Samples were non-paired, source overlap was not serialized, and the amendment followed automatic summarization but preceded annotation. The audit therefore cannot estimate a common-source grounding effect and is inconclusive about system-level improvement or harm. Hard filtering already achieved 0.660 accuracy, 0.530 macro-F1, and 0.135 conditional unsafe rate. The implemented weighted arm showed no demonstrated incremental decision benefit over hard filtering. This fixed-matrix failure analysis shows decision redistribution with lost label functionality; the available human audit does not establish a grounding gain.

AI.tldr: Correctness-gated multi-teacher distillation yields modest gains in accuracy and macro-F1 but no robust grounding benefit; hard filtering outperforms the weighted approach, and evaluation evidence for grounding remains inconclusive due to audit limitations.
AI.motivation: To determine whether gating decisions by correctness in a multi-teacher distillation setup improve decision accuracy and provide reliable grounding for outputs, versus unfiltered distillation and hard filtering.
AI.method: Fixed experimental design with eight arms sharing 4,330 sources, a 63.9M-parameter student, 12,990 optimization rows, 406 updates, evidence inputs, and a decoder. Seven teacher-based arms use one fixed three-response pool. Three seeds evaluated on 267 held-out examples. Comparisons include correctness-weighted distillation versus unfiltered distillation; evaluation on accuracy, five-label macro-F1, and task-defined conditional unsafe-action rate. Source-label SFT used as a baseline with highest macro-F1. An availability-amended audit assessed grounding with a limited, non-paired, partially overlapping sample after summarization and before annotation. Hard filtering performance reported for comparison.
AI.result: Relative to unfiltered distillation, the correctness-weighted arm increased accuracy by 0.1660, macro-F1 by 0.1323, and reduced conditional unsafe-action rate by 0.4979 (with confidence intervals). However, these shifts are not uniformly beneficial; the weighted approach did not yield universally better behavior. Source-label SFT had the highest mean macro-F1 (0.586). The weighted arm showed zero Refuted recall across seeds, and two seeds labeled all 167 claim examples as NotEnoughInfo. In the availability-amended audit, weighted and unfiltered outputs had 0/20 vs 1/20 evidence-supported positives and 20/20 vs 19/20 positives containing unsupported material. The audit could not estimate common-source grounding and was inconclusive about system-level improvement or harm. Hard filtering achieved 0.660 accuracy, 0.530 macro-F1, and 0.135 conditional unsafe rate, outperforming the weighted arm. Overall, the fixed-matrix, correctness-gated approach redistributed decisions with loss of label functionality, and there is no demonstrated incremental grounding benefit given the available human audit.
AI.conclusion: In this fixed-matrix setup, correctness gating does not provide robust, consistent grounding benefits. Hard filtering remains effective, and the available audit cannot establish a clear grounding gain or system-level improvement. More rigorous, grounded evaluation with diverse seeds, sources, and evaluation protocols is needed to draw conclusions about decision-grounding benefits.

title: Cascading Gradient Inversion via LT-Code Inspired Peeling in Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning shares model updates rather than raw data, yet these updates can be inverted to reconstruct the clients' training data. Analytic reconstruction attacks, which invert a gradient in closed form, degrade as the batch grows: prior single-round attacks recover only about half of a batch of size $100$ even when the attacker fully controls the network parameters, and known upper bounds limit what any such method can recover. We establish a connection between gradient inversion and the theory of erasure-correcting codes, and use it to construct attacks that exceed these bounds. Our attacks recover batches exactly, together with every sample's label, from a single FedSGD round, and certify each recovery without ground-truth data. On eight image and tabular benchmarks they outperform prior single-round attacks by a wide margin. Even a passive attacker who only observes an honestly trained network recovers $94$--$100\%$ of ImageNet batches at sizes up to $128$, more than prior single-round attacks achieve even with active manipulation of the model, and in the active setting more than $90\%$ is recovered at batch sizes of several hundred. These results show that the privacy leakage of federated learning has been underestimated.

AI.tldr: A novel gradient-inversion attack framed via erasure-correcting codes that fully reconstructs training batches and labels from a single FedSGD round, surpassing prior bounds and revealing significant privacy leakage in federated learning.
AI.motivation: Address underestimated privacy risks in federated learning by improving reconstruction attacks, certifying results without ground-truth data, and highlighting potential leakage even from passive observations.
AI.method: Establish a connection between gradient inversion and erasure-correcting codes; design attacks that exploit this link to recover exact data batches and per-sample labels from a single round; provide recovery certifications; evaluate on multiple benchmarks and attacker scenarios.
AI.result: Attacks recover batches exactly with labels from one FedSGD round; certify recoveries without ground-truth data; outperform prior single-round attacks across eight benchmarks; passive attacker recovers 94–100% of ImageNet batches for batch sizes up to 128; active attacker recovers >90% for batch sizes of several hundred.
AI.conclusion: Federated-learning privacy leakage is larger than previously believed; existing analyses and defenses may be insufficient; motivates reevaluation of privacy guarantees and development of stronger defenses.

title: Grounding Generated Video Plans in Simulation Towards Versatile Dexterous Controllers
summary: Generated hand-object interaction (HOI) videos provide a controllable way to propose manipulation motions. Simulation-based HOI tracking can translate such kinematic references into feasible low-level control, but its scalability is limited by the lack of reliable reference motions. We therefore combine generated videos with simulation-based HOI grounding: during training, generated videos provide diverse motion references for learning a multi-object, multi-trajectory HOI tracker, and at deployment, the video model produces motion plans that are executed by the learned tracker. In particular, we propose a method that enables scalable reference generation by HOI reconstruction with minimal manual intervention and successfully grounds more than 1,500 generated videos in simulation, achieving success rates over 25 percentage points higher than those of baselines during simulation-based training. In real-world closed-loop experiments, it achieves diverse grasps, including functional grasps, non-prehensile manipulation, and post-grasp object-pose tracking. Videos and code are available at https://boyuan-an.github.io/GALATEA/.

AI.tldr: Proposes scalable generation of hand-object interaction (HOI) references by reconstructing HOI from generated videos and grounding them in simulation, enabling training of a multi-object, multi-trajectory HOI tracker; achieves 25+ percentage point improvement over baselines and demonstrates real-world diverse grasps; provides videos and code.
AI.motivation: The lack of reliable, scalable reference motions hampers simulation-based HOI tracking; there is a need for diverse, high-quality references to train a multi-object, multi-trajectory HOI tracker and to enable deployment via grounded motion plans.
AI.method: Use generated HOI videos as training references and ground them in simulation via HOI reconstruction with minimal manual intervention; train a tracker that handles multiple objects and trajectories; at deployment, the video model outputs motion plans that the tracker executes.
AI.result: Grounded over 1,500 generated videos in simulation; improved success rates by >25 percentage points over baselines during training; in real-world closed-loop tests, demonstrated diverse grasps (functional, non-prehensile) and post-grasp object-pose tracking.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables scalable, simulated grounding of HOI references and transfer to real-world manipulation, enabling robust, diverse manipulation behaviors; resources (videos, code) are released.

title: Hyperbolic Geometry for Open-World Object Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery
summary: Open-world object detection (OWOD) extends closed-set detection by requiring models to identify unknown objects and incrementally learn them once annotations become available. In remote sensing imagery, object categories often exhibit latent hierarchical relationships that may be inadequately represented in the Euclidean spaces commonly adopted by existing methods, limiting unknown-object recall and incremental-learning performance. To address this issue, we investigate hyperbolic geometry for OWOD in remote sensing imagery and propose HyRS-OWOD. To improve unknown object recall, we design a two-step unknown-object discovery mechanism: a Decoupled Objectness Learning (DOL) module that disentangles foreground perception from semantic information to separate foreground proposals from background regions, followed by a Hyperbolic Uncertainty Learning (HUL) component that leverages the radius of hyperbolic embeddings as an uncertainty-aware cue for known-unknown discrimination. For incremental learning, we develop a Hyperbolic Metric Learning (HML) strategy that enhances inter-class separability, facilitating the incorporation of novel categories while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Experiments on three remote sensing benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in unknown recall and incremental learning over state-of-the-art OWOD methods.

AI.tldr: HyRS-OWOD uses hyperbolic geometry for open-world object detection in remote sensing, introducing Decoupled Objectness Learning (DOL), Hyperbolic Uncertainty Learning (HUL), and Hyperbolic Metric Learning (HML) to improve unknown-object recall and incremental learning across three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Remote sensing object categories often form latent hierarchical relationships that Euclidean embeddings struggle to capture, hindering unknown-object recall and incremental learning in OWOD.
AI.method: Introduce HyRS-OWOD with: (1) DOL to separate foreground/objectness from semantics; (2) HUL to use hyperbolic embedding radii as uncertainty cues for known-vs-unknown discrimination; (3) HML to strengthen inter-class separability for better integration of new categories and reduced forgetting.
AI.result: Experiments on three remote sensing benchmarks show consistent improvements in unknown recall and incremental learning compared with state-of-the-art OWOD methods.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic representations and the proposed modules effectively capture hierarchical relationships in remote sensing data, improving open-world detection by enhancing unknown object recall and mitigating catastrophic forgetting during incremental learning.

title: Which Tokens Should SFT Actually Learn? A Token-Trimming Perspective on Mathematical Reasoning
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. 14 pages. Code available at https://github.com/karpning/TrimSFT
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) applies a uniform cross-entropy loss to all target tokens, even though different tokens provide unequal learning signals for mathematical reasoning. This uniform treatment can over-sharpen already mastered tokens while amplifying learning pressure on uncertain, low-confidence tokens, leading to suboptimal training dynamics. We propose Trimmed Logit-Gap SFT (TrimSFT), a simple token-level reweighting method that scales the SFT loss according to the logit gap between the gold token and its strongest competitor. TrimSFT trims supervision away from both extremes: tokens already mastered (large logit gap) and tokens weakly supported by the current model (small or negative logit gap), concentrating learning within an intermediate logit-gap region between them. We instantiate this principle with a Gaussian weight centered at margin m with bandwidth τ, requiring no reference model or additional forward pass. We evaluate TrimSFT on six base models from the Llama, Qwen, and DeepMath families across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks. TrimSFT consistently improves over standard SFT, achieving the best average performance on five out of six models, with gains of up to +26.9 points over SFT on MATH500. Further analyses show that the bandwidth τ matters more than the exact margin location, and that half-trim variants that remove supervision pressure from only one side yield inferior trade-offs. A token-level logit-gap distribution analysis suggests that TrimSFT reshapes model confidence in a more balanced way than uniform SFT or monotonic reweighting methods. These results suggest that reasoning SFT can benefit from trimming both extremes rather than treating all tokens uniformly.

AI.tldr: TrimSFT reweights token-level supervision in supervised fine-tuning by scaling the loss with the logit gap to the strongest competitor, trimming extremes to focus learning on intermediate tokens; improves reasoning SFT across multiple models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Uniform cross-entropy treats all target tokens equally, but tokens provide unequal learning signals for mathematical reasoning; trimming aims to allocate supervision where it is most informative.
AI.method: Apply a Gaussian weight to the per-token SFT loss, centered at margin m with bandwidth τ, based on the logit gap between the gold token and its strongest competitor. No reference model or extra forward pass required; weights computed from the current model outputs during training.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over standard SFT across six base models (Llama, Qwen, DeepMath) and five mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Best average performance on five of six models; gains up to +26.9 points over SFT on MATH500. Bandwidth τ matters more than the exact margin location; half-trim variants underperform. Token-level gap distribution analysis suggests TrimSFT yields a more balanced confidence profile than uniform SFT or monotonic reweighting.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning SFT benefits from trimming supervision away from both extremes—mastered tokens and weakly supported tokens—concentrating learning in an intermediate logit-gap region, with a simple, model-agnostic approach that does not require extra forward passes.

title: PELM: Power Efficient On-Device LLM Inference with Speculative Decoding and Dynamic Voltage Frequency Scaling
summary: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) directly on mobile platforms at the edge is gaining traction due to a myriad of benefits, such as increased privacy, personalization, and reduced latency. However, LLMs have heavy computational requirements, which are difficult for resource-constrained mobile and edge platforms to fulfill. In addition to limited compute resources, mobile and edge systems often have a compact form factor and lack physical mechanisms to dissipate heat generated from high processor usage rates (e.g., fans) to prevent throttling and reduced processing power, which LLMs can easily cause. To mitigate these effects, prior works have proposed various power governing strategies, such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), for reducing power and heat generation for heavy computational tasks on mobile platforms. Recently, DVFS methods tailored for mobile LLMs have also been proposed. However, these methods mostly focus on optimizing hardware parameters and processor frequencies, and they fall short under some thermally constrained scenarios. Drawing from recent advances in machine learning, we identify and take advantage of the key insight that not all tokens require full-depth inference to maintain high-quality generation. Motivated by this, we present PELM, a solution that augments traditional DVFS processor frequency tuning with two additional workload-specific knobs: 1) speculative decoding and 2) variable verification depth to expand the optimization space to multiple dimensions for more power efficient on-device LLM inference. In extensive evaluations across hardware platforms and datasets, PELM demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art power governing methods, with up to 23.1% speedup and 52.4% reduction in energy consumption, while maintaining comparable task performance. The source code is available at https://github.com/imec-nu/PELM.

AI.tldr: PELM augments DVFS-based on-device LLM inference with two workload-specific knobs—speculative decoding and variable verification depth—creating a multi-dimensional optimization space that further reduces energy/heat while preserving generation quality.
AI.motivation: Mobile/edge platforms struggle with heat and limited compute; standard DVFS tunes hardware parameters but often fails under thermally constrained scenarios, hindering on-device LLM viability.
AI.method: Introduce two knobs on top of DVFS: speculative decoding (processing fewer tokens with possible early exit) and variable verification depth (adjusting the depth of output verification). Search over a multi-dimensional space to optimize power/throughput/quality; evaluate across hardware and datasets; compare to state-of-the-art power governs methods.
AI.result: Across multiple hardware platforms and datasets, PELM achieves up to 23.1% speedup and 52.4% energy reduction relative to baselines, while maintaining comparable task performance to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: PELM demonstrates that extending DVFS with workload-aware controls yields meaningful power and performance gains for on-device LLMs, with practical code available for adoption; potential limitations include generalization to diverse models, overhead of added controls, and the need for robust evaluation across dynamic workloads.

title: Automatic Reproducible Camera Intrinsic Calibration
summary: Accurate camera intrinsic calibration is fundamental to robot perception, and the accuracy depends on the quality of the collected images. However, existing target-based calibration methods often require the practitioner to manually filter out high-quality images and to specify an appropriate radial distortion order. This paper presents a fully automatic intrinsic calibration pipeline that determines both from the collected data. We adopt an iterative rejection scheme that estimates parameters on a candidate image set and removes views whose mean residual exceeds a multiple of the median. Crucially, this process runs independently under each candidate distortion order, so that the retained image set is consistent with the residual scale of that order. Further, the distortion order is selected on held-out images, with the intrinsics and distortion fixed and only the board pose re-estimated, ensuring that an added coefficient is supported by independent observations. Finally, we integrate both steps into an interactive calibration tool that supports full-pipeline data inspection and parameter estimation. Experiments on our own camera data and five public real-world datasets show that image filtering reduces the held-out reprojection error by 25\%, the order selection further by 5\%, achieving the lowest held-out mean among four compared configurations without manual image selection. We will release the code and data to facilitate future research.

AI.tldr: A fully automatic intrinsic calibration pipeline that jointly filters images and selects distortion order without manual intervention, using per-order iterative residual rejection and held-out validation, achieving lower reprojection error.
AI.motivation: Eliminate manual steps in target-based camera calibration (image quality filtering and radial distortion order selection) and ensure consistency between data and distortion model to improve accuracy.
AI.method: An iterative rejection scheme that estimates intrinsics for a candidate image set and discards views whose mean residual exceeds k times the median. The process runs independently for each candidate distortion order. Distortion order is chosen using held-out images by fixing intrinsics/distortion and re-estimating only the board pose, ensuring added coefficients are supported by independent observations. The steps are integrated into an interactive tool for data inspection and parameter estimation.
AI.result: Image filtering reduces held-out reprojection error by 25%; order selection adds 5%; achieves the lowest held-out mean among four configurations without manual image selection, demonstrated on one camera dataset and five public real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fully automatic calibration pipeline improves robustness and accuracy of camera intrinsic calibration by combining per-order residual-based image selection with held-out validation, enabling automatic, reliable calibration without manual data curation.

title: LightMedSeg-ISLES: Stroke Lesion Segmentation with 81x Fewer Parameters than nnU-Net
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to ISLES 2026 challenge. To be published in Nature Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS)
summary: Large networks and ensembles often lead medical image segmentation challenges, but their storage and inference demands complicate deployment. We present LightMedSeg-ISLES, a 1.26-million-parameter pipeline for T1-weighted stroke lesion segmentation in ISLES'26. On a 146-case held-out cohort, flip test-time augmentation produces 0.618 mean Dice and 0.599 lesion-wise F1. A 102.35-million-parameter nnU-Net ResEnc-L produces 0.634 Dice and 0.544 lesion-wise F1 after size filtering. LightMedSeg therefore retains 97.5\% of nnU-Net's Dice with 81.4$\times$ fewer parameters while improving lesion-wise F1 by 0.055. Its four-pass TTA operating point requires 4.7$\times$ fewer FLOPs per standardized patch than nnU-Net. It also slightly exceeds filtered UNETR++ and nnFormer. Longer training and stronger augmentation add 0.0358 Dice without increasing capacity, establishing a strong single-checkpoint alternative to much larger models.

AI.tldr: LightMedSeg-ISLES: a 1.26M-parameter segmentation pipeline for stroke lesions achieving competitive Dice and improved lesion-wise F1 on ISLES'26, with massive parameter and FLOPs reductions compared to nnU-Net; near-parity in Dice, better lesion-wise F1, and strong single-checkpoint performance; enhancement with longer training and augmentation.
AI.motivation: Reduce model size and inference cost for large medical image segmentation models, enabling practical deployment on limited hardware while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Proposes LightMedSeg-ISLES pipeline (1.26M params) with four-pass test-time augmentation (TTA) including flip; evaluates on 146-case held-out ISLES'26 cohort; compares against 102.35M-parameter nnU-Net ResEnc-L after size filtering; reports Dice and lesion-wise F1; analyzes FLOPs per standardized patch; investigates impact of longer training and stronger augmentation.
AI.result: LightMedSeg-ISLES achieves 0.618 mean Dice and 0.599 lesion-wise F1 (flip TTA). nnU-Net ResEnc-L (102.35M params) achieves 0.634 Dice and 0.544 lesion-wise F1 after size filtering. LightMedSeg retains 97.5% of nnU-Net's Dice with 81.4× fewer parameters and improves lesion-wise F1 by 0.055. Four-pass TTA requires 4.7× fewer FLOPs per standardized patch than nnU-Net. LightMedSeg slightly exceeds filtered UNETR++ and nnFormer. Longer training and stronger augmentation add 0.0358 Dice without increasing capacity, providing a strong single-checkpoint alternative to larger models.
AI.conclusion: A strong lightweight competitor in medical image segmentation: near-parity in Dice with the much larger nnU-Net and superior lesion-wise F1, with substantial efficiency gains in parameters and FLOPs; longer training and augmentation offer additional boosts, suggesting robust performance as a single-checkpoint baseline for deployment on constrained hardware.

title: Can Artificial Intelligence Support Healthcare and Mental Health Through Early Cyberbullying Detection ? The Impact of Emotion-Aware AI on Proactive Online Safety
summary: Healthcare systems, mental health, and public well-being are increasingly affected by cyberbullying and harmful online interactions. This paper presents CareGuard, an early-warning framework designed to support healthcare-driven mental health protection and proactive online safety through the detection of cyberbullying-related content using advanced natural language processing techniques. CareGuard integrates zero-shot semantic labeling with fine-tuned transformer-based models, including BERT, DistilBERT, and RoBERTa, to enable robust and context-aware classification across sensitive cyberbullying categories. To improve efficiency and reduce unnecessary computation in healthcare-oriented monitoring settings, the framework incorporates an emotion-aware filtering mechanism alongside cosine similarity-based semantic screening, allowing the system to focus on semantically relevant and emotionally salient content. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that CareGuard effectively balances detection accuracy and computational efficiency, highlighting its potential for scalable deployment in healthcare systems, mental health monitoring, and online safety applications.

AI.tldr: CareGuard is a framework that detects cyberbullying-related content for healthcare contexts using zero-shot labeling and fine-tuned transformers, with emotion-aware filtering and cosine-based screening to balance accuracy and efficiency, showing promising benchmark results for scalable online-safety in healthcare and mental-health monitoring.
AI.motivation: Cyberbullying and harmful online interactions threaten mental health and public well-being, particularly in healthcare settings. There is a need for an efficient, context-aware detection system that can operate in healthcare monitoring pipelines.
AI.method: Integrates zero-shot semantic labeling with fine-tuned transformer models (BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa). Adds an emotion-aware filtering mechanism and cosine similarity-based semantic screening to prioritize semantically relevant and emotionally salient content, reducing unnecessary computation in healthcare monitoring scenarios.
AI.result: Experiments on benchmark datasets indicate that CareGuard achieves a favorable balance between detection accuracy and computational efficiency, supporting scalable deployment in healthcare systems, mental health monitoring, and online safety applications.
AI.conclusion: CareGuard presents a promising approach for proactive online safety in healthcare contexts, with demonstrated efficiency and accuracy; future work could further validate in real-world deployments and explore broader datasets and deployment considerations.

title: Muon-C: Operator-Aligned Muon for Convolutional Kernels
summary: Muon replaces matrix momentum with an approximately orthogonal polar direction, but its geometry depends on the matrix representation. For convolution, standard unfolding describes a local patch map rather than the convolution operator. We introduce Muon-C, an operator-aligned optimizer that represents kernel momentum as frequency-wise channel-transfer matrices, polarizes these blocks independently, and uses a critical Fourier grid to return updates exactly to the original finite kernel support. We show that the new geometry arises from combining the block partition and Fourier coordinates. The exact-polar direction is a linear minimization oracle under the critically sampled convolution norm. Its worst-case guarantee relative to the continuous convolution-operator norm is never weaker than unfolding and is strictly stronger for $3\times3$ kernels. On CIFAR-10 flow matching with matched applied-update RMS, Muon-C reaches 9.87 FID at 40k iterations, compared with 22.26 for unfolded Muon and 51.31 for Adam. It reaches their final quality using $0.62\times$ and $0.64\times$ their model FLOPs, respectively. Under equal tuning budgets, Muon-C achieves 3.42 FID.
