Gains persist across data scales and transfer to classification across convolutional architectures.

AI.tldr: Muon-C is an operator-aligned optimizer for convolution kernels that uses frequency-wise channel-transfer matrices and a Fourier-grid to achieve exact-polar updates, yielding strong theoretical guarantees and substantial empirical gains over unfolding and Adam with lower FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Standard unfolding describes local patch maps and does not align with the convolution operator's geometry; a representation that exposes the operator structure can improve optimization efficiency and accuracy while reducing compute.
AI.method: Kernel momentum is represented as frequency-wise channel-transfer blocks; blocks polarized independently; a critical Fourier grid ensures updates map back to finite kernel support; the exact-polar direction is obtained via a linear minimization oracle under a critically sampled convolution norm.
AI.result: The worst-case guarantee relative to the continuous convolution-operator norm is no weaker than unfolding, and strictly stronger for 3×3 kernels. Empirically on CIFAR-10, Muon-C achieves 9.87 FID at 40k iterations vs 22.26 for unfolded Muon and 51.31 for Adam. It achieves comparable final quality with 0.62× and 0.64× the FLOPs of the baselines, respectively. Under equal tuning budgets, Muon-C achieves 3.42 FID. Gains persist across data scales and transfer to classification across architectures.
AI.conclusion: Muon-C introduces a geometry derived from block partition and Fourier coordinates, yielding an efficient, theoretically grounded optimizer with strong empirical performance; its gains generalize across data scales and convolutional architectures.

title: Assembling Two Parts in One Hand
comment: To appear on Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project website: https://ltbgbird.github.io/in-hand-assembly-page/
summary: A hallmark of human dexterity is the cooperative use of fingers, where different fingers take on distinct yet coordinated roles to accomplish fine manipu- lation, such as capping a pen with the hand that holds it. We study this finger-level coordination through in-hand assembly: mating two rigid objects within a single dexterous hand, with no second arm and no fixture. We present a reinforcement learning formulation to solve this problem in a unified framework, which is driven by a goal relative pose between the two parts. Finger coordination is shaped by a function-based auxiliary reward and regularized toward a single human reference pose, while domain randomization and a fusion of historical proprioception and object observation confer robustness to occlusion-induced estimation noise. The same recipe solves three different assembly tasks (Bottle, Syringe, and Marker). Trained purely in simulation, the policies transfer zero-shot to hardware with a single camera, demonstrating robustness to state-estimation errors caused by oc- clusion. Our experiments also reveal that in-hand assembly places demands on hand morphology and can serve as a benchmark for modern robotic hand systems. Videos and code are available at https://ltbgbird.github.io/in-hand-assembly-page/.

AI.tldr: A unified reinforcement learning framework for in-hand assembly within a single dexterous hand, using a goal relative pose objective, function-based auxiliary rewards with human pose regularization, domain randomization, and sensor fusion to handle occlusion. It solves three tasks (Bottle, Syringe, Marker) in simulation and transfers zero-shot to hardware with a single camera, highlighting hand morphology implications and providing a benchmark for modern robotic hands.
AI.motivation: Understanding and enabling dexterous, finger-level coordination for assembling rigid parts entirely within a single hand, a hallmark of human dexterity, and establishing a robust, transferable RL-based approach for such in-hand manipulation tasks.
AI.method: A reinforcement learning formulation driven by a goal relative pose between two parts. Finger coordination is guided by a function-based auxiliary reward and regularized toward a single human reference pose. Robustness is achieved via domain randomization and fusion of historical proprioception and object observations. The approach is applied to three tasks (Bottle, Syringe, Marker) and trained purely in simulation.
AI.result: Policies trained in simulation transfer zero-shot to hardware using a single camera, robust to occlusion-induced state-estimation noise. The method solves all three tasks with the same recipe. The experiments indicate that in-hand assembly constrains hand morphology and can serve as a practical benchmark for modern robotic hands.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a unified RL framework for complex in-hand assembly, achieving sim-to-real transfer with minimal observation hardware, and suggests that in-hand assembly tasks can drive the design of future robotic hand systems and benchmarks.

title: Recovering Biomechanical Signals from Missing Keypoints Using Temporal Interpolation in Monocular Gait Analysis
summary: Monocular pose estimation enables low-cost gait analysis but is sensitive to missing keypoints caused by occlusion, detection errors, or efficiency-driven model reduction. While prior work on recovering missing joints focuses on complex learned models, the effectiveness of simple temporal methods remains underexplored. We evaluate knee-angle estimation under a missing-ankle-keypoint condition and test a first-order temporal interpolation scheme as a recovery mechanism. Across 527 frames of monocular walking video (428 with valid baseline detections), removing the ankle keypoint increased mean angular error to 23.4° +/- 46.7° and collapsed signal variance to near zero. Temporal interpolation reduced error to 1.1° +/- 6.7° and restored variance and smoothness to within a few percent of baseline. These results indicate that gait signals possess sufficient temporal redundancy for a simple, computationally trivial interpolation scheme to recover a critical missing joint, without resorting to learned reconstruction models. The findings support low-complexity, real-time-compatible designs for gait analysis in resource-constrained or occlusion-prone monocular settings.

AI.tldr: A simple first-order temporal interpolation can recover missing ankle keypoints in monocular gait analysis, achieving near-baseline knee-angle accuracy and restored variance, suggesting low-complexity methods suffice in occlusion-prone settings.
AI.motivation: Monocular pose estimation is sensitive to missing keypoints (occlusions, detection errors). Previous work relies on complex learned models; this work probes whether a simple temporal method can recover missing joints.
AI.method: Evaluate knee-angle estimation under a missing-ankle-keypoint condition across 527 frames of monocular walking video (428 valid baselines). Remove ankle keypoint, apply first-order temporal interpolation, compare to baseline on angular error and variance.
AI.result: Without ankle keypoint: mean angular error 23.4° ± 46.7° and near-zero variance. With temporal interpolation: error reduced to 1.1° ± 6.7°, variance and smoothness restored to within a few percent of baseline.
AI.conclusion: Gait signals contain temporal redundancy that enables simple, real-time-compatible interpolation to recover missing joints, avoiding learned reconstruction models and benefiting resource-constrained or occlusion-prone monocular gait analysis.

title: LexAgentHallu: A Hierarchical Benchmark for Profiling Hallucinations in Legal Agents
summary: As large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-augmented legal agents, they introduce agentic hallucinations where tool-call and reasoning errors cascade into fabricated holdings and miscited authority. However, existing legal benchmarks evaluate only single-turn QA with outcome-level metrics, while agentic hallucination benchmarks lack legal-specific diagnostic capability. Neither answers to what extent and how a legal agent hallucinates along its trajectory. To address these limitations, we introduce LexAgentHallu, a legal agentic hallucination benchmark designed to evaluate to what extent and how legal agents fail along multi-step trajectories. Built through a four-stage expert-in-the-loop pipeline, LexAgentHallu contains 3414 instances across 17 legal categories and 6 task types. Each instance is annotated under a dual-layer hallucination taxonomy of 7 high-level categories and 27 fine-grained subclasses, covering both substantive errors and agent-procedural failures. We further design fine-grained metrics that quantify to what extent and localize how each failure occurs along an agent's execution path. Our evaluation across 18 proprietary and open-source agents uncovers a Right-Answer-Wrong-Reason effect and reveals that hallucination subclasses cluster rather than scatter, forming distinct agentic framework, legal task, and category profiles. These findings, invisible to outcome-level evaluation, validate the diagnostic power of LexAgentHallu for evaluating agentic hallucination in law.

AI.tldr: A multi-step, diagnostic benchmark (LexAgentHallu) assesses legal agentic hallucinations along execution trajectories using a four-stage expert-in-the-loop pipeline, a two-layer taxonomy (7 high-level + 27 fine-grained subclasses), 3414 instances across 17 legal categories and 6 task types, and path-localized metrics. It reveals a Right-Answer-Wrong-Reason pattern and clustering of hallucination types, demonstrating diagnostic value beyond outcome-level evaluation.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of current legal benchmarks that focus on single-turn QA and outcome-level metrics, by diagnosing how and where legal agents hallucinate along their reasoning and tool-use trajectories.
AI.method: Four-stage expert-in-the-loop data construction; large, diverse dataset (3414 instances, 17 categories, 6 tasks); dual-layer taxonomy (7 high-level, 27 fine-grained); design of path-localized, fine-grained metrics; evaluation on 18 proprietary/open-source agents.
AI.result: Identification of structured hallucination patterns; path-localized failure attribution; Right-Answer-Wrong-Reason effect; distinct agentic profiles shaped by task, category, and framework; diagnostic power exceeded traditional outcome metrics.
AI.conclusion: LexAgentHallu provides a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating agentic hallucination in law, enabling finer-grained analysis of error modalities along agent trajectories and facilitating more targeted improvements in tool-augmented legal AI.

title: Settling: Equilibrium Inference for Non-Convex Validity Sets
summary: Many learning systems return a single point estimate even when admissible outputs form disconnected or non-convex sets. Under squared loss, an ambiguous conditional distribution can therefore have a Bayes-optimal conditional mean that is invalid. We formalize this failure as conditional mean collapse and introduce Settling, an equilibrium-based inference operator that separates proposal generation, consistency evaluation, and test-time equilibrium selection. The operator treats a mean-seeking proposal as an initialization and refines it toward a locally stable configuration; conditional on initialization, refinement is deterministic. We establish exact-gradient descent, local convergence, and an inexact-gradient robustness condition relevant to learned consistency critics. In a reproducible 100-context geometric diagnostic, the mean-seeking baseline succeeds in 0/100 contexts, stochastic denoising in 100/100, and Settling in 99/100 while producing substantially lower trajectory roughness. A 1,200-run sensitivity study yields 97-100% success across obstacle-jitter ranges up to 0.20 and 94-100% across one-time initialization perturbations from 0.05 to 0.50. Cross-domain panels remain mechanism illustrations; learned high-dimensional validation remains an open empirical test.

AI.tldr: Introduces Settling, an equilibrium-based inference operator to prevent conditional mean collapse under squared loss by refining mean-seeking proposals to stable equilibria; shows near-perfect empirical robustness in a 100-context geometric diagnostic and broad sensitivity tests, with open high-dimensional validation.
AI.motivation: Under squared loss, admissible outputs can form disconnected/non-convex sets, causing the Bayes-optimal conditional mean to be invalid. This leads to conditional mean collapse where a single point estimate fails to capture multiple plausible outputs. The work formalizes this failure and proposes an inference mechanism (Settling) to separate proposal generation, consistency evaluation, and test-time equilibrium selection to obtain stable, plausible outputs.
AI.method: Introduce Settling: an equilibrium-based inference operator that separates proposal generation, consistency evaluation, and test-time equilibrium selection. It starts from a mean-seeking proposal and refines it toward a locally stable configuration; refinement is deterministic given the initialization. The approach includes exact-gradient descent, local convergence, and an inexact-gradient robustness condition for learned consistency critics. Experimental validation includes a reproducible 100-context geometric diagnostic (mean-seeking baseline 0/100, stochastic denoising 100/100, Settling 99/100) and a 1,200-run sensitivity study across obstacle-jitter and initialization perturbations.
AI.result: Settling achieves near-perfect robustness in the stated diagnostic: 99/100 success; mean-seeking baseline fails entirely; stochastic denoising succeeds fully. Across 1,200 runs, success rates are 97–100% for obstacle jitter up to 0.20 and 94–100% across initialization perturbations from 0.05 to 0.50. It yields substantially lower trajectory roughness than alternatives. Cross-domain panels illustrate mechanism; high-dimensional validation remains an open empirical test.
AI.conclusion: Settling provides a practical, robust inference mechanism to avoid conditional mean collapse under non-convex admissible outputs by separating proposal, consistency, and equilibrium selection and refining, with strong empirical performance in controlled diagnostics and broad robustness to perturbations. Validation in high-dimensional settings remains an important future step.

title: Future-Aware Flow Planning for Safe UAV Target Following
summary: UAV target following in cluttered environments is inherently predictive: current-state followers can lag behind turns, choose blocked corridors, or trade tracking for unsafe near-horizon motion. We propose a future-aware flow planning framework for state-informed UAV target following. Predicted target futures guide clean UAV trajectory generation as horizon-aligned residual signals, while risk-scored executable-prefix repair is embedded inside the sampling loop. On fixed ID/OOD receding-horizon benchmarks, the planner improves the intended safety--tracking trade-off rather than dominating every metric: it matches zero measured ID collision rate with the highest ID safe-tracking time, and gives the lowest OOD macro collision rate and final tracking error among the displayed methods, while Future-MPC remains smoother and stronger on some thresholded OOD success metrics under its hand-designed objective. Ablations show that future adaptation improves candidate generation before safety repair, and simulator-facing stress tests probe interface, sensing, and controller-execution effects. These results support horizon-aligned future adaptation and embedded prefix repair as complementary ingredients for safe UAV target following under the tested simulation conditions.

AI.tldr: Future-aware, horizon-aligned UAV target following with predictive target futures; integrates risk-aware, executable-prefix repair into sampling; achieves favorable safety-tracking trade-offs in receding-horizon benchmarks and ablations highlight the benefit of future adaptation before safety repair.
AI.motivation: Current state-only UAV followers lag during turns or in cluttered corridors, forcing unsafe near-horizon behavior or suboptimal tracking. A predictive, horizon-aligned planning approach is needed to balance safety and tracking in dynamic, cluttered environments.
AI.method: Proposes a future-aware flow planning framework where predicted target futures guide horizon-aligned trajectory generation via residual signals, with risk-scored executable-prefix repair embedded inside the sampling loop. Evaluated on fixed ID/OOD receding-horizon benchmarks.
AI.result: The planner improves the intended safety–tracking trade-off, matching zero ID collisions while achieving the highest ID safe-tracking time, and obtaining the lowest OOD macro collision rate and final tracking error among displayed methods. Future-MPC remains smoother and stronger on some OOD metrics. Ablations indicate future adaptation improves candidate generation before safety repair; stress tests probe interface, sensing, and controller-execution effects.
AI.conclusion: Horizon-aligned future adaptation and embedded prefix repair are complementary ingredients for safe UAV target following in the tested simulation conditions.

title: Cross-Species Animal Re-Identification with Semantic Consistency Learning
summary: Generalizable animal Re-Identification (ReID) aims to recognize individual animals across species with diverse morphologies and ecological contexts. Unlike person ReID, where different domains share similar body structures, animal species often exhibit drastically different anatomical structures and visual patterns, making it difficult to establish shared visual correspondences. As a result, representations learned across species tend to form fragmented embedding spaces, which severely limits cross-species generalization. To address this challenge, we propose Semantic Consistency Learning (SCL), a framework designed to learn representations that remain stable across appearance variations while preserving semantic structures shared across species. SCL consists of two complementary components. Foreground-Background Decoupled Spectral Normalization (FDSNorm) stabilizes feature statistics by suppressing environment-induced style variations in a region-aware manner, while Cross-species Neighborhood Modeling (CNM) captures transferable relational structures across species through dynamic feature neighborhoods. Extensive experiments on 11 public animal ReID datasets demonstrate that SCL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods under multiple cross-species evaluation protocols and generalizes effectively to previously unseen species and ecological domains. Code is available at https://github.com/Kemalau/ECCV-26-SCL.

AI.tldr: Introduce Semantic Consistency Learning (SCL) for generalizable animal ReID, with two components to stabilize features and model cross-species relations, achieving state-of-the-art across 11 datasets and unseen species.
AI.motivation: Cross-species generalization in animal ReID is challenging due to drastic anatomical differences that create fragmented embedding spaces; robust representations must be stable to appearance changes while preserving shared semantic structure across species.
AI.method: Two components: (1) Foreground-Background Decoupled Spectral Normalization (FDSNorm) to suppress environment-induced style variations in a region-aware way; (2) Cross-species Neighborhood Modeling (CNM) to capture transferable relational structures across species via dynamic feature neighborhoods.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 11 public animal ReID datasets show SCL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods under multiple cross-species evaluation protocols and generalizes to unseen species and ecological domains; code is released.
AI.conclusion: SCL provides a robust framework for cross-species animal ReID, balancing appearance invariance with semantic structure preservation and showing strong cross-domain generalization.

title: Procedural Memory Under Change: Reuse and Interference in Controlled Web Tasks
summary: Procedural memory lets language agents reuse successful routines, but reuse presumes that a stored routine remains applicable. We study what happens when that presumption is deliberately violated. The study combines a retrospective, human-assisted interface-adaptation case from BrowserGym TimeWarp with controlled frozen-memory comparisons on synthetic shopping decisions. During the documented WebShop V1-V6 development path, interface-specific code was adapted while the separately stored high-level procedure was not reported to change; this phase does not constitute an autonomous memory-agent evaluation. In the controlled phase, an early pilot produced one task on which two memory conditions selected a more expensive item while the no-memory condition selected the reference minimum. Follow-up probes did not establish a recurring row-order or identity-binding pattern. We then tested four forms of mismatch: changed quantities, a different evidence representation, a conflict between local and global optimization, and distributed promotion evidence, across 32 formal cells. Each cell used one temperature-0 generation with the same local qwen3:8b configuration and no adaptive retry. Across these pairs, none of the predefined diagnostic interference signatures appeared on the tasks for which they were defined when current-task evidence was explicit and sufficient. The result identifies a tested region of non-interference: a procedural memory can be mismatched without becoming behaviorally disruptive. It does not establish general safety or a mechanism. The remaining question is which additional conditions turn applicability mismatch into observable, memory-caused error.

AI.tldr: Procedural memory can be mismatched without immediate behavioral interference under controlled conditions; study identifies a non-interference region but does not establish safety or mechanisms, leaving open what conditions would turn mismatch into memory-caused errors.
AI.motivation: Assess how procedural memory reuse behaves when stored routines become inapplicable, and whether mismatches cause observable errors in memory-augmented agents.
AI.method: Retrospective, human-assisted interface-adaptation using BrowserGym TimeWarp; controlled frozen-memory comparisons on synthetic shopping decisions; development path V1–V6 with interface adaptations but stable high-level procedures; four mismatch forms (changed quantities, different evidence representation, conflict between local/global optimization, distributed promotion evidence) across 32 formal cells; each cell used a temperature-0 generation with the same local qwen3:8b configuration and no adaptive retry.
AI.result: Across task-cell pairs, predefined diagnostic interference signatures did not appear when current-task evidence was explicit and sufficient; evidence suggests a region of non-interference where procedural memory can be mismatched without immediate disruption.
AI.conclusion: The study does not establish general safety or mechanism for memory-applied mismatches; the remaining question is which additional conditions turn applicability mismatch into observable, memory-caused errors.

title: ALIGN-HOLD: Experience Alignment for Real-Time Hold Control in Large-Scale Ride-Hailing Matching at DiDi
summary:
Real-time hold control is a high-leverage mechanism in large-scale ride-hailing systems: by selectively deferring driver-order pairs, the platform can wait for better matching opportunities and improve end-to-end passenger-driver experience. Existing production systems such as EXHOLD learn bandit-based hold policies from handcrafted combinations of trip completion, cancellations, waiting time, and driver effort. However, designing such rewards becomes increasingly difficult as marketplace preferences are heterogeneous and observed passenger-driver behavior can be sparse, noisy, and affected by dynamic supply-demand conditions.
  We present ALIGN-HOLD, a production-scale experience alignment framework that learns hold policy from implicit marketplace preferences. ALIGN-HOLD constructs complementary preference pairs from order trajectories, driver trajectories, and contemporaneous local matching graphs, and trains an experience Reward Model (RM) using balanced multi-view sampling and model-adaptive hard preference sampling. During simulator-based policy learning, the frozen RM provides a dense, context-dependent reward and supports label-free filtering of low-identifiability interactions whose behavioral feedback is difficult to attribute to matching quality.
  We deploy ALIGN-HOLD on DiDi's ride-hailing platform and evaluate it in a 28-day randomized A/B experiment, covering approximately 100,000 passenger requests per day. Compared with the deployed production policy, ALIGN-HOLD achieves statistically significant improvements in trip completion rate and driver income, while significantly reducing passenger cancellations before and after driver acceptance. Complementary ablations, RM diagnostics, and behavioral analyses validate the contributions of the proposed components. ALIGN-HOLD has been fully ramped up and is currently serving DiDi's Brazil marketplace.

AI.tldr: ALIGN-HOLD learns real-time hold policies from implicit marketplace preferences, using a Reward Model trained with balanced multi-view sampling and hard preference sampling. It enables simulator-based policy learning and label-free filtering of low-identifiability interactions. Deployed on DiDi, it improves trip completion and driver income while reducing cancellations in a 28-day A/B across Brazil.
AI.motivation: Ride-hailing hold control can significantly impact user experience and platform efficiency, but existing reward designs are brittle in the face of heterogeneous preferences, sparse/noisy feedback, and dynamic supply-demand. There is a need to infer rewards from implicit marketplace signals rather than handcrafted surrogates.
AI.method: Construct complementary preference pairs from order trajectories, driver trajectories, and local matching graphs. Train an Experience Reward Model (RM) using balanced multi-view sampling and model-adaptive hard preference sampling. Use the frozen RM to provide dense, context-dependent rewards during simulator-based policy learning and to filter low-identifiability interactions. Deploy in production with Ab initio A/B evaluation and ablations.
AI.result: In 28 days, across ~100k passenger requests/day, ALIGN-HOLD improved trip completion rate and driver income, while reducing passenger cancellations before and after driver acceptance, compared to the deployed production policy. Complementary ablations and diagnostics validate component contributions. Fully deployed in DiDi’s Brazil marketplace.
AI.conclusion: ALIGN-HOLD demonstrates effective learning of hold policies from implicit preferences at production scale, with a robust reward signal and components that tolerate sparse/noisy feedback, achieving measurable improvements in key customer and driver metrics.

title: Multi-Robot Scanner for Automated Full-Body Dermoscopic Imaging
summary: This paper outlines the specifications and design approach used to construct a full body imaging scanner capable of capturing skin lesions at a dermatoscopic level using cameras mounted on the end-effectors of four UR10 manipulators. The system possesses a view-planning algorithm capable of appropriately selecting the best camera position to acquire images of moles, a high-level controller to allow the manipulators to work simultaneously and a collision-detector that halts the manipulators when they make contact with an object or a person. We evaluate the system through real-patient full-body scans, comparing acquired images against contact dermoscopy and an existing total-body photography system (Vectra) across clinically relevant lesion features, and quantify true optical resolving power using a USAF 1951 resolution target, yielding a smallest resolvable feature size of 22.1 microns for our scanner compared to 8.8 microns for contact dermoscopy. Results show the scanner consistently outperforms Vectra across most clinically relevant features and achieves comparable performance to contact dermoscopy for the majority of features assessed. By acquiring dermatoscopic-quality images automatically and without contact, and without requiring a separate manual dermoscopic examination, the scanner closes part of the gap between total-body photography and handheld dermoscopy, suggesting potential for future integration into screening workflows.

AI.tldr: A robotic four-arm full-body imaging system captures dermatoscopic-quality, non-contact skin lesion images using end-effector cameras, with view-planning, parallel manipulation, and collision detection; evaluated against contact dermoscopy and Vectra, achieving 22.1 µm resolution versus 8.8 µm for contact dermoscopy; generally outperforms Vectra and rivals contact dermoscopy for many features; supports integration into screening workflows.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between non-contact total-body photography and handheld dermoscopy by providing automated dermatoscopic-quality imaging over the full body without patient contact, to streamline screening workflows.
AI.method: Robotic platform with four UR10 manipulators carrying imaging cameras. A view-planning algorithm selects optimal camera positions; a high-level controller enables simultaneous multi-arm operation; a collision detector halts motion on contact. Evaluation on real-patient scans comparing against contact dermoscopy and the Vectra system, plus a USAF 1951 resolution target to quantify optical resolving power.
AI.result: Achieves 22.1 µm smallest resolvable feature; contact dermoscopy resolves 8.8 µm. The scanner outperforms Vectra on most clinically relevant features and is comparable to contact dermoscopy for the majority of assessed features.
AI.conclusion: Automated, non-contact dermatoscopic-quality full-body imaging can close part of the gap between total-body photography and handheld dermoscopy, with potential for integration into screening workflows.

title: VFNet: Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Model for Void Fraction Estimation in Gas-Liquid Two-Phase Flow
summary: Void fraction, which quantifies the proportion of the fluid flow volume occupied by the gas phase, is a key parameter in the characterization of gas-liquid two-phase flow. Existing estimation methods either rely on flow assumptions that do not generalize across different fluids or on intrusive sensing that disturbs the flow behavior. We propose VFNet, a dual-branch spatio-temporal neural network for void-fraction prediction from synchronized multi-view videos of two-phase flow. A local branch extracts features from confined spatial regions and fuses the synchronized dual views, while a spatio-temporal branch captures the global evolution of the flow across space and time to refine a coarse geometric estimate. Trained on simulated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) data with known ground-truth void fractions and evaluated against both learning-based and traditional baselines, VFNet achieves the best performance across a broad range of metrics and also improves downstream flow-pattern classification on real two-phase flow data.

AI.tldr: VFNet is a dual-branch spatio-temporal neural network that predicts void fraction from synchronized multi-view videos of two-phase flow, outperforming baselines and aiding downstream flow-pattern classification.
AI.motivation: Void fraction is a key metric for gas-liquid two-phase flow, but existing non-intrusive estimation methods either rely on flow-specific assumptions or disturb the flow. A generalizable, non-intrusive method using synchronized multi-view video and spatio-temporal modeling is needed.
AI.method: VFNet comprises a local branch that extracts features from confined spatial regions and fuses synchronized dual views, and a spatio-temporal branch that models the global space-time evolution to refine a coarse geometric estimate. It is trained on simulated CFD data with ground-truth void fractions and evaluated against learning-based and traditional baselines, with an emphasis on generalization to real data.
AI.result: VFNet achieves the best performance across multiple metrics compared to both learning-based and traditional baselines and also improves downstream flow-pattern classification on real two-phase flow data.
AI.conclusion: A dual-branch spatio-temporal architecture effectively estimates void fraction from multi-view videos, leveraging both local region features and global flow evolution; training on CFD data yields robust performance and improves downstream analyses.

title: Proof-Carrying Cognition: Closing the Verification Gap with Reality-Settled Reward
summary: Frontier gains in language-model reasoning come from reinforcement learning on reasoning traces and are concentrated in domains with a cheap, sound verifier. We argue the field's binding constraint is the verification gap: no scalable, incorruptible reward for reasoning outside formal domains. We make four contributions. (1) Theory: in a joint-Gaussian model of best-of-N selection, verifier-gold correlation rho is the exact exchange rate between test-time compute and capability, and an unsound verifier pays a polynomial penalty N^(1/rho^2); a margin-free copula form predicts realized soundness of real LLM judges to 4% median error. (2) Demonstration: in program-synthesis testbeds with executable ground truth, including a pre-registered scaled replication, unsound verifiers lose Soundness-under-Pressure as optimization grows (0.94 to 0.32 at N=4096) while a sound verifier improves monotonically; reality-anchored settlement beats a frozen verifier under i.i.d. and adversarial pressure, driving the hacking gap from ~0.27 to ~0; soundness scales log-linearly with settled labels, with on-policy settlement ~10x more label-efficient than random labeling. With real LLM judges and unit-test execution as gold, a weak judge loses soundness under best-of-N (p<0.001), a stronger judge is more robust, and selection alone manufactures +0.53 hacking gaps from honest samples. Under real GRPO training, a frozen reward model traces the full overoptimization curve (executed reward collapses 90%) while the same model refit on a 10% settlement stream preserves 6x the executed reward. (3) Paradigm: proof-carrying cognition, where reasoning steps are typed probabilistic claims priced by a self-built world model trained only on held-out reality and settled by proper scoring rules. (4) Benchmark: we specify Soundness-under-Pressure as the headline metric for a reality-settled reasoning benchmark.

AI.tldr: Verifier quality and feedback stability are the bottlenecks for RL-based reasoning in LLMs; the paper formalizes this, demonstrates robustness costs of unsound verifiers, and proposes a proof-carrying cognition paradigm with a reality-grounded, soundness-focused benchmark.
AI.motivation: Address the verification gap in LLM reasoning: lack of scalable, incorruptible rewards for reasoning beyond formal domains, which limits gains from reasoning traces.
AI.method: Theoretical model: joint-Gaussian Best-of-N with verifier-gold correlation rho; a copula form predicts real-world judge soundness. Empirical: program-synthesis testbeds with executable ground truth and a pre-registered replication; real LLM judges with unit-test gold under i.i.d. and adversarial pressure; GRPO training experiments; on-policy vs frozen settlement; measurement of soundness, hacking gap, label efficiency; development of proof-carrying cognition and a reality-settled benchmark.
AI.result: Unsound verifiers degrade soundness as optimization scales (e.g., 0.94 → 0.32 at N=4096); sound verifiers improve monotically. Reality-anchored settlement beats frozen verifiers; hacking gap falls from ~0.27 to 0; soundness scales roughly log-linearly with settled labels; on-policy settlement yields ~10x label efficiency. With real judges and unit tests, weak judges lose soundness under best-of-N; stronger judges show robustness; selection alone can create +0.53 hacking gaps. Under GRPO training, the reward model tracks the full overoptimization curve (90% collapse) but a 10% settlement refit preserves ~6x the reward. Towards a paradigm, proof-carrying cognition and a reality-settled reasoning benchmark via Soundness-under-Pressure.
AI.conclusion: The work advocates proof-carrying cognition and a soundness-focused, reality-grounded framework for evaluating and improving LLM reasoning. It introduces Soundness-under-Pressure as a headline metric and highlights the central role of verifiers in enabling robust, label-efficient reasoning in real-world settings.

title: Kernel-Complexity Edge Sanitization for Training-Free Defense against Structural Graph Attacks
comment: 12 pages. Accepted at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM 2026)
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse applications, yet they remain highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks that maliciously perturb graph structure. Existing defenses often lack rigorous theoretical grounding, rely on attack-specific heuristics, or require costly retraining procedures such as adversarial training. To address these limitations, we propose Kernel-Complexity Edge Sanitization (KCES), a training-free and model-agnostic framework for defending against structural attacks. KCES is built upon Graph Kernel Complexity (GKC), a principled metric derived from the graph Gram matrix that appears in a generalization upper bound on the GNN test error. From this bound, we define an edge-specific KC score that quantifies each edge's structural influence via its induced change in GKC. KCES then identifies and prunes high-KC edges, which are empirically enriched with adversarial perturbations under structural attacks, to mitigate their harmful impact. Computationally efficient and scalable, KCES operates as a lightweight preprocessing step without retraining and can be seamlessly integrated with existing defenses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KCES consistently outperforms representative robust baselines across diverse attack settings and scales effectively to large graphs. Supported by theoretical analysis and extensive empirical validation, KCES provides a principled and efficient framework for securing GNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/karpning/KCScore.

AI.tldr: KCES provides a training-free, model-agnostic defense against structural attacks on GNNs by pruning edges with high Graph Kernel Complexity (GKC) scores, derived from the graph Gram matrix bound on GNN generalization error.
AI.motivation: To overcome the lack of theory-grounded, training-free defenses for structural attacks on GNNs and avoid costly retraining like adversarial training.
AI.method: Define Graph Kernel Complexity (GKC) from the graph Gram matrix bound; compute an edge-specific KC score as the induced change in GKC when an edge is perturbed; prune edges with high KC scores as a preprocessing step; works without retraining and can be integrated with existing defenses.
AI.result: Empirically, KCES consistently outperforms representative robust baselines across diverse attack settings and scales to large graphs; supported by theoretical analysis and extensive empirical validation.
AI.conclusion: KCES offers a principled, efficient preprocessing defense for GNNs that is training-free and model-agnostic, with code available for replication.

title: Adaptive Shared Control with Online Bounded-Rational Human Behavior Estimation
summary: This work considers adaptive shared human-robot control for nonlinear control-affine systems, where the assumption of a fully rational human is relaxed and the robot adapts its assistance to observed boundedly rational human behavior. We use a level-k bounded-rationality model of the two-player game to construct a finite bank of candidate human and robot policies through alternating best-response computations, with the associated value functions and policies approximated using adaptive dynamic programming. During the shared-control interaction, state-transition residuals compare the measured system evolution with the trajectories predicted by the candidate human policies. The residuals are accumulated using a forgetting factor and mapped to a probabilistic human-behavior model over the finite candidate bank. Rather than selecting a single candidate or averaging stored robot policies, the robot computes a distribution-aware one-step best response by minimizing an expected cooperative cost over the complete estimated human behavior distribution. For a quadratic terminal-value approximation and Euler state propagation, this response admits a closed-form solution expressed in terms of the expected human input. The proposed methods are evaluated in simulations of a benchmark nonlinear system stabilization task, and of a planar manipulator shared control setup. The reported results show decreasing Kullback-Leibler divergence between the estimated and simulated human behavior distributions, and a lower accumulated running cost for the robot agent over the shared control interaction period, than the maximum-probability and probability-weighted alternative policies baseline.

AI.tldr: Adaptive shared-control for nonlinear control-affine systems with boundedly rational humans. Builds a finite bank of candidate policies, uses adaptive dynamic programming, and a distribution-aware one-step best response to minimize expected cost. Validated in simulations showing improved behavior modeling and reduced cost.
AI.motivation: Model human-robot interaction where humans are not fully rational. Exploit level-k bounded rationality to maintain cooperation; use distributional reasoning over a bank of candidate policies to improve adaptability and robustness.
AI.method: Construct a finite bank of candidate human and robot policies via alternating best-responses. Approximate value functions with adaptive dynamic programming. Use state-transition residuals between measured and predicted trajectories, accumulate with a forgetting factor, map to a probabilistic human-behavior distribution over the policy bank. Compute a distribution-aware one-step best response by minimizing an expected cooperative cost over the estimated human distribution; for quadratic terminal value and Euler propagation, obtain a closed-form solution in terms of the expected human input.
AI.result: Simulation experiments on a nonlinear system stabilization task and a planar manipulator shared-control setup show decreasing KL divergence between estimated and simulated human distributions. The proposed method yields lower accumulated running cost for the robot compared to maximum-probability and probability-weighted baselines.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a principled, distribution-aware approach to adaptive shared control under bounded-rational human behavior, improving alignment with observed behavior and reducing robot cost; demonstrated feasibility and potential for robust human-robot collaboration.

title: IAE-VTG: Interaction-Aligned Action-Entity Video Temporal Grounding
summary: Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) localizes the video segment that matches a natural-language query. Many queries describe an action performed by a particular entity. Existing methods often encode the query as a whole or use general video-text interactions, without explicitly checking whether the action and entity occur together. They may therefore select a segment that contains both concepts but not the event described by the query. We propose Interaction Aligned Action-Entity Video Temporal Grounding (IAE-VTG), which models this rela?tionship at both the representation and training assignment levels. First, the Fine-grained Disentangled Interaction Module (FDIM) separates action and entity related query information and aligns it with complementary motion and appearance features. It then combines token-level interactions to build representations that capture the relationship between the action and entity. Second, Interaction-Sensitive Assignment (ISA) adds this interaction evidence to bipartite matching, so training targets are selected using both temporal overlap and semantic compatibility. This reduces supervision from temporally plausible but semantically incorrect proposals. Experiments on QVHighlights, Charades?STA, and TACoS show that IAE-VTG consistently improves strong baselines and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on standard grounding metrics. Additional analyses show that the method is especially effective when similar actions or entities appear at multiple times and produces more reliable assignments for complex events.

AI.tldr: IAE-VTG introduces a two-stage approach to VTG: a Fine-grained Disentangled Interaction Module (FDIM) to align action and entity cues with motion and appearance, and an Interaction-Sensitive Assignment (ISA) to enforce semantic compatibility during training, yielding better grounding performance across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing VTG methods often rely on holistic query representations and temporal overlap, which can yield semantically incorrect proposals where the action and entity do not co-occur as described. There is a need to explicitly model action-entity co-occurrence and incorporate semantic compatibility into supervision.
AI.method: FDIM disentangles action- and entity-related query components and aligns them with complementary motion and appearance features, building token-level interactions to capture action–entity relationships. ISA integrates these interactions into the bipartite matching training objective by selecting targets based on both temporal overlap and semantic compatibility, reducing supervision from temporally plausible but semantically wrong proposals.
AI.result: IAE-VTG consistently improves strong baselines on QVHighlights, Charades-STA, and TACoS, achieving competitive or state-of-the-art performance on standard grounding metrics. Analyses show enhanced robustness when similar actions or entities appear at multiple times and more reliable assignments for complex events.
AI.conclusion: Modeling action–entity interactions at both representation and training assignment levels yields more semantically coherent VTG, reduces incorrect proposals, and generalizes well across datasets.

title: UnitBoost: Managing Compound LLM Systems with a Merge Operator, Not a Model
summary: Compound LLM systems often solve a coordination problem by adding a higher-level LLM. The resulting meta-agent reads workers' outputs, writes the final answer, allocates later calls, and decides when to stop. It is expressive, but it also concentrates three control decisions in an opaque, order-sensitive model call. We ask whether the manager needs to be generative at all. UnitBoost replaces that model with a defined meta-level operator: a task-given unit map turns worker outputs into slot-value proposals, a constrained argmax assembles the output, and the slots left unfilled or unsupported become an explicit residual for the next round. The operator is order-free, records unit provenance, and gives a simple guarantee: without coupling constraints, unit-wise maximization under the same admission score dominates selection of any complete candidate. On three held-out benchmarks, it exceeds the best single candidate chosen with gold labels by 0.060-0.195 absolute task-score points and input-matched generative managers by 0.048-0.076. Replacing only the management step improves six compound-system configurations by 0.013-0.182. Residual-directed rounds raise FanOutQA cell F1 from 0.4778 to 0.5524; matched controls show that the true residual outperforms random targets and ordinary rereading, while a label-free supply signal flags exhaustion after one unproductive round. The same analysis measures three conditions in which no such gain is available (one indivisible unit, unavailable unit identity, and an endpoint that charges for every emitted unit) and quantifies cross-unit coupling as a repair cost. The manager gives up semantic freedom and gains order invariance, unit provenance, and testable failure conditions.

AI.tldr: UnitBoost replaces a generative meta-manager in multi-LLM systems with a non-generative meta-operator that maps unit outputs to slot-value proposals, uses a constrained argmax, and propagates residuals; it yields robust improvements and explicit failure signals in compound LLM systems.
AI.motivation: Reduce opacity, order sensitivity, and semantic overreach of a generative meta-agent; provide provenance-tracked, order-free coordination with testable failure conditions and residual-driven iterations.
AI.method: Define a meta-level operator: a task-given unit map converts worker outputs into slot-value proposals; a constrained argmax assembles the final output; unfilled/unsupported slots become an explicit residual for the next round. The operator is order-free and records unit provenance. Evaluate on three held-out benchmarks, compare to gold-label best single candidate and input-matched generative managers, and analyze residual-directed rounds, three degenerate conditions (indivisible unit, unavailable unit identity, and endpoint pricing), and cross-unit repair costs.
AI.result: UnitBoost yields 0.060–0.195 absolute task-score improvements over the best single candidate with gold labels and 0.048–0.076 over input-matched generative managers; modifying only the management step improves six compound-system configurations by 0.013–0.182. In FanOutQA, F1 rises from 0.4778 to 0.5524; residual targets outperform random targets and rereading; a label-free supply signal flags exhaustion after a single unproductive round. The three degenerate cases show where gains may vanish, and cross-unit coupling is quantified as a repair cost.
AI.conclusion: The manager sacrifices semantic freedom in exchange for order invariance, unit provenance, and testable failure conditions, while unit-wise maximization under the same admission score can dominate complete candidate selection in the absence of coupling constraints.

title: EFQ-Softmax: Exp-Free Quantization for Softmax
summary: Low-bit attention accelerates Transformer inference by moving the $QK^\top$ and $PV$ matrix multiplications to FP8 or FP4 matrix engines. However, the softmax path often evaluates shifted-score exponentials in higher precision, forms a temporary probability block, and quantizes it before low-bit $PV$ multiplication. This exp-then-quantize path creates a mismatch between a high-precision probability producer and a low-bit matrix consumer. We propose EFQ-Softmax (Exp-Free Quantization for Softmax), a low-bit probability-generation method that directly maps shifted attention scores to block-scaled E2M1 operands. For each microscaling block, EFQ-Softmax selects an exponent-only scale from the local maximum, maps the shifted scores to a normalized residual domain, and generates nonnegative E2M1 probability codes using a single affine rule. The resulting operand is used consistently in both the $\widetilde{P}V$ numerator update and the $\widetilde{P}\mathbf{1}$ denominator update. The FlashAttention-style row-maximum update, historical rescaling, high-precision accumulation, and final normalization remain unchanged. We evaluate end-to-end quality on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and WAN2.2-TI2V-5B, and separately measure kernel-level performance on the A5 vector unit. EFQ-Softmax improves the Qwen3-8B seven-task mean from 0.6749 with MXFP4 to 0.6773 and the Qwen3-VL nine-task mean from 0.7826 to 0.8000. On WAN2.2, it maintains temporal consistency and visual quality comparable to the FP16 and MXFP4 baselines under VBench. On the A5 vector unit, EFQ-Softmax reduces the vector-stage latency of the fused probability-generation kernel by 40.33% on average across sequence lengths from 16K to 128K. These results show that direct low-bit probability generation can replace the conventional exp-then-quantize path while preserving end-to-end model quality.

AI.tldr: A low-bit EFQ-Softmax method for Transformer attention that maps shifted scores directly to nonnegative E2M1 probability codes, eliminating exp-then-quantize mismatch and enabling end-to-end low-bit inference with preserved accuracy and notable speedups.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between high-precision probability production and low-bit PV computation in low-bit attention by enabling direct low-bit probability generation.
AI.method: Introduce EFQ-Softmax (Exp-Free Quantization for Softmax). For each microscaling block, select an exponent-only scale from the local maximum, map shifted scores to a normalized residual domain, and generate nonnegative E2M1 probability codes via a single affine rule. The same operand is used for both the PV numerator update and the 1-denominator update. Maintains FlashAttention-style row-maximum update, historical rescaling, high-precision accumulation, and final normalization.
AI.result: End-to-end quality improvements on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and WAN2.2-TI2V-5B. Kernel-level performance gains on the A5 vector unit, with fused probability-generation latency reduced by 40.33% on average across sequence lengths 16K–128K.
AI.conclusion: Direct low-bit probability generation can replace the exp-then-quantize path without sacrificing end-to-end model quality; EFQ-Softmax yields measurable quality gains and substantial speedups.

title: CougarTail & CUB: A General-Purpose Mast and Central Utility Board for Cylindrical Underwater Enclosures
summary: Cylindrical watertight enclosures are widely used across various underwater systems, from unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs), to remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), to various sensor platforms. However, electronics are typically built on rectangular PCBs arranged in horizontal stacks, which inefficiently occupy the circular cross-section volume that is critical for both payload capacity and buoyancy management. This paper presents CUB (Central Utility Board) and CougarTail, a general-purpose system designed to address this gap. CUB is a circular PCB sized for 4-inch-diameter enclosures that consolidates a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 (CM5) and an STM32 microcontroller, while also providing power management features and auxiliary connections. Mounted coaxially, CUB reduces the electronics stack of our CougUV from 200 mm of tube length and 709 g to 25 mm and 156 g, returning that length and mass budget to payload and buoyancy trim. CougarTail is an open-source companion sensor mast that houses a GPS antenna and two dual-band (2.4 and 5 GHz) omnidirectional PCB antennas. Both components are validated through bench testing and integration on a CougUV platform, our small open-sourced torpedo UUVs.

AI.tldr: Circular Central Utility Board (CUB) and CougarTail reduce electronics footprint in cylindrical UUV enclosures by using a circular 4-inch PCB and an open-source sensor mast, dramatically saving space and mass.
AI.motivation: Rectangular PCB stacks waste circular cross-section in cylindrical watertight enclosures, limiting payload capacity and buoyancy; a compact, integrated electronics solution is needed for UUVs.
AI.method: CUB is a circular 4-inch-diameter PCB housing a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 and an STM32 MCU with power management and IO; mounted coaxially to shrink the electronics stack. CougarTail is an open-source sensor mast housing a GPS antenna and two dual-band (2.4/5 GHz) PCB antennas.
AI.result: Bench-tested and integrated on CougUV; electronics stack shortened from 200 mm to 25 mm; mass reduced from 709 g to 156 g, reclaiming payload and buoyancy margin.
AI.conclusion: Provides a general-purpose, open-source packaging solution for cylindrical UUV enclosures, enabling greater payload capacity and buoyancy management; validated on small torpedo-like UUVs (CougUV).

title: Distilling Image Prototypes for Guided Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enhances the robustness of models against distribution shifts but faces two critical challenges: error accumulation from noisy pseudo-labels and catastrophic forgetting of source knowledge. Uncertainty-based approaches designed to mitigate error accumulation often yield overconfident or computationally expensive estimates, while strategies intended to prevent forgetting via prototype replay rely on static representations that easily become misaligned as the model adapts. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel framework, Distilling Image Prototype for Guided Test-Time Adaptation (DIPTTA). The core of the proposed approach is the introduction of a Distill Image Prototype (DIP), a compact set of synthetic images that serves as a dynamic and regenerative anchor of source knowledge. This prototype enables a dynamic feature replay mechanism that continuously generates feature prototypes aligned with the current state of the model, thus effectively preventing catastrophic forgetting. Furthermore, the DIP anchors a source-calibrated uncertainty estimation method, which provides a less biased measure of sample reliability by leveraging stable source knowledge, thereby robustly suppressing error accumulation. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DIPTTA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly under severe domain shifts. The source code is available at https://github.com/LiwenWang919/DIPTTA.

AI.tldr: Proposes DIPTTA, a test-time adaptation framework using a Distill Image Prototype to provide dynamic feature replay and source-calibrated uncertainty, improving robustness to domain shifts.
AI.motivation: Addresses error accumulation from noisy pseudo-labels and catastrophic forgetting in Test-Time Adaptation. Existing uncertainty-based approaches can be overconfident or computationally expensive, and prototype replay methods rely on static representations that misalign during adaptation.
AI.method: Introduces Distill Image Prototype (DIP): a compact set of synthetic images that serve as a dynamic, regenerative anchor of source knowledge. Uses DIP for (i) dynamic feature replay aligned with the current model state to prevent forgetting, and (ii) source-calibrated uncertainty estimation leveraging stable source knowledge to curb error accumulation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show DIPTTA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, especially under severe domain shifts.
AI.conclusion: DIPTTA provides a dynamic, regenerative source-knowledge anchor via Distill Image Prototypes and a calibrated uncertainty mechanism, yielding robust test-time adaptation. Source code available at the provided GitHub link.

title: The Era by Eon Benchmark: A Generated Enterprise Estate with Exact Ground Truth for Benchmarking LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents for enterprise systems of record cannot be evaluated on customer production data, and no existing substitute provides ground truth. We present the Era by Eon Benchmark for evaluating LLM agents that use enterprise tools. The benchmark is built around a complete fictional company. It includes product simulators, company-specific internal databases, benchmark questions, and computed answer keys. Industry, company size, business model, application portfolio, and a seed define each company. One seeded entity graph supplies shared company data to simulators of Salesforce, Zendesk, Slack, Gong, and other products. A questionconditioned generator creates the schemas and records for internal databases. It takes shared entities, keys, and values from the same graph before generating database-specific facts. Both mechanisms therefore describe one consistent enterprise estate. Every expected answer is computed from the final records, so grading is exact. Design and answer-key checks validate the internal databases. A realism scorecard and adversarial detector validate the entity graph. Across 23 generated companies, the mean realism score rose from 61.8 to 97.0, with zero records flagged as synthetic. In the reported simulator-track comparison, nine models answered the same 33 questions three times each. Accuracy estimates ranged from 42.4% to 76.8%, and three of 36 pairwise differences remained supported after correction.

AI.tldr: A ground-truth, enterprise-focused benchmark (Era by Eon) uses a fully synthetic but realistic enterprise estate to evaluate LLM agents with enterprise tools, enabling exact grading across 23 companies and multiple tools; results show varying model accuracy and strong realism validation.
AI.motivation: To enable objective evaluation of LLM agents operating on enterprise systems of record without exposing or relying on real customer data, by providing a consistent, ground-truth benchmark with realistic, verifiable data.
AI.method: Build a fictitious company with seed-defined industry/size/model; generate a shared entity graph; simulate a suite of enterprise tools (Salesforce, Zendesk, Slack, Gong, etc.) with internal databases created by a question-conditioned generator that uses the entity graph; produce computed answer keys from final records; validate schemas with design and answer-key checks; assess realism via a scorecard and detect synthetic entities with an adversarial detector; evaluate 23 generated companies using 33 questions answered thrice by nine models, and compare accuracy with statistical correction.
AI.result: Realism improved from 61.8 to 97.0 across the 23 companies, with no records flagged as synthetic; model accuracy on the 33 questions ranged 42.4%–76.8%, and 3 of 36 pairwise model differences remained statistically significant after correction.
AI.conclusion: The Era by Eon Benchmark provides a rigorous, ground-truth benchmark for evaluating LLM agents against enterprise toolchains, enabling exact grading and robust realism validation; it reveals substantial performance variability across models and demonstrates a scalable, configurable approach adaptable to other enterprise toolsets.

title: EEGBind: Detecting Source-Level Interictal Epileptiform Discharges via EEG-Centric Multimodal Binding
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '26)
summary: Source-level analysis of interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) is relevant to presurgical evaluation and treatment planning because it helps characterize where epileptiform activity is likely to arise. Beyond detecting whether an IED is present, this setting requires assigning IED-positive activity to clinically meaningful brain-region categories. This setting is challenging because source-region evidence in short electroencephalography (EEG) windows can be subtle, partial, and affected by subject variability, class imbalance, and imperfect multimodal context. We present EEGBind, an EEG-centric multimodal binding framework for five-class source-level IED classification. EEGBind treats EEG as the primary modality and binds synchronized video-context features around an EEG-centric representation. Instead of relying on early or overly strong multimodal fusion, which may perturb the source-sensitive EEG representation, EEGBind uses video context as auxiliary evidence for robust classification. A view-consistent repair stage is further used to improve hidden-set robustness while preserving the learned source-class boundary. On the NeuroMM 2026 Grand Challenge Track 3 NMM-Source-IED benchmark, EEGBind achieves 0.8395 on weighted-F1 and outperforms strong competitors. These results support EEG-centric multimodal binding as a practical strategy for source-level IED classification. The open-source code is available at https://github.com/HKUSTGZ-ML4Health-Lab/NeuroMM2026_IED_Detection.

AI.tldr: EEGBind: an EEG-centric multimodal binding method for five-class source-level IED classification using synchronized video context; achieves 0.8395 weighted-F1 on NeuroMM 2026 benchmark; includes view-consistent repair; open-source.
AI.motivation: Precise localization of interictal activity for presurgical planning; challenges include subtle/partial source-level evidence, subject variability, class imbalance, and imperfect multimodal context; EEG is the primary modality.
AI.method: EEG is treated as the primary modality and is bound with synchronized video-context features around an EEG-centric representation. Avoids early or overly strong multimodal fusion to prevent perturbing EEG representations; incorporates a view-consistent repair stage to improve robustness of hidden-set classification while preserving the source-class boundary.
AI.result: 0.8395 weighted-F1 on NeuroMM 2026 Grand Challenge Track 3 NMM-Source-IED benchmark; outperforms strong competitors.
AI.conclusion: EEG-centric multimodal binding is a practical and effective strategy for source-level IED classification; code is open-source.

title: FolDeX: A Physical-World Benchmark for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects
summary: Embodied AI, including vision-language-action and world-action models, must operate reliably in the physical world. Yet methods that perform well in simulation can degrade substantially on real robots, especially in long-horizon deformable-object manipulation, where policies must track changing states and execute reliable multi-stage bimanual interactions. Existing real-robot benchmarks mainly focus on short-horizon rigid-object tasks and offer limited coverage of long-horizon deformable manipulation. We introduce FolDeX, a physical-world benchmark built entirely from real-robot data, with garment folding as its primary task. Since real-robot data collection is costly, FolDeX studies how heterogeneous physical experience can be reused efficiently. The benchmark is organized around four research axes: leveraging human intervention and recovery data collected during deployment; transferring data across tasks, including across garment categories and from rigid to deformable-object manipulation; reusing data across scenes with changes in lighting, background, and layout; and transferring data across robotic embodiments. FolDeX provides 2,000+ hours of real-robot data spanning 20+ tasks and 10+ embodiments. We also establish a fair real-robot evaluation platform for externally submitted policies, with standardized tasks, held-out physical objects, controlled initializations, and a unified execution protocol. The platform is publicly accessible at https://ai.midea.com/#/fold-challenge. We hope FolDeX will serve as a unified testbed for heterogeneous real-robot data reuse and reliable long-horizon deformable manipulation.

AI.tldr: FolDeX is a real-robot benchmark for long-horizon deformable-object manipulation (garment folding), offering 2,000+ hours of data across 20+ tasks and 10+ embodiments, with data reuse across interventions, tasks, scenes, and embodiments, plus a fair evaluation platform; publicly available.
AI.motivation: Real-world performance gaps after sim-to-real transfer for long-horizon deformable manipulation; existing benchmarks emphasize short-horizon rigid tasks; costly real-robot data necessitates efficient reuse and broad coverage.
AI.method: Build FolDeX from real-robot data focused on garment folding; define four research axes for data reuse: intervention/recovery data; cross-task and cross-category transfer (rigid to deformable); cross-scene reuse with lighting/background/layout changes; cross-embodiment transfer. Provide 2,000+ hours across 20+ tasks and 10+ embodiments. Establish a fair evaluation platform with standardized tasks, held-out objects, controlled initializations, and unified execution protocol; make public at provided URL.
AI.result: Contributes a new real-robot benchmark and evaluation platform enabling heterogeneous data reuse and long-horizon deformable manipulation; demonstrates potential for transfer and generalization via the dataset and protocol.
AI.conclusion: FolDeX is proposed as a unified testbed for heterogeneous real-robot data reuse and reliable long-horizon deformable manipulation; aims to accelerate progress by providing real-robot data and a standardized evaluation.

title: MethaneFuse: Learning from Multi-Sensor Satellite Observations for Methane Plume Detection
summary:
Methane plume detection from satellite imagery is constrained by incomplete observations: public satellites provide complementary spatial, spectral, and atmospheric evidence, but real plume cases rarely contain fully paired multi-sensor measurements because of revisit schedules, cloud coverage, acquisition quality, and the transient nature of emissions. Most learning-based detectors rely on single-sensor inputs, especially Sentinel-2 (S2), leaving many reported plume cases unusable.
  We construct MethaneUnion, a temporal multi-sensor dataset built from Carbon Mapper plume reports and matched S2, Landsat 8/9 (L8/9), EMIT, and Sentinel-5P (S5P) observations. Built on MethaneUnion, MethaneFuse learns from heterogeneous satellite observations under partial sensor availability without requiring complete four-sensor measurements.
  MethaneUnion expands usable coverage from 3,211 valid S2-matched plume cases to 8,981 reported plume cases with multi-sensor observations. At the representative 480 m setting, MethaneFuse achieves 84.87 F1 and 93.62 AUROC, improving over the strongest baseline by 5.65 F1 and 8.30 AUROC points while reducing false positives by 8.19 points. Sensor-availability experiments show that MethaneFuse improves detection when S2 is available and transfers plume knowledge to L8/9, EMIT, and S5P when S2 is unavailable. These results demonstrate the value of learning from incomplete heterogeneous sensor observations for practical methane plume detection.

AI.tldr: Temporal multi-sensor methane plume dataset MethaneUnion enables robust detection with partial sensor availability via MethaneFuse, improving coverage and detection performance over single-sensor baselines.
AI.motivation: Public satellites offer complementary evidence for methane plumes but rarely provide fully paired multi-sensor data due to revisit schedules, clouds, and transient emissions. Learning from incomplete heterogeneous sensor observations is needed to improve practical plume detection.
AI.method: Construct MethaneUnion by linking Carbon Mapper plume reports with matched observations from Sentinel-2, Landsat 8/9, EMIT, and Sentinel-5P. Train MethaneFuse to learn from heterogeneous sensor inputs without requiring complete four-sensor measurements (i.e., partial modality availability) and evaluate at 480 m resolution.
AI.result: Expansion of usable plume cases from 3,211 (S2-only matches) to 8,981 with multi-sensor observations. MethaneFuse achieves 84.87 F1 and 93.62 AUROC at 480 m, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.65 F1 and 8.30 AUROC and reducing false positives by 8.19. Sensor-availability experiments show better detection with S2 and knowledge transfer to L8/9, EMIT, and S5P when S2 is unavailable.
AI.conclusion: Learning from incomplete heterogeneous sensor observations is valuable for practical methane plume detection. MethaneFuse provides robust cross-sensor performance and improves detection under partial sensor availability.

title: Shifting Relational Paradigms for Affective Computing: Affective Resonance, Vitality Affects, and Vocal Interaction Fields
comment: Accepted at Interspeech 2026 for poster presentation. 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
summary: Affective computing has largely followed an individual-state paradigm, extracting discrete emotion labels or arousal/valence from isolated speakers. We argue this framing is incomplete for interaction. Drawing on affective resonance and vitality-contour accounts, we propose a relational framework in which the primary unit of affective analysis is the interactional field constituted within vocal dynamics. As a proof of concept, we present a preliminary empirical study using continuous self-supervised speech representations to detect directional expressive coupling in multi-party conversation. Coupling is regime-specific, concentrated at sub-second timescales, and collapses under exclusive-speech negative controls, consistent with a relational account of affective dynamics. We introduce design frameworks for Artificial Affective Resonance Intelligence grounded in Affective Resonance Dynamic Ontologies, supported by null-calibrated directional coupling analyses across interaction regimes.

AI.tldr: Proposes a relational, interaction-centric framework for affective dynamics in vocal interaction, moving beyond isolated emotion labels to an interactional field; provides a preliminary multi-party study showing sub-second, regime-specific directional expressive coupling via continuous self-supervised speech representations, and outlines design frameworks for Artificial Affective Resonance Intelligence based on affective resonance ontologies and null-calibrated coupling analyses.
AI.motivation: Current affective computing largely adopts an individual-state paradigm, focusing on discrete emotions or arousal/valence for isolated speakers. This misses the interactional, field-level dynamics that emerge in conversations.
AI.method: Introduce a relational framework grounded in affective resonance and vitality-contour theories; conduct a preliminary empirical study using continuous self-supervised speech representations to detect directional expressive coupling in multi-party conversation; assess coupling across interaction regimes and under negative controls; propose null-calibrated directional coupling analyses.
AI.result: Findings indicate coupling is regime-specific, concentrated at sub-second timescales, and collapses under exclusive-speech negative controls, supporting a relational perspective on affective dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Propose design frameworks for Artificial Affective Resonance Intelligence and Affective Resonance Dynamic Ontologies, supported by null-calibrated directional coupling analyses across interaction regimes.

title: Fine-Tuning a KV Cache Concatenation-Aware Model or Recomputing KV Caches? Why Not Both?
summary: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, a large number of retrieved chunks are concatenated to form the input context so that users can receive high-quality responses based on external knowledge. As a result, the input context length increases substantially, leading to a larger prefill workload and, in turn, a longer time to first token (TTFT). While previous works that reuse precomputed key-value (KV) caches effectively reduce TTFT for long-context inputs, it remains unclear whether response quality is preserved when the input context becomes very long. In this paper, we propose a combined approach that (i) fine-tunes the model while taking KV cache concatenation into account and (ii) selectively recomputes a subset of the KV caches. By applying both techniques, we demonstrate improved accuracy for long-context inputs. Experiments on the RULER benchmark show that, for a 124k-token input, our method improves the RULER score by 9.7 point over the baseline that recomputes KV caches only. Moreover, TTFT is reduced by 80% compared with full attention.

AI.tldr: A two-fold approach—KV-cache concatenation-aware fine-tuning and selective KV-cache recomputation—improves long-context RAG performance. On 124k-token inputs (RULER), it gains 9.7 points in RULER score over a KV-recompute baseline and cuts time-to-first-token by 80% vs full attention.
AI.motivation: Long-context retrieval-augmented generation scales input size, increasing prefill and TTFT. While KV-cache reuse can speed up inference, it may degrade answer quality for very long contexts. There is a need to preserve response quality while achieving substantial latency reductions.
AI.method: 1) Fine-tune the model with explicit consideration of concatenated KV caches in the attention mechanism. 2) Implement selective recomputation of a subset of KV caches during inference, rather than recomputing all. Evaluate on the RULER benchmark with extremely long inputs (up to 124k tokens). Compare to baselines that recompute KV caches only and to full attention.
AI.result: For 124k-token inputs, the proposed method improves the RULER score by 9.7 points over the baseline that recomputes KV caches only, and reduces TTFT by 80% compared with full attention.
AI.conclusion: Joint KV-cache-aware fine-tuning and selective KV recomputation effectively preserve or improve answer quality for very long inputs while delivering substantial latency reductions, suggesting practical viability for long-context RAG deployments.

title: SwingBot: Learning Whole-Body Brachiation for Humanoid Robots
summary: Brachiation enables primates to move across overhead supports when ground paths are blocked, suggesting a complementary locomotion mode for robots operating in cluttered or hazardous environments. Bringing this capabil?ity to high-DoF humanoid robots is difficult because the controller must discover a long-horizon release-swing-capture sequence, coordinate alternating contacts with whole-body momentum, and act without reliable measurements of segment?relative displacement or hook-contact state. We present SwingBot, a learning framework for continuous humanoid brachiation with passive wrist hooks. Swing?Bot makes the task trainable by organizing learning around the structure of brachi?ation: biomimetic keyframes make rare release-swing-capture transitions reach?able during early exploration, and recurrent privileged-state estimation provides compact position and contact latents for deployment. Hardware experiments demonstrate continuous bar traversal and robustness to payload, external distur?bances and different bar spacings, showing that this formulation offers a practical route to whole-body robotic brachiation.

AI.tldr: SwingBot enables continuous humanoid brachiation with passive wrist hooks via a learning framework that leverages biomimetic keyframes and privileged-state estimation, demonstrated on hardware across varying bars and payloads.
AI.motivation: Brachiation offers a complementary locomotion mode for robots in cluttered or hazardous environments; high-DoF humanoid robots face long-horizon control with uncertain contact states and measurements, hindering practical deployment.
AI.method: Organize learning around brachiation structure using biomimetic keyframes to enable rare release-swing-capture transitions during early exploration, and use recurrent privileged-state estimation to learn compact position and contact latent representations for deployment, with passive wrist hooks.
AI.result: Hardware experiments show continuous bar traversal and robustness to payload, external disturbances, and different bar spacings, indicating the approach is a practical route to whole-body robotic brachiation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SwingBot framework provides a viable, trainable path to continuous humanoid brachiation with passive hooks, addressing long-horizon coordination and uncertain sensing, and enabling robust performance on hardware.

title: LogiScope-VQA: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Logistics Hazard Identification in Industrial Scenarios
summary: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) large-scale deployment in industrial warehouse settings specifically necessitates that models exhibit human-expert-level hazard-oriented perception, understanding, and reasoning capabilities.
