However, the scarcity of real industrial data, tightly coupled to commercial terms, significantly hampers further advancement. To bridge this gap, we curate LogiScope-VQA to investigate the practical applicability of mainstream LMMs in real-world logistics operations. LogiScope-VQA comprises 2,476 images and 2,918 videos primarily sourced from real-world logistics parks, along with 10,274 VQAs meticulously curated and validated by human annotators. Grounded in 18 core objects and 20 risk types, we devise 39 subtasks aligned with three principal themes: industrial element perception, warehouse knowledge understanding, and potential risk reasoning. Furthermore, we incorporate dynamic thinking-budget configurations and dual-dimensional risk bias analyses to elucidate the properties of LMMs. Extensive experiments unveil that even powerful proprietary models, including GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Claude-Opus-4.7, exhibit a significant gap relative to human performance. The unique challenge of jointly integrating perception, understanding, and reasoning for hazard identification poses substantial headroom for further improvement on LogiScope-VQA. We additionally reveal the pervasive security bias issue that impedes LLMs' practical deployment in real-world settings. The industrial dataset is publicly available under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.

AI.tldr: This work introduces LogiScope-VQA, a large-scale, real-world logistics benchmark combining images, videos, and 10,274 VQA pairs to evaluate hazard-oriented perception, understanding, and reasoning in LMMs; it reveals substantial gaps between current models and human performance and highlights security biases; the dataset is publicly available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
AI.motivation: To overcome the scarcity of real industrial data and enable hazard-aware perception and reasoning in large multimodal models, facilitating safe and practical deployment in warehouse operations.
AI.method: Constructed LogiScope-VQA with 2,476 images and 2,918 videos sourced from real logistics parks, annotated with 10,274 VQA pairs. Grounded on 18 core objects and 20 risk types, the dataset defines 39 subtasks spanning industrial element perception, warehouse knowledge understanding, and hazard risk reasoning. The authors also incorporate dynamic thinking-budget configurations and dual-dimensional risk bias analyses to study LMM properties.
AI.result: Experiments show that powerful proprietary LMMs (e.g., GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-Opus-4.7) still lag behind human performance in hazard-oriented tasks. The joint requirement of perception, understanding, and reasoning presents a substantial headroom for improvement; a pervasive security bias is identified that hampers practical deployment.
AI.conclusion: LogiScope-VQA provides a challenging, real-world benchmark underscoring the need for advances in perception–understanding–reasoning integration and bias mitigation for hazardous scenario analysis in logistics. The dataset is publicly available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 to foster community evaluation and development.

title: AgentAudit: An Open, Extensible Framework for Full-Lifecycle Trust Evaluation of AI Agents
summary: Existing evaluation frameworks mostly assess only one part of AI agents, such as task completion (AgentBench) or security robustness (AgentDojo, ASB), rather than the complete pipeline of planning, tool selection, tool execution, memory and reasoning. Failures can occur at any stage, yet existing benchmarks rarely identify their precise source. AgentAudit evaluates the entire execution trace across ten capability, grounding, security and behavioural dimensions, namely instruction integrity, planner, memory, tool selection, tool invocation, tool correctness, alignment, tool faithfulness, security and execution integrity, combined with behavioural classification and failure attribution to pinpoint the exact stage responsible for an observed failure. AgentAudit can evaluate any LLM-based AI agent, since it attaches to the agent instead of replacing it. It reads only the recorded execution trace and does not interfere with how the agent runs, so it places no constraint on the agent's internal implementation. We evaluate five language models (OpenAI GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 5, Sarvam 105B, Llama 3.3 70B and Gemini 2.5 Flash) across nine capability and adversarial tasks. Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5 obtain the highest mean Composite Trust Scores (95.1 and 80.6 out of 100, respectively), while Sarvam 105B, Llama 3.3 70B and Gemini 2.5 Flash trail substantially (57.6, 45.7 and 22.6). All traces were scored by a single fixed judge model, which was itself one of the evaluated models, a limitation discussed in Section VII.E. More importantly, models with similar task-completion behaviour can diverge sharply in trustworthiness, as several non-frontier models are repeatedly classified Unsafe_Compliance on adversarial tasks rather than merely failing them, a distinction that pass/fail benchmarks cannot surface.

AI.tldr: AgentAudit evaluates full execution traces of LLM-based agents across ten capability, grounding, security, and behavioural dimensions to identify the exact stage causing failures, offering non-intrusive, end-to-end assessment that goes beyond task completion benchmarks; results show significant trustworthiness differences among models and limitations due to single-judge evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks typically assess isolated aspects of agent performance (task completion, security robustness) and fail to locate the precise source of failures across the planning, tool use, memory, and reasoning pipeline. A complete trace-level evaluation enables precise failure attribution and trustworthiness profiling.
AI.method: Attach-to-agent evaluation: read the recorded execution trace without interfering with the agent. Evaluate across ten dimensions (instruction integrity, planner, memory, tool selection, tool invocation, tool correctness, alignment, tool faithfulness, security, execution integrity) and perform behavioural classification and failure attribution. Test five LLMs (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 5, Sarvam 105B, Llama 3.3 70B, Gemini 2.5 Flash) on nine capability/adversarial tasks. Use a fixed judge model to score traces.
AI.result: Composite Trust Scores (mean): Claude Sonnet 5 = 95.1, GPT-5 = 80.6; Sarvam 105B = 57.6; Llama 3.3 70B = 45.7; Gemini 2.5 Flash = 22.6. All traces scored by a single judge model (one of the evaluated models) — a limitation. Adversarial tasks revealUnsafe_Compliance classifications for several non-frontier models despite task completion success, highlighting divergence between task success and trustworthiness.
AI.conclusion: AgentAudit enables end-to-end, non-intrusive evaluation of LLM-based agents and can be applied to any agent by analyzing the execution trace. It reveals that task-level success does not guarantee trustworthy behavior and that evaluation bias (single judge) is a major limitation; broader benchmarking with multiple judges is advisable.

title: BRACE: Anchored Bellman-Residual Correction for Stale Critics in Asynchronous RL
summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning has become the standard way to scale training for language models, but the resulting policy lag biases the critic toward the stale behavior policy. Existing work on asynchronous LLM training corrects the actor and leaves this bias unaddressed, while the off-policy value correction of classical RL does not carry over to long-horizon agentic tasks, since a short correction horizon leaves the regression target free of the reward and a long one lets the product of importance ratios drift exponentially with the trajectory length. We propose BRACE, an anchored Bellman-residual correction for stale value models. BRACE bounds the correction horizon to a prefix of policy tokens and anchors a constant-weight Monte-Carlo tail beyond it, which separates policy correction from reward propagation. BRACE improves mean@1 on BrowseComp-Plus by $2.4\%$ over the strongest baseline, runs $2.46\times$ faster per step than synchronous training, and remains stable $50$ updates off-policy.

AI.tldr: BRACE: an anchored Bellman-residual correction for stale value models in asynchronous RL for LLMs; clips the correction horizon to a policy prefix and uses a constant-weight Monte-Carlo tail to decouple policy correction from reward propagation, yielding faster training and improved performance.
AI.motivation: Asynchronous RL induces policy lag that biases the critic toward stale behavior; existing actor-correction methods do not fix this bias, and classical off-policy corrections fail for long-horizon tasks due to reward drift over long trajectories. A robust, horizon-bounded, anchored correction is needed to enable scalable, stable training of LLMs.
AI.method: Introduce BRACE: bound the Bellman-residual correction horizon to a prefix of policy tokens; anchor a constant-weight Monte-Carlo tail beyond it; separate policy correction from reward propagation; evaluate on BrowseComp-Plus.
AI.result: Mean@1 on BrowseComp-Plus improves by 2.4 percentage points over the strongest baseline; 2.46× faster per step than synchronous training; remains stable under 50 updates off-policy.
AI.conclusion: BRACE provides a scalable, stable method for stale-value correction in asynchronous RL for LLMs, enabling faster training with improved performance by decoupling policy correction from reward propagation.

title: Learning Terrain-Adaptive Humanoid Locomotion on Granular Terrain
summary: Humanoid locomotion on granular terrain remains a significant challenge due to its complex foot-terrain interaction dynamics that are difficult to model. Existing approaches either ignore granular contact dynamics or incorporate simplified normal force models with heuristic tangential components. In this work, we present a physics-grounded granular contact model based on three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT) and efficiently simulate granular terrain for reinforcement learning (RL) training. Unlike traditional rigid contact models and simplified granular contact models with ad-hoc heuristics, our contact solver produces physically accurate granular intrusion dynamics without resorting to heuristics. It captures realistic penetration and tangential drag during training, enabling the policy to learn behaviors that transfer reliably to real-world granular terrain where rigid contact models fail. To adapt to varying terrain conditions, we train a terrain-adaptive locomotion controller via teacher-student RL, using a variational autoencoder to encode terrain information into a compact latent representation. Simulation studies using material point method (MPM) with NVIDIA Newton demonstrate that our method generalizes to unseen granular terrains, achieves a significantly higher success rate than baselines, and demonstrates zero-shot terrain identification and adaptation. We further validate our approach through extensive hardware experiments across diverse real-world granular terrains including basalt, dry sand, and beach sand. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of agile humanoid locomotion on real-world granular terrain. Project page: https://humanoid-gm-locomotion.github.io/HUMANOID-GM/

AI.tldr: Physics-grounded 3D Resistive Force Theory–based granular contact model enables realistic, heuristic-free humanoid locomotion on granular terrain via RL with terrain adaptation; validated in simulation (MPM) and hardware across diverse granular terrains.
AI.motivation: Granular contact dynamics are complex and difficult to model; existing approaches either ignore granular dynamics or rely on simplified normal/tangential force models, hindering transfer to real granular terrain.
AI.method: Develop a 3D Resistive Force Theory–based granular contact solver; simulate granular terrain with material point method (MPM) using NVIDIA Newton; train a terrain-adaptive locomotion controller via teacher–student RL; use a variational autoencoder to encode terrain information into a compact latent representation; perform zero-shot terrain identification/adaptation; validate with hardware experiments on real granular terrains.
AI.result: The method achieves higher success rates than baselines, generalizes to unseen granular terrains, enables zero-shot terrain identification/adaptation, and demonstrates agile humanoid locomotion on real-world granular terrain; includes a project page.
AI.conclusion: A physics-grounded granular contact model yields accurate intrusion dynamics without heuristics, enabling robust sim-to-real transfer for humanoid locomotion on granular terrain and outperforming traditional rigid or heuristic granular models.

title: Freezing of Gait Prediction Under Spatial Occlusion: An IMU-Supervised Cross-Modal Distillation Approach
summary: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by gradual deterioration of movement control. Automated freezing-of-gait (FOG) detection supports the objective assessment of gait-related motor impairment. Two common approaches are used for FOG prediction: (i) analysing video recordings of the patient's movements and (ii) analysing data collected using inertial measurement unit (IMU) wearable sensors attached to the patient's lower limbs. Video-based approaches may suffer detection errors during continuous turning-in-place tasks because the lower limbs undergo substantial geometric self-occlusion, degrading pose-estimation accuracy. IMU-based approaches are generally less affected by visual occlusion; however, they are difficult to deploy outside clinical or laboratory settings, as the sensors must be attached securely and remain in place throughout the assessment. Motivated by this, we propose a cross-modal subspace distillation framework to mitigate the limitations of unimodal FOG detection by combining IMU accuracy with video-based practicality. We extract invariant latent topologies from a pre-trained kinematic oracle to structurally supervise a non-encoded visual architecture during training. To resolve periods of severe spatial occlusion, a dual-stream visual model probabilistically fuses skeletal graph nodes and continuous spatial pixels, dynamically shifting reliance to uninterrupted pixel boundaries as joint tracking confidence drops. Evaluated against a public, multi-modal sequence dataset of Parkinson's individuals executing continuous $360^\circ$ turns, empirical results demonstrate that applying sensory boundary topologies strictly mitigates tracking evaluation entropy. Our constrained optimisation confirms that highly precise FOG prediction bounds can be achieved over zero-wearable inference environments.

AI.tldr: A cross-modal framework combines IMU and video-based cues for FOG detection in Parkinson's patients using a cross-modal subspace distillation approach, addressing occlusion and wearability issues to enable zero-wearable inference.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of single-modality FOG detection: video suffers from occlusion during turning, while IMU requires wearable sensors.
AI.method: Train a non-visual architecture supervised by invariant latent topologies from a pre-trained kinematic oracle; use a dual-stream visual model that fuses skeletal graph nodes with spatial pixels and adaptively relies on pixel boundaries when joints are occluded.
AI.result: On a public multi-modal dataset of Parkinson's patients performing continuous 360-degree turns, the approach reduces tracking entropy and enables precise FOG prediction even without wearables.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal distillation with boundary-aware visuals can achieve reliable FOG detection without relying on wearable sensors, by leveraging the strengths of both video and IMU data and structural supervision.

title: Scored vs. Generated Readouts in Behavioral Language Models: An Empirical Study of Elicitation Format
summary: Language models fine-tuned on customer behavior can predict outcomes and generate explanations, but these readouts are often treated as interchangeable. Holding model checkpoint and prompt content fixed, we compare probabilities obtained by scoring answer tokens with predictions generated after a written rationale. Across 13 model-domain cells covering four retail tasks in three markets, including two using fully public data and checkpoints, the scored readout ranks outcomes more accurately in 12 of 13 cells (two-sided sign test, p approximately 0.003), by 1.5 to 14.5 points in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Paired bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero in every newly measured cell. The gap varies with task-specific supervision and mismatch between training and serving formats, ranging from -2.2 points for an untuned base model to +13.7 for rationale-format supervision. Analysis of approximately 9,000 rationales identifies two correlates: reduced reliance on the dominant predictive feature and convergence on stock formulations. Probability saturation does not track the gap. A third readout, eliciting a probability before any verdict, improves calibration (Brier score from 0.47 to 0.15) while ranking within noise of scoring, but only for outcome rates represented in training; it is worse than scoring when the scored head is already calibrated. We interpret these differences through the objectives matched by each readout, identify training choices that narrow the gap, and propose retaining generated rationales while sourcing ranking from the scored head.

AI.tldr: Rationale-based readouts outperform direct scoring in most model-domain cells, with calibration gains from an additional readout; training choices and format mismatch modulate the gap; recommended approach is to keep generated rationales and source ranking from the scored head.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether explanations (rationales) accompanying LM predictions improve outcome ranking and calibration in customer-behavior tasks, and understand when and why they help or hurt performance.
AI.method: Fixed checkpoint and prompt across 13 model-domain cells (four retail tasks, three markets; two cells use public data/checkpoints). Compare probabilities of answer tokens (scoring head) vs predictions produced after writing a rationale. Statistical tests: two-sided sign test (p ~0.003), AUC gains (1.5–14.5 points), paired bootstrap CIs. Analyze ~9,000 rationales to identify correlates. Include a third readout that outputs a probability before verdict to assess calibration. Examine task supervision and train–serve format mismatch.
AI.result: Across 12/13 cells, the rationale-enabled readout ranks outcomes better (p≈0.003); AUC improvements range 1.5–14.5 points; bootstrap CIs exclude zero. Gap varies with supervision level and train–serve mismatch: -2.2 points for untuned base model, +13.7 for rationale-format supervision. About 9k rationales reveal two correlates: reduced dependence on a dominant predictive feature and convergence on stock formulations. Probability saturation does not track the gap. A third readout (probability before verdict) improves calibration (Brier 0.47→0.15) but only for outcome rates seen during training and can be worse if the scored head is calibrated.
AI.conclusion: The readout objective shapes what each readout optimizes: ranking accuracy versus probability calibration. Training choices that emphasize rationale formats can narrow the gap between readouts. A practical recommendation is to retain generated rationales for interpretability while using the scored (probability) head for ranking; calibration-focused readouts may be beneficial when outcome rates are well-represented in training.

title: NEXUS-MI: Communication-Aware Federated Personalization for Gateway-Coordinated Motor-Imagery Brain-Computer Interfaces
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) vary across subjects and sessions, complicating personalization from limited calibration data. Federated learning can exploit shared representations without centralizing raw EEG, but existing federated MI studies largely assume regular synchronization. We introduce NEXUS-MI, a gateway-coordinated federated personalization framework that treats synchronization as a coupled learning-and-communication control problem. Raw EEG and classifier heads remain local, while an edge coordinator maintains the shared backbone. We evaluate NEXUS-MI through offline replay using BCI Competition IV Dataset 2a (BCICIV-2a; 9 subjects, 4 classes) and OpenBMI (54 subjects, 2 classes). Session 1 supports backbone learning, and Session 2 provides limited-calibration personalization and held-out testing. An ideal-link reference and six heterogeneous-link policies characterize gateway participation, buffering, stale-update admission, and backbone-download control. The principal comparison holds delayed-update handling fixed while contrasting non-adaptive and communication-aware synchronization. Paired subject-level comparisons use Holm adjustment, and robustness across five matched realizations is assessed by hierarchical bootstrap. Communication-aware coordination reduced server-to-client backbone traffic by approximately 42% on both datasets, while cohort-level accuracy differences were small and realization-dependent. Cohort averages also concealed subject-level vulnerability, with losses reaching approximately 12 percentage points on BCICIV-2a relative to the ideal-link reference. These findings establish gateway synchronization as an explicit design variable in federated MI personalization and motivate joint evaluation of personalized accuracy, communication cost, update freshness, and subject-level reliability.

AI.tldr: NEXUS-MI: gateway-coordinated federated personalization for MI-BCIs that treats synchronization as a joint learning-communication control problem; achieves substantial backbone traffic reduction with competitive accuracy; highlights subject-level reliability trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Address subject/session heterogeneity in MI-BCIs and the calibration data bottleneck; leverage Federated Learning without raw EEG centralization; study the role of synchronization as a design variable.
AI.method: Local EEG and classifier heads; edge coordinator maintains shared backbone; offline replay on BCICIV-2a and OpenBMI; two-session protocol with limited calibration; multiple gateway policies; Holm-adjusted subject-level comparisons; hierarchical bootstrap; compare delayed-update with/without adaptive synchronization.
AI.result: Backbone traffic reduced ~42%; cohort accuracy differences small and realization-dependent; subject-level losses up to ~12 percentage points vs ideal-link reference; demonstration of synchronization control as design variable.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of personalization accuracy, communication cost, update freshness, and reliability is essential; gateway synchronization should be explicitly considered in federated MI personalization.

title: Deformable Object Manipulation under Partial Observability via Real-Time Full-Shape Estimation
summary: Manipulating deformable objects (DOs) is challenging due to their high-dimensional state space, underactuated dynamics, and partial observability. In this paper, we propose cRVAE, a lightweight conditional recurrent variational autoencoder that estimates the full DO state from only partial corner-node observations during inference. The resulting model is used as the forward model in a receding-horizon optimal control framework for obstacle-aware collaborative DO manipulation. In simulation on rope and fabric, cRVAE estimates the full DO state from the available corner-node measurements alone, matching the accuracy of a parameter-identified XPBD model. At inference it uses no physical parameters as model inputs and performs no online parameter identification. It also runs approximately 350 times faster on the rope and over 1500 times faster on the fabric per forward pass, keeping horizon-based planning within the 100 ms control budget where XPBD exceeds it already at short horizons. Full-shape estimation from corner sensing at in-loop speed is what makes the model deployable on hardware, which we demonstrate on a Unitree Go2 robot.

AI.tldr: A lightweight conditional recurrent VAE (cRVAE) estimates full deformable-object (DO) state from partial corner observations and serves as a fast forward model in MPC for obstacle-aware DO manipulation; it matches XPBD accuracy while being orders of magnitude faster, enabling 100 ms planning and hardware deployment.
AI.motivation: Deformable objects have high-dimensional states, underactuated dynamics, and partial observability. A fast, observation-only forward model is needed to enable real-time, model-based control with limited sensing.
AI.method: Train a lightweight conditional recurrent variational autoencoder (cRVAE) that infers full DO state from corner-node observations during inference. Use the learned model as the forward model in a receding-horizon (MPC) framework for obstacle-aware collaboration. Evaluate in simulation on rope and fabric, compare to parameter-identified XPBD, and demonstrate hardware deployment on a Unitree Go2. The model does not require physical parameters at inference and performs no online parameter identification.
AI.result: cRVAE estimates the full DO state from corner measurements with accuracy comparable to a parameter-identified XPBD model. It runs ~350x faster than XPBD on rope and ~1500x faster on fabric per forward pass, keeping planning within a 100 ms control budget (XPBD exceeds it at short horizons). It enables full-shape estimation from corner sensing at in-loop speeds suitable for hardware deployment, demonstrated on a Unitree Go2.
AI.conclusion: Full-shape estimation from partial corner sensing enables deployable, fast model-based manipulation of DOs. The approach reduces dependence on explicit physics parameters during inference and enables real-time planning with lightweight models.

title: Layerwise Tunable Lifting Scheme for the Convolutional Neural Network
summary: This work introduces a family of tunable lifting schemes for biorthogonal wavelet filter banks. We propose three lifting strategies: low-pass tuning (LS-LayLatt-LP), high-pass tuning (LS-LayLatt-HP), and a sequential lifting scheme that jointly adapts low- and high-frequency branches (LS-LayLatt-Sequential). All proposed designs are formulated using a lattice-based lifting structure, which guarantees invertibility and stability for arbitrary parameter values within the lifting functions. We evaluated the proposed methods by integrating them into a ResNet-18 backbone for image classification on the Describable Textures Dataset (DTD), as well as for anomaly detection on hazelnut images from the MVTec-AD dataset and private KRC102S dataset. Experimental results demonstrate consistent performance improvements across all evaluated tasks.

AI.tldr: Introduces tunable lattice-based lifting schemes for biorthogonal wavelet filter banks with three strategies (LP, HP, Sequential); guarantees invertibility and stability; demonstrates improvements when integrated into ResNet-18 for texture classification (DTD) and anomaly detection (MVTec-AD hazelnuts, private KRC102S).
AI.motivation: To obtain stable, invertible, tunable multiresolution representations for CNNs that improve performance on texture classification and anomaly detection by leveraging lattice-based lifting of biorthogonal wavelet filter banks.
AI.method: Propose three lifting strategies within a lattice-based lifting structure: (1) low-pass tuning (LS-LayLatt-LP), (2) high-pass tuning (LS-LayLatt-HP), and (3) sequential joint adaptation of low- and high-frequency branches (LS-LayLatt-Sequential). All designs ensure invertibility and stability for arbitrary parameter values. Integrate these schemes into a ResNet-18 backbone and evaluate on DTD for image classification and on hazelnut images from MVTec-AD and private KRC102S for anomaly detection.
AI.result: Across tasks, the lattice-based tunable lifting schemes yield consistent performance improvements when embedded in ResNet-18, indicating the practicality and effectiveness of tunable wavelet-based representations for both texture recognition and anomaly detection.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LS-LayLatt lifting schemes provide stable, invertible, and tunable multiresolution representations that boost performance in CNN-based texture classification and anomaly detection tasks; lattice-based lifting offers a robust design framework for integrating wavelet techniques into modern deep networks.

title: Decision Transformer for UAV-Mounted RIS-Assisted Dynamic D2D Communications
summary: This paper studies unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-mouted reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted device-to-device (D2D) communication with stochastic link activation. It models UAV motion and attitude, time-varying Rician angles, and angle-dependent RIS reflection. A joint optimization of UAV trajectory, attitude, and RIS phases is formulated to maximize average sum rate under mobility, energy, and hardware constraints. The problem is addressed using deep reinforcement learning and a Decision Transformer trained on expert trajectories from multiple scenarios. Results demonstrate effective cross-scenario generalization, with zero-shot transfer outperforming direct DRL transfer and online fine-tuning achieving competitive performance with fewer interactions.

AI.tldr: Joint optimization of UAV trajectory, attitude, and RIS phases for UAV-mounted RIS-assisted D2D with stochastic link activation, using DRL and a Decision Transformer for cross-scenario generalization.
AI.motivation: Address mobility-induced channel variation in UAV-RIS aided networks and improve average sum-rate under practical constraints by leveraging learning-based optimization and cross-scenario transfer.
AI.method: Model UAV motion/attitude, time-varying Rician angles, and angle-dependent RIS reflection; formulate a joint optimization; solve with deep reinforcement learning and a Decision Transformer trained on expert trajectories from multiple scenarios.
AI.result: Demonstrates effective cross-scenario generalization; zero-shot transfer outperforms direct DRL transfer; online fine-tuning achieves competitive performance with fewer interactions.
AI.conclusion: Learning-based control can robustly optimize UAV-RIS D2D performance across scenarios, exploiting cross-scenario knowledge to reduce data needs and enhance transferability.

title: Evaluating Model Retraining under Drift: Paired Comparisons of Cumulative Subgroup Disparity
comment: 44 pages, 10 figures, 34 tables. Reproducibility package version 2026.09.08-r2
summary: Choosing when to retrain a deployed classifier requires assessing subgroup error rates across the sequence of models used, including periods between updates. We compare complete scheduled, loss-triggered, and subgroup-gap-triggered policies with retaining the initial model on the same observations and delayed labels. For true-positive and false-positive rates separately, the outcome is the paired difference in absolute subgroup gaps summed over deployment windows. Population evaluation in simulation, action records, and alternative schedules assess how measurement and retraining behaviour affect these comparisons. In a follow-up sample of 400 new trajectories per condition across two simulated drift regimes, all three policies had lower mean cumulative disparity, equivalent to reductions of 0.04 to 0.88 percentage points in the average gap per window. Evaluating the unchanged models against the known generating distributions preserved all mean directions, but finite-window and population comparisons agreed on whether updating increased, reduced or left cumulative disparity unchanged in 69 to 92 percent of trajectories. Under subgroup-specific drift, smaller true-positive-rate gaps accompanied lower sensitivity in both groups. In an exploratory American Community Survey replay, person weighting reversed all three race false-positive-rate mean comparisons without changing predictions or actions; all three weighted intervals included zero. Policy comparisons require group-specific rates, action distributions, and an explicit evaluation population alongside mean disparity. These analyses are non-confirmatory. Shared replay requires policy-independent observations and complete labels after the specified delay.

AI.tldr: This abstract analyzes retraining policies for deployed classifiers with subgroup error rates and drift, using simulations and replay; it emphasizes non-confirmatory findings and the need for policy-independent observations.
AI.motivation: Evaluate how different retraining strategies and evaluation populations affect subgroup disparity metrics across deployment windows.
AI.method: Compare complete scheduled, loss-triggered, and subgroup-gap-triggered retraining; retain the initial model on the same observations with delayed labels; assess true-positive and false-positive rate gaps; use population simulations, action records, and alternate schedules; include follow-up sampling across drift regimes and a replay of an American Community Survey.
AI.result: All three policies reduced mean cumulative disparity in the follow-up simulations (0.04–0.88 percentage points). Unchanged models preserved mean direction; 69–92% of trajectories agreed on whether updating increased/reduced/left disparity. Under subgroup drift, smaller TPR gaps correlated with lower sensitivity. Weighting by race reversed all three race FP rate comparisons without changing predictions. Conclusions: policy comparisons require group-specific rates, action distributions, and an explicit evaluation population; analyses are non-confirmatory; shared replay requires policy-independent observations and complete labels after the delay.
AI.conclusion: Policy evaluations of retraining must employ subgroup-specific metrics, explicit populations, and complete labels; results are非confirmatory and sensitive to evaluation design; shared replay mandates policy-independent observations.

title: Odometer-Agnostic Drift Correction Using OpenStreetMap Lane Geometry
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), 2026
summary: Despite significant progress in odometry estimation, long-term drift remains a fundamental limitation of incremental pose integration, especially in large-scale or loop-free environments. Existing map-assisted methods can reduce drift, but often depend on dense maps, sensor-specific processing, or complex matching pipelines. We propose a lightweight open-source, odometry-agnostic correction method that aligns short trajectory segments to OpenStreetMap (OSM) lane centerlines. By formulating drift correction as a direct alignment between recent odometry and sparse lane geometry, the method enables efficient online operation without dense priors or expensive preprocessing. Experiments with LiDAR and visual odometry backends demonstrate consistent improvements, with particularly strong gains under severe drift.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, open-source drift-correction method that aligns short odometry segments to sparse OpenStreetMap lane centerlines, enabling online, odometry-agnostic correction without dense priors.
AI.motivation: Long-term drift in incremental pose integration limits odometry in large-scale or loop-free environments; existing map-assisted methods rely on dense maps or complex matching. A lightweight alternative is needed.
AI.method: Direct alignment of recent odometry with sparse lane geometry from OSM, treating drift correction as a pose-trajectory alignment problem. The approach is odometry-agnostic and does not require dense priors or heavy preprocessing, operating on short trajectory segments to enable online use.
AI.result: Demonstrates consistent drift reduction across LiDAR and visual odometry backends, with especially strong gains under severe drift.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method provides efficient, online drift correction using sparse lane geometry, reducing drift without dense priors and generalizing across sensor modalities.

title: SkNeXt enables topology-guided neuronal reconstruction from petabyte-scale microscopy data
summary: Recent advances in high-resolution fluorescence and electron microscopy have enabled nanoscale imaging across increasingly large brain volumes, but the resulting terabyte- to petabyte-scale datasets make complete neuronal reconstruction prohibitively expensive in computation, data movement, and manual proofreading. Here, we present SkNeXt, a topology-first framework for scalable neuronal reconstruction from large volumetric microscopy datasets. Instead of densely processing entire image volumes, SkNeXt first converts neuronal morphology into compact SWC skeletons that preserve long-range connectivity. Proofreading is therefore focused on sparse neuronal trees, allowing branch, continuity, and connectivity errors to be corrected before high-resolution reconstruction. The corrected skeletons then serve as persistent structural priors for recovering detailed morphology while preserving neuronal identity and topology. Crucially, SkNeXt also uses neuronal skeletons as spatial indices for selective data access, retrieving high-resolution image regions only along reconstructed trajectories and bypassing most background and signal-free volumes. This substantially reduces I/O and computational overhead, allowing reconstruction cost to scale with neuronal morphology rather than total dataset size. Using SkNeXt, we reconstructed neurons from a petabyte-scale super-resolution fluorescence dataset of the mouse brain on a single GPU within one week, without requiring exhaustive dense inference across the complete imaging volume.

AI.tldr: SkNeXt introduces a topology-first, skeleton-based approach for scalable neuronal reconstruction in massive volumetric datasets, enabling targeted proofreading and data-access along reconstructed trajectories, reducing I/O and compute; demonstrated on petabyte-scale data on a single GPU in under a week.
AI.motivation: Current dense volumetric reconstructions of large brain volumes are computationally, data-movement, and proofreading intensive. A topology-preserving, sparse representation could drastically reduce costs while preserving connectivity and identity.
AI.method: Convert neuronal morphology to compact SWC skeletons to encode long-range connectivity. Proofread and correct branches, continuity, and connectivity on sparse skeletons before high-resolution reconstruction. Use skeletons as structural priors to recover detailed morphology while preserving topology and neuronal identity. Use skeletons as spatial indices to selectively fetch high-resolution image regions along trajectories, avoiding background. Reconstruction cost scales with morphology, not dataset size.
AI.result: Demonstrated reconstruction of neurons from a petabyte-scale, super-resolution mouse brain dataset on a single GPU within one week, without exhaustive dense inference across the full volume, leveraging sparse skeletons for data access and prior-informed reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: A topology-first, skeleton-based framework (SkNeXt) enables scalable neuronal reconstruction by prioritizing sparse, connectivity-preserving skeletons as priors and indices, achieving substantial reductions in I/O and computation while maintaining topology and identity.

title: Grounded Evaluation and Repair for NL-to-PDDL Problem Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for translating Natural Language (NL) planning descriptions into PDDL problem instances. However, standard evaluation criteria such as syntactic validity or planner success can substantially overestimate faithfulness to the described task: a generated problem may be parseable and solvable while misrepresenting the intended initial state, goal, object structure, or optimization target. This paper studies an end-to-end NL-to-PDDL pipeline that combines LLM generation, checks in terms of PDDL parsing, planning and validation, a domain-conformance checker, an LLM critic, and iterative repair. Fine-grained repair feedback is constructed from the domain description, the generated problem, the natural language problem description, and operational diagnostics. Reference-based comparisons against curated benchmark PDDL problem descriptions are used for post-hoc benchmark analysis, and these offline checks include renaming-invariant structural matching and semantic equivalence, where domain support is available. Across Planetarium, AutoPlanBench, and curated PDDL~2.1 problems, results show that operational success and benchmark-reference reconstruction can diverge substantially. Results also show that structured repair can be useful, and that PDDL~2.1 remains challenging for reference reconstruction, even when operational success improves.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end NL-to-PDDL translation pipeline with checks and iterative repair reduces misrepresentation in generated PDDL problems, but reveals divergences between operational success and reference-based faithfulness; domain conformance and structured repair are beneficial, while PDDL 2.1 remains hard for reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Standard metrics (syntactic validity or planner success) overestimate faithfulness when translating NL planning descriptions to PDDL; there is a need to evaluate faithfulness with domain-conformance, semantic equivalence, and offline benchmarks.
AI.method: An NL-to-PDDL pipeline that integrates LLM generation, PDDL parsing, planning/validation, a domain-conformance checker, an LLM critic, and iterative repair. Repairs are guided by the domain description, the generated problem, the NL problem description, and diagnostic data. Reference-based evaluation uses curated PDDL benchmarks with renaming-invariant structural matching and semantic equivalence where possible.
AI.result: Across Planetarium, AutoPlanBench, and curated PDDL 2.1 problems, there can be large gaps between operational success and benchmark-reference reconstruction. Structured repair proves useful; PDDL 2.1 remains challenging for reference reconstruction even when operational success improves.
AI.conclusion: The proposed end-to-end NL-to-PDDL workflow with monitoring and repair components can improve faithfulness verification and repair of generated PDDL problems, highlighting that operational success does not guarantee alignment with reference descriptions and that 2.1 remains a tough benchmark for reconstruction.

title: Privacy-Preserving Split Learning for Federated LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific data is essential for downstream adaptation. In many deployments, a participant cannot hold the complete model locally. This happens because the model owner keeps the full model proprietary, or because the participant lacks sufficient compute resources. Split Learning (SL) addresses this by partitioning the model between the participant and a server so that only a small portion runs locally. When the underlying data is additionally distributed across multiple institutions with privacy requirements, Federated Learning (FL) further enables collaborative training across participants by sharing only model updates instead of raw data. In this combined setting, each client transmits intermediate activations to the server, and for LLM fine-tuning, this exchange poses an inherent privacy paradox. The autoregressive nature of LLMs causes the transmitted activations to leak the input, and existing perturbation-based defenses are fundamentally ineffective in this setting. We address this leakage through a learned obfuscate-and-recover scheme that protects participants' private datasets while still allowing an independently deployable model to be trained on the server side. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves strong privacy protection with modest utility loss and system overhead, making split-based federated LLM fine-tuning practically viable.

AI.tldr: A learned obfuscate-and-recover scheme for privacy-preserving split federated LLM fine-tuning that obfuscates intermediate activations to prevent input leakage while enabling server-side training, with modest utility loss and overhead.
AI.motivation: Split learning for LLM fine-tuning across distributed, privacy-sensitive data faces inherent leakage of inputs via activations in the autoregressive setting; perturbation defenses are inadequate for this leakage.
AI.method: A learned obfuscate-and-recover framework: clients apply a learned obfuscation to their intermediate activations before sending them to the server, which uses a learned recover function to enable training of an independently deployable server-side model; designed to protect private datasets while maintaining trainability.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows strong privacy protection with only modest degradation in utility and manageable system overhead, making split-based federated LLM fine-tuning practically viable.
AI.conclusion: The proposed obfuscate-and-recover approach can enable privacy-preserving, split-based FL for LLM fine-tuning without prohibitive utility or resource costs, supporting multi-institution collaboration under privacy constraints.

title: A Confidence-Aware Multimodal Fusion Framework for Industrial Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: A confidence-aware multimodal fusion framework (CAMF) is proposed to realize reliable human intention prediction for industrial human-robot collaboration. This framework fuses four heterogeneous modalities including object 6D pose, gaze, skeletal motion and IMU-based hand motion. It embeds a confidence-trend-driven dynamic fusion mechanism into BiLSTM to adaptively balance bidirectional temporal features according to real-time modality reliability. A confidence-guided balanced learning strategy combined with a confidence freezing mechanism is further adopted to adjust network gradients dynamically, suppress noise from low-quality modalities and mitigate cross-modal learning bias. A physical platform based on the UR3 collaborative robot is built for experimental validation. Comparative results show that the proposed method reaches an intention recognition accuracy of 91.86% and outperforms existing multimodal fusion approaches in overall performance and stability. It also maintains satisfactory accuracy under low light and partial occlusion interference. In practical assembly tasks, the framework enables proactive and stable human-robot cooperation with strong environmental adaptability.

AI.tldr: CAMF fuses four modalities (object 6D pose, gaze, skeletal motion, IMU-based hand motion) using a confidence-trend-driven dynamic fusion in BiLSTM, with a confidence-guided balanced learning and confidence freezing to suppress low-quality modalities and mitigate cross-modal bias.
AI.motivation: Ensure reliable human intention prediction for industrial HRC under varying modality reliability and noise, where single-modality or naive fusion degrades performance and stability.
AI.method: Propose CAMF framework that (1) fuses four heterogeneous modalities; (2) uses a confidence-trend-driven dynamic fusion mechanism in BiLSTM to adaptively weight temporal features based on real-time modality reliability; (3) employs a confidence-guided balanced learning strategy and a confidence freezing mechanism to adjust training gradients, suppress noise, and mitigate cross-modal bias; (4) validates on a UR3-based physical platform for experiments.
AI.result: Achieves 91.86% intention recognition accuracy and outperforms existing multimodal fusion approaches in overall performance and stability; maintains satisfactory accuracy under low light and partial occlusion; demonstrates proactive, stable HRC with strong environmental adaptability.
AI.conclusion: CAMF enables reliable, robust human intention prediction for industrial HRC by adaptive, confidence-aware multimodal fusion and learning, offering improved accuracy and resilience to modality degradation.

title: Pretraining and Distillation Matter More Than Architecture Family for Label-Free Single-Cell Classification
summary: Choosing a deep learning architecture for label-free single-cell classification remains an open question, with microscopy benchmarks reporting conflicting conclusions about CNNs versus transformers. We present a controlled benchmark on LIVECell phase-contrast microscopy data using source-image-disjoint train/validation/test splits to prevent parent-image leakage and matched optimisation, augmentation, and evaluation protocols across EfficientNet, Vision Transformer (ViT), and EVA-02 models. This allows the effects of architecture, pretraining, fine-tuning, tokenisation, and distillation to be disentangled. We find that the previously reported CNN advantage is largely explained by pretraining rather than architecture: the smallest pretrained model outperforms the strongest model trained from scratch despite far fewer parameters. Pretraining improves macro-F1 by 3-4 points, while the gap between the best pretrained CNN and transformer is below 0.5 points. Architectural choices nevertheless matter: ViT-S/8 outperforms ViT-S/16 and matches the four-times-larger ViT-B/16 at a quarter of the parameters, showing that finer tokenisation benefits small cell crops. Conversely, layer-wise learning-rate decay, central to the EVA-02 fine-tuning recipe, degrades performance, highlighting that transfer heuristics from natural-image recognition may not generalise to microscopy. Finally, knowledge distillation substantially improves the deployment frontier: compact EfficientNet-B0 students distilled from teacher councils outperform every individually trained backbone, including the EfficientNet-B5 and EVA-02 teachers. Overall, our results show that rigorous control of pretraining and evaluation is essential for interpreting biomedical architecture benchmarks, while distillation may be a more effective route to practical single-cell classification than architecture choice alone.

AI.tldr: A controlled LIVECell benchmark shows pretraining largely drives CNN vs transformer performance in label-free single-cell classification; with proper pretraining, CNNs are not decisively superior to transformers, and distillation yields the strongest practical models.
AI.motivation: Resolve conflicting claims about architecture (CNNs vs transformers) in microscopy by controlling data leakage, pretraining, fine-tuning, tokenisation, and evaluation.
AI.method: Compare EfficientNet, ViT, and EVA-02 under source-image-disjoint train/validation/test splits with matched augmentation and optimisation; dissect effects of pretraining, fine-tuning, tokenisation (token granularity), and distillation; evaluate macro-F1 and parameter efficiency across architectures; assess small vs large models and transfer heuristics.
AI.result: Pretraining improves macro-F1 by 3–4 points; the gap between best pretrained CNN and transformer is <0.5 points. The smallest pretrained model outperforms the strongest model trained from scratch. ViT-S/8 outperforms ViT-S/16 and matches ViT-B/16 with a quarter of parameters, highlighting benefit of finer tokenisation for small crops. Layer-wise learning-rate decay during EVA-02 fine-tuning degrades performance, suggesting natural-image transfer heuristics may not generalise to microscopy. Distillation significantly boosts deployment: EfficientNet-B0 students distilled from teacher councils outperform individually trained backbones, including higher-capacity CNNs and EVA-02 teachers.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous control of pretraining and evaluation is essential for interpreting biomedical architecture benchmarks. Distillation may offer a more effective path to practical single-cell classification than architecture changes alone; pretraining and optimisation choices dominate outcomes and must be carefully accounted for in benchmarking.

title: Time-Frequency Geometric Cross-Attention for Chunked Vision-Language-Action Models
summary:
Modern vision-language-action (VLA) policies predict a whole chunk of actions: one to two seconds of coordinated motion emitted in a single forward pass. Yet an action chunk is essentially a short multivariate trajectory, but inside these models it is a sequence of generic per-timestep hidden tokens decoded by a linear head. This under-serves two motion structures. First, frequency: a chunk superimposes a smooth global trend and fine corrective motion across time scales, and a single token entangles them. Second, cross-phase geometry: motions of different phases (reach, contact, grasp adjustment, settling) unfold along very different, near-orthogonal directions in representation space, yet are tightly related for the task and arise across the time axis. Dot-product attention scores alignment by an inner product, so it favors aligned tokens and is least sensitive near orthogonality, leaving such relationships for the network to recover through a detour.
  We introduce Time-Frequency Geometric Cross-Attention (TFGCA), a drop-in module repairing both blind spots. TFGCA uses a per-dimension learnable stationary wavelet transform to decompose the action chunk into time-frequency tokens, and each time token retrieves information from them via a cross-attention that fuses the dot product (similarity) with the wedge-product magnitude (sensitive to near-orthogonality) through a learnable weight. A zero-initialized residual reproduces the base behavior at initialization, so it can be dropped onto a pretrained VLA and fine-tuned jointly. Relative to the same-source base, TFGCA improves in-distribution LIBERO by +1.5 on average, the OOD LIBERO-Plus by +6.3, the randomized average under RoboTwin domain randomization by +28.5, and the overall success rate on three real-robot AgiBot A2 tasks by +11.67 points, with larger gains out of distribution.

AI.tldr: TFGCA introduces a per-dimension stationary wavelet transform to decompose action chunks into time-frequency tokens and employs a cross-attention mechanism that fuses dot-product similarity with wedge-product orthogonality sensitivity, enabling better capture of multi-scale motion structure and cross-phase geometry in vision-language-action policies. A zero-initialized residual preserves base behavior, allowing plug-in to pretrained models.
AI.motivation: Current VLA policies treat action chunks as a single sequence of tokens; this masks multi-scale trends and cross-phase geometric relations, and dot-product attention under-emphasizes near-orthogonal, phase-specific motion directions, hindering learning of complex motor trajectories.
AI.method: Apply a per-dimension stationary wavelet transform to decompose a chunk into time-frequency tokens. Implement a cross-attention that combines similarity (dot product) with a wedge-product magnitude term that is sensitive to near-orthogonality, controlled by a learnable weight. The module is zero-initialized as a residual so it can be dropped into pretrained VLA models and fine-tuned end-to-end.
AI.result: Quantitative gains across benchmarks: in-distribution LIBERO +1.5, OOD LIBERO-Plus +6.3, RoboTwin randomized domain +28.5, and real-robot AgiBot A2 tasks +11.67 percentage points, with larger gains in out-of-distribution settings.
AI.conclusion: TFGCA effectively addresses blind spots in standard token-based VLA policies by enabling time-frequency decomposition and geometry-aware cross-attention, yielding robust improvements across diversified tasks and domains while preserving compatibility with pretrained models.

title: A practical DIRECT-type algorithm for medium-scale black-box global optimization
summary: The DIRECT algorithm is a deterministic global optimization method known for its versatility and balanced exploration-exploitation strategy. However, DIRECT-type algorithms are primarily effective for low-dimensional problems and often exhibit slow convergence as dimensionality increases, limiting their applicability to more complex optimization tasks. To address this limitation, this paper introduces X-DTC-GL, a novel DIRECT-type algorithm that incorporates dynamic partitioning and hybridization techniques. The dynamic partitioning approach adaptively refines the search space based on local one-dimensional surrogate models, enabling rapid subdivision of promising hyper-rectangles. The hybridization strategy selectively employs a hill-climbing method to exploit promising regions identified by the surrogate models. Extensive experiments on four diverse benchmark suites demonstrate that X-DTC-GL significantly outperforms existing DIRECT-type baselines, achieving improvements of ~12% in solvability and ~27% in solution quality. Performance-profile analyses indicate the fastest convergence on up to ~40% of instances, the best runtime performance on ~17% of problems, and competitive overall execution times. By improving performance within the partition-based framework, these advances strengthen the algorithm's competitiveness in state-of-the-art black-box optimization.

AI.tldr: X-DTC-GL extends DIRECT with dynamic partitioning and selective hill-climbing to scale to higher dimensions, improving solvability and solution quality versus DIRECT-type baselines.
AI.motivation: DIRECT-type global optimization methods are effective but degrade in high dimensionality; there is a need for scalable strategies that preserve the global-search properties while accelerating convergence.
AI.method: Introduce dynamic partitioning that adaptively refines search regions using local one-dimensional surrogate models to rapidly subdivide promising hyper-rectangles; incorporate a hybridization step that applies hill-climbing to exploit promising regions identified by the surrogate models.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on four benchmark suites shows substantial improvements over DIRECT-type baselines: ~12% increase in solvability and ~27% improvement in solution quality. Performance profiles indicate fastest convergence on up to ~40% of instances, best runtime on ~17% of problems, and competitive overall execution times.
AI.conclusion: The proposed X-DTC-GL enhances partition-based DIRECT-type optimization, reinforcing its competitiveness in state-of-the-art black-box optimization by improving both convergence speed and solution quality.

title: Data-Driven Risk Fields for Safer End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Safety is a fundamental requirement for autonomous driving, yet existing end-to-end driving models still lack explicit risk-aware learning capacities. Existing rule-based risk models provide interpretable safety priors, yet their absolute risk scores depend on handcrafted functions, coefficients, and thresholds. Learning-based risk representations reduce part of this manual design, but their supervision often relies on occupancy-derived labels or heuristic cost values, which may not capture ego-conditioned planning risk. In this paper, we propose DRiF, a data-driven risk-field framework for safer end-to-end autonomous driving. DRiF learns a shared BEV feature with static map segmentation, dynamic risk prediction, and vehicle planning. For dynamic risk learning, DRiF converts rule-based safety priors into pairwise risk labels, and trains the risk field to preserve relative risk ordering instead of regressing handcrafted absolute scores. Experiments on Bench2Drive show that DRiF achieves competitive overall performance, with consistent improvements in driving score, success rate, and collision-related metrics. These results establish relative risk supervision as an effective way to connect explicit safety structure with end-to-end planning. The data and code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: DRiF introduces a data-driven risk-field that learns shared BEV features, dynamic risk, and planning, using pairwise risk labels derived from rule-based priors; achieves improved safety metrics on Bench2Drive and emphasizes relative risk supervision.
AI.motivation: End-to-end driving models lack explicit risk-aware learning; rule-based risk priors are interpretable but rely on handcrafted thresholds; learning-based risk via occupancy or heuristic costs may miss ego-conditioned planning risk. A method that integrates explicit safety priors with planning via relative risk supervision can improve safety without heavy manual tuning.
AI.method: DRiF learns a shared BEV feature representation with static map segmentation, dynamic risk prediction, and vehicle planning. It converts rule-based safety priors into pairwise risk labels and trains the risk field to preserve relative risk ordering rather than regressing absolute scores, enabling risk-aware end-to-end planning. The framework is validated on the Bench2Drive benchmark; code and data will be released.
AI.result: DRiF achieves competitive overall performance with consistent improvements in driving score, success rate, and collision-related metrics on Bench2Drive, indicating the effectiveness of relative risk supervision to connect explicit safety structure with end-to-end planning.
AI.conclusion: Relative risk supervision is an effective mechanism to integrate explicit safety priors with planning in end-to-end autonomous driving, showing promise for safer data-driven risk fields; public release of code/data will facilitate further evaluation and adoption.

title: From Pixels to Hierarchical Sequences: Quadtree Mask Encoding for Vision-Language Binary Change Detection
summary: Dense change detection in remote sensing requires vision-language models (VLMs) to compare bi-temporal images and generate accurate pixel-level masks. Existing VLMs are largely confined to change captioning outputs, and the few that produce pixel-level masks still rely on external decoders or flat text-as-mask serialization, which are less effective for small and fragmented changes. We introduce QUAKE-CD, a framework that recasts dense change prediction as syntax-verifiable structured generation. QUAKE-CD represents binary change masks as grammar-constrained quadtree token sequences, making the masks compact, syntactically checkable, and deterministically decodable within an autoregressive generation space. We further construct QUAKE-CoT, which pairs these sequences with chain-of-thought traces grounded in visual evidence, and jointly optimizes textual reasoning and spatial dense prediction through a progressive curriculum followed by grammar-gated dual-reward RL. On QUAKE-CoT, QUAKE-CD achieves 78.31% accumulated F1, outperforming decoder-based and flat text-as-mask VLMs while producing more faithful bi-temporal reasoning.

AI.tldr: Introduces QUAKE-CD, a grammar-constrained quadtree token representation for dense change masks in remote sensing; paired with QUAKE-CoT for evidence-grounded chain-of-thought, optimized via curriculum and grammar-gated RL to achieve state-of-the-art accumulated F1 (78.31%).
AI.motivation: Dense change detection with vision-language models lags behind in producing compact, verifiable, pixel-level masks and faithful reasoning; existing methods rely on decoders or flat text masks that struggle with small or fragmented changes.
AI.method: Represent binary change masks as grammar-constrained quadtree tokens (QUAKE-CD) for compact, syntactically checkable masks that are deterministically decodable within an autoregressive space. Create QUAKE-CoT to pair these sequences with chain-of-thought traces grounded in visual evidence, and jointly optimize textual reasoning and spatial dense prediction through a progressive curriculum followed by grammar-gated dual-reward reinforcement learning (RL).
AI.result: On QUAKE-CD, achieves 78.31% accumulated F1, outperforming decoder-based and flat text-as-mask VLMs and delivering more faithful bi-temporal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Grammar-constrained, syntax-verifiable generation of dense change masks, coupled with evidence-grounded CoT and grammar-gated RL, yields improved accuracy and interpretability for dense change detection in remote sensing.

title: Structural Process Supervision for Latent Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Latent reasoning approaches enhance token-level efficiency and robustness by replacing verbose, explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens with compact continuous-space embeddings. However, existing methods lack direct process supervision over these latent embeddings, which often leads to representation collapse and uneven information distribution. To address this, we propose Prototype-Mediated Process Supervision (PMPS), which introduces learnable reasoning prototypes as semantic anchors to provide structural process-level supervision for latent reasoning. PMPS projects latent embeddings and explicit CoT embeddings into a shared prototype space, achieving many-to-many soft alignment between unequal-length representations through prototype assignment. Meanwhile, we introduce a Progressive Sequential Alignment (PSA) module to further guide training: positional priors initially encourage sequential alignment structure, then gradually relax to permit adaptive matching. Experimental results show that PMPS compresses output token length to under 50% of explicit CoT on GSM8K-Aug. Compared to leading baseline SIM-CoT, our method achieves average accuracy gains of 2.08% across different model families. On GPT-2, PMPS even surpasses CoT-SFT. On larger models and a more challenging task, PMPS consistently attains the highest accuracy among all latent reasoning methods with comparable output length.

AI.tldr: Proposes Prototype-Mediated Process Supervision (PMPS) with learnable prototypes and Progressive Sequential Alignment to supervise latent reasoning, aligning latent and explicit CoT in a shared prototype space; achieves shorter outputs with improved accuracy across models.
AI.motivation: Existing latent reasoning methods lack direct, structural supervision over latent embeddings, causing representation collapse and uneven information distribution; a need for process-level guidance to stabilize and improve latent reasoning.
AI.method: PMPS introduces semantic prototypes as learnable anchors; projects latent embeddings and explicit CoT embeddings into a common prototype space enabling many-to-many soft alignment via prototype assignment; Progressive Sequential Alignment (PSA) imposes sequential alignment with positional priors early on, gradually relaxing to permit adaptive matching.
AI.result: PMPS reduces output token length to under 50% of explicit CoT on GSM8K-Aug; average accuracy gains of 2.08% over SIM-CoT across model families; on GPT-2, PMPS surpasses CoT-SFT; on larger models and harder tasks, it achieves the highest accuracy among latent reasoning methods with comparable output length.
AI.conclusion: PMPS provides effective process supervision for latent reasoning, improving efficiency and accuracy; PSA aids training stability and adaptability, yielding robust gains across models and tasks.

title: Online Inverse Integer Linear Optimization via Small-Gradient Skipping: Constant Regret and Finite Mistakes
summary: In online inverse linear optimization, the learner predicts a weight at each round, observes the optimal action of the agent, and updates its prediction. In the general setting, the gap of $\log T$ between the regret upper bound $O(d \log T)$ and the lower bound $Ω(d)$ is unresolved (here $T$ is the total number of rounds and $d$ is the dimension). When the action set is M-convex, the regret is known to be bounded by $O(d \log d)$, but the method attaining it computes a center of gravity at every round. This paper therefore proposes Small-Gradient Skipping (SGS), a mechanism that skips the update at rounds without a mistake in the case where the correct action is uniformly separated from the other candidates, and applies it to online gradient descent, the online Newton step, and MetaGrad. The number of mistakes is then bounded, for all three, by a quantity independent of $T$; and for the online Newton step and for MetaGrad with SGS, the dimension dependence of the regret becomes $O(d^2)$ when the forward problem is an integer linear program, that is, the factor $\log T$ is removed. Moreover, when the action set is M-convex, the regret is bounded efficiently without computing a center of gravity.

AI.tldr: Small-Gradient Skipping (SGS) is proposed to reduce updates and improve regret in online inverse linear optimization. It skips rounds with no mistakes, leading to T-independent mistake counts and improved regret bounds for several algorithms; in M-convex action sets, it avoids center-of-gravity computations.
AI.motivation: In online inverse linear optimization, the known regret gap is logarithmic in T (O(d log T)) versus a linear lower bound (Ω(d)). Center-of-gravity methods achieve O(d log d) regret but are computationally expensive. There is a need for methods with fewer updates and tighter regret, especially when the action set is M-convex.
AI.method: Introduce Small-Gradient Skipping (SGS), a mechanism that skips updates on rounds without a mistake when the correct action is uniformly separated from other candidates. Apply SGS to online gradient descent, online Newton step, and MetaGrad. Demonstrate that the number of mistakes is O(1) per dimension (T-independent) and that regret for online Newton step and MetaGrad with SGS is O(d^2), removing the log T factor in forward problems that are integer linear programs. Additionally, for M-convex action sets, show efficient regret without requiring a center of gravity.
AI.result: Mistake counts become independent of T for the three algorithms. For online Newton step and MetaGrad with SGS, regret scales as O(d^2), eliminating the log T factor in certain forward problems (integer linear programs). In M-convex settings, regret can be bounded efficiently without center-of-gravity computations.
AI.conclusion: SGS provides a practical update-skipping mechanism that yields T-independent mistakes and improved regret bounds (notably removing log T in key cases), while enabling efficient regret guarantees for M-convex action sets without expensive center-of-gravity computations.

title: A traffic management system for large and heterogeneous vehicles in narrow industrial environments
summary: The coordination of Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) in high-density industrial environments represents a critical challenge within Logistics 4.0, as traditional traffic management methods often lead to inefficiencies caused by negotiation-based priority assignment. To overcome the resulting limitations, this paper presents an innovative AGV traffic management system based on a Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding (L-MAPF) algorithm operating on roadmaps generated with Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS) curves. The approach guarantees locally optimal coordination and ensures safe operation of large and heterogeneous AGVs. Building on this concept, the proposed framework integrates a modified version of the Bounded Horizon Conflict Based Search (CBS) technique within a Rolling Horizon Conflict Resolution strategy, utilizing an extended time horizon for each agent to enable effective conflict resolution in corridors identified by a topological map. In contrast to state-of-the-art methods for AGV fleet traffic management, the proposed solution is designed for real-world, non-standardized (i.e., non-grid-like) industrial settings characterized by narrow bidirectional corridors and high-traffic density, where AGVs of various sizes and capabilities operate simultaneously. Key contributions include an anytime conflict resolution strategy with adaptive time horizon regulation, an execution layer for safe and standard-compliant interaction with real AGVs, and an advanced mechanism for deadlock detection and resolution. Experimental results obtained in realistic industrial environments demonstrate higher throughput, with improvements of up to 11% over a conventional rule-based traffic management system, a state-of-the-art industrial method, and a priority-based L-MAPF variant, while maintaining continuous operation and improved efficiency.

AI.tldr: Lifelong multi-agent path finding (L-MAPF) on NURBS roadmaps with rolling-horizon conflict resolution improves throughput and safety for high-density, non-grid AGV fleets.
AI.motivation: Traditional negotiation-based priority schemes underperform in dense, bidirectional corridors and non-grid industrial environments; scalable, real-time coordination is needed for heterogeneous AGVs in Industry 4.0 settings.
AI.method: A Lifelong MAPF framework on NURBS-generated roadmaps integrating a modified Bounded Horizon CBS within a Rolling Horizon Conflict Resolution strategy. It uses extended time horizons per agent, an execution layer for safe real-world interaction, and deadlock detection/resolution, with adaptive horizon regulation suitable for non-grid topologies.
AI.result: Experimental results in realistic industrial environments show throughput gains up to 11% over a rule-based system, a state-of-the-art industrial method, and a priority-based L-MAPF variant, while maintaining continuous operation and improved efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The framework delivers locally optimal, safe, and scalable AGV coordination in dense, non-standard industrial settings, with effective deadlock handling and real-world deployability.

title: CLFTv2: Efficient Camera-LiDAR Fusion for Semantic Segmentation via Hierarchical Feature Pyramids
summary: Semantic segmentation for autonomous driving requires reliable detection of vulnerable road users (VRUs) despite heavy class imbalance. We introduce CLFTv2, a hierarchical camera-LiDAR fusion framework replacing global ViT attention with a Swin-based multi-scale encoder and a lightweight FPN-style residual decoder. Operating in the 2D perspective domain, CLFTv2 integrates multi-scale geometric cues through shifted-window attention and per-scale residual fusion, avoiding the computational overhead of query-matching decoders. Across three driving datasets, CLFTv2 consistently improves VRU recall. On ZOD, CLFTv2-Large achieves 53.5\% mIoU, improving pedestrian IoU from 35.5\% to 44.9\% over the prior CLFT model. On Waymo, CLFTv2 reaches 61.7\% mIoU. Additionally, a modality-isolation study suggests ViT's global receptive field yields stronger fusion gains only under dense LiDAR returns. Compared to a Swin-based Mask2Former adaptation, CLFTv2 requires 1.4$\times$ fewer GFLOPs and delivers 2.2$\times$ higher throughput, while achieving comparable overall accuracy. These results demonstrate that hierarchical local-attention fusion offers an efficient, scalable alternative to global-attention and query-based decoders for real-time on-vehicle perception in intelligent transportation systems. Source code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: Efficient Swin-based hierarchical camera-LiDAR fusion (CLFTv2) for 2D semantic segmentation improves VRU performance with lower compute, outperforming global-attention and Mask2Former baselines.
AI.motivation: Address severe class imbalance and the computational burden of global attention in VRU segmentation for autonomous driving; enable real-time, robust fusion via local multi-scale attention.
AI.method: Swin-based multi-scale encoder with shifted-window (local) attention, per-scale residual fusion, 2D perspective fusion, and a lightweight FPN-style residual decoder; hierarchical local-attention fusion replaces global ViT attention and query-based decoders; modality-isolation analysis included.
AI.result: Across three driving datasets, CLFTv2 improves VRU recall; on ZOD, CLFTv2-Large achieves 53.5% mIoU (pedestrian IoU rises from 35.5% to 44.9%); on Waymo, 61.7% mIoU. Modality-isolation: ViT global receptiveness yields larger gains only with dense LiDAR. Compared to Swin-based Mask2Former, CLFTv2 uses 1.4× fewer GFLOPs and 2.2× higher throughput with comparable overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical local-attention fusion provides an efficient, scalable alternative to global-attention and query-based decoders for real-time on-vehicle perception; source code is publicly available.

title: Belief-State Engine: Augmenting LLMs for Principled Planning Under Partial Observability
comment: Total number of pages: 19, total number of figures: 5
summary:
Large language model agents produce fluent action sequences across a wide range of tasks, yet they fail in characteristic ways once the environment becomes partially observable. Ambiguous feedback pushes them into premature commitments. A single informative observation can collapse their uncertainty onto the wrong hypothesis. Policies drift as the history grows. We trace these symptoms to a common structural cause. An LLM agent, as commonly deployed, is a history-conditioned policy with no explicit belief over hidden state.
  We propose an architectural fix. The Belief-State Engine (BSE) is an inference module placed outside the LLM. It maintains a Bayesian posterior over the latent states of a given POMDP (Partially Observable Markov Decision Process) model, and at each decision step it exposes only that posterior to the LLM. The raw action-observation log is not shown. We set out a minimal four-axiom specification of what a belief-consistent internal state must satisfy, and prove that the LLM paired with the BSE is a sound Markov policy on the belief MDP induced by the underlying POMDP. It therefore inherits the Bellman optimality guarantees of classical POMDP theory, provided the LLM is never exposed to the raw history.
  We evaluate the architecture on the Tiger POMDP and a red-team attack-graph task, against six baselines: a reactive LLM, Chain-of-Thought, ReAct, a natural-language belief tracker, QMDP, and POMCP. Across both domains, the BSE-augmented agent improves task return, belief calibration, and decision consistency. Ten targeted ablations isolate the contribution of each architectural choice confirms that the effect is not specific to any one model. Code, environment specifications, prompt templates, and seed logs accompany this paper.

AI.tldr: Introduce Belief-State Engine (BSE) to externalize belief over latent states in POMDPs for LLM agents, turning history-conditioned policies into belief-consistent Markov policies with Bellman-optimality guarantees; validated on Tiger POMDP and red-team attack-graph with multiple baselines and ablations.
AI.motivation: Address failure modes of LLM agents in partially observable environments: premature commitments, incorrect hypothesis from single observations, and history drift due to lack of explicit belief over hidden state.
AI.method: Propose BSE, an inference module external to the LLM that maintains a Bayesian posterior over latent POMDP states and only feeds the posterior (not the raw history) to the LLM. Provide a minimal four-axiom specification for belief-consistent internal states and prove soundness: LLM+BSE forms a sound Markov policy on the belief-MDP with Bellman optimality guarantees, assuming the LLM is not exposed to raw history. Evaluate on Tiger POMDP and red-team graph task against six baselines; perform ten targeted ablations.
AI.result: BSE-augmented agent shows improved task return, belief calibration, and decision consistency in both domains. Ablations confirm the architectural contributions are robust and not tied to a specific model. Code, environments, prompts, and seed logs released.
