AI.conclusion: Isolating belief state as an external inference module enables sound planning with LLMs in partially observable settings, preserving classical POMDP guarantees and improving practical performance across tasks and attackers.

title: In Medical Claims Data, Enhancing Predictive Performance for Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events Using Cross Attention
comment: 13pages, 3 figures. Accepted to KDD 2024 AIDSH workshop
summary: Medical claims data comprise the financial details, including the expenses and billing information, as well as the clinical information, such as the diagnoses and treatments, of patients visiting medical facilities. Recently, it has been acknowledged that large databases can be constructed from medical claims data for medical research purposes. However, the clinical information within these datasets is often medically unstructured, limiting its application in comprehensive analyses. This study enhances predictive model performance for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), a leading cause of death worldwide. Models that predict MACE are crucial to clinical practice guidelines. We utilize a cross-attention mechanism to develop a method that effectively weights the relationships between diagnoses and treatments. Effectively repre- senting the clinical information contained in medical claims data, this approach generates more representative features for predicting MACE. The ROC-AUC score of our proposed cross-attention-based model was 0.7720, higher than other benchmark models including the conventional atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease model, the light gradient boosting machine, and a self-attention-based model. These results indicate that integrating the clinical structure of medical claims data using a cross-attention mechanism significantly enhances the performance of predictive models.

AI.tldr: Cross-attention on medical claims data improves MACE prediction; ROC-AUC 0.7720 surpasses baselines.
AI.motivation: Medical claims contain unstructured clinical data; better representation needed to utilize large claims databases for MACE prediction.
AI.method: Cross-attention mechanism to weight relations between diagnoses and treatments; develops representative features from clinical structure; compares to ASCVD model, LightGBM, and self-attention model.
AI.result: ROC-AUC 0.7720, higher than baselines; demonstrates effectiveness of incorporating cross-attention to model clinical structure.
AI.conclusion: Integrating clinical structure via cross-attention enhances predictive performance for MACE using medical claims data.

title: Frequency-Conditioned Flow Matching for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Robot actions are temporally correlated trajectories whose frequency components encode motion at different scales with highly non-uniform energy distributions. Yet Flow Matching--based vision-language-action (VLA) models typically generate actions in temporal coordinates, without explicitly modeling or systematically leveraging this frequency heterogeneity. We introduce \emph{FreqFM}, a frequency-conditioned Flow Matching framework for VLA models. It raises action frequency from an implicit trajectory property to an explicit conditioning dimension that spans the entire generation pipeline. Concretely, in DCT frequency coordinates, FreqFM constructs a spectrum-matched source distribution, adaptively balances the objective across frequencies, and constrains per-frequency guidance residuals using the corresponding reference transport scales. FreqFM integrates into existing Flow Matching action experts without changing the VLA backbone. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLA-Arena, FreqFM consistently improves performance, including a 9.3-point gain on LIBERO-Plus, and further demonstrates its effectiveness on six real-robot tasks.

AI.tldr: FreqFM introduces a frequency-conditioned Flow Matching framework for vision-language-action (VLA) models, explicitly conditioning action generation on action frequency via DCT coordinates. It constructs a spectrum-matched source distribution, balances the objective across frequencies, and constrains per-frequency guidance residuals with reference transport scales, integrating without backbone changes and yielding consistent gains across datasets, including a 9.3-point improvement on LIBERO-Plus and success on six real-robot tasks.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of explicit modeling of temporal frequency heterogeneity in Flow Matching-based VLA models, where action trajectories have non-uniform, multi-scale energy distributions that are not leveraged during generation.
AI.method: Introduce frequency conditioning (FreqFM) by operating in DCT frequency coordinates; create a spectrum-matched source distribution; adaptively balance losses across frequencies; constrain per-frequency guidance residuals using corresponding reference transport scales; integrate into existing Flow Matching action experts without modifying the VLA backbone.
AI.result: Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLA-Arena, FreqFM yields consistent performance gains, including a 9.3-point boost on LIBERO-Plus, and demonstrates effectiveness on six real-robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling and conditioning on action frequency in a Flow Matching VLA framework improves generation performance and generalizes across datasets and real-robot tasks, highlighting frequency-aware conditioning as a robust strategy for action generation.

title: Albedo Estimation via Latent Bridge Matching
comment: Accpeted at the Color and Imaging Conference (CIC 2026), hosted by the Society for Imaging Science and Technology (IS&T)
summary: Recent advances in Intrinsic Image Decomposition (IID) have increasingly relied on generative models. However, progress remains limited by three key challenges: (a) insufficient physical consistency, (b) high computational cost at inference time, and (c) limited generalization capabilities. In this work, we show that latent bridge matching (LBM) effectively addresses these limitations for albedo estimation. We introduce a novel LBM-based architecture that enforces physical consistency through a pixel reconstruction loss, benefits from the inherent efficiency of LBM low-cost inference, and improves generalization across diverse datasets by incorporating a shading conditioning. In this extended version, we additionally show that conditioning the shading estimator itself on the predicted albedo further improves reconstruction fidelity, and we benchmark our best model against stateof-the-art IID methods across five real and synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: LBM-based architecture for intrinsic image decomposition (IID) that yields physically consistent albedo estimates with low-cost inference and improved generalization via shading conditioning; extended version shows the shading estimator conditioned on predicted albedo; evaluated against state-of-the-art on five real/synthetic datasets.
AI.motivation: IID methods struggle with physical consistency, computational cost at inference, and generalization across datasets. A physically grounded, efficient approach with better generalization is desired for robust albedo estimation.
AI.method: Propose latent bridge matching (LBM) architecture that enforces physical consistency through a pixel reconstruction loss, leveraging LBM for fast inference. Introduce shading conditioning to improve generalization and, in the extended version, condition the shading estimator on the predicted albedo to further boost reconstruction fidelity.
AI.result: Best model benchmarked against state-of-the-art IID methods across five real and synthetic datasets, demonstrating improved reconstruction fidelity and generalization.
AI.conclusion: LBM effectively addresses physical consistency, inference efficiency, and generalization in IID albedo estimation; the shading-conditioned variants offer additional gains, with strong empirical performance on diverse datasets.

title: OntologyAligner: Ontology-Aligned Retrieval and Hierarchy-Guided Large Language Model Reranking for Biomedical Ontology Normalization
summary: Biomedical ontology normalization maps free-text expressions to standardized concepts, enabling consistent integration and analysis of biomedical data. This task remains challenging because lexical variation and subtle distinctions among hierarchically related concepts can obscure concept boundaries. We present OntologyAligner, a three-stage framework that combines ontology-aligned retrieval, large language model candidate reranking, and selective hierarchy-guided refinement. We also construct PhenoNormBench, a unified benchmark comprising 13,390 samples from seven Human Phenotype Ontology datasets. OntologyAligner achieved state-of-the-art performance on HPO normalization, with 88.78% Macro Top-1 Accuracy and 86.75% Micro Top-1 Accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.85 and 5.07 percentage points, respectively. Ablation analyses showed complementary contributions from all three stages, and sensitivity analyses demonstrated stability across candidate-set sizes and model backbones. Applications to MONDO, MEDIC, and NCBITaxon further established portability to other ontologies. OntologyAligner offers a generalizable framework for accurate mapping of biomedical text to structured ontology concepts. PhenoNormBench and the code are publicly available at https://github.com/zhelishisongjie/OntologyAligner.

AI.tldr: OntologyAligner is a three-stage framework for biomedical ontology normalization that achieves state-of-the-art performance on HPO normalization; introduces PhenoNormBench benchmark; code released.
AI.motivation: Biomedical textual mentions exhibit lexical variation and subtle distinctions within hierarchies, causing concept-boundary ambiguity in ontology mapping; robust, portable, and reproducible normalization is needed.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) ontology-aligned retrieval to fetch candidate concepts; (2) large language model candidate reranking to re-order candidates using semantic cues; (3) selective hierarchy-guided refinement to enforce ontological structure. PhenoNormBench is constructed from seven HPO datasets (13,390 samples) to benchmark normalization.
AI.result: State-of-the-art on HPO normalization: Macro Top-1 88.78%, Micro Top-1 86.75%; surpasses strongest baseline by 4.85 and 5.07 percentage points. Ablation shows each stage contributes; sensitivity analyses indicate stability across candidate-set sizes and model backbones. Demonstrates portability to MONDO, MEDIC, and NCBITaxon.
AI.conclusion: OntologyAligner offers a generalizable framework for accurate biomedical text-to-ontology mapping; PhenoNormBench and the code are publicly available at the provided GitHub link.

title: TempTPI: Informer-Based trajectory prediction for maritime vessels
comment: Accepted to IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) 2026. \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media
summary: Accurate long-term trajectory prediction for maritime vessels is essential for safety and logistical efficiency. While deep learning models, particularly Transformers, have shown promise in processing Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, they often struggle with the quadratic computational complexity of self-attention and the loss of accuracy over extended forecasting horizons. This study proposes TempTPI, a novel prediction framework that integrates an Informer-based encoder with a multi-channel temporal encoding mechanism. The Informer architecture leverages a ProbSparse self-attention mechanism to reduce computational overhead and focus on the most significant dependencies, while the temporal encoder utilizes Fourier-like frequency expansions to capture cyclic patterns (hourly, daily, and seasonal) in vessel behavior. We evaluate our model against the state-of-the-art TPTrans architecture using AIS data from Danish waters. Experimental results demonstrate that TempTPI consistently outperforms existing methods across prediction windows of 1 to 5 hours. Notably, at a 5-hour horizon, the proposed model achieves a 55% improvement in Mean Squared Error (MSE), offering a robust solution for long-range maritime situational awareness.

AI.tldr: TempTPI introduces an Informer-based encoder with a multi-channel Fourier-like temporal encoding for long-horizon AIS trajectory prediction, achieving significant MSE gains over TPTrans especially at 5 hours.
AI.motivation: Need accurate, efficient long-range maritime trajectory prediction due to safety and logistics; standard self-attention is costly and accuracy drops with horizon.
AI.method: Uses an Informer-based encoder with ProbSparse self-attention to reduce complexity and a multi-channel temporal encoder employing Fourier-like frequency expansions to capture cyclic vessel behavior (hourly, daily, seasonal). Evaluated against TPTrans on Danish AIS data.
AI.result: TempTPI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art across 1–5 hour horizons; at 5 hours, MSE improves by 55%.
AI.conclusion: Combining ProbSparse attention with Fourier-like temporal encoding yields robust long-horizon AIS predictions, enhancing maritime situational awareness.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous UAV Exploration in Wildfire Response
summary: This study develops a deep reinforcement learning framework for training Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) agents to navigate and monitor simulated wildfire environments. Results show that agents learn increasingly stable and effective behaviors over time, as demonstrated by converging loss trends, improved reward signals, and more consistent navigation patterns such as fire-boundary tracking. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) based UAV systems for autonomous wildfire monitoring and suggest that environmental structure and reward design influence policy effectiveness.

AI.tldr: A DRL-based UAV framework for wildfire monitoring trained in simulation; agents achieve stable, effective policies with converging loss and better rewards, particularly in fire-boundary tracking, showing promise for autonomous monitoring; policy quality depends on environmental structure and reward design.
AI.motivation: Enable autonomous, scalable wildfire monitoring using UAVs guided by deep reinforcement learning to operate in dynamic, partially observable, hazardous environments.
AI.method: Design and train a deep reinforcement learning framework for UAV control in a simulated wildfire environment, monitoring learning dynamics (loss, rewards) and evaluating navigation behavior (e.g., boundary tracking).
AI.result: Agents exhibit increasingly stable and effective policies with converging loss, improved reward signals, and consistent navigation patterns such as fire-boundary tracking, indicating the approach can learn useful monitoring behaviors.
AI.conclusion: DRL-based UAV systems can automate wildfire monitoring, with policy effectiveness shaped by the environment’s structure and the reward design.

title: StreetDiff: Multi-view Street Scenes Generation via Cross-view Consistent Multi-view Stable Diffusion with Structure Prompts
summary: Multi-view diffusion models have shown strong performance in scenes with strong geometric priors and sparse semantics, such as indoor rooms or simple outdoor environments (e.g., fields, courtyards). However, they often fail to maintain cross-view consistency under camera rotation, especially in structurally complex urban environments. Without explicit modeling of spherical correspondence across views, existing approaches tend to produce object duplication, structural distortion, and layout inconsistency. To address this limitation, we propose StreetDiff, a multi-view diffusion framework that explicitly enforces cross-view alignment during denoising. StreetDiff introduces a Panorama--Perspective Synergy design to decouple global layout reasoning from local detail synthesis, and incorporates a Panorama Alignment Module (PAM) that establishes spherical-projection-based attention constraints across views. By injecting structured alignment constraints without modifying the diffusion backbone, our framework achieves robust cross-view coherence in challenging urban street scene generation tasks. In addition, we construct Street360, a large-scale HDR multi-view urban panorama dataset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that StreetDiff significantly improves structural consistency and visual fidelity compared to prior multi-view diffusion generation methods.

AI.tldr: StreetDiff is a diffusion-based multi-view framework for urban street scenes that enforces cross-view spherical alignment via a Panorama Alignment Module, decoupling global layout reasoning from local detail synthesis; accompanied by Street360, a large-scale HDR multi-view urban panorama dataset; it yields improved cross-view coherence and visual fidelity over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Current multi-view diffusion methods struggle to maintain cross-view consistency under camera rotations in structurally complex urban scenes due to the lack of explicit spherical correspondence across views, causing object duplication, distortion, and layout inconsistencies.
AI.method: Introduce Panorama–Perspective Synergy with a Panorama Alignment Module (PAM) that uses spherical-projection-based attention constraints to enforce cross-view alignment across views. The design decouples global layout reasoning from local detail synthesis and injects alignment constraints without modifying the diffusion backbone.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that StreetDiff significantly improves structural consistency and visual fidelity compared with prior multi-view diffusion generation methods on challenging urban street scene tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed cross-view alignment paradigm yields robust cross-view coherence in urban street generation, and Street360 provides a large-scale dataset to support such diffusion-based rendering in complex environments.

title: Reference-Based Bias Detection in LLMs via Relative Representations of Hidden States
summary: Existing bias auditing methods typically rely on model outputs, requiring costly benchmarks or judge models and potentially missing internal shifts that never appear in generated text. We propose a reference-based method that audits bias in hidden-state representations across related model variants, for example before and after fine-tuning. Because fine-tuning reshapes representation geometry, absolute hidden states are not directly comparable, so we encode each sentence by its similarities to a fixed set of anchor sentences, yielding relative representations in a shared comparison space. There we measure how target groups shift in their association with positive and negative attributes, a quantity we call the Representational Bias Shift $ΔB$. Across three model families and the WildGuardMix, DecodingTrust and ToxiGen benchmarks, $ΔB$ correlates with output-level bias change in 15 of the 18 settings we test, reaching $|r| = 0.84$ ($p < 0.001$) under full fine-tuning and becoming more model-dependent under parameter-efficient adaptation. Thresholding $ΔB$ detects checkpoints whose bias increased with ROC AUC between $0.65$ and $0.99$, and on WildGuardMix and DecodingTrust it separates them better than a SEAT-based baseline for all three families. $ΔB$ is also stable under changes to the anchor set, attribute sets and target templates. Our method requires no task-specific evaluation data and audits a model in about three minutes, using $3$-$50\times$ less compute than the output-level benchmarks considered here. We view it as complementary to output-based auditing rather than a replacement for it.

AI.tldr: Represents representational bias shifts (ΔB) using anchor-based similarities to audit hidden-state biases across model variants; correlates with output bias changes and is fast and data-free to use.
AI.motivation: Relying on output-based audits can miss internal distributional shifts and requires task benchmarks; a reference-based approach can detect bias embedded in representations before instantiating outputs, and be robust to fine-tuning or adaptation.
AI.method: Encode sentences by their similarities to a fixed anchor set to obtain a shared comparison space across models. Compute Representational Bias Shift ΔB for target groups in relation to valenced attributes. Relate ΔB to output-level bias changes across several model families and benchmarks. Use thresholding on ΔB for bias detection, and compare performance to SEAT; evaluate stability to anchor/attribute/template choices; report speed and compute savings.
AI.result: ΔB correlates with output bias change in 15 of 18 settings, with |r| up to 0.84 (p<0.001) under full fine-tuning; less correlated under parameter-efficient adaptation. Thresholding ΔB yields ROC AUC between 0.65 and 0.99 for detecting bias increase. On WildGuardMix and DecodingTrust, ΔB separates biased vs. unbiased checkpoints better than SEAT across all three model families. ΔB is stable to changes in anchor sets, attribute sets, and target templates. Auditing requires no task-specific evaluation data, takes about 3 minutes, and uses 3–50x less compute than the benchmarks. Concludes that ΔB complements but does not replace output-based auditing.
AI.conclusion: Represents a robust, fast, and task-agnostic audit of hidden-state bias that supplements output-based methods. Its anchor-based representation space and stability across variations enable scalable monitoring of representational biases during model development and fine-tuning.

title: Exact Degeneracy Under Balanced k-Shot Sampling:Consequences for Small-Sample Discriminant Analysis on LLM Embeddings
summary:
Balanced k-shot sampling draws exactly k labeled examples per class. We show that it induces an exact, provable degeneracy in a family of small-sample discriminant estimators. Under balanced sampling, the within-class scatter operator of Kernelized Linear Principal Component Discriminant Analysis (KLPCDA) is not merely rank-deficient but exactly a scaled orthogonal projector. We derive the consequences in closed form: two of KLPCDA's seven variants have every signal eigenvalue exactly equal, so their eigenvector selection criterion is provably indifferent rather than ill-conditioned, and a third has a provably void objective. This follows from the estimators' construction, not any dataset; we confirm it on frozen sentence embeddings and, separately, on residual-stream activations from a decoder-only generative model. An in-formula tie-break repairs the two repairable variants, with recovery gated by class count: the residual subspace constraint costs 5x more on few-class than many-class datasets (p=0.000001).
  We then evaluate the repaired framework on few-shot text classification on frozen LLM embeddings (n much smaller than d, up to 4096), across four datasets, three embedding sizes, and three trained baselines (SetFit, LoRA, in-context learning). A properly cross-validated logistic-regression probe still beats every KLPCDA variant on three of four datasets, at every embedding size; guidance carried from pixel, vibration-signal, and gene-expression data does not directly generalize to this feature space. Three independent geometric separability metrics fail to explain why one high-dimensional decoder-based embedding model underperforms smaller bidirectional encoders, ruling out anisotropy; the gap is substantially an estimation-efficiency effect, not a permanent ceiling, closing by more than 80% when the support set grows from k<=10 to k=30-50 (p=0.00195, both many-class datasets).

AI.tldr: Balanced k-shot sampling induces exact degeneracy in small-sample discriminant estimators, specifically turning KLPCDA's within-class scatter into a scaled orthogonal projector. Two KLPCDA variants become eigenvalue-indifferent, one has a void objective; an in-formula tie-break repairs the two repairable variants, with costs rising for few-class data. The repaired framework underperforms compared with a cross-validated logistic-regression probe on most datasets, and the performance gap is attributed mainly to estimation efficiency rather than representational limits. Increasing the number of support examples (k) substantially mitigates the gap (≈80% recovery when k grows from ≤10 to 30–50). Empirical validation spans frozen LLM embeddings and residual decoder activations, across four datasets, three embedding sizes, and three baselines. In summary: sampling choice can induce degeneracy in discriminant methods; standard prognoses like logistic regression remain robust in few-shot regimes, and larger k alleviates degeneracy-driven deficiencies.
AI.motivation: To understand how balanced k-shot sampling affects small-sample discriminant estimators, particularly KLPCDA, and to quantify the practical impact on few-shot text classification using high-dimensional embeddings.
AI.method: The authors derive the exact form of the within-class scatter under balanced sampling, showing it becomes a scaled orthogonal projector, and extract closed-form consequences for KLPCDA variants. They identify two indeterminate eigenvalue scenarios and one void objective, propose an in-formula tie-break to repair the first two variants, and validate the theory on frozen sentence embeddings and residual activations. They then evaluate repaired KLPCDA against cross-validated logistic regression on four datasets, three embedding sizes, and three baselines, with cross-validated probes.
AI.result: Under balanced sampling, KLPCDA variants exhibit exact degeneracy: two variants have all signal eigenvalues equal (indifferent eigenvector selection), one variant has a void objective. The in-formula tie-break partially repairs the degeneracy; costs of applying the repair are higher for few-class datasets. Empirically, a properly cross-validated logistic-regression probe beats KLPCDA across most settings; the gap shrinks by >80% as k increases from ≤10 to 30–50. Geometric separability metrics do not explain performance differences; the main effect is estimation efficiency rather than a fixed ceiling in representational capacity.
AI.conclusion: Balanced k-shot sampling can causally induce exact degeneracy in a family of small-sample discriminants like KLPCDA, explaining why KLPCDA often underperforms a simple regularized classifier in few-shot text classification. A principled tie-break can repair some degeneracy, but overall robustness is governed by estimation efficiency and sample size rather than intrinsic model capacity. Increasing k markedly mitigates the degradation, indicating the degeneracy is a solvable data-collection issue rather than a fundamental limitation.

title: Coastal Environment Generation with HoloOcean
summary: Marine robotic simulation provides a safe and inexpensive method of developing and testing algorithms for unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) and unmanned surface vessel (USV) autonomy and perception before full field deployment. However, these simulations are often limited by the availability of simulated environments. Current marine robotics simulation suites offer manual ways to edit or create environments, but they require existing data or specialized knowledge of the environment system. To address these issues, we introduce a novel Unreal Engine 5 level generation pipeline that enables automatic creation of coastal environments for HoloOcean. Our pipeline relies on a user-provided overhead image of a coastal scene. The pipeline then uses the image to generate height map data, as well as automatically select assets and place them in the environment.

AI.tldr: An Unreal Engine 5 pipeline automatically generates coastal environments for HoloOcean from overhead images, enabling automatic height-map creation and asset placement to expand simulation environments for UUV/USV testing.
AI.motivation: Marine robotics simulations are constrained by scarce, hard-to-edit environments. An automatic, image-driven pipeline can rapidly create diverse, realistic coastal scenes, reducing manual data and expertise requirements.
AI.method: Input: user-provided overhead coastal image. Process: generate height-map data from the image; automatically select and place assets in Unreal Engine 5 to build a coastal scene for HoloOcean; integrates with the HoloOcean simulation workflow.
AI.result: Introduces a complete pipeline that produces usable coastal environments from overhead imagery, automating height-map generation and asset placement to enable rapid, scalable environment creation for marine robotics simulations.
AI.conclusion: The approach lowers manual effort, increases environmental diversity, and broadens the set of test terrains for UUV/USV autonomy and perception research.

title: Can We Trust Video Hallucination Detectors? VidHalLoc for Evaluating the Evaluators
summary: Video-language models and video agents can produce hallucinations that conflict with spatiotemporal evidence. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate model hallucinations, and heterogeneous mechanisms make detector reliability difficult to compare. We introduce VidHalLoc, a benchmark that evaluates hallucination detection methods under a unified diagnostic evaluation protocol using 2,000 adversarial hallucination samples across Video Question Answering and Video Captioning tasks, spanning Ontology and Dynamic hallucination categories. To construct VidHalLoc efficiently, we introduce VideoHALO, a Harness Engineering-informed multi-agent workflow that decomposes data construction into four executable stages supported by a memory system and a communication protocol. Evaluation of fifteen methods reveals that the four dedicated detectors peak at an Overall accuracy of only 34.63%, indicating limited reliability across video hallucination types [Dataset Repository: https://huggingface.co/datasets/wesfggfd/VidHalLoc].

AI.tldr: VidHalLoc provides a unified benchmark for detecting video hallucinations across VQA and video captioning, using 2,000 adversarial samples and a VideoHALO multi-agent data-construction workflow; detectors perform poorly, with about 34.6% overall accuracy.
AI.motivation: Video-language models frequently hallucinate and current detectors differ in tasks, datasets, and evaluation protocols, making cross-study comparisons unreliable. A unified diagnostic benchmark is needed to rigorously evaluate hallucination detectors across spatiotemporal evidence.
AI.method: Construct VidHalLoc with 2,000 adversarial hallucination samples spanning VQA and video captioning, covering Ontology and Dynamic hallucination types. Data construction is powered by VideoHALO, a harness-engineering multi-agent workflow with four executable stages, supported by a memory system and a communication protocol.
AI.result: Fifteen detectors were evaluated; the best overall accuracy is 34.63%, indicating limited reliability across hallucination types and suggesting that current detectors do not generalize well.
AI.conclusion: VidHalLoc establishes a unified, diagnostic evaluation protocol for video hallucination detectors and demonstrates the need for more robust methods. The dataset is available at HuggingFace.

title: RAP: Research Attention Prediction Reveals Target-Conditioned Evidence Acquisition Biases
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as research agents, yet their ability to track shifts in research attention is difficult to evaluate because reviews and research ideas lack uniquely verifiable outcomes. We introduce Research Attention Prediction (RAP), a rolling benchmark covering 278 AI/ML fields and 1,390 episodes. At each cut-off, an LLM agent searches a temporally restricted arXiv corpus and predicts the next six months' paper shares across eight frozen research directions. Search generally helps, but all four diagnostic models perform worse than an exact-count exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) baseline in compositional accuracy. We identify two linked bottlenecks. Under cumulative-history access, State carry-forward outperforms direct Forecast for all four diagnostic models; frozen-evidence replay links a shared component of this reversal to Forecast-oriented policies retrieving a smaller share of recent evidence. Even with exact historical activity, future-specific updating remains limited, with only GPT-5.5 plus reopened Search slightly surpassing EWMA. Fine-tuning on realised outcomes improves Qwen3-4B's forecast Spearman correlation by 0.105 on held-out fields at later origins, with gains also on change-rich episodes.

AI.tldr: Introduces RAP, a rolling benchmark to evaluate LLMs on predicting future AI/ML research attention across many fields; shows LLMs generally underperform an EWMA baseline and identifies bottlenecks in memory and evidence retrieval; reports modest gains from fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To provide an objective, verifiable evaluation of how well LLMs can track shifts in research attention, addressing the lack of outcomes in reviews and ideas by using a temporally restricted, field-wide forecasting benchmark.
AI.method: Construct RAP with 278 AI/ML fields and 1,390 episodes. At each cut-off, an LLM agent searches a temporally restricted arXiv corpus and predicts the next six months' paper shares across eight frozen directions. Compare four diagnostic models against an exact-count EWMA baseline. Analyze bottlenecks: cumulative-history (state carry-forward vs direct forecast) and frozen-evidence replay. Evaluate with GPT-5.5 plus reopened Search; assess fine-tuning on realised outcomes for Qwen3-4B.
AI.result: Findings: (1) Search helps but all four diagnostic models perform worse than the EWMA baseline in compositional accuracy. (2) Under cumulative-history access, state carry-forward outperforms direct forecast; frozen-evidence replay links a shared component to Forecast-oriented policies that retrieve a smaller share of recent evidence. (3) Even with exact historical activity, future updating remains limited; GPT-5.5 with reopened Search only slightly surpasses EWMA. (4) Fine-tuning realised outcomes improves Qwen3-4B’s forecast Spearman correlation by 0.105 on held-out fields, with gains on change-rich episodes.
AI.conclusion: Forecasting research attention with LLMs remains challenging; simple historical baselines (EWMA) are strong, but certain architectural choices (state carry-forward, evidence replay) and targeted fine-tuning yield incremental improvements. The work highlights the need for better updating mechanisms and evidence integration to surpass baseline trends.

title: Forward-Free LLM Depth Pruning via Weight Redundancy
summary: Depth pruning reduces large language model (LLM) inference cost by removing complete Transformer blocks. Activation-based methods collect hidden states through forward passes on calibration data, while existing forward-free methods score each Transformer block separately without measuring similarity between blocks. We propose Weight-Redundancy Pruning (WRP), a forward-free depth-pruning method that estimates inter-layer redundancy from checkpoint weights to select blocks without calibration data or model forward passes. WRP compares attention output and MLP down-projection weights across layers and combines their pairwise similarities with relative projection-scale information. The resulting all-pairs similarity matrix guides layer grouping and block selection. Across multiple pruning settings, model families, and downstream tasks, WRP consistently outperforms existing forward-free magnitude pruning and approaches the performance of activation-based methods.

AI.tldr: Weight-Redundancy Pruning (WRP) is a forward-free depth-pruning method that uses inter-layer weight redundancy to select Transformer blocks without calibration data or forward passes, delivering competitive performance to activation-based methods.
AI.motivation: Reduce LLM inference cost by pruning depth without relying on calibration data or run-time forward passes; bridge the gap between forward-free and activation-based pruning methods.
AI.method: Compute inter-layer redundancy by comparing attention output and MLP down-projection weights across layers; create pairwise similarity across layers; combine with relative projection-scale information; form an all-pairs similarity matrix to guide layer grouping and block selection.
AI.result: WRP consistently outperforms existing forward-free magnitude pruning and approaches the performance of activation-based methods across multiple pruning settings, model families, and downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: WRP provides a practical, weight-based forward-free depth-pruning strategy that leverages inter-layer redundancy to enable effective Transformer block pruning without calibration data.

title: DUET-DINO: Simultaneous Cross-View World Modeling for Latent Planning in Robot Manipulation
summary: Action-conditioned latent world models predict future visual representations, enabling zero-shot goal-conditioned robot planning and control. However, their predictions for fine-grained spatial and rotational actions are unreliable for full 7-DoF end-effector control. To address this gap, we introduce DUET-DINO, a simultaneous cross-view latent world model that jointly learns action-conditioned predictions from static side- and wrist-camera observations through cross-view conditioning. By exploiting complementary global scene and gripper-centric information, DUET-DINO enables latent planning over the full 7-DoF action space. Across spatially diverse reach, orientation-intensive angled-reach, and multi-goal grasp-and-lift tasks, DUET-DINO consistently outperforms single-view and independent dual-view baselines, achieving 92% success on reach, 72.5% on angled-reach, and 60.0% on lift tasks. DUET-DINO is trained from scratch on DROID and RoboArena datasets and generalizes robustly under visual distribution shifts. We further show that while V-JEPA 2 wrist-view predictions underestimate visual dynamics induced by fine-grained actions, DINOv3 predictions better capture action-conditioned scene changes, leading to stronger downstream planning. The code and model checkpoints will be open-sourced. Project page: https://utn-air.github.io/DUET-DINO

AI.tldr: A cross-view latent world model (DUET-DINO) fuses static side and wrist camera views to enable 7-DoF action-conditioned planning, outperforming single-view baselines on reach (92%), angled-reach (72.5%), and lift (60%) tasks; trained on DROID and RoboArena, with robust generalization and plans to open-source.
AI.motivation: Existing action-conditioned latent world models struggle with fine-grained spatial and rotational (7-DoF) end-effector control. Leveraging complementary global scene and gripper-centric cues from dual static views can improve prediction fidelity and planning.
AI.method: DUET-DINO jointly learns action-conditioned predictions from static side- and wrist-camera observations via cross-view conditioning. It enables latent planning over the full 7-DoF action space and is evaluated on diverse reach, angled-reach, and grasp-and-lift tasks; compared against single-view and independent dual-view baselines; includes ablations comparing DINOv3 wrist-view dynamics to V-JEPA 2.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines across tasks: reach 92% success, angled-reach 72.5%, lift 60%. Demonstrates robustness to visual distribution shifts. DINOv3 better captures action-conditioned scene changes than V-JEPA 2 wrist-view predictions. Trained from scratch on DROID and RoboArena; code and checkpoints to be open-sourced.
AI.conclusion: Cross-view latent modeling with DUET-DINO effectively enables 7-DoF planning by combining global scene and gripper-centric information, yielding stronger action-conditioned predictions and downstream planning; supports generalization across distribution shifts and diverse tasks; release planned.

title: Interpreting Object-Dependent Concept Brittleness in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
comment: Accepted at ACM MM 2026. 27 pages, 17 figures, including appendices
summary: Although text-to-image diffusion models generally exhibit strong prompt-following ability, we identify a persistent and previously underexplored failure pattern in which a small subset of prompts differing only in the object consistently fails to realize the same target concept under identical generation settings. We term this phenomenon object-dependent concept brittleness. Such cases suggest systematic internal blind spots rather than random sampling noise. In this paper, we present an interpretability-oriented framework to audit and minimally correct these failures. Our key idea is to analyze denoising trajectories in a step-wise sparse autoencoder (SAE) space, where abstract style and attribute concepts become more separable than in the raw denoising representation. This sparse space enables us to compare successful and failed generations, identify concept dimensions whose evidence is missing, weakened, or temporally delayed, and construct class-level concept prototypes from reliable class-consistent samples. Based on this audit process, we introduce a lightweight inference-time correction strategy that interpolates denoising features toward the corresponding prototype in SAE space. Rather than serving as a task-specific retraining method, this intervention acts as a validation of the diagnosed concept deficiency. We evaluate the proposed framework on style and attribute failure cases across multiple diffusion backbones, with significant improvements in concept consistency, text fidelity, and repair success. Further analyses show that deeper denoising representations provide clearer concept structure, while early-stage intervention offers the strongest correction leverage. Code is available at https://github.com/Metecade/Object-Dependent-Concept-Brittleness.

AI.tldr: Identify and fix object-dependent concept brittleness in text-to-image diffusion via an interpretability-aided, sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature audit and a lightweight inference-time correction.
AI.motivation: Address a systematic failure pattern where similar prompts fail to realize the same target concept under identical settings, implying internal blind spots rather than stochastic noise.
AI.method: Audit denoising trajectories in a step-wise SAE space where abstract concepts are more separable; compare successful and failed generations to identify missing/weakened/delayed concept evidence; construct class-level prototypes from reliable samples; apply interpolation of denoising features toward prototypes at inference without retraining.
AI.result: Significant improvements in concept consistency, text fidelity, and repair success across multiple diffusion backbones; deeper denoising representations yield clearer concept structure; early-stage interventions offer the strongest correction leverage; code available.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a lightweight, interpretable framework to diagnose and partially repair object-dependent concept brittleness without task-specific retraining, validating the diagnose-correct paradigm for diffusion model failures.

title: Agent-Based ML-LLM Fusion with Self-Optimizing Prompts for Plateau Weather Alerts
summary: To address insufficient contextualization, weak generalization, and poor scenario adaptation in tourism meteorological services, we propose SmartWeatherAgent--a unified three-stage architecture integrating intent recognition, hazard prediction, and reasoning-enhanced generation. The system fuses rule-based methods with large language models to parse queries at multiple granularities and employs a LightGBM model enriched with highland-specific features (e.g., wind speed abruptness rate), achieving an F1-Macro score of 0.605 with 1.60 ms latency on high-wind, precipitation, and low-temperature events. A 12-round micro-step prompt self-optimization loop boosts the composite warning quality score S_final from 4.2 (B01) to 8.9 (B12, +112%). Key improvements include a sharp rise in B08 from data source citation (6.5 -> 8.5), sustained high performance in B10 via physical mechanism explanation, and a peak scientific rigor score of 9.2 in B12 through explicit uncertainty statements. The system autonomously generates structured warnings that integrate causal mechanisms, spatiotemporal evolution, quantitative evidence, regulatory references, and confidence statements--enhancing professional depth, logical rigor, and scientific soundness, and advancing meteorological services toward proactive perception, explainable decision-making, and intelligent agency.

AI.tldr: SmartWeatherAgent introduces a unified three-stage architecture that fuses rule-based methods with LLMs for intent recognition, hazard prediction, and reasoning-enabled generation, achieving improved warning quality and speed in tourism meteorological services.
AI.motivation: Address insufficient contextualization, weak generalization, and poor scenario adaptation in tourism meteorological services.
AI.method: A three-stage architecture: (1) intent recognition, (2) hazard prediction, (3) reasoning-enhanced generation. Combines rule-based methods with large language models. Uses LightGBM with highland-specific features (e.g., wind speed abruptness rate). Employs a 12-round micro-step prompt self-optimization loop.
AI.result: F1-Macro 0.605 with 1.60 ms latency for high-wind, precipitation, and low-temperature events. S_final rises from 4.2 (B01) to 8.9 (B12, +112%). B08 improves data source citation (6.5→8.5). B10 maintains high performance via physical mechanism explanations. Peak scientific rigor score reaches 9.2 in B12 with explicit uncertainty statements. Autonomously generates structured warnings with causal mechanisms, spatiotemporal evolution, quantitative evidence, regulatory references, and confidence statements.
AI.conclusion: Advances meteorological services toward proactive perception, explainable decision-making, and intelligent agency through integrated, rigorous warning generation.

title: ProMeta: Few-shot PROTAC-targeted degradation prediction across E3 ligases
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, and 2 tables. Source code and reproducibility resources are available at https://github.com/yeyufeiyyf/prometa and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21371599
summary: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) have emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy that selectively degrades historically ''undruggable'' targets via the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Despite growing efforts to develop computational predictors of PROTAC degradation activity, existing supervised approaches remain severely challenged by data scarcity and imbalance across E3 ligases, limiting their ability to generalize beyond well-studied ligase contexts. In practice, labeled data are heavily concentrated on a few ligases (e.g., CRBN and VHL), while the majority of E3 ligases remain underexplored yet are critical for expanding the design space of targeted degraders. Developing methods that enable robust cross-ligase generalization with minimal labeled data is therefore essential for improving the practical utility of computational PROTAC discovery. We reformulate PROTAC degradation activity prediction across E3 ligases as a few-shot meta-learning problem and present ProMeta, a prototype-based graph neural network trained through episodic meta-learning on source-E3 tasks and evaluated on held-out target-E3 tasks through support-conditioned inference. ProMeta performs inference without updating the encoder by dynamically estimating class prototypes from minimal target-ligase support samples. On the CRBN-to-VHL benchmark, ProMeta achieves AUROC values of 0.796 under K=2, Q=3 and 0.883 under K=2, Q=5, improving by 19.9% and 6.8%, respectively, over the corresponding supervised GNN baseline. Reverse VHL-to-CRBN transfer under the same protocol yielded AUROC values of 0.702 (K=2, Q=3) and 0.821 (K=2, Q=5), confirming bidirectional applicability while revealing direction and data-regime dependence. Together, these results support ProMeta as a practical framework for cross-ligase few-shot prediction under the evaluated support/query protocols.

AI.tldr: ProMeta is a prototype-based graph neural network for cross-ligase few-shot PROTAC degradation prediction, enabling robust generalization with minimal labeled data.
AI.motivation: Overcome data scarcity and heavy ligase imbalance in PROTAC degradation prediction to extend design space to underexplored E3 ligases.
AI.method: Prototype-based GNN trained with episodic meta-learning on source E3 tasks; at test time, support-conditioned inference estimates class prototypes from a small target-ligase support set with no encoder updates.
AI.result: CRBN→VHL: AUROC 0.796 (K=2,Q=3) and 0.883 (K=2,Q=5), outperforming supervised GNN by 19.9% and 6.8%; VHL→CRBN: AUROC 0.702 (K=2,Q=3) and 0.821 (K=2,Q=5). Demonstrates bidirectional cross-ligase generalization with direction/data-regime dependence.
AI.conclusion: ProMeta offers a practical encoder-free framework for cross-ligase few-shot PROTAC degradation prediction, expanding the actionable degrader design space, though performance varies by ligase direction and data regime.

title: Show-Harness: Just a VLM Agent Can Play Robots
summary: Foundation vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit broad intelligence about the world, yet translating this intelligence into robot control remains challenging. We present Show-Harness, an Embodied Harness that enables VLMs to "play" robots through a compact semantic interface linking intent to action. Show-Harness exposes discrete semantic action units that VLMs can naturally reason over, while embodiment-specific interpreters deterministically ground them into local robot actions, keeping the VLM directly responsible for fine-grained physical decisions. Through the same interface, Show-Harness demonstrates the feasibility of (1) directly unlocking closed-source frontier VLMs for zero-shot robot control, and (2) adapting small-scale open-source VLMs for low-cost deployment with just a few GPU-hours of fine-tuning. We further develop GUMI (GUI Manipulation Interface), which extends the same semantic action space to GUI-based demonstration collection, allowing humans and agents to "play" robots across embodiments without specialized teleoperation hardware. Extensive experiments show that Show-Harness-equipped VLM agents generalize robustly across tasks, embodiments, and environments, outperforming representative agentic and VLA paradigms. These results suggest that the right interface can unlock substantial embodied capability from foundation VLMs, without requiring additional model capacity or costly embodiment-specific pretraining.

AI.tldr: Show-Harness introduces an Embodied Harness that connects foundation vision-language models to robot control via discrete semantic action units, with embodiment-specific interpreters grounding actions deterministically. It enables zero-shot control of frontier VLMs and cost-efficient fine-tuning of open-source VLMs. GUMI extends the interface to GUI-based demonstrations. Experiments show robust generalization across tasks, embodiments, and environments, suggesting the right interface unlocks embodied capability without extra model capacity or costly pretraining.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between capable but general-purpose foundation VLMs and concrete embodied robot control. Exploit a compact, semantically meaningful action interface so VLMs can reason about actions while interpreters ground them into safe, executable robot commands, enabling zero-shot control of frontier models and efficient adaptation of smaller models.
AI.method: Introduce discrete semantic action units that VLMs reason over. Use embodiment-specific interpreters to deterministically ground these actions into local robot commands. Develop Show-Harness as the interfacing framework. Create GUMI (GUI Manipulation Interface) to extend the same semantic action space to GUI-based demonstrations for cross-embodiment play. Evaluate zero-shot control of frontier VLMs and few-GPU-hours fine-tuning of open-source VLMs, and benchmark against representative agentic and VLA methods.
AI.result: Show-Harness enables robust generalization across tasks, embodiments, and environments. Demonstrates feasibility of zero-shot control for closed-source frontier VLMs and practical fine-tuning for small open-source VLMs. Outperforms selected baselines in embodied task settings.
AI.conclusion: A carefully designed semantic-action interface can unlock substantial embodied capabilities from foundation VLMs without increasing model capacity or needing extensive embodiment-specific pretraining.

title: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversations via Class-Wise Adaptive Modality Fusion and Affective Geometry
comment: Accepted at the 11th Workshop and Competition on Affective Behavior Analysis in-the-Wild (ABAW) at ECCV 2026
summary: Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC) requires integrating heterogeneous textual, audio, and visual cues while accounting for conversational context and emotional dynamics. We extend the Self-Distillation Transformer architecture for ERC with appearance+geometry visual representations, class-wise adaptive modality fusion, and a valence-arousal prior for affective transitions. On the MELD and IEMOCAP datasets, geometry-enhanced visual representations improve weighted F1 by 0.27 and 4.36 points over appearance-only features, respectively, while class-wise adaptive fusion provides further gains of 0.17 and 0.25 points over the original softmax gate. The valence-arousal prior yields targeted improvements of 0.30 and 0.74 accuracy points on emotionally shifted utterances while preserving performance on stable turns. These results indicate that structured facial cues, emotion-dependent modality weighting, and affective geometry provide complementary benefits for multimodal ERC.

AI.tldr: Multimodal ERC enhancement via geometry-informed visuals, adaptive modality fusion, and valence-arousal priors; reports dataset-specific gains on MELD and IEMOCAP.
AI.motivation: ERC requires integrating heterogeneous textual, audio, and visual cues within conversational context; appearance-only features and simple fusion may miss structured facial cues and affective transitions.
AI.method: Extend Self-Distillation Transformer for ERC with (1) geometry-enhanced visual representations alongside appearance, (2) class-wise adaptive modality fusion beyond a softmax gate, (3) a valence-arousal prior to model affective transitions; evaluated on MELD and IEMOCAP.
AI.result: Geometry-enhanced visuals improve weighted F1 by 0.27 (MELD) and 4.36 points (IEMOCAP) over appearance-only features. Class-wise adaptive fusion adds 0.17 (MELD) and 0.25 points (IEMOCAP) beyond the original softmax gate. Valence-arousal prior yields improvements of 0.30 (MELD) and 0.74 accuracy points (IEMOCAP) on emotionally shifted utterances, while preserving performance on stable turns.
AI.conclusion: Structured facial cues, emotion-aware modality weighting, and affective geometry complement each other to enhance multimodal ERC across datasets.

title: Kernel-Managed Shared Memory for System-Wide Personalization
summary: AI systems become more useful when they can adapt to the people using them, but in multi-agent systems, useful context learned by one agent often remains unavailable to others. We present kernel-managed shared memory, a system-level abstraction in which specialized agents write structured, tagged memories while the agent-system kernel, not individual agents, governs retrieval, privacy enforcement, and prompt injection. We implement and evaluate this design on AIOS and compare it against three alternatives across three assistant models (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, Qwen-2.5:7B) and 1,800 total trials. Against an unmanaged external memory backend (Mem0) using identical underlying storage, kernel-managed retrieval and injection improve personalization scores by 2.4-4.0 points on a 5-point scale (e.g., 1.05 to 4.69 profile usage on GPT-4o), with every comparison significant at p < 10^-18. Against standard retrieval-augmented injection, gains are similarly large and consistent across all three models. Against full, unfiltered context concatenation, a soft ceiling on available context rather than on response quality, kernel-managed injection statistically matches performance on two of three models and shows a small, model-specific deficit on the third, while using substantially shorter prompts: end-to-end latency is 15-61% lower across all three models, with corresponding reductions in per-call token usage and inference cost. These results indicate that centralizing memory management in the agent-system kernel, rather than leaving retrieval and privacy enforcement to individual agents, delivers most of the personalization benefit of unconstrained context at a fraction of its cost.

AI.tldr: Centralizing memory management in the agent-system kernel enables cross-agent personalization with built-in privacy controls, delivering large personalization gains and notable efficiency savings over unmanaged memory and standard RAG, while approaching unconstrained-context performance at lower cost.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent AI systems, context learned by one agent is often unavailable to others, limiting personalization and reuse. A system-level, kernel-governed memory abstraction can enable controlled sharing, privacy, and prompt management.
AI.method: Introduce kernel-managed shared memory as a system-level abstraction where agents write structured, tagged memories; the kernel governs retrieval, privacy enforcement, and prompt injection. Implemented on AIOS; evaluated across GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, Qwen-2.5:7B (1,800 trials); compared against Mem0 (unmanaged external memory), standard retrieval-augmented injection, and full-context concatenation baselines.
AI.result: Personalization scores improved by 2.4–4.0 points on a 5-point scale (e.g., GPT-4o: 1.05 → 4.69); all comparisons significant (p < 1e-18). Gains robust across all three models and against standard RAG. Against full-context concatenation, the approach matches performance on two models and shows a small deficit on the third, while using much shorter prompts. End-to-end latency reduced 15–61% across models, with lower per-call token usage and inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Centralizing memory management in the agent-system kernel yields most of the personalization benefits of unconstrained context at a fraction of its cost.

title: Strangers to Themselves: What Language Models Say About Themselves Is Generic
summary: Language models can fluently describe how they would behave: whether they would cave to pushback, misuse a tool, or lie under pressure. Is that description actually about the model speaking? We turn self-knowledge into a prediction test. Across nine behavioral evaluations, we measure how a model behaves under different conditions, ask it to predict those rates, and compare its predictions with controls that remove the self from the question. We find that: (i) Direct self-report is weak (r = +0.04), and even showing the model the exact items only raises prediction to +0.24. Crucially, the same item-informed question about "capable AI agents in general" does just as well (+0.28), while other models' answers about themselves predict the target model at least as well as its own. (ii) Frontier scale does not detectably change this pattern: any gains in prediction are not self-specific, and are consistent with a better theory of how AI assistants behave rather than better self-knowledge. (iii) First-person framing does have one robust effect: it shifts reports in the flattering direction, understating harmful behavior relative to the same question about a generic agent. (iv) Finetuning on a model's own behavioral record can teach narrow self-predictions, but it also changes the behavior being predicted and the gains do not transfer broadly. The practical implication is simple: asking a model what it would do mostly reveals a theory of AI assistants in general, plus a favorable bias, rather than privileged knowledge of that model.

AI.tldr: Asking a model to predict its own behavior largely reveals a general theory of AI assistants and a favorable bias, not privileged self-knowledge.
AI.motivation: To test whether self-descriptions or predictions by language models reflect true model self-knowledge or merely a generalizable theory about AI behavior and biases, across multiple evaluation setups.
AI.method: Nine behavioral evaluations where the model’s actual behavior under different conditions is measured; the model is asked to predict those rates; predictions are compared to controls that remove the self from the question; experiments include direct self-report, item-informed self-prediction, predictions about capable AI agents in general, frontier scaling, first-person framing, and finetuning on the model’s own behavioral record.
AI.result: (i) Direct self-report is weak (r ≈ 0.04); item-informed self-prediction raises prediction to ≈0.24; questions about “capable AI agents in general” perform similarly or better (≈0.28); other models predicting the target model perform as well or better. (ii) Frontier scale shows no robust self-specific gains; better predictive theory rather than self-knowledge. (iii) First-person framing biases predictions in a flattering direction, understating harmful behavior vs. generic agent. (iv) Finetuning on the model’s own behavior yields narrow self-predictions that do not transfer broadly and also alters the behavior being predicted.
AI.conclusion: Asking a model what it would do mainly reveals a general theory of AI assistants and a favorable bias, not privileged knowledge about that specific model.

title: Vague2Detect: Handling Ambiguous Prompts in Knowledge-Based Open-World Detection
summary: Real-world detectors must often interpret functional or ambiguous prompts, yet conventional models such as YOLO remain restricted to fixed class lists. Even open-vocabulary models like YOLO-World frequently misalign vague language with the intended objects. Building on our prior work Commonsense-Guided Open-World Object Detection Using LLMs and Visual-Semantic Matching, we address YOLO-World's limitations in grounding task-driven queries. We propose Vague2Detect, a hybrid pipeline in which a fine-tuned Sentence-BERT retrieves candidates from a structured household Knowledge Base (KB), and YOLO-World verifies their presence in the image. For prompts outside the KB, a large language model (GPT-3.5-turbo) generates candidate descriptions, dynamically expanding the KB to cover novel concepts. On a benchmark of household scenes using custom images and an Open Images V7 subset, YOLO-World alone achieves only 32% Vague Prompt Success Rate (VPSR), the ability to map ambiguous queries to correct detections. In contrast, Vague2Detect improves performance to 61% VPSR with high precision, and up to 85% when augmented with GPT fallback.

AI.tldr: Hybrid Vague2Detect combines a structured knowledge-base with Sentence-BERT retrieval, YOLO-World verification, and GPT-3.5-turbo-based expansion to map vague prompts to detections, achieving VPSR improvements from 32% (YOLO-World) to 61% (plus up to 85% with GPT fallback).
AI.motivation: Address the gap where real-world, task-driven, ambiguous prompts are not well grounded by fixed-class detectors or open-vocabulary models, reducing misalignment between language and image content.
AI.method: A two-stage hybrid pipeline: (1) recover candidate objects from a structured household KB using fine-tuned Sentence-BERT; (2) verify candidates in the image with YOLO-World; (3) for prompts outside the KB, a GPT-3.5-turbo module generates candidate descriptions and dynamically expands the KB; (4) optionally use GPT fallback to further augment candidates; (5) evaluate on household scenes (custom images and Open Images V7 subset).
AI.result: YOLO-World baseline achieves 32% VPSR; Vague2Detect raises VPSR to 61% with high precision, and up to 85% when GPT fallback is used.
AI.conclusion: Vague2Detect substantially improves grounding of vague, task-driven prompts in open-world object detection by integrating structured knowledge with LLM-assisted expansion and a vision-language verifier, showing strong gains over a strong baseline.

title: Beyond Surface Imitation: Contrastive Modeling for Reasoning Path Alignment in Multimodal In-Context Learning
summary: In-context learning (ICL) is widely used in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and achieves strong performance across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, existing multimodal ICL methods often rely on surface level imitation of in-context demonstrations, making it difficult for MLLMs to align their responses with the reasoning path required by the given multimodal input. This limitation becomes more pronounced in complex multimodal tasks, thereby restricting further improvements in MLLM performance. To address this issue, we propose a new multimodal ICL framework that combines contrastive demonstration modeling with the self-refinement capability of MLLMs. Specifically, our framework reformulates each demonstration by explicitly contrasting a suboptimal response with a better response under the same input, together with a reasoning path that reveals how the response should be refined. This contrastive formulation makes the reasoning path toward the desired response more explicit and guides the MLLM beyond superficial imitation. Furthermore, because effective refinement depends on the current response, we introduce a response-conditioned retrieval mechanism to select demonstrations whose reasoning paths are more relevant to the current response. In addition, we use a lightweight alignment controller to predict response quality and determine whether further refinement is needed. Experiments on three types of multimodal tasks show that the proposed framework consistently improves MLLM performance, with particularly notable gains on visual question answering (VQA).

AI.tldr: A contrastive, self-refining multimodal in-context learning framework that reformulates demonstrations as contrastive suboptimal/better responses plus reasoning paths, coupled with response-conditioned retrieval and an alignment controller, yielding consistent gains across multimodal tasks, especially VQA.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal ICL relies on superficial imitation and lacks explicit reasoning guidance, hindering performance on complex multimodal tasks.
AI.method: Reformulate each demonstration as a contrastive pair (suboptimal vs better response) with a reasoning path; use response-conditioned retrieval to pick demonstrations aligned to the current input; employ a lightweight alignment controller to predict response quality and decide refinement steps.
AI.result: Consistent improvements across three multimodal tasks, with particularly notable gains in visual question answering.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive demonstration modeling with self-refinement and dynamic retrieval enhances MLLM alignment to reasoning paths, improving performance; the approach leverages current response context and selective refinement.

title: Beyond Conventional Federated Learning via High-Order Regularization
summary: Federated clients that perform several local optimization steps can return parameter displacements with widely different magnitudes. The quadratic regularization of FedProx grows linearly with displacement and therefore offers limited control over the contrast between ordinary and unusually large client movements. We here introduce HiFedProx, which replaces the quadratic penalty with a scale-matched power-type regularizer indexed by $p\geq2$. All powers have the same regularization-gradient magnitude at a reference displacement $R$, while every $p>2$ gives a weaker response below $R$ and a stronger response above it. An exact affine reference calculation shows that increasing $p$ compresses relative displacement disparities, although very large powers approach fixed-radius behavior and increase local curvature. HiFedProx combines this geometry with finite-budget stochastic client optimization and same-minibatch Armijo backtracking. In paired five-seed experiments on a frozen 60-writer FEMNIST subset, a common-parameter study over $p\in\{2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}$ shows similar clean-training performance but substantial gains under composite stress. The lowest moderate- and severe-stress losses occur at $p=7$ and $p=6$, improving over $p=2$ by $11.44\%$ and $23.16\%$, respectively. Although displacement-tail ratios continue to decrease through $p=8$, predictive performance peaks in an intermediate range and Armijo trial cost increases with $p$. These results indicate that the exponent should be calibrated rather than maximized. In our experiments, $p=5$--$7$ provides the most useful range.

AI.tldr: HiFedProx uses a scale-matched power-type regularizer (p>=2) to compress client-displacement disparities in FedProx, improving robustness under stress while preserving training performance; optimal p lies in 5–7.
AI.motivation: Federated learning with FedProx shows widely varying local displacements; quadratic regularization offers limited control over large vs. typical movements. A regulizer that better regularizes extreme displacements and is tunable could improve robustness under finite-budget optimization.
AI.method: Replace FedProx's quadratic penalty with a scale-matched power-type regularizer indexed by p>=2. All powers share the same regularization-gradient magnitude at a reference displacement R; p>2 weakens the penalty below R and strengthens it above R. An exact affine reference analysis shows that increasing p compresses relative displacement disparities; very large p tends toward fixed-radius behavior and increases local curvature. Combine with finite-budget stochastic client optimization and Armijo backtracking on minibatches. Conduct a common-parameter sweep over p in {2,3,4,5,6,7,8} on a frozen 60-writer FEMNIST subset across five seeds.
AI.result: Under composite stress, similar clean-training performance is observed across p, but substantial gains occur for moderate/severe stress at p=6–7 (e.g., p=7 reduces moderate-stress loss by 11.44% and p=6 reduces severe-stress loss by 23.16% compared with p=2). Displacement-tail ratios continue to decrease with p up to 8, but predictive performance peaks at an intermediate p, and Armijo trial cost grows with p. Recommendation: calibrate p rather than maximize; p in the 5–7 range provides the most useful trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The exponent p should be calibrated to the task; an intermediate range (5–7) offers the best balance between reducing displacement disparities and maintaining training efficiency, yielding robustness under stress with minimal loss in clean training.

title: Putting Captions to the Test: Evaluating Video Caption Quality through Multiple-Choice Question Answering
summary: Evaluating video captioning remains a critical challenge for Visual Large Language Models (VLLMs). Existing metrics primarily rely on matching generated text against ground-truth references. This paradigm suffers from the ``one-to-many'' nature of video description, where high-quality captions are often penalized for lexical mismatches or valid shifts in visual focus. Furthermore, such assessments are typically one-dimensional, failing to provide a fine-grained analysis of caption quality. To address this, we redefine caption quality through the lens of information fidelity: A caption must maximize the coverage of salient visual information while ensuring strict factuality. We introduce CapQuiz, a novel reference-free benchmark that assesses captions based on their utility in answering human-verified, fine-grained, multiple-choice questions derived from the video. CapQuiz features a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 question types (spanning Descriptive and Inferential categories) across 24 diverse video domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CapQuiz correlates significantly better with human judgments than existing metrics and offers interpretable insights into model performance.

AI.tldr: CapQuiz is a reference-free benchmark for video captioning that evaluates captions by their ability to answer human-verified multiple-choice questions, capturing information fidelity and factuality.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of text-based, ground-truth–dependent metrics which penalize lexical variation and shifts in visual focus due to the one-to-many nature of video descriptions; need a fine-grained, human-aligned evaluation.
AI.method: Develop CapQuiz with a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 question types (Descriptive and Inferential) spanning 24 video domains; generate multiple-choice questions from videos; measure caption utility by answering these questions; compare to existing metrics and human judgments.
AI.result: CapQuiz correlates significantly better with human judgments than existing metrics; provides interpretable, fine-grained diagnostics of model performance across domains.
AI.conclusion: CapQuiz offers a robust, reference-free evaluation framework for video captioning emphasizing information fidelity and factuality.

title: Why Sample What You Can Enumerate? Exact Policy Optimization for Genomic Tool Selection
summary: Reinforcement learning over a frozen reasoner has become a common recipe for teaching a policy which external tools to invoke. We show that this recipe becomes structurally mismatched in specialist scientific settings where the complete tool-subset space is enumerable. There, a small set of recurring computational capabilities covers the domain, so the space of tool subsets is combinatorial yet small enough to enumerate, and GRPO still estimates an action expectation from a handful of sampled rollouts. Worse, the approximation degrades as training succeeds: as the policy concentrates on preferred subsets it resamples them, sampled rewards collide, and the group-normalized advantage vanishes. On genomic reasoning the fraction of questions yielding no reward signal rises from 0.2% under a uniform reference policy to 20.8% after GRPO training. As a remedy, we introduce FGPO (Full-Group Policy Optimization), which (1) scores every tool subset and optimizes the exact action expectation, so each update sees the complete action space, and (2) precomputes the reward of each question--subset pair into an exhaustive table, removing frozen-reasoner calls from the training loop entirely. Across five frozen reasoners and three genomic benchmarks, FGPO outperforms GRPO in all 15 settings by 6.75 points on average and up to 14.20, while a standard on-demand GRPO schedule would require 2.4 times as many frozen-reasoner reward evaluations and, on GenomeQA, FGPO cuts invoked tools per question from 2.36 to 1.40.

AI.tldr: FGPO addresses mismatch issues of GRPO in enumerable tool-subset spaces by exhaustively evaluating action subsets and precomputing rewards, improving performance and efficiency.
AI.motivation: In specialist scientific settings, the complete tool-subset space is enumerable and small; GRPO's sample-based action-value estimation degrades as the policy concentrates on certain subsets, leading to reward-signal sparsity and wasted evaluations.
AI.method: Introduce FGPO: (1) score every tool subset to optimize the exact action expectation over the full action space; (2) precompute the reward for each question–subset pair into an exhaustive table, removing frozen-reasoner calls from training.
AI.result: FGPO outperforms GRPO across five frozen reasoners and three genomic benchmarks (15 settings) by 6.75 points on average (up to 14.20); GRPO would require about 2.4× as many frozen-reasoner reward evaluations; GenomeQA shows tool-invocation reduction from 2.36 to 1.40 per question.
AI.conclusion: In domains with enumerable tool-subset spaces, FGPO provides more stable, efficient training and higher performance by eliminating reward-signal sparsity and resampling issues that plague GRPO.

title: Meta-LinEXP3: Online-within-Online Learning for Adversarial Linear Contextual Bandits
summary: Meta-learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for transferring knowledge across sequential bandit tasks. While substantial progress has been made for stochastic bandits and non-contextual adversarial bandits, meta-learning for adversarial linear contextual bandits (ALCBs) with random action sets remains largely unexplored. To address this problem, we propose Meta-LinEXP3, an online-within-online algorithm that constructs a predictable task-level prior from completed tasks to guide the inner LinEXP3 learner. For known context distributions, we develop a policy-centered estimator that achieves an intrinsic-dimension $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$ per-task regret bound. For unknown distributions, we introduce a past-only regularized moment estimator with an $\mathcal{O}(n^{2/3})$ leading regret term and explicit finite-sample error. We further establish a direct connection between prior accuracy and transfer regret, showing that increasingly accurate priors yield sublinear transfer-dependent regret across tasks. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Meta-LinEXP3, including its application to structured hyperspectral tensor sampling.

AI.tldr: Meta-LinEXP3 is a meta-learning framework for adversarial linear contextual bandits with random action sets, using a task-level prior to guide an inner LinEXP3 learner. It provides two estimators for different knowledge of context distributions, achieving sublinear per-task regret and sublinear transfer regret as priors improve, with validation on hyperspectral tensor sampling.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient knowledge transfer across sequential adversarial linear contextual bandit tasks when actions are randomly drawn, filling a gap where prior work mainly addresses stochastic or non-contextual/adversarial settings without random action sets.
AI.method: An online-within-online approach that constructs a predictive task-level prior from completed tasks to guide an inner LinEXP3 learner. For known context distributions, a policy-centered estimator achieves intrinsic-dimension O(sqrt(n)) per-task regret. For unknown distributions, a past-only regularized moment estimator achieves leading regret O(n^{2/3}) with explicit finite-sample error. Establishes a link between prior accuracy and transfer regret, and validates the method with experiments including structured hyperspectral tensor sampling.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees: per-task regret bounds of O(sqrt(n)) with known context distributions and O(n^{2/3}) leading term with finite-sample error for unknown distributions; transfer regret is sublinear in the number of tasks as priors become more accurate. Empirical results demonstrate Meta-LinEXP3’s effectiveness, including in structured hyperspectral tensor sampling.
AI.conclusion: Meta-LinEXP3 provides a principled meta-learning solution for ALCBs with random action sets, delivering sublinear transfer-dependent regret via task-level priors and two estimators tailored to the availability of context distribution information; applicable to real-world structured sensing tasks.

title: From Few-Shot Segmentation to Clinician-in-the-Loop Medical Image Analysis
summary: Few-shot medical image segmentation (FSMIS) seeks to delineate unseen structures from a small support set, but its standard formulation fixes task-defining evidence before inference.
