AI.method: Comprehensive literature review of VideoLLMs and related frame-sampling, vision-encoder, and LLM-prompt/decoder techniques since late 2022 and earlier components; taxonomy by pipeline stage; synthesis of accuracy-cost metrics where possible; compilation of a community resource repository.
AI.result: Provides a structured taxonomy of efficiency approaches, aggregates reported accuracy-cost data across papers when feasible, and identifies gaps such as audiovisual efficiency and the lack of standardized evaluation protocols; releases a repository with curated resources (momentslab/awesome-efficient-videollm).
AI.conclusion: Efforts to improve VideoLLM efficiency are progressing, with multiple independent strategies across stages. However, standardized benchmarks and comprehensive audiovisual efficiency coverage remain underdeveloped, necessitating coordinated evaluation practices and more holistic optimization.

title: A Dominant Diffuse Phase in the Sparse Autoencoder Phase Diagram
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly used to recover interpretable features from neural-network activations, yet systematic feature co-occurrence can cause distinct features to be absorbed or merged. The MAIS-O43 open problem proposes a controlled experiment to characterize when recovery of a true synthetic dictionary gives way to feature merging as the nesting fraction $γ$, sparsity penalty $λ$, and dictionary size $M$ vary. We implement the specified protocol and evaluate 200 independently initialized fits across ten of the 165 grid cells. We observe zero full-dictionary recoveries and zero merges. Instead, every run converges to a reproducible diffuse phase: reconstruction is nearly perfect, but learned atoms typically remain far from the true features (median best cosine 0.5-0.7 against a 0.95 recovery criterion) and learned codes are an order of magnitude denser than the ground truth. This behavior persists under robustness checks and across the full 165-cell grid using standard minibatch Adam (3,300 additional fits). Since the global optimum of the exact sparse-coding objective is known to merge nested features in the two-feature case, these results suggest that trained SAEs need not reach the corresponding minima, and that the phase diagram of trained models may differ fundamentally from that of objective minimizers.

AI.tldr: Sparse autoencoders under the MAIS-O43 protocol rarely recover the true dictionary; they converge to a diffuse phase with near-perfect reconstruction and dense codes, implying trained SAEs may not reach the exact objective minima and that the phase diagram differs from that of minimizers.
AI.motivation: Characterize when recovery of a true synthetic dictionary occurs versus feature merging as nesting fraction γ, sparsity penalty λ, and dictionary size M vary; assess robustness across initializations and grid coverage.
AI.method: Implement the MAIS-O43 protocol; evaluate 200 independently initialized fits across ten grid cells; perform robustness checks with 3,300 additional fits across the full 165-cell grid; train using standard minibatch Adam; assess dictionary recovery (cosine similarity to true features), evidence of merges, reconstruction quality, and code sparsity.
AI.result: Zero full-dictionary recoveries and zero merges observed; all runs converge to a reproducible diffuse phase: reconstruction nearly perfect, learned atoms remain far from true features (median best cosine 0.5–0.7 against 0.95 recovery criterion); learned codes are an order of magnitude denser than ground truth; results robust across robustness checks and grid; global optimum of exact sparse coding in the two-feature case is known to merge nested features.
AI.conclusion: Trained SAEs may not reach the minima of the exact sparse-coding objective; the phase diagram of trained models can differ fundamentally from objective minimizers, calling into question the applicability of objective-minimization intuition to trained autoencoders.

title: Spot-the-shift: Evaluating Grounded Image Difference Captioning of Long-term Changes
summary: Long-term change understanding from images of the same place revisited over time is a challenging task with applications in map maintenance and urban infrastructure monitoring. Prior work addresses it either through pixel-level prediction or difference captioning, neither of which is sufficient to reliably measure how well models detect and describe such changes. We introduce SPOT-THE-SHIFT, a human-verified benchmark for grounded image difference captioning of long-term changes in real-world driving scenes. Our benchmark provides natural language captions and spatial masks for structural changes across each image pair. We further propose an evaluation protocol that reliably assesses models' captioning ability, validated through human studies. Benchmarking state-of-the-art MLLMs, we find that models struggle with the fine-grained multi-image spatial capability required for this task. Finally, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that improves an off-the-shelf MLLM without sacrificing general capabilities.

AI.tldr: A grounded, long-term change-detection benchmark for driving scenes (SPOT-THE-SHIFT) with human-verified captions and spatial masks, plus an evaluation protocol and a synthetic-data augmentation pipeline; results show current MLLMs struggle with fine-grained multi-image spatial reasoning, which is addressed by the synthetic data approach.
AI.motivation: To reliably measure how well models detect and describe long-term changes across image pairs, addressing limitations of pixel-level predictions and generic difference captions in real-world driving contexts used for map maintenance and infrastructure monitoring.
AI.method: Introduce SPOT-THE-SHIFT with natural language change captions and spatial masks; develop a robust evaluation protocol validated by human studies; benchmark state-of-the-art multimodal large language models (MLLMs); create a synthetic data generation pipeline to augment training and improve model performance.
AI.result: Current MLLMs perform poorly on fine-grained, spatially grounded change captioning; the synthetic data pipeline improves an off-the-shelf MLLM while preserving broad capabilities.
AI.conclusion: SPOT-THE-SHIFT provides a valuable benchmark for grounded, spatially-aware long-term change understanding and reveals a gap in current MLLMs; synthetic data can enhance performance without compromising general capabilities, suggesting directions for future research and model development.

title: View-Structured Conformal Prediction for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders novel views in real time, but an uncertainty heatmap does not certify that a rendered view meets a certain prediction coverage. We treat novel-view synthesis as structured regression and ask that, with probability at least $1-α$, RGB prediction boxes cover at least a $1-β$ fraction of pixels in a new view. We propose View-Structured Conformal Prediction (VSCP). It splits the pre-calibration scale into a spatial shape from the renderer and a transferable view-difficulty factor, which predicts the smallest view-wise multiplier that shape needs. A held-out quantile over views (View-CP) then gives finite-sample validity even when transferring to new scenes. The same factorization makes the analysis exact: a conformity score is the ratio of oracle to predicted view difficulty, and excess width separates into a test-side and a calibration-side term. Across 13 real scenes, pixel-pooled calibration reaches 89.9\% marginal pixel coverage but only 61.4\% view-event coverage at a 90\% target, while View-CP reaches 91.7--92.0\%. At matched coverage VSCP cuts width by 22.1\% against a constant scale, and matches a ten-model ensemble's 21.0\% reduction using only one model per scene and four rather than ten rasterization passes per query. VSCP also improves on the closest single-model baseline, the 3DGS-U field, by 4.7 points ($p=0.0225$). The view predictor transfers from bounded source families to all nine unbounded Mip-NeRF~360 scenes. There the full scale beats the constant scale with 20.7\% width saving on all nine scenes. It also keeps an 18.3\% saving under a different densification backbone and runs at 216--280 FPS on an RTX~4090.

AI.tldr: VSCP extends conformal prediction to 3D view synthesis by factoring scale into a renderer-shape and a view-difficulty predictor; achieves finite-sample validity with robust coverage and reduced interval width across scenes, with real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty heatmaps for 3D Gaussian Splatting do not certify prediction coverage for novel views; need a coverage guarantee for structured regression in novel-view synthesis.
AI.method: Split pre-calibration scale into spatial shape + transferable view-difficulty factor; train/estimate view-difficulty; use held-out quantile View-CP across views for finite-sample validity; analysis yields that conformity score is ratio oracle/predicted view difficulty; width decomposes into test-side and calibration-side terms.
AI.result: Pixel-level calibration achieves 89.9% coverage; view-event coverage 61.4% at 90% target; View-CP 91.7-92.0%; VSCP reduces width by 22.1% vs constant scale; matches 10-model ensemble's 21% width reduction with much less compute; improves on 3DGS-U by 4.7 points (p=0.0225); transfers to Mip-NeRF 360 with 20.7% width saving; 18.3% saving under another backbone; 216-280 FPS on RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: Factorized VSCP provides finite-sample validity for novel-view predictions with improved coverage and significantly reduced predictive widths, enabling fast, reliable uncertainty quantification in real-time neural rendering and transferability across scenes and backbones.

title: SceneHI: High-Resolution 3D-Consistent Scene Texturing with Controllable Illumination
summary: SceneHI is a framework that lifts high-resolution, illumination-aware priors from 2D diffusion models to perform 3D texture synthesis. It is the first to demonstrate that high-resolution textures, previously limited to 2D synthesis, can be generated directly on 3D objects without model fine-tuning or optimization. Designed for complex, multi-object environments, SceneHI uniquely combines 3D-consistency, high-resolution fidelity, and physically plausible baked shadows within a single generative pipeline. To enforce strict geometric coherence, we introduce an exact analytical pixel-to-texel mapping that aligns diffusion trajectories across multiple viewpoints. We utilize High-Resolution Latent Textures (HRLTs) as a persistent canvas for gradually denoised textures, while camera views perform the denoising steps in latent pixel space. This ensures a shared base texture that can be subsequently refined to high resolution without compromising multi-view consistency. Finally, a light-aware generative pass embeds realistic geometry-consistent shadows directly into the atlases, bridging the gap to production workflows. SceneHI achieves high visual fidelity while reducing generation time by 80% compared to existing scene-level methods.

AI.tldr: SceneHI enables high-resolution 3D texture synthesis by lifting illumination-aware priors from 2D diffusion models into a unified pipeline, achieving 3D-consistent, shadow-aware textures on complex scenes without fine-tuning and with ~80% faster generation than prior methods.
AI.motivation: To generate high-fidelity, multi-view-consistent textures directly on 3D objects using diffusion priors, addressing the limitations of 2D-only textures and the need for efficient, production-friendly workflows.
AI.method: Introduce an exact pixel-to-texel mapping for cross-view diffusion trajectory alignment; use High-Resolution Latent Textures (HRLTs) as a persistent texture canvas; perform denoising in latent pixel space across camera views; apply a light-aware generative pass to bake geometry-consistent shadows into atlases; integrate into a single end-to-end pipeline without model fine-tuning.
AI.result: Demonstrates high visual fidelity, 3D-consistency, high-resolution textures, and baked shadows; achieves ~80% reduction in generation time versus existing scene-level methods in complex, multi-object environments.
AI.conclusion: SceneHI proves that high-resolution 3D textures can be synthesized directly from 2D diffusion priors in a coherent, production-friendly framework, combining 3D-consistency, high-res detail, and physically plausible lighting within a single generative pipeline.

title: One Loop, Two Gains: Can Active Learning win the Lottery for Free?
summary: The lottery ticket hypothesis posits the existence of winning tickets: sparse subnetworks that, when trained in isolation from their original initialization, match the accuracy of the full dense network. The predominant method for discovering such tickets, iterative magnitude pruning, alternates pruning with full retraining from scratch until convergence over many cycles. Similarly, deep active learning also retrains a model from scratch after each acquisition round as new labels become available. Despite this shared reliance on iterative retraining with a substantial computational overhead, the two paradigms have been studied separately. We observe that the iterative training loop inherent to pool-based active learning already provides the exact computational structure that iterative magnitude pruning exploits, and propose Improve & Prune (I&P), a method that integrates magnitude pruning into each active learning retraining cycle at practically no additional cost. This raises a key empirical question: can iterative magnitude pruning produce winning tickets under the non-stationary data regime of active learning? We investigate this question across multiple acquisition functions, architecture families, and image classification datasets, including an active fine-tuning scenario. Our results demonstrate that I&P yields sparse, deployable models at each active learning iteration. Those match the accuracy of their dense counterparts at sparsities up to 95%, effectively obtaining winning tickets as a byproduct of the active learning pipeline. These per-iteration sparse models can address two computational bottlenecks - per-round model retraining and acquisition scoring over the unlabeled pool - that currently prevent the practical adoption of DAL on large architectures and large unlabeled pools.

AI.tldr: Integrating magnitude pruning into each active-learning retraining cycle yields per-iteration winning tickets, enabling sparse models that match dense accuracy up to 95% sparsity with minimal extra cost.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational burden of deep active learning (DAL) by exploiting the iterative retraining structure common to both pruning (IMP) and pool-based AL, and test whether pruning can produce winning tickets under AL's non-stationary data regime.
AI.method: Introduce Improve & Prune (I&P): integrate magnitude pruning into every retraining step inside the AL loop, performing pruning and retraining concurrently with negligible overhead.
AI.result: Across multiple acquisition functions, architectures, and image datasets (including active fine-tuning), I&P yields sparse, deployable models at each AL iteration that match dense-model accuracy at sparsities up to 95%, effectively yielding winning tickets within the AL pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Iterative magnitude pruning can produce winning tickets in non-stationary AL settings; per-iteration sparse models address key bottlenecks in DAL, aiding practical deployment on large architectures and unlabeled pools.

title: Beyond Weak Labels: Prompt-Guided Local Refinement for Weakly Supervised Water Segmentation in High-Resolution Multispectral Imagery
comment: Accepted for presentation at ICIP Workshop 2026 and to be published as part of the conference proceedings
summary: High-resolution water mapping supports environmental monitoring and related applications, but accurate pixel-level labels are difficult and costly to produce. Official hydrographic vectors provide scalable weak supervision, but they contain artifacts like boundary noise, temporal mismatch, and omissions of small water structures. We propose a two-stage framework for weakly supervised water segmentation in high resolution multispectral imagery. Stage 1 learns initial masks from rasterized vector pseudo-labels, and Stage 2 converts these masks into structured component-wise prompts for localized refinement. On a manually corrected validation set, refinement improves SegFormer-B0 from 0.9509 to 0.9535 IoU and U-Net from 0.9408 to 0.9486 IoU, with corresponding F1 gains from 0.9749 to 0.9762 and 0.9695 to 0.9736. It leads to sharper shorelines, reduced boundary spillover, and better thin-structure delineation. The results indicate that prompt-guided refinement can improve pseudo-label-based water segmentation by targeting local errors that are poorly captured by global training supervision.

AI.tldr: Two-stage weak supervision for water segmentation: rasterized vector pseudo-labels provide initial masks, then component-wise prompts guide localized refinement. Small but consistent IoU/F1 gains on SegFormer-B0 and U-Net, with sharper shorelines and better thin-structure delineation.
AI.motivation: Leverage scalable but noisy official hydrographic vectors to generate pseudo-labels for high-resolution water mapping. Address boundary errors, temporal mismatch, and omissions through localized, prompt-based refinement.
AI.method: Stage 1: rasterize vector-derived pseudo-labels to train initial masks. Stage 2: derive structured component-wise prompts from masks to refine predictions locally. Evaluate on SegFormer-B0 and U-Net using a manually corrected validation set.
AI.result: Refinement yields IoU increases: SegFormer-B0 0.9509→0.9535; U-Net 0.9408→0.9486. F1 increases: SegFormer-B0 0.9749→0.9762; U-Net 0.9695→0.9736. Qualitative gains include sharper shorelines, reduced boundary spillover, improved delineation of thin water structures.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-guided refinement effectively improves pseudo-label-based water segmentation by targeting local errors not captured by global training, indicating promise for scalable high-resolution water mapping with weak supervision.

title: A Later Test Set Is Not a New Domain: Pretraining Familiarity Survives a Contamination-Free Hold-Out
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code, data fetchers and per-series results: https://github.com/mahdinaser/tsfm-bench
summary:
Time-series foundation models are evaluated almost exclusively on public archives that predate them, so a strong score cannot be separated from having seen the test set during pretraining. The obvious remedy is a hold-out that postdates the models. We build one: thirteen forecasters -- four classical, three trained per dataset, six pretrained -- on seven groups drawn from five domains, every observation published after the last model was released, and every dataset rebuildable without an API key. Under this protocol pretrained models win 5 of 7 groups, lose one to a Theta baseline, and on daily exchange rates are indistinguishable from a seasonal naive forecast, along with every other method tested.
  We then ask what separates the wins from the losses, and report a negative result: the two intrinsic properties one would reach for -- seasonal strength and spectral entropy, measured on the input window -- do not account for the pattern, and seasonal strength is if anything negatively associated with the advantage. What does track it is corpus familiarity. Our largest gain (28% lower MASE than the best classical method, on weekly Wikipedia pageviews) falls on Wikipedia pageviews, the domain TimesFM's authors describe as the bulk of its pretraining corpus, at the same granularities and differing only in time window. Within the pretrained family, where every model forecasts identical series so that series difficulty cancels, the TimesFM family outranks the Chronos family by -0.53 ranks on Wikipedia against -0.09 everywhere else (1,500 vs. 754 series, Mann-Whitney p < 1e-5). We conclude that a temporal hold-out removes memorisation of a window but not familiarity with a domain, that benchmarks therefore need domain hold-outs stated relative to disclosed corpora, and that the practitioner's question is less which model is better than whether their domain is one the model was raised on.

AI.tldr: Pretrained time-series foundation models often beat classical baselines on post-release hold-out data, but gains stem from corpus familiarity with the domain rather than intrinsic properties; domain-aware, post-dated hold-outs are needed for fair evaluation.
AI.motivation: Assess whether time-series foundation model gains come from memorizing test windows or genuine generalization, and determine what factors drive performance beyond model type.
AI.method: Construct a post-dated hold-out evaluation across 13 forecasters (4 classical, 3 trained per dataset, 6 pretrained) on 7 groups from 5 domains, with observations published after the last model release and datasets rebuildable without API keys. Compare pretrained vs classical baselines, measure MASE, rank differences (Mann–Whitney), and analyze correlation with seasonal strength, spectral entropy, and corpus familiarity (domain of the training data).
AI.result: Pretrained models win 5 of 7 groups, lose 1 to a Theta baseline, and are indistinguishable from seasonal naive on daily exchange rates. The strongest gains (e.g., 28% lower MASE) occur in Wikipedia pageviews, a domain heavily represented in the pretraining corpus. Within pretrained models, TimesFM outperforms Chronos on Wikipedia but not elsewhere; partitioning by series shows that platform advantages stem from domain familiarity rather than intrinsic properties. Seasonal strength and spectral entropy do not explain the pattern.
AI.conclusion: Temporal, post-dated hold-outs reduce memorization of a specific window but do not remove domain familiarity effects; evaluation should include domain-revealing hold-outs tied to disclosed corpora, and practitioners should consider whether the target domain matches the model’s training data rather than assuming a general model superiority.

title: OmniMed-FL: A Robust Multimodal Federated Learning Framework for Clinical Diagnosis
summary: Simultaneous assessment of medical imaging and patient records is often required in clinical diagnosis. However, standard machine learning algorithms cannot analyze these data types together. Meanwhile, compliance with HIPAA and GDPR can constrain centralized aggregation of sensitive patient data. This leaves a crucial void of secure fusion of visual and textual context across distant networks. Thus, we present OmniMed-FL, a controlled systems study of multimodal federated learning for five-class clinical condition classification (Normal, Pneumonia, COVID-19, Pleural Effusion, Cardiomegaly). Our proxy corpus pairs 3,000 public chest radiographs with 3,000 class-conditioned synthetic notes, matched by class, not by patient. The framework benchmarks eight fusion strategies, three initializations, four missing-text imputation rules, and matched federated baselines under non-IID Dirichlet partitioning across 3 to 20 hospital clients. As all notes are synthetic and pairing is not patient-level, these are descriptive proxy comparisons, not estimates of diagnostic performance or deployment readiness. Within those limits with clients ($K=5$) and severe skew ($α=0.1$), local-only training achieves a macro-F1 score of 0.297, FedAvg achieves $0.662\pm0.074$, FedProx $0.737\pm0.085$, a matched FedMME-style one-shot ensemble $0.647\pm0.080$, and our SCAFFOLD-AdamW adaptation $0.070\pm0.015$, the 0.075 FedProx-FedAvg gap falling inside the wider of the two two-seed standard deviations. Over a $4\times3$ grid, label skew costs up to 0.27 F1 whereas a near-sevenfold client increase costs at most 0.10, while bidirectional volume grows linearly to 183.5 GiB at $K=20$. Multimodal fusion leads on both corpora, scoring 0.956 against 0.934 for text and 0.664 for images on the synthetic corpus and 0.906 against 0.880 and 0.737 on the radiograph corpus, for $2.3\times$ the model state of text alone.

AI.tldr: OmniMed-FL studies multimodal federated learning for clinical condition classification using synthetic image-text pairs to benchmark fusion under non-IID settings; finds fusion improves macro-F1 over unimodal baselines, but results are descriptive due to synthetic data and proxy pairings.
AI.motivation: Privacy constraints (HIPAA/GDPR) impede centralized fusion of radiology images and clinical notes. Multimodal federated learning across distributed hospitals could enable joint modeling without data pooling; the study benchmarks fusion methods and robustness under non-IID data.
AI.method: Constructed a proxy corpus of 3,000 chest radiographs paired with 3,000 class-conditioned synthetic notes (not patient-matched). Five-class labels: Normal, Pneumonia, COVID-19, Pleural Effusion, Cardiomegaly. Evaluates across 3–20 hospital clients (K=5 default). Non-IID Dirichlet partitioning. Benchmarks eight fusion strategies, three initializations, four missing-text imputation rules, and matched federated baselines. Comparisons include FedAvg, FedProx, a matched FedMME-style one-shot ensemble, and SCAFFOLD-AdamW adaptation. Reported macro-F1 scores for both unimodal and multimodal setups on synthetic and radiograph corpora.
AI.result: Key results include: local-only macro-F1 = 0.297; FedAvg = 0.662 ± 0.074; FedProx = 0.737 ± 0.085; matched FedMME-like ensemble = 0.647 ± 0.080; SCAFFOLD-AdamW = 0.070 ± 0.015. Over a 4×3 grid, label skew costs up to 0.27 F1; increasing client count to K=20 increases bandwidth up to 183.5 GiB. Multimodal fusion outperforms unimodal baselines: on the synthetic corpus, fusion = 0.956 vs text 0.934 and image 0.664; on the radiograph corpus, fusion = 0.906 vs text 0.880 and image 0.737. This yields ~2.3× the model state of text alone.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal fusion in a federated, privacy-conscious setting shows substantial performance gains over unimodal baselines in these proxy experiments, suggesting potential for clinical utility. However, results derive from synthetic, non-patient-level pairings and are descriptive; real-world generalization, patient-level alignment, and deployment readiness require further validation. Potential limitations include variable SCAFFOLD performance, non-IID data effects, and bandwidth considerations.

title: Shape-guided Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View X-ray 3D Reconstruction
comment: Accepted at: Off-Grid: 1st Workshop on Continuous Representations and Grid-Free Methods in Medical Imaging, MICCAI 2026
summary: Sparse-view X-ray 3D reconstruction is essential for reducing radiation exposure, but recovering a density field from a handful of X-ray projections is severely ill-posed. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting has achieved state-of-the-art performance in sparse-view reconstruction by representing the volume using explicit, optimized primitives, but it requires dozens of projected views. With fewer views, reconstruction quality degrades severely since the explicit primitives are optimized freely without any anatomical information. Anatomical structures, in contrast, share similar geometry and density across a population. Their variations are bounded within a limited range that statistical shape models can capture. This paper proposes a shape-guided Gaussian splatting framework for sparse-view X-ray 3D reconstructions. Our contribution lies in driving Gaussian positions toward anatomically valid configurations, alongside atlas-based density regularization. Our method ensures anatomically consistent reconstruction and improves PSNR by 2.83 dB over a state-of-the-art Gaussian splatting baseline with as few as 5 views. Code Available: https://github.com/polyshape-lab/ShapeGuidedGaussian

AI.tldr: Shape-guided Gaussian splatting with atlas-based density regularization improves sparse-view X-ray 3D reconstruction, achieving +2.83 dB PSNR with 5 views.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view X-ray 3D reconstruction is severely ill-posed due to limited projections. While 3D Gaussian Splatting achieves strong results, it relies on primitive optimization without anatomical priors. Anatomical structures exhibit bounded geometric variability across populations, which can be captured by statistical shape models.
AI.method: Introduce shape-guided Gaussian splatting that steers Gaussian positions toward anatomically valid configurations using an atlas-based density prior, coupled with density regularization to enforce plausible anatomy during optimization for sparse-view reconstruction.
AI.result: Achieves a PSNR improvement of 2.83 dB over a state-of-the-art Gaussian splatting baseline using as few as 5 views; code is available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating anatomical priors via atlas-based regularization with Gaussian splatting yields more anatomically consistent reconstructions in sparse-view X-ray 3D imaging and enables higher quality results with very few views.

title: Forgetting Only What Matters: Layer-Selective Unlearning toward Robust LLMs
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables, AACL-IJCNLP 2026, conference paper
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or otherwise undesirable training content, creating privacy, safety, and regulatory concerns. Machine unlearning offers a practical alternative to full retraining, but many existing methods apply broad or fixed parameter updates that can degrade utility and remain brittle under deployment changes such as post-training quantization, where forgotten knowledge may partially re-emerge. We propose Forgetting Only What Matters via Unlearning Layers (FOM-UL), a layer-level unlearning framework that selects transformer layers using a forget-to-retain significance score. This score identifies layers with high influence on the forget set and low sensitivity to the retain set, allowing FOM-UL to concentrate updates where they are most effective while leaving most of the model unchanged. This targeted update strategy improves the forgetting-utility trade-off and provides an empirical path toward quantization-resilient unlearning by reducing the chance that small, diffuse updates are erased by low-bit rounding. Across TOFU, KnowUnDo, and MUSE-style evaluations, FOM-UL reduces residual memorization compared with strong GA, NPO, KLD, SURE, ReLearn, and LUNAR-based baselines while preserving retain-set utility close to the vanilla model. Under 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization, FOM-UL maintains stronger memorization suppression and utility preservation than competing methods, and adversarial prompt evaluations show lower recovery of forgotten content. Overall, FOM-UL provides an efficient unlearning strategy that improves targeted forgetting, utility preservation, and deployment robustness without claiming formal guarantees of erasure.

AI.tldr: FOM-UL is a layer-level unlearning method that targets transformer layers using a forget-to-retain significance score to improve forgetting with minimal utility loss, showing robustness to post-training quantization and better protection against recovered forgotten content without formal erasure guarantees.
AI.motivation: LLMs memorize sensitive or copyrighted content, creating privacy and safety concerns; existing unlearning methods can degrade utility and are brittle under deployment changes like quantization; a targeted, deployment-robust approach is needed.
AI.method: Compute a forget-to-retain significance score per transformer layer to identify layers with high influence on forgotten data and low sensitivity to retained data; update only those layers to erase memorized content while leaving others unchanged, aiming for efficient, quantization-resilient unlearning.
AI.result: FOM-UL reduces residual memorization compared with strong baselines (GA, NPO, KLD, SURE, ReLearn, LUNAR) and preserves retain-set utility close to vanilla; under 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization, memorization suppression and utility preservation are stronger than competing methods; adversarial prompts show lower recovery of forgotten content across TOFU, KnowUnDo, and MUSE-style evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Targeted, layer-level forgetting improves forgetting efficacy and deployment robustness without claiming formal erasure guarantees, offering a practical path toward quantization-resilient unlearning.

title: Enhanced Deformable Convolution with Center-invariant Offset and Edge-aware Mask
summary: Deformable convolution networks have recently become popular for many computer vision tasks, especially for semantic segmentation, because of their exceptional capabilities in dynamic spatial modeling. However, due to the dense deformable offsets and the lack of longer-range dependencies, they can not fully adopt proper and precise deformations for feature representations. To tackle the issues, in this paper, we propose Enhanced Deformable ConvNets (EDCN) for semantic segmentation. Specifically, a novel Enhanced Deformable Convolution (EDC) is exploited in the decoder, which integrates the Center-invariant Offset Module (COM) and Edge-aware Mask Module (EMM). The COM employs larger kernels and eliminates deformations at the kernel center, obtaining offsets that are more in line with the target from richer spatial information. Concurrently, the EMM obtains the significance of image content via Sobel edge detection, then selectively applies deformations based on the content significance, minimizing unnecessary deformations associated with relatively less important information, thereby avoiding impact from less informative regions. Experiments show that EDC outperforms state-of-the-art deformable convolution variants, including Deformable ConvNets V1-V4 and Entire Deformable ConvNets, across mainstream segmentation datasets with various decoder settings. Moreover, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. In addition, visualizations illustrate that EDC enhances spatial adaptation and target focus. We further analyze the extendibility of EDC to larger kernels on the image classification benchmark. Code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: EDC enhances deformable convolutions for semantic segmentation by introducing COM and EMM, improving spatial adaptation and content-aware deformation, with strong empirical gains and extendibility to larger kernels.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of dense deformable offsets and lack of long-range dependencies in deformable ConvNets, aiming for more accurate and targeted feature deformations in segmentation.
AI.method: Propose Enhanced Deformable Convolution (EDC) with two modules: Center-invariant Offset Module (COM) using larger kernels and removing center deformation to align offsets with target; Edge-aware Mask Module (EMM) using Sobel edge detection to weigh deformation by content significance, applied in the decoder.
AI.result: EDC outperforms state-of-the-art deformable convolution variants (including Deformable ConvNets V1–V4 and Entire Deformable ConvNets) across mainstream segmentation datasets under various decoder configurations; ablation validates contributions; visualizations show improved spatial adaptation and target focus; extendibility to larger kernels demonstrated on image classification benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: EDC provides more accurate, content-aware spatial deformations for segmentation, reducing deformation in less informative regions while enhancing alignment to targets; results suggest good generalization and potential for broader kernel sizes, with code to be released.

title: Semigroup-JEPA: Latent Dynamics Consistency for Zero-Shot Physics Generalization
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models learn a compact latent representation of the world that supports prediction and planning, but their capability to learn physics and generate physically realistic dynamics remains hitherto untested. In this work, we introduce SemiGroup-JEPA (SG-JEPA), which extends the LeWorldModel framework by supplying the parameter governing the physics to the temporal model via action-conditioning and jointly training an encoder and predictor through an autoregressive latent rollout. To evaluate the model's ability to generalize out of distribution, we design dynamical tasks under different gravitational fields that, despite obeying the same physical law, exhibit qualitatively different dynamics, ranging from floating motion in weak gravitational fields to rapid bouncing in strong ones. In contrast to DINO-WM, SG-JEPA reduces open-loop prediction error by up to 2 times on two-dimensional datasets, and increases control success rate up to 2.5 times for three-dimensional robotic datasets, for which we train independent diffusion policies. To explain this advantage, we develop a linear feature model that separates local law-conditioned error from its recursive amplification under rollout. Guided by this model, we find that back-propagating the multi-step rollout loss into the representation trains the encoder to keep the features that the predictor can carry forward, and that those are the features the dynamics depend on, so most of the gain comes from the encoder learning better features rather than from the predictor learning better dynamics. See project page at https://sg-jepa.github.io.

AI.tldr: SG-JEPA extends JEPA by conditioning the temporal model on physics parameters and jointly training encoder/predictor with autoregressive latent rollouts, improving out-of-distribution physics generalization and planning performance.
AI.motivation: Test whether world models can learn physically realistic dynamics and generalize under varying gravity, addressing the gap in evaluating physics-capable latent dynamics within JEPA-style architectures.
AI.method: Introduce SemiGroup-JEPA (SG-JEPA) by conditioning the latent dynamics on a physics parameter (gravity) via the action-conditioned temporal model, and train encoder and predictor jointly through autoregressive latent rollouts. Compare against DINO-WM and evaluate on 2D datasets (prediction error) and 3D robotic datasets (control with diffusion policies). Develop a linear feature model to separate local law-conditioned error from recursive rollout amplification and analyze where gains originate.
AI.result: SG-JEPA reduces open-loop prediction error by up to 2x on 2D datasets and increases control success rate by up to 2.5x on 3D robotic datasets with independent diffusion policies, compared to DINO-WM.
AI.conclusion: Backpropagating the multi-step rollout loss into the encoder yields features that the predictor can carry forward and that dynamics depend on; most gains come from improved encoder representations rather than the predictor's dynamics. A linear analysis clarifies how policy- and physics-conditioned errors propagate through rollouts, guiding encoder-focused improvements.

title: Advanced Brain Tissue Imaging with Data-Consistent Diffusion Priors in Laminographic X-Ray Nanoimaging
summary: Nanoscale imaging of mammalian brains is critical for connectomics. X-ray laminography enables high-throughput imaging of extended, plate-like biological specimens. However, the tilted acquisition geometry leads to incomplete Fourier-space coverage, giving rise to a missing-cone of information. Conventional reconstruction methods cannot recover unmeasured information within the cone, resulting in artifacts that distort fine brain structures. While resolving these requires modeling 3D structure, direct 3D deep learning approaches are limited by data scarcity and computational cost. Here we introduce LUCID (Laminography with Unified Consistent Diffusion), a framework that combines multi-view diffusion priors with projection-domain data consistency. LUCID integrates complementary 3D structural information while enforcing strict alignment with the laminography forward model. On simulated datasets, LUCID substantially improves spatial fidelity and restores missing Fourier components, outperforming baseline methods. Applied to experimental laminography data, LUCID generalizes robustly despite being trained exclusively on fully sampled tomographic volumes, and effectively recovers unmeasured Fourier information.

AI.tldr: LUCID fuses multi-view diffusion priors with projection-domain data consistency to address missing-cone artifacts in X-ray laminography for nanoscale brain imaging, restoring unmeasured Fourier components and improving spatial fidelity.
AI.motivation: Overcome incomplete Fourier coverage in laminography due to tilted acquisition and data scarcity for 3D deep learning, enabling accurate nanoscale connectomics.
AI.method: Integrates diffusion-based priors learned from fully sampled volumes with projection-domain data consistency across multiple laminography views, enforcing strict alignment with the laminography forward model.
AI.result: In simulations, substantially improved spatial fidelity and missing Fourier reconstruction, outperforming baselines; applied to experimental laminography data, showed robust generalization despite training only on fully sampled volumes and effective recovery of unmeasured Fourier information.
AI.conclusion: LUCID provides a unified framework that leverages 3D structural priors while honoring the measurement model to mitigate missing-cone artifacts in laminography, with strong potential for high-throughput nanoscale brain imaging.

title: Nonmaximal sums of maximally monotone operators under Rockafellar's constraint qualification
summary: We construct counterexamples to Rockafellar's sum conjecture in which two maximally monotone operators satisfy the interior-domain condition but their sum is not maximally monotone. We give one counterexample on $c_0$ and another on $\ell^1$ with its usual norm. We establish a general construction theorem that computes the entire monotone polar of a class of graphs, gives a necessary and sufficient condition for their maximal monotonicity, and shows how a positive rank-one perturbation yields a nonmaximal sum under this condition. We verify the theorem's hypotheses and its maximality criterion on $c_0$, thereby obtaining a counterexample to the conjecture. Furthermore, we construct a bounded linear surjection from $\ell^1$ onto $c_0$ and use it to obtain the counterexample on $\ell^1$.

AI.tldr: The paper presents counterexamples to Rockafellar's sum conjecture in which two maximally monotone operators with interior-domain condition have a sum that is not maximally monotone, first on c0 and then on l1 via a surjection from l1 to c0. It introduces a general construction that computes the monotone polar of a class of graphs, provides a necessary and sufficient criterion for maximal monotonicity, and shows how positive rank-one perturbations can destroy maximality. The results are validated on c0 and extended to l1 using the surjection.
AI.motivation: To test the limits of Rockafellar's sum theorem by constructing explicit counterexamples under the interior-domain hypothesis, and to develop a general, verifiable framework (via monotone polar and perturbations) for assessing maximal monotonicity of operator sums.
AI.method: Develops a general construction theorem that computes the entire monotone polar of a class of monotone graphs; derives a necessary and sufficient condition for maximal monotonicity of sums; analyzes the effect of positive rank-one perturbations; applies the framework to obtain counterexamples on c0; uses a bounded linear surjection from l1 onto c0 to transfer the counterexample to l1.
AI.result: Explicit counterexamples to the conjecture: two maximally monotone operators with interior-domain condition whose sum is not maximally monotone, first on c0 and then on l1; a general monotone-polar-based criterion for maximality; demonstration that rank-one perturbations can yield nonmaximal sums under the criterion.
AI.conclusion: Rockafellar's sum conjecture fails under the interior-domain condition; the paper provides a robust framework (monotone polar and perturbation analysis) to decide maximality and to generate further counterexamples, including extending the construction from c0 to l1.

title: AgroVisNet: A lightweight Convolutional Network and the BD-PlantDX Expert-Validated Benchmark for Radish, Potato and Pointed Gourd Disease Classification
summary: Automated plant disease diagnosis is increasingly deployed on farmer-held devices in regions where agronomic expertise is scarce and network connectivity is unreliable. Three obstacles limit its practical value: public benchmarks are dominated by a small set of non-native crops, region-specific datasets are rarely validated by domain experts, and the architectures that reach competitive accuracy carry parameter budgets that are unsuited to low-cost hardware. We propose AgroVisNet, a compact convolutional network trained from scratch, together with BD-PlantDX, an expert-validated benchmark of 12,432 field images spanning 12 classes of radish, potato and pointed gourd in healthy and diseased states, collected across the Bogura and Nilphamari districts of Bangladesh. AgroVisNet couples grouped bottleneck residual blocks carrying sequential channel and spatial attention with multi-scale depthwise blocks and a dual-pooling classification head, reaching 290,572 trainable parameters. On BD-PlantDX the model attains 99.52% test accuracy and 99.52% weighted F1, exceeding all six ImageNet-pretrained lightweight backbones evaluated under an identical protocol while using 8.7 to 16.8 times fewer parameters and 1.3 to 8.5 times fewer multiply-accumulate operations. Exported for deployment, the model quantises to a 0.46 MB full-integer network at a 0.22 percentage-point accuracy cost and classifies an image in 8.40 ms on a single CPU. Across five random seeds accuracy remains at 99.57 +- 0.10%, a ten-variant ablation isolates the contribution of each component, and the same architecture transfers without redesign to two independently collected datasets at 98.71% and 99.05% accuracy. Grad-CAM evidence indicates that predictions rest on lesion-bearing leaf regions rather than on background cues.

AI.tldr: Compact AgroVisNet achieves near-state-of-the-art accuracy for field plant disease diagnosis with far fewer parameters and on-device efficiency, validated on a dedicated field benchmark (BD-PlantDX) and transferable to other datasets.
AI.motivation: Address three practical obstacles: over-reliance on limited crop benchmarks, lack of expert validation on region-specific data, and heavy parameter budgets hindering deployment on low-cost devices.
AI.method: Proposes AgroVisNet: a compact CNN with grouped bottleneck residual blocks, sequential channel and spatial attention, multi-scale depthwise blocks, and a dual-pooling classification head; 290,572 parameters. BD-PlantDX: 12,432 field images, 12 classes across healthy/diseased for radish, potato, pointed gourd, collected in Bangladesh. Deployment considerations include quantisation to 0.46 MB and CPU inference 8.40 ms. Performance evaluation under identical protocol against six ImageNet-pretrained lightweight backbones; cross-seed and cross-dataset ablations.
AI.result: Achieves 99.52% test accuracy and 99.52% weighted F1 on BD-PlantDX, surpassing all baselines; 8.7-16.8x fewer parameters and 1.3-8.5x fewer MACs; single-CPU inference 8.40 ms; cross-seed accuracy 99.57 +- 0.10%; architecture transfers to two independent datasets with 98.71% and 99.05% accuracy; Grad-CAM shows focus on lesion regions.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a practical, domain-tailored, resource-efficient model and benchmark for on-device plant disease recognition, with strong accuracy, robustness across seeds, and transferability; supports real-world deployment in resource-constrained settings.

title: Learning with Covariance Matrices: Principal Component Analysis Meets Learning with Graphs
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Signal Processing Magazine
summary: This feature article provides an overview of the theoretical foundations for coVariance neural networks (VNNs), i.e., graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on covariance matrices as graphs. Covariance matrices are ubiquitous across domains, and hence, the deployment of GNNs often leverages graphs of pairwise statistical dependencies. Existing theoretical contributions on GNNs consider abstract graph representations and cannot accommodate the data-driven nuances associated with covariance matrices. This tutorial brings into focus various novel theoretical insights via mathematical analyses of VNNs that have broad signal processing implications, including: (i) a conceptual equivalence between VNNs and principal component analysis (PCA)-based information processing; (ii) refined stability bounds on predictive outcomes in the presence of finite sample-induced covariance matrix perturbations; and (iii) refined characterization of transferability of VNNs across multiscale datasets. The theoretical insights discussed herein provide the underlying principles and justification towards adopting VNNs over workhorse PCA-based learning pipelines, in applications where covariance matrices are useful descriptors of data structure. We also convey how impact of these foundational advances permeates to \textit{principled} designs and applications of learning methods across broad domains where covariance matrices emerge. Notably, we elucidate the conceptual insights facilitated by VNNs to the specific task of characterizing brain age gap for neurodegenerative conditions using neuroimaging datasets, a timely problem in computational neuroscience. Broader impacts to other application domains are discussed as well.

AI.tldr: The abstract surveys theoretical foundations of covariance-based GNNs (VNNs), linking them to PCA, and detailing stability and transferability analyses with a neuroimaging application, arguing for principled VNN-based designs over PCA pipelines.
AI.motivation: Covariance matrices are pervasive and often serve as graphs of pairwise statistical dependencies. Existing GNN theory uses abstract graphs and may not capture covariance-driven data nuances, necessitating a theoretical treatment of VNNs.
AI.method: Theoretical analyses establishing: (i) an equivalence between VNNs and PCA-based information processing, (ii) refined stability bounds under finite-sample covariance perturbations, and (iii) refined transferability across multiscale datasets; plus discussion of principled design implications and a neuroimaging example (brain age gap).
AI.result: Characterizes VNNs as offering principled information processing aligned with PCA, improved understanding of stability and transferability under realistic covariance estimation, and a roadmap for applying VNNs in neuroscience and other domains where covariance descriptors are informative.
AI.conclusion: VNNs provide a robust theoretical foundation that justifies their use over PCA pipelines in covariance-centric learning, with broad applicability and explicit design insights for multiscale data and biomedical imaging tasks.

title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework
summary: AI literacy provides foundational competencies that support ethical, transparent, and sustainable technological development, although higher-order capabilities such as governance, critical evaluation, and strategic decision-making extend beyond basic literacy into advanced levels of AI competency. This study positions AI literacy as a governance capacity that complements and strengthens all 17 SDGs. It introduces a six-level taxonomy of artificial intelligence reasoning and ethics that extends traditional learning models by incorporating ethical judgement and strategic foresight. This taxonomy forms the foundation of an integrated framework linking education, governance, and sustainable development. A survey of 300 participants from diverse professional backgrounds within a national context which reveals strong technical awareness but limited ethical and governance readiness, highlighting critical gaps in public capacity to manage artificial intelligence responsibly. Findings show that ethical reasoning and reflective thinking are the strongest predictors of sustainable and trustworthy artificial intelligence use. The study proposed to embed literacy-based competencies into curricula, institutional policies, and governance mechanisms to accelerate equitable and responsible progress toward sustainable development goals

AI.tldr: AI literacy framed as governance capacity linked to all 17 SDGs; introduces a six-level AI reasoning and ethics taxonomy; reveals gaps in public readiness; ethical reasoning and reflective thinking predict trustworthy AI; recommends embedding literacy in curricula, policies, and governance.
AI.motivation: Advance responsible AI development by elevating literacy to governance-relevant competencies and aligning with sustainable development goals; address public capacity shortfalls.
AI.method: Theoretical framework development (AI literacy as governance capacity) plus a six-level taxonomy; integrated framework connecting education, governance, SDGs; empirical component: survey of 300 professionals in a national context.
AI.result: High technical awareness but limited ethical/governance readiness; ethical reasoning and reflective thinking are strongest predictors of sustainable, trustworthy AI use; identifies critical gaps in public capacity.
AI.conclusion: Embed literacy-based competencies into curricula, institutional policies, and governance mechanisms to accelerate equitable and responsible progress toward SDGs.

title: Quantum Feature Engineering for Credit Default Prediction: When and Why IQP Circuits Help Linear Classifiers
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing Conference (HPEC 2026)
summary: Credit default prediction is a tabular classification problem in which modest gains in F1 translate directly into reduced financial exposure. We ask whether Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits can produce features that improve a classifier over both its raw classical baseline and Kernel PCA - the strongest unsupervised classical non-linear alternative - at an equal feature budget. The dataset provides 23 financial attributes per client; for an n-qubit circuit we select n of them, encode each as a rotation angle, and read 2n expectation values back out as new features. The motivation for using a quantum circuit is computational: an n-qubit IQP circuit runs in constant depth and encodes feature correlations in a 2^n-dimensional Hilbert space, whereas classical simulation of its exact output statistics scales exponentially in n. Using the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset and five-fold cross-validation, we find that appending 16 IQP features (n = 8 qubits) to a Logistic Regression model raises F1 from 0.462 to 0.517 (+0.055, p < 0.0001). Kernel PCA, the next-best method, reaches only 0.493 at the same feature count; the gap survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 12 tests (p = 0.00007). No other classifier - Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost, or k-NN - benefits, which points to a linear-expressivity mechanism rather than a generic improvement. We also show that how the 8 input features are chosen matters: Random Forest importance-guided selection reaches F1 = 0.523, while encoding maximally uncorrelated features drops it to 0.496, demonstrating that the circuit amplifies informative structure rather than creating it from scratch.

AI.tldr: IQP-derived features improve logistic regression for credit default prediction; 8-qubit features outperform kernel PCA and other classifiers; feature selection quality matters.
AI.motivation: Assess whether IQP circuit-based features can provide a linear, informative feature expansion that improves classification at a fixed feature budget, given exponential quantum encoding advantages vs classical methods.
AI.method: Use UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset; select n of 23 attributes as input to an n-qubit IQP circuit; encode each as a rotation angle; read 2n expectation values as features; evaluate several classifiers with and without IQP features using five-fold CV; compare against kernel PCA; test random-forest-guided vs uncorrelated feature selections.
AI.result: With 16 IQP features (n=8), logistic regression F1 rises from 0.462 to 0.517 (Δ=0.055, p<0.0001); kernel PCA reaches 0.493; multiple testing corrected p=0.00007; other classifiers gain nothing; RF-feature selection yields F1=0.523 while maximizing uncorrelated features yields 0.496.
AI.conclusion: Results support a linear-expressivity mechanism: quantum features improve a linear classifier at fixed feature budget; the choice of input features is crucial; the circuit amplifies informative structure rather than creating it anew.

title: Cross-Model Agreement as a Deployment-Time Reliability Signal for Automatic Polyp Segmentation
summary: In real-time colonoscopy, ground-truth annotations are unavailable at inference, so polyp segmentation models can fail silently. We propose Referee-Based Quality Estimation (RBQE), a reference-free framework measuring agreement between a primary segmentation model and an independently trained referee on the same image. RBQE is evaluated on a standardized 1,223-image external benchmark drawn from four public datasets, using four referee configurations chosen to separate two design axes: referee independence and architectural diversity. Using a common Agreement Dice descriptor, a same-architecture referee differing from the primary model only in random initialization already yields a useful reliability signal (ROC-AUC = 0.923), showing that independent training alone is sufficient. Cross-architecture referees improve further: SegFormer-B0 achieves the strongest performance (ROC-AUC = 0.960), significantly outperforming the same-architecture control and UNet++, and exceeding a representative Test-Time Augmentation baseline by 0.055 ROC-AUC under an identical protocol, whereas a prompt-coupled MedSAM referee underperforms despite maximal architectural diversity. Because empty-mask agreement is trivially separable, we also report a restricted evaluation excluding such cases: ROC-AUC falls to 0.876 (SegFormer-B0, 1,046 images) and 0.783 (same-architecture control, 975 images), yet RBQE's margin over both baselines widens on this identical subset. RBQE additionally increases the mean Dice of retained predictions as low-agreement cases are progressively rejected, supporting selective prediction, and requires only one additional deterministic referee forward pass at inference. Our study therefore supports cross-model agreement as a practical, interpretable reliability framework for automated polyp segmentation.

AI.tldr: RBQE uses cross-model agreement between a primary segmentation model and a referee to estimate reliability in real-time polyp segmentation without ground-truth. Cross-architecture referees yield stronger reliability signals than same-architecture ones, improving ROC-AUC on a 1,223-image external benchmark; restricted evaluation excluding empty masks lowers absolute performance but widens RBQE’s margin vs baselines. RBQE requires only one extra deterministic referee pass and supports selective prediction by discarding low-agreement cases.
AI.motivation: In real-time colonoscopy, ground-truth segmentation is unavailable at inference, risking silent failures. A practical reliability signal is needed to indicate when the primary model’s predictions should be trusted.
AI.method: Train an independent referee model(s) on the same images but with different architecture than the primary model. Measure agreement using an Agreement Dice descriptor between the primary segmentation and the referee’s segmentation on a standardized external benchmark (1,223 images from four public datasets). Evaluate four referee configurations varying independence and architectural diversity, including same-architecture with random initialization and cross-architecture configurations like SegFormer-B0, UNet++, and MedSAM. Perform a restricted evaluation excluding empty masks. At inference, perform one additional deterministic forward pass for the referee to obtain the reliability signal and use agreement to gate predictions (selective prediction).
AI.result: Same-architecture referee with random initialization yields ROC-AUC 0.923. Cross-architecture referees improve to ROC-AUC 0.960 (SegFormer-B0 strongest), outperforming same-architecture control and UNet++. Cross-architecture also beats a representative Test-Time Augmentation baseline by 0.055 ROC-AUC under an identical protocol. In restricted evaluation (excluding empty masks), ROC-AUC drops to 0.876 for SegFormer-B0 and 0.783 for the same-architecture control, but RBQE’s margin over baselines widens on this subset. RBQE increases mean Dice of retained predictions as low-agreement cases are rejected, and only requires one additional referee forward pass per inference.
AI.conclusion: Cross-model agreement is a practical, interpretable reliability framework for automated polyp segmentation. RBQE can provide a reliable uncertainty signal using minimal additional inference cost and supports selective prediction by discarding low-agreement results.

title: A positive resolution of the gap-entropy conjecture
summary: We prove the gap-entropy conjecture for fixed-confidence best-arm identification with independent unit-variance Gaussian arms, means in $[0,1]$, and a unique optimal arm. For each suboptimal arm $i$, let $Δ_i=μ_*-μ_i$ be its gap from the optimal mean, and write $H=\sum_{i\ne *}Δ_i^{-2}$. Let $p_r$ be the fraction of $H$ contributed by arms with $2^{-(r+1)}<Δ_i\le2^{-r}$, and let $\mathrm{Ent}(I)=\sum_{r:p_r>0} p_r\log(1/p_r)$. Among all algorithms that identify the optimal arm with probability at least $1-δ$ on every Gaussian instance, the optimal expected number of samples on a given instance, averaged over all permutations of the arm labels, is within absolute constant factors of $H(\log(1/δ)+\mathrm{Ent}(I))$. Moreover, there is an algorithm, independent of the instance, whose expected number of samples is bounded by a constant multiple of this quantity plus $g^{-2}\log\log(e^e/g)$, where $g=\min_{i\ne *}Δ_i$ is the gap to the closest competitor.

AI.tldr: Proof of the gap-entropy conjecture for fixed-confidence best-arm identification with independent unit-variance Gaussian arms; optimal sample complexity scales with H(log(1/δ)+Ent(I)); plus a universal algorithm achieving this up to a g-dependent additive term.
AI.motivation: Understand the fundamental sample complexity of identifying the best arm under fixed confidence by incorporating the distribution of gaps via the gap-entropy measure; connect lower bounds to achievable algorithms in Gaussian bandits with a unique optimum.
AI.method: Information-theoretic analysis to derive lower bounds via change-of-measure and gap-partitioning; define H and Ent(I) from the gaps; construct an instance-independent arm-selection algorithm achieving the bound up to constants plus a g^{-2} log log term.
AI.result: The optimal expected sample complexity (averaged over arm-label permutations) is within constant factors of H(log(1/δ)+Ent(I)); and there exists an instance-independent algorithm with expected samples bounded by a constant multiple of this quantity plus g^{-2} log log(e^e/g).
AI.conclusion: Gap-entropy provides a refined characterization of fixed-confidence BAI complexity, linking it to the distribution of gaps and yielding tight (up to constants) lower and upper bounds and a universal algorithm.

title: Field Converter: Geometry-Initialized Temporal Residual Refinement for World-Grounded Player Pose Estimation from Soccer Broadcasts
summary: Recovering 3D human pose from monocular sports broadcasts remains challenging when players must be localized in a shared metric world coordinate system rather than only reconstructed relative to their own body. We introduce Field Converter, a geometry-initialized temporal residual framework for world-grounded 3D player pose estimation from calibrated soccer broadcasts. Our method first uses camera and pitch geometry to initialize the player root through ray-ground intersection, then predicts a temporal residual correction from pose, image, camera, and geometric cues. On match-disjoint evaluation sequences, residual refinement reduces root error from 49cm with geometry alone to 14cm with a frame-wise MLP and 10cm with a TCN, while a Transformer achieves a comparable 11cm. The resulting world-space MPJPE reaches 13.2cm, and ablations show that residual prediction clearly outperforms direct global-root regression while temporal context matters more than the specific temporal backbone. Failure analysis further identifies airborne motion as the main limitation of the ground-based geometric initialization.

AI.tldr: A geometry-initialized temporal residual framework (Field Converter) for world-grounded 3D player pose estimation from monocular soccer broadcasts, combining camera/pitch geometry with temporal residuals to achieve precise world-space MPJPE (13.2 cm) and sub-10 cm root errors in lookups, outperforming direct regression; airborne motion is a key failure mode.
AI.motivation: Recover 3D human pose in a shared metric world from monocular broadcasts remains challenging; need accurate world-grounded root initialization and temporal refinement to robustly estimate field-grounded player poses.
AI.method: Initialize the root via ray-ground intersection using camera and pitch geometry; predict temporal residuals using pose, image, camera, and geometric cues with light-weight temporal backbones (MLP, TCN, Transformer) to correct ground-truth root and propagate across frames.
AI.result: On match-disjoint sequences, geometry alone yields ~49 cm root error; residual refiners reduce to 14 cm (frame-wise MLP) and 10 cm (TCN); Transformer ~11 cm; world-space MPJPE = 13.2 cm; ablations show residuals outperform global-root regression; temporal context more critical than backbone type.
AI.conclusion: Residual temporal prediction is superior to direct regression for world-grounded 3D pose; temporal context is crucial; airborne motion is the primary limitation of geometry-based root initialization; Field Converter offers solid advances for sports pose estimation.

title: BrainTaskonomy: Learning How to Pretrain and What to Transfer in fMRI Foundation Models
summary: fMRI foundation models increasingly aggregate heterogeneous data across brain states, cohorts, and acquisition settings, yet pretraining domains are commonly treated as a flat mixture and downstream tasks are adapted independently. We study whether measured learning relations can organize both stages without modifying the backbone. During pretraining, a lightweight Brain-DiT proxy estimates difficulty and directed facilitation across ten fMRI domains, yielding a priority-guided cumulative domain curriculum combined with high-to-low-noise timestep scheduling and joint consolidation. During adaptation, controlled first- and higher-order transfer across fifteen tasks constructs a directed taskonomy, from which budgeted integer programming (BIP) selects directly supervised source tasks and target-specific routes. The joint priority-domain and high-to-low-timestep curriculum reduces v-NMSE, PSD-NMSE, and FC-MSE by 6.5%, 16.3%, and 10.5%, respectively, relative to uniform sampling over both dimensions, and shows strong downstream performance across six in- and out-of-domain tasks. The taskonomy reveals asymmetric, target-dependent transfer, while exploratory sealed-test evaluation shows larger descriptive gains for BIP policies when higher-order route spaces are available than for matched random controls. Together, these findings support organizing fMRI pretraining and adaptation by measured learning relations rather than treating domains and tasks as independent flat sets.

AI.tldr: A learning-relations–guided framework jointly organizes fMRI pretraining and adaptation: a domain curriculum guided by a Brain-DiT proxy and a taskonomy-driven adaptation via budgeted integer programming, yielding consistent reductions in error metrics and improved cross-domain transfer.
AI.motivation: To overcome the conventional flat treatment of heterogeneous fMRI domains during pretraining and downstream tasks, and to exploit measured learning relations to improve efficiency and generalization across in-/out-of-domain data.
AI.method: Pretraining uses a Brain-DiT proxy to estimate domain difficulty and directed facilitation across 10 fMRI domains, forming a priority-guided cumulative domain curriculum with high-to-low-noise timestep scheduling and joint consolidation. Adaptation builds a directed taskonomy across 15 tasks using controlled first- and higher-order transfer; budgeted integer programming selects directly supervised source tasks and target-specific routes for efficient transfer.
AI.result: The joint domain-priority and timesteps curriculum reduces v-NMSE by 6.5%, PSD-NMSE by 16.3%, and FC-MSE by 10.5% relative to uniform sampling. Demonstrates strong downstream performance across six in-domain and out-of-domain tasks. The taskonomy shows asymmetric, target-dependent transfer; sealed-test evaluation shows larger gains for BIP policies when higher-order route spaces are available compared to matched random controls.
AI.conclusion: Organizing fMRI pretraining and adaptation by measured learning relations—rather than treating domains and tasks as independent flat sets—yields consistent performance gains and reveals asymmetric transfer patterns that can guide efficient, targeted adaptation.

title: Precision in Rice Variety Classification using Stacking-Based Ensemble Learning
summary: Rice, a staple food for a significant portion of the global population, exhibits remarkable diversity in its varieties, presenting substantial challenges for accurate identification by consumers, traders, and farmers. This complexity often facilitates fraudulent practices, such as the unauthorized mixing of rice types, which undermines quality and trust in the supply chain. Despite its critical importance, existing research falls short of providing robust and efficient methods for precise rice variety classification based on external characteristics like color, size, and texture. To address this gap, our study introduces a comprehensive rice variety identification framework designed to enhance transparency and quality assurance. We developed a stacked ensemble model tailored for rice variety classification and curated a comprehensive dataset comprising 20 rice varieties, each distinguished by unique visual attributes. The proposed approach achieved an unprecedented classification accuracy of 100%. Furthermore, we integrated our model into a mobile application, enabling even novice users to effortlessly identify rice varieties using grain images from a smartphone camera. These findings underscore the transformative potential of advanced machine learning techniques in mitigating fraudulent practices and ensuring stringent rice quality control. Our work holds significant implications for agricultural stakeholders, paving the way for automated crop identification systems and advancing precision agriculture practices.

AI.tldr: Stacked ensemble approach for rice variety classification achieving claimed 100% accuracy on a 20-variety image dataset, with mobile app deployment.
AI.motivation: Address mislabeling and fraud in rice supply chains due to reliance on external visual traits; improve transparency and quality assurance in agricultural value chains.
AI.method: Proposes a stacked ensemble classifier using color, texture, and size features from grain images; dataset of 20 varieties; reported 100% accuracy; mobile application interface.
AI.result: Reported accuracy 100% on their dataset; mobile app enabling novice users to identify varieties via smartphone images.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates potential of ML/ensemble methods for automated rice identification; implications for quality control and precision agriculture; still requires rigorous validation for generalization.

title: Guiding Image-to-3D Generation with Test-Time Partial Observations
summary: Image-to-3D models can generate visually compelling 3D assets from a single RGB image, but their geometry is often only loosely constrained by the available observations, limiting their use in applications that require geometric fidelity. In many real-world settings, however, partial geometric observations of the object may be available at test time. We introduce a training-free framework for incorporating such evidence into pretrained image-to-3D generative models without retraining or finetuning. To do this, we guide generation using a ray-consistent observation likelihood defined over the model's occupancy representation, combining surface occupancy and free-space evidence. Applied to SAM 3D and its multi-view extension, our approach substantially improves geometric fidelity across different levels of observability, as well as visual quality. Our results demonstrate that pretrained image-to-3D models can effectively integrate partial geometric observations through explicit test-time guidance, complementing their learned generative priors without modifying the underlying model.

AI.tldr: Training-free integration of partial geometric observations into pretrained image-to-3D generators at test-time, improving geometry without retraining by ray-consistent occupancy likelihood.
AI.motivation: Image-to-3D models often produce geometries loosely constrained by observations; in practice, partial geometry is available, and leveraging it without retraining is highly desirable to improve fidelity.
AI.method: Introduce a ray-consistent observation likelihood over the model's occupancy representation that fuses surface occupancy and free-space evidence; apply at test-time to SAM 3D and its multi-view extension; no retraining of the pretrained model; uses occupancy-based guidance to steer generation.
AI.result: Significant improvement in geometric fidelity across varying observability and improved visual quality; demonstrates that pretrained image-to-3D models can utilize partial geometric cues via explicit test-time guidance without modifying priors.
AI.conclusion: Test-time geometric guidance can substantially enhance geometry of image-to-3D generators with partial observations, providing a practical, training-free pathway to fuse data-driven priors with explicit cues.

title: Programmable World Model
summary: Recent video world models generate increasingly realistic and interactive visual experiences, yet lack reliable mechanisms for maintaining persistent world state and enforcing programmable rules over extended interactions. We introduce Programmable World Model, a framework that decouples world-state evolution from visual observation generation. An agent translates natural-language instructions into executable programs that specify entity states and state-transition rules, enabling direct control over individual entities and their interactions. A lightweight engine executes these programs to update and maintain an explicit, persistent global world state, including off-screen entities and non-visual attributes. To connect world state with visual generation, we introduce state-augmented 3D oriented bounding boxes (OBBs) as an intermediate representation. This representation, together with the target camera trajectory, is deterministically compiled into pixel-aligned spatiotemporal conditioning signals for a pretrained video model serving as the generative renderer. This design allows users to create playable games with predefined mechanics, direct control over individual entities, and persistent world state throughout gameplay. We further introduce CombatStateBench, a benchmark for evaluating programmable world models. On CombatStateBench, our method achieves 94% Count Accuracy and 98% State Accuracy, substantially outperforming existing interactive video world models while supporting coherent long-horizon generation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of separating explicit state evolution from generative rendering for building persistent, programmable worlds.

AI.tldr: A framework that decouples world-state evolution from visual rendering by translating natural-language instructions into executable programs that manage a persistent global world state; connects to a pretrained video renderer via state-augmented 3D OBBs; introduces CombatStateBench benchmark with strong results.
AI.motivation: Current video world models struggle with persistent state, long-horizon interactions, explicit rules, and off-screen entities; a programmable, persistent world state is needed to support coherent, rule-governed gameplay and reliable long-term generation.
AI.method: An agent translates NL instructions into executable programs specifying entity states and state-transition rules; a lightweight engine executes these programs to update a persistent global world state (including off-screen entities and non-visual attributes). State-augmented 3D oriented bounding boxes (OBBs) plus a target camera trajectory are deterministically compiled into pixel-aligned spatiotemporal conditioning signals for a pretrained video model that serves as the rendering engine.
AI.result: On CombatStateBench, the method achieves 94% Count Accuracy and 98% State Accuracy, substantially outperforming existing interactive video world models while supporting coherent long-horizon generation.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that separating explicit state evolution from generative rendering is effective for building persistent, programmable worlds and enabling playable, rule-governed interactions.

title: DCReg: Decoupled Characterization for Efficient Degenerate LiDAR Registration
summary: LiDAR point cloud registration is fundamental to robotic perception and navigation. In geometrically degenerate environments (e.g., corridors), registration becomes ill-conditioned: certain motion directions are weakly constrained, causing unstable solutions and degraded accuracy. Existing detect-then-mitigate methods fail to reliably detect, physically interpret, and stabilize this ill-conditioning without corrupting the optimization. We introduce DCReg (Decoupled Characterization for Ill-conditioned Registration), establishing a detect-characterize-mitigate paradigm that systematically addresses ill-conditioned registration via three innovations. First, DCReg achieves reliable ill-conditioning detection by employing Schur complement decomposition on the Hessian matrix. This decouples the 6-DoF registration into 3-DoF clean rotational and translational subspaces, eliminating coupling effects that mask degeneracy in full-Hessian analyses. Second, within these subspaces, we develop interpretable characterization techniques resolving eigen-basis ambiguities via basis alignment. This establishes stable mappings between eigenspaces and physical motion directions, providing actionable insights on which motions lack constraints and to what extent. Third, leveraging this spectral information, we design a targeted mitigation via a structured preconditioner. Guided by MAP regularization, we implement eigenvalue clamping exclusively within the preconditioner rather than modifying the original problem. This preserves the least-squares objective and minimizer, enabling efficient optimization via Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient with a single interpretable parameter. Experiments demonstrate DCReg achieves 20-50% higher long-duration localization accuracy and 5-30x speedups (up to 116x) over degeneracy-aware baselines across diverse environments. Code: https://github.com/JokerJohn/DCReg

AI.tldr: DCReg decouples 6-DoF registration using Schur complement to 3-DoF subspaces, provides interpretable eigenbasis mapping, and uses an eigenvalue-clamped preconditioner for stable, efficient optimization, yielding substantial accuracy and speed gains.
AI.motivation: Ill-conditioning in geometrically degenerate LiDAR registration (e.g., corridors) causes unstable solutions and degraded accuracy. Existing detect-then-mitigate methods struggle to reliably detect, interpret, and stabilize degeneracy without corrupting the optimization.
AI.method: 1) Schur complement decomposition of the Hessian to decouple rotation and translation into 3-DoF subspaces, removing coupling that hides degeneracy; 2) in subspaces, recover eigen-basis ambiguities through basis alignment to map eigenspaces to physical motion directions; 3) design a structured preconditioner with eigenvalue clamping guided by MAP regularization, modifying only the preconditioner to preserve the least-squares objective; optimization via Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient with a single interpretable parameter.
AI.result: Empirically, DCReg achieves 20-50% higher long-duration localization accuracy and 5-30x speedups (up to 116x) over degeneracy-aware baselines across diverse environments.
AI.conclusion: DCReg establishes a principled detect-characterize-mitigate framework for ill-conditioned registration by decoupling the problem, providing interpretable subspace mappings, and applying targeted preconditioner-based mitigation that preserves the objective while enhancing robustness and efficiency; code available at the provided repository.
